concepts.name: A posteriori knowledge
concepts.summary: Knowledge whose justification depends on experience, observation, or testimony about how the world is.
concepts.body:
A posteriori knowledge is justified through evidence about particular facts rather than through reflection on meanings or logical form alone. Perception, measurement, memory of an observation, experiment, and reliable testimony can all supply the relevant evidence. The category concerns the route of justification, not whether the resulting belief is weak or provisional.

An empirical claim can become extremely well supported while remaining sensitive to new evidence. That makes a posteriori different from a claim's being contingent: contingency concerns whether it could have been otherwise, while a posteriori concerns how we are justified in believing it.

examples.text: A geologist knows that a particular fault moved during an earthquake by combining field observations, seismograms, and dated rock evidence.
examples.note: The conclusion depends on evidence about an actual event, so conceptual competence alone would not settle it.

commonMisreadings: A posteriori does not mean merely personal or uncertain; repeatable measurement and good testimony can provide strong justification.
A proposition can be necessary in some philosophical accounts yet still be learned through an empirical route, so the label is not interchangeable with contingent.
criticisms: The boundary is disputed when reasoning uses learned concepts, perception, and background theory together, because justification is rarely supplied by a completely pure source.

lookalikes.note: The contrast concerns whether particular experience is required for justification.
Analyticity concerns meaning or form, whereas a posteriori status concerns epistemic dependence on experience.

concepts.name: A priori knowledge
concepts.summary: Knowledge justified without depending on particular sensory experience of the relevant fact.
concepts.body:
A priori knowledge is justified by reasoning, conceptual competence, or a structure of thought that does not require checking the particular world-state in question. A person can establish that a contradiction follows from given premises without inspecting objects, and can recognize some logical or mathematical consequences by understanding the relevant rules. This does not mean that language learning, education, or the possession of concepts has no history.

A priori and necessary are distinct classifications. A priori describes the basis of justification; necessary describes how a proposition could be true across possibilities. Likewise, analytic and a priori often overlap but are not simply synonymous, especially in Kantian accounts of synthetic a priori judgment.

examples.text: After stipulating that every member of a committee is present, one can infer a contradiction from the claim that a committee member is absent without visiting the meeting.
examples.note: The inference is settled by the meanings and relations in the premises, not by observing the committee.

commonMisreadings: A priori does not mean innate, psychologically effortless, or immune to every error.
It is not the same as necessary: the epistemic route and the modal status answer different questions.
criticisms: Quinean critics argue that the distinction can be difficult to isolate because even logic and meanings are embedded in revisable networks of belief.

lookalikes.note: The contrast is whether particular experience is needed to justify the claim.
Analyticity classifies a proposition by meaning or form, not directly by its route of knowing.

concepts.name: Abductive reasoning
concepts.summary: Inference that selects the explanation which best accounts for the available evidence.
concepts.body:
Abductive reasoning begins with observations and asks which hypothesis would make them intelligible with the least unexplained residue. Explanatory scope, fit with the evidence, simplicity, background plausibility, and predictive success may all matter. Unlike deduction, abduction does not preserve truth from premises to conclusion; unlike a bare guess, it is constrained by a comparison among candidate explanations.

The conclusion remains defeasible. A diagnosis can be the best current explanation and still be overturned by a laboratory result or by a rival theory that explains more symptoms with fewer assumptions.

examples.text: A mechanic infers a failing alternator after a dimming dashboard, a dead battery after a short drive, and a charging test below specification.
examples.note: The alternator hypothesis unifies several signs and is tested against competing causes such as a loose belt or damaged battery.

commonMisreadings: Abduction is not proof of the favored explanation; it ranks hypotheses under current evidence.
The simplest story is not automatically best if it leaves important observations unexplained.
criticisms: There is no universally accepted numerical rule for weighing explanatory virtues, so different investigators can rationally rank the same hypotheses differently.

lookalikes.note: Deduction guarantees its conclusion when the premises and form are valid; abduction does not.
Induction projects patterns or frequencies, while abduction evaluates explanatory hypotheses.

concepts.name: Abolitionism
concepts.summary: A movement that seeks to end a coercive institution rather than merely administer or soften it.
concepts.body:
Abolitionism is most closely associated with the campaigns against chattel slavery, but the general idea is a demand for institutional elimination. Historical abolitionists combined moral arguments about personhood and domination with political work: organizing, petitioning, publishing, aiding escape, and pressing for legal change. The term therefore names both a normative judgment and a strategy for transforming law and social power.

Abolitionist reasoning can conflict with gradualism when incremental measures stabilize the institution they are meant to replace. It can also raise hard questions about transition: ending a legal status does not by itself repair dispossession, racial hierarchy, or economic dependence that the institution created.

Contemporary prison abolition extends the question to incarceration and the institutions that reproduce it. Thinkers such as Angela Davis ask how housing, education, health care, and responses to violence might be organized so that imprisonment ceases to serve as the default solution to social problems. The shared commitment is institutional replacement; the history, proposed alternatives, and practical controversies differ from those of slavery abolition.

examples.text: A campaign that demands the legal emancipation of enslaved people and rejects compensation schemes that preserve ownership is abolitionist.
examples.note: Its objective is to remove the property relation itself, not only to regulate cruelty within it.

commonMisreadings: Abolitionism is not synonymous with any reform that makes a coercive institution less harsh.
The historical abolition of slavery did not automatically abolish the social and economic inequalities built around slavery.
criticisms: Critics of abolitionist transitions argue that abrupt institutional change can leave affected people without material protection; abolitionists reply that protection cannot depend on preserving domination.

lookalikes.note: Reformism seeks improvement within an institution, while abolitionism makes the institution's end the central aim.

concepts.name: Abstract object
concepts.summary: A purported entity that is not a concrete object located in ordinary physical space and time.
concepts.body:
An abstract object is posited to explain what statements about numbers, propositions, sets, or properties are about without treating those entities as physical bodies. The number seven, for example, can be instantiated by many changing collections without itself being one of those collections. Abstract-object theories differ over whether such entities exist independently of minds, language, or practices.

The classification is ontological, not dismissive. Calling something abstract does not call it fictional, useless, or unknowable; it says that its mode of being is unlike the mode of being of a rock or a planet. The central dispute is whether mathematical and semantic practice needs this kind of ontology.

examples.text: The proposition that snow is white can be asserted in many languages and written on many surfaces without being identical to any inscription.
examples.note: The candidate object is the truth-bearer or content, not a particular physical mark that expresses it.

commonMisreadings: Abstract does not mean imaginary; fictional characters and numbers raise different existence questions.
A physical representation of a number is not the number itself, even though it can instantiate or denote it.
criticisms: Nominalists argue that mathematics can be reconstructed using concrete inscriptions, linguistic rules, or structural roles without a realm of abstract entities.

concepts.name: Absurdism
concepts.summary: The view that human demands for final meaning confront a world that offers no guaranteed answer.
concepts.body:
Absurdism names a conflict, not simply a conclusion that life is worthless. Human beings seek intelligibility, justification, and durable purpose, while the universe appears indifferent to those demands. In Camus's formulation, the absurd arises from the relation between the seeker and the silent world rather than from either side alone.

The characteristic response is lucid revolt: refusing false consolation while continuing to live, choose, and create local meanings. Absurdism therefore differs from nihilism, which can deny value, and from religious existentialism, which locates ultimate meaning in transcendence.

examples.text: A person recognizes that no cosmic verdict will certify their work yet continues composing music and caring for friends without pretending those activities have eternal guarantees.
examples.note: The example preserves commitment while accepting the absence of a final, externally supplied meaning.

commonMisreadings: Absurdism is not a claim that nothing matters; it rejects guaranteed cosmic meaning while allowing situated value.
It is not identical to depression or generalized pessimism, which are psychological or evaluative conditions rather than the philosophical position.
criticisms: Critics argue that the move from silence about cosmic purpose to a life of revolt may require normative commitments that absurdism itself does not fully ground.

lookalikes.note: Nihilism denies or suspends value more broadly, whereas absurdism focuses on the clash between meaning-seeking and indifference.

concepts.name: Academic skepticism
concepts.summary: The skeptical tradition of Plato's Academy that challenged claims to certain knowledge and explored how to act without an infallible criterion of truth.
concepts.body:
Academic skepticism developed within Plato's Academy under Arcesilaus and Carneades, especially in opposition to the Stoic claim that some impressions carry an unmistakable guarantee of truth. Arcesilaus used arguments on both sides of a question to challenge such guarantees and defend suspension of assent. Carneades developed a more elaborate account of persuasive impressions that could guide action without becoming an infallible criterion of knowledge. These positions survive largely through later reports, so distinguishing a dialectical argument from a philosopher's own commitment can be difficult.

The tradition should not be reduced to ordinary caution about fallible scientific findings. Its central problem is whether rational assent requires a kind of certainty that human cognition cannot supply. Critics pressed the practical objection that withholding assent would make action impossible; Academic responses appealed to what appears reasonable or persuasive. Pyrrhonian skepticism shares some methods but constitutes a distinct historical tradition, and Sextus Empiricus criticized the Academics rather than belonging to their school.

examples.text: Asked how a traveler can choose a route without certain knowledge, an Academic skeptic allows following the route supported by several mutually consistent reports while withholding the claim that those reports are incapable of error.
examples.note: The case illustrates practical guidance by persuasive impressions, the response associated with Carneades, rather than a modern research policy alone.

commonMisreadings: Academic skepticism names a historical phase of Plato's Academy; it does not mean skepticism practiced by academics in general.
Arcesilaus and Carneades did not present one uniform doctrine. Later reports disagree about how far their arguments expressed personal commitments.
criticisms: Opponents argue that deciding what is more persuasive already relies on standards of rationality that look like commitments rather than complete suspension.

lookalikes.note: Both suspend dogmatic assent, but their historical methods and claims about practical guidance differ.
Dogmatism asserts settled conclusions where academic skepticism emphasizes the insufficiency of available justification.

concepts.name: Accelerationism
concepts.summary: A family of theories that treats intensifying technological, economic, or social forces as potentially transformative.
concepts.body:
Accelerationism is not one program. Some versions argue that existing capitalist or technological dynamics should be intensified to expose contradictions or create post-capitalist capacities; others treat acceleration as a destructive tendency to be managed, redirected, or resisted. The shared question is whether speed and scale can become political instruments rather than merely symptoms of a system.

The doctrine is difficult to evaluate because acceleration can distribute benefits and harms unevenly. Automation may reduce necessary labor under collective control, yet intensify surveillance and precarious work under private control. The same technical increase therefore does not determine a political outcome by itself.

examples.text: A left accelerationist proposal treats publicly governed automation as a way to shorten the working week and expand time for democratic activity.
examples.note: The proposal redirects an existing productive tendency toward a specified social end rather than praising speed in the abstract.

commonMisreadings: Accelerationism does not uniformly mean making everything faster or welcoming collapse.
It is not a technological determinism: institutions and ownership shape what intensified capacity does.
criticisms: Critics warn that deliberately intensifying crisis can magnify suffering before any transformative capacity appears, and that the promised endpoint may be politically under-specified.

lookalikes.note: Accelerationist arguments can intensify or redirect capitalist dynamics, while capitalism is the economic system under discussion.

concepts.name: Access consciousness
concepts.summary: The availability of mental information for reasoning, reporting, decision, and deliberate control.
concepts.body:
Access consciousness concerns what a representation can do in a cognitive system. Information is access-conscious when it is available to processes such as verbal report, inference, planning, memory-guided action, or voluntary control. The notion is functional: it asks whether information is globally usable, not whether it has a particular felt quality.

This distinction permits a theory in which a person can consciously access that a traffic light is red while the phenomenal character of seeing red is analyzed separately. A state may influence behavior without being available for report, so behavioral control alone does not establish access consciousness.

examples.text: A driver notices a red warning light, tells a passenger about it, and chooses to pull over based on the information.
examples.note: The representation is available across speech, deliberation, and action rather than remaining an isolated sensorimotor response.

commonMisreadings: Access consciousness is not a synonym for vivid sensation; phenomenal consciousness asks what an experience feels like.
Information can be accessed by one specialized process without being globally available for flexible reasoning.
criticisms: Critics question whether functional availability explains subjective experience or merely redescribes the cognitive abilities that accompany it.

lookalikes.note: Unconscious processing can guide behavior without making its representations available for report and deliberation.

concepts.name: Achilles and the tortoise
concepts.summary: Zeno's paradox in which infinitely many pursuit stages seem to prevent a faster runner from overtaking a head start.
concepts.body:
In the paradox, Achilles must first reach the point where the tortoise began, then the point the tortoise reached during that interval, and so on. The construction yields infinitely many sub-tasks, each apparently necessary before overtaking occurs. It tests whether an infinite division of a path entails an infinite duration and whether motion can be composed from infinitely many parts.

Modern calculus answers one central pressure by showing that an infinite series of shrinking intervals can converge to a finite sum. That mathematical result models the completion of the stages, but philosophical disputes remain about what the series represents and whether the paradox targets time, space, continuity, or the logic of change.

examples.text: If the tortoise has a ten-metre lead and moves one-tenth as far during each pursuit interval, the required distances form 10 + 1 + 0.1 + 0.01 and continue indefinitely.
examples.note: The stages are infinite in number while their convergent total can remain finite.

commonMisreadings: The paradox does not show that Achilles literally fails to pass the tortoise in ordinary conditions.
An infinite number of parts is not automatically an infinite total length or duration.
criticisms: A calculus solution may explain the numerical convergence without settling the metaphysical question of whether a continuum is composed of completed parts.

concepts.name: Acquaintance knowledge
concepts.summary: Knowledge by direct familiarity or experience, distinguished from knowing a proposition about the thing.
concepts.body:
Acquaintance knowledge is a relation of direct familiarity: knowing a person, a place, a sensation, or an object through experience rather than merely possessing a description. Russell used the distinction to separate immediate awareness from knowledge by description, though later uses vary. Acquaintance can supply material for recognition without itself being a complete set of true propositions.

The distinction matters because a detailed description of cinnamon does not guarantee that someone knows its taste by acquaintance. Conversely, direct familiarity does not ensure accurate theoretical beliefs about what the familiar thing is or why it has its properties.

examples.text: Someone who has repeatedly tasted fresh ginger has acquaintance with its distinctive heat even if they cannot chemically explain capsaicin-like sensations.
examples.note: Direct sensory familiarity and scientific propositional knowledge come apart in the example.

commonMisreadings: Acquaintance is not the same as expertise; familiarity can exist without skilled explanation.
It is not automatically infallible, since recognition and memory of a familiar item can still be mistaken.
criticisms: Some philosophers doubt that acquaintance is a separate kind of knowledge rather than a non-propositional relation or a cluster of perceptual abilities.

lookalikes.note: Propositional knowledge is knowledge that a statement is true; acquaintance is direct familiarity with something.

concepts.name: Act consequentialism
concepts.summary: The view that each act is right or wrong according to the value of its consequences compared with available alternatives.
concepts.body:
Act consequentialism assesses an individual choice directly by its expected or actual results, depending on the theory's treatment of uncertainty. An act is permissible when its consequences are at least as good as those of the alternatives, with the relevant value possibly involving welfare, equality, preference satisfaction, or another good. Rules matter only insofar as following them affects outcomes in the case at hand.

This makes the view sensitive to context: keeping a promise usually helps trust, but breaking one may be required if it prevents a catastrophe. The same feature creates pressure to justify demanding sacrifices and to explain how agents can estimate consequences without bias.

examples.text: A medic diverts a scarce dose to the patient who will otherwise die within minutes when the alternative patient can safely receive treatment later.
examples.note: The act is judged by the comparative consequences of allocating the dose in each available way.

commonMisreadings: Act consequentialism does not say that any useful act is right; it requires comparison with the consequences of alternatives.
It can recognize rules as valuable habits while still treating their authority as dependent on their effects.
criticisms: The theory may permit violating rights or promises when doing so produces a sufficiently large aggregate benefit, and critics dispute whether that trade is morally acceptable.

lookalikes.note: Act utilitarianism is a welfare-maximizing species of the broader act-consequentialist family.
Rule utilitarianism evaluates practices or rules rather than each isolated act directly.

concepts.name: Act utilitarianism
concepts.summary: A form of act consequentialism that selects the available act with the greatest expected aggregate utility.
concepts.body:
Act utilitarianism applies the utility principle to each decision: choose the act whose consequences contain at least as much overall welfare as every alternative. Classical versions identify utility with pleasure and the absence of pain, while later versions use preference satisfaction or objective well-being. The calculation is impartial in its basic structure: each person's welfare counts rather than receiving weight from the agent's identity.

The theory must specify how to compare uncertain outcomes, how to count future people, and whether distribution matters apart from total welfare. Its directness can make it flexible in emergencies, but it can also demand actions that ordinary morality treats as exploitative or excessively sacrificial.

examples.text: A disaster coordinator sends the only available rescue boat to the route where it can save twenty stranded people rather than the route where it can save three.
examples.note: The choice compares total expected benefit across the available actions, not the coordinator's personal ties.

commonMisreadings: Utilitarian calculation is not the same as pursuing short-term usefulness; indirect effects and long-run welfare count too.
Act utilitarianism differs from rule utilitarianism because a generally beneficial rule can be overridden in an individual case.
criticisms: Critics argue that maximizing totals can justify sacrificing an innocent person or imposing severe burdens on a minority, even when doing so seems unjust.

lookalikes.note: Act utilitarianism is a welfare-maximizing species of the broader act-consequentialist family.
Rule utilitarianism asks which rules maximize welfare rather than recalculating every act directly.

concepts.name: Actualism
concepts.summary: The modal view that only actual entities exist, while possibilities describe ways the actual world could have been.
concepts.body:
Actualism denies that merely possible people, objects, or worlds are additional inhabitants of reality. It can still accept ordinary modal claims: saying that a particular person could have become a musician describes an alternative way the actual person might have lived, not a currently existing counterpart in another realm. Actualists therefore need an account of how modal language works without quantifying over nonactual objects.

The view contrasts with possibilism, which treats some merely possible entities as genuine objects of quantification. The dispute affects the semantics of counterfactuals, de re possibility, and statements about what someone could have done.

examples.text: An actualist can say that this oak could have grown taller without saying that a taller, merely possible oak exists somewhere as a second object.
examples.note: The modal claim modifies the actual oak's possible history rather than adding a nonactual oak to the inventory.

commonMisreadings: Actualism does not deny possibility; it denies that merely possible entities exist in the same ontological sense as actual ones.
It is not the claim that everything actual is necessary or unchangeable.
criticisms: Possibilists argue that actualist paraphrases can become technically complex and may fail to preserve the apparent object-directed content of modal claims.

lookalikes.note: Modal realism treats possible worlds as real, a stronger commitment than actualism accepts.

concepts.name: Administered society
concepts.summary: A critical-theory diagnosis of social life increasingly organized by bureaucratic, economic, and technological administration that narrows individual autonomy.
concepts.body:
The administered society describes domination that operates through systems of classification, planning, expertise, media, and economic management rather than only through a visible sovereign command. In Adorno's critical theory, people encounter institutions as procedures that define needs, allocate opportunities, and translate singular lives into standardized cases. Administration can appear rational because it solves real coordination problems, yet its categories can make the person serve the system instead of the system serving the person.

The diagnosis does not reject every public service or rule. Administration can protect people from arbitrary private power and make rights actionable. The critical question is whether procedures remain answerable to those affected, allow exceptions to be argued, and preserve spaces for nonconforming judgment. Critics see a risk of romanticizing unorganized freedom; the concept is more precise when it identifies how efficiency, expertise, and convenience narrow the capacity to contest the ends being administered.

examples.text: A benefits system assigns a person's life to rigid eligibility codes and automated risk scores, leaving no meaningful route to explain circumstances outside the categories.
examples.note: The example shows administration becoming domination when the person must fit the system rather than the system answer to the person.

commonMisreadings: Administered society is not simply any society with public administration or technology.
The concept does not claim that every rule or service is oppressive; its target is totalizing management that narrows autonomy and dissent.
criticisms: Critics argue that the diagnosis can idealize unadministered freedom and understate how public administration protects people from arbitrary private power.

concepts.name: Advaita Vedanta
concepts.summary: A Vedanta school holding that Brahman is ultimate reality and the deepest self is not ultimately separate from it.
concepts.body:
Advaita Vedanta, developed in its classical form by Shankara, interprets the Upanishadic teaching of nonduality through the identity of Atman and Brahman. Ignorance makes embodied persons identify with limited mental and physical attributes; liberating knowledge recognizes that the self's ultimate nature is not an independently bounded entity. This is an account of bondage and release, not merely the slogan that everything looks alike.

Advaita distinguishes levels of description. Ordinary transactions, persons, duties, and causal relations function at the conventional level, while Brahman is ultimate reality beyond such differentiation. The world is therefore not simply nonexistent: its status is dependent and misapprehended when treated as final, self-subsistent reality.

examples.text: A rope mistaken for a snake illustrates how a real basis can support a misidentified appearance until discriminating knowledge corrects the perception.
examples.note: The analogy models error and correction; it does not mean ordinary persons are literally hallucinations.

commonMisreadings: Advaita is not the crude claim that nothing exists or that ethical conduct is irrelevant at the conventional level.
Nonduality does not mean that individual differences disappear from everyday transactions; it concerns their ultimate status.
criticisms: Other Vedanta schools object that Advaita makes plurality and devotion too derivative, while Buddhist critics question its appeal to an enduring self or Brahman.

lookalikes.note: Both challenge ordinary reification, but Advaita grounds nonduality in Brahman whereas anatta denies an enduring self.

concepts.name: Aesthetic experience
concepts.summary: An attentive experience of an object or event through its perceptual, expressive, or formal qualities.
concepts.body:
Aesthetic experience involves attending to how something is presented and organized: color, rhythm, proportion, texture, expression, atmosphere, or the way parts develop over time. It can include pleasure, emotion, imagination, bodily response, and thought, but none is individually required. A disturbing tragedy can be aesthetically powerful without being pleasant.

The concept asks about a mode of engagement rather than a special class of museum objects. A coastline, interface, ceremony, or ordinary tool can invite aesthetic attention when its sensible and expressive features become salient, even while practical and moral concerns remain present.

examples.text: While listening to a string quartet, a listener tracks the return of a theme, the tension of dissonance, and the changing balance among instruments.
examples.note: The attention follows formal and expressive relations in the experience rather than treating the music only as background or information.

commonMisreadings: Aesthetic experience need not be pleasant, passive, or free of conceptual thought.
It is not defined by the object's institutional status; natural scenes and designed artifacts can also sustain it.
criticisms: Some theorists doubt that aesthetic experience has a single distinctive psychological character, since attention, emotion, and practical interest can overlap.

lookalikes.note: An experience is an episode of engagement; a judgment makes an evaluative claim about what was encountered.

concepts.name: Aesthetic judgment
concepts.summary: An evaluative judgment about beauty, elegance, expressive force, or another aesthetic quality.
concepts.body:
An aesthetic judgment says that an object or performance is beautiful, graceful, garish, moving, balanced, or otherwise aesthetically qualified. It is more than reporting a private preference because it typically presents the judgment as answerable to reasons that others can consider: composition, rhythm, unity, contrast, historical convention, or expressive achievement. Yet its normativity does not operate like a measurement with a universally agreed procedure.

Aesthetic judgment therefore combines subject-involvement with a claim to shareability. Disagreement can be genuine without making every judgment equally good, because attention, comparison, and criticism can improve or weaken the reasons offered.

examples.text: A critic argues that a film's long take is aesthetically effective because its sustained duration makes the character's isolation perceptible rather than merely stating a preference for long shots.
examples.note: The judgment gives an interpretable reason connecting a formal feature to an experienced effect.

commonMisreadings: An aesthetic judgment is not identical to a report of liking, although liking can motivate one.
Its claim to validity does not imply that aesthetic evaluation can be settled by a ruler or a vote.
criticisms: Relativists and subjectivists argue that apparent reasons often reflect training and cultural norms rather than properties that bind evaluators independently of response.

lookalikes.note: Aesthetic value is what an object may possess; judgment is the act of evaluating or asserting that value.

concepts.name: Aesthetic realism
concepts.summary: The view that at least some aesthetic qualities or values are not reducible to individual preference.
concepts.body:
Aesthetic realism holds that features such as unity, expressiveness, beauty, or artistic achievement can provide reasons that constrain judgment independently of any one person's immediate response. A realist need not claim that every work has a single obvious ranking or that aesthetic properties are physical properties in the manner of mass. The claim is that evaluation can be answerable to the work and to standards of attention rather than being made true solely by liking.

Realism thus explains why criticism can be corrective: a viewer may learn to notice a structural relation that was present before they appreciated it. The theory must still explain how cultural practices, historical knowledge, and perceptual training contribute to access to those qualities.

examples.text: A realist can argue that the counterpoint in a fugue is a genuine source of musical coherence even when a first-time listener finds the piece confusing.
examples.note: The judgment appeals to an intelligible relation in the work that education may reveal rather than create by preference alone.

commonMisreadings: Aesthetic realism does not require unanimous taste or a mechanical test for every dispute.
It does not say that aesthetic qualities are independent of all human practices in the same way as chemical elements.
criticisms: Anti-realist critics ask how aesthetic properties can be identified without circularly relying on the very responses and practices that realism claims they constrain.

lookalikes.note: Relativism makes standards framework-dependent, while realism treats at least some aesthetic reasons as more than local preference.
Both are realist positions, but one concerns aesthetic value and the other moral facts or reasons.

concepts.name: Aesthetic relativism
concepts.summary: The view that aesthetic standards or verdicts depend on persons, cultures, practices, or evaluative frameworks.
concepts.body:
Aesthetic relativism denies that one wholly context-free standard must govern every evaluation. What counts as graceful, appropriate, moving, or successful may depend on a tradition's purposes, conventions, materials, and learned forms of attention. A relativist can still distinguish better and worse judgments within a practice; the denial is of a single standard that overrides every framework from nowhere.

The position helps explain why the same mask, melody, or architectural form can be evaluated differently when its social function and history change. It also faces the problem of criticism across cultures: if standards are too insulated, it becomes difficult to explain genuine learning or justified criticism between traditions.

examples.text: A ritual mask may be judged successful within a community because it performs an ancestral and ceremonial role that a museum visitor, treating it as a detached sculpture, misses.
examples.note: The evaluative standard is tied to a practice and purpose rather than to isolated visual preference.

commonMisreadings: Relativism does not entail that judgments are random or that criticism within a culture is impossible.
It does not require treating every cultural practice as beyond interpretation or ethical criticism.
criticisms: Critics argue that strong relativism cannot explain why outsiders may expose internal distortions or why cross-cultural criticism can sometimes be better informed than local approval.

lookalikes.note: Realism posits aesthetic reasons that are not exhausted by frameworks, while relativism makes their authority framework-dependent.
Aesthetic relativism concerns evaluation of aesthetic qualities; cultural relativism is a broader thesis about norms and values.

concepts.name: Aesthetic value
concepts.summary: The value an object, event, or experience has through qualities such as beauty, expressiveness, or formal coherence.
concepts.body:
Aesthetic value is the kind of worth attributed to an object's appearance, organization, expressive power, or mode of presentation. It can belong to artworks, landscapes, performances, interfaces, ceremonies, and ordinary activities. The value may be intrinsic to an experience, relational to a work's context, or intertwined with moral, historical, practical, or social value without being reducible to any one of them.

The concept distinguishes what makes something aesthetically worthwhile from its price, usefulness, or moral goodness. A beautiful object can be morally objectionable, and a morally admirable act can be aesthetically unremarkable; particular cases may combine these dimensions but should not collapse them.

examples.text: A public garden can have aesthetic value because its paths, seasonal colors, and borrowed views create a coherent experience even when it has no commercial rarity.
examples.note: The value arises from perceptual and spatial organization, not from market price or scarcity.

commonMisreadings: Aesthetic value is not limited to beauty or pleasure; tragedy, severity, and strangeness can also be aesthetically valuable.
It is not the same as monetary value, popularity, or moral approval.
criticisms: Debates over aesthetic value question whether it is a property of objects, a relation involving trained responses, or a construction of cultural institutions and practices.

lookalikes.note: Value is the wider category of worth; aesthetic value specifies worth grounded in aesthetic qualities or experience.

concepts.name: Aestheticism
concepts.summary: A doctrine or movement that gives artistic autonomy and aesthetic experience priority over practical or moral purposes.
concepts.body:
Aestheticism treats art's value as not requiring service to moral instruction, politics, religion, or utility. The slogan of art for art's sake captures its resistance to judging a poem or painting solely by what it teaches or accomplishes outside the aesthetic domain. Historically, the movement also cultivated style, sensation, refinement, and an oppositional distance from bourgeois usefulness.

Its strongest version raises a conflict between artistic autonomy and moral criticism. An aestheticist may defend a work's formal achievement even when its subject matter is troubling, while critics argue that production, representation, and reception are themselves socially and ethically situated.

examples.text: A critic evaluates a decadent poem for its imagery, rhythm, and tonal precision without treating moral instruction as a requirement for its success.
examples.note: The standard of assessment is internal artistic achievement rather than usefulness as a lesson or civic tool.

commonMisreadings: Aestheticism is not merely enjoying beautiful things; it is a position about the priority and autonomy of aesthetic value.
It need not deny that art can have political or moral effects; it denies that those effects exhaust its justification.
criticisms: Critics argue that claims of autonomy can conceal class privilege, labor conditions, or political commitments embedded in the supposedly self-contained work.

lookalikes.note: Formalism emphasizes form in analysis, while aestheticism is a broader cultural and normative commitment about art's priority.

concepts.name: Aesthetics
concepts.summary: The branch of philosophy that studies art, beauty, aesthetic experience, judgment, and value.
concepts.body:
Aesthetics investigates several connected but distinct questions: what aesthetic properties are, how artworks and natural objects are experienced, what makes a judgment of taste reasoned, and how aesthetic value relates to moral, cognitive, or practical value. It also examines interpretation, artistic expression, representation, originality, genre, and the role of institutions. The field is therefore not reducible to a theory of beauty.

Aesthetic inquiry ranges from classical questions about imitation to contemporary questions about digital works, popular culture, design, and the politics of exhibition. It can analyze both the object and the practices through which people learn to attend, classify, and evaluate.

examples.text: An aesthetics seminar compares whether a protest song's political force is part of its artistic value or a separate value that interacts with its music.
examples.note: The question separates aesthetic evaluation from neighboring moral and political evaluations without assuming they are unrelated.

commonMisreadings: Aesthetics is not confined to fine art, museums, or beauty; it also covers nature, design, media, and ordinary experience.
It is not a purely subjective study of preference, because many aesthetic theories analyze reasons, standards, and public disagreement.
criticisms: Some critics argue that traditional aesthetics universalized narrow European art categories and neglected social power, craft, popular forms, and non-Western traditions.

lookalikes.note: Philosophy of art is a major part of aesthetics, while aesthetics also studies nature and everyday experience.

concepts.name: Agency
concepts.summary: The capacity of a person or group to initiate, guide, and control action toward purposes.
concepts.body:
Agency concerns action as something organized by an agent's reasons, intentions, and practical control rather than as a mere event happening to a body. It can involve forming goals, selecting among options, monitoring progress, and revising conduct. Agency is a matter of degree and can be distributed across individuals, groups, tools, and institutions; it does not require unlimited choice or independence from circumstances.

The concept supports debates about responsibility and autonomy. A person may exercise agency under coercive conditions while having diminished alternatives, and a group may act through procedures that no single member controls. A good analysis therefore separates initiation, intention, control, and the social conditions that make action possible.

examples.text: Tenants who organize, choose negotiators, and vote on a rent strike exercise collective agency even though landlords, law, and income constrain their options.
examples.note: The group forms intentions and coordinates action without requiring that every external constraint disappear.

commonMisreadings: Agency is not identical to unrestricted free will or total self-sufficiency.
Being caused by reasons, upbringing, or institutions does not by itself eliminate agency; the relevant issue is how the action is organized and controlled.
criticisms: Structural theorists warn that agency-centered explanations can blame individuals for outcomes produced by institutions, while strong structural views risk making organized resistance unintelligible.

lookalikes.note: Autonomy emphasizes self-government or independence of judgment; agency is the wider capacity to act intentionally.
Free will concerns the conditions of responsibility and choice, while agency also applies to constrained and collective action.

concepts.name: Agent-neutral reasons
concepts.summary: Normative reasons whose force does not depend on which particular agent is considering them.
concepts.body:
An agent-neutral reason can be stated without an essential reference to the evaluator's personal projects, relationships, or location. If unnecessary suffering counts against an outcome, it counts as a reason for anyone deliberating about that outcome, even when no special relationship is involved. Agent-neutrality concerns the structure of a reason, not whether every agent must perform the same act: different information or opportunity can change what each person can do.

The idea often supports impartial consequentialism and universalist ethics. It is contested by theories that give special weight to commitments, promises, personal projects, or the claims of those to whom an agent stands in a relationship.

examples.text: The avoidable death of a distant child gives a passerby a reason to help when assistance costs little, even though the child is a stranger.
examples.note: The reason arises from the child's plight rather than from a special tie to the passerby.

commonMisreadings: Agent-neutral does not mean that every agent has identical duties when their abilities, evidence, or costs differ.
It does not require emotional detachment; empathy can help an agent recognize an impartial reason.
criticisms: Agent-relative theorists argue that strict impartiality can distort the moral significance of personal commitments and make ordinary relationships demand too much sacrifice.

lookalikes.note: Impartiality is a related ethical ideal, while agent-neutrality classifies the structure of a reason.

concepts.name: Agent-relative reasons
concepts.summary: Normative reasons whose force depends on an agent's commitments, relationships, projects, or position.
concepts.body:
An agent-relative reason gives a particular agent a reason that need not apply to everyone in the same way. A promise creates a reason for the promisor; a parent has special responsibilities toward a child; and a person may have reason to protect a project they have undertaken. These reasons can be moral rather than merely selfish, because relationships and commitments can generate legitimate obligations.

Agent-relativity does not mean that anything an agent wants is justified. The reason must arise from an appropriate commitment or relation, and it can be limited by competing duties, rights, or the seriousness of harm to others. The central issue is whether morality permits partiality as part of a good life.

examples.text: A teacher has a special reason to write a recommendation for a student whose work they supervised, even though the teacher has no identical duty toward every applicant.
examples.note: The reason is generated by an actual professional relationship and responsibility, not by arbitrary preference.

commonMisreadings: Agent-relative reasons are not automatically selfish; care, fidelity, and responsibility can be morally valuable.
They do not make impartial reasons disappear, especially when the agent's project would impose grave harm on others.
criticisms: Impartial theorists worry that agent-relative permissions can rationalize favoritism or allow many people to disregard large harms by citing personal projects.

lookalikes.note: Agent-neutral reasons retain their force regardless of the identity or relationships of the deliberator.

concepts.name: Agnosticism
concepts.summary: A position that suspends or denies knowledge of whether a deity or deities exist.
concepts.body:
Agnosticism is primarily an epistemic position about the knowability or known status of divine existence. Someone can be agnostic because they suspend judgment, because the available arguments seem inconclusive, or because they think the question exceeds human cognitive limits. Agnosticism can combine with theism or atheism when those terms describe belief rather than knowledge.

The strength of the position varies. Weak agnosticism says that the person does not currently know; strong agnosticism says that the matter cannot be known. Neither version automatically gives equal credibility to every religious claim, since evidence and coherence can still be assessed comparatively.

examples.text: A person believes that a creator may exist but says that neither revelation nor natural theology has established the claim as knowledge.
examples.note: The person separates a tentative belief from the stronger epistemic status of knowing.

commonMisreadings: Agnosticism is not necessarily indecision, apathy, or equal confidence in all religious propositions.
It is not identical to atheism unless atheism is being used broadly for lack of theistic belief rather than denial.
criticisms: Critics argue that suspending judgment can conceal a practical evidential conclusion when the available evidence is sufficiently uneven, while agnostics reply that uncertainty can be the rational result.

lookalikes.note: Atheism concerns belief or denial about gods; agnosticism concerns knowledge and can coexist with either belief status.
Fideism treats faith as independent of or superior to evidential knowledge, whereas agnosticism withholds a knowledge claim.

concepts.name: Agnotology
concepts.summary: The study of how ignorance, doubt, and non-knowledge are produced or maintained socially.
concepts.body:
Agnotology examines ignorance as an object with a history rather than as a simple absence of information. Institutions can cultivate uncertainty through selective research, strategic public relations, suppression, confusing messaging, or the unequal distribution of attention. The field asks who benefits from a population not knowing, which mechanisms produce that condition, and how knowledge claims are blocked or delayed.

It does not imply that every gap in knowledge is manufactured. Natural difficulty, limited resources, and honest disagreement also matter. The analytical distinction is between ignorance that emerges accidentally and ignorance that is organized through incentives, practices, and power.

examples.text: A corporation funds public campaigns that emphasize uncertainty about a product's harms while withholding internal studies that would clarify the risk.
examples.note: The ignorance is studied as an outcome of information selection and institutional strategy, not merely as a missing fact.

commonMisreadings: Agnotology is not a theory that all ignorance is deliberate or that every scientific disagreement is propaganda.
It studies social production of non-knowledge, not only individual ignorance or lack of education.
criticisms: Critics warn that attributing ignorance to organized power can become unfalsifiable unless researchers specify evidence distinguishing deliberate cultivation from ordinary uncertainty.

lookalikes.note: Epistemic injustice concerns unfair treatment as a knower, while agnotology focuses on how ignorance or doubt is produced and maintained.

concepts.name: Agrarianism
concepts.summary: A political and social outlook that treats cultivation, land stewardship, and rural community as central goods.
concepts.body:
Agrarianism values a society organized around direct relationships with land, food production, seasonal work, and the independence associated with owning or cultivating productive resources. Its versions can be conservative, republican, ecological, or egalitarian. Common targets include speculative landholding, concentrated corporate power, urban dependency, and the loss of practical skills.

Agrarianism is not simply nostalgia for a rural past. Its strongest arguments concern scale, stewardship, and political independence: who controls land, how soil and water are renewed, and whether people have meaningful access to the conditions of self-rule. It must still address mechanization, urban livelihoods, and the historical exclusions hidden by idealized images of the countryside.

examples.text: An agrarian policy might protect small farms through land trusts, soil-restoration grants, and limits on speculative absentee ownership.
examples.note: The program treats land as an ecological and civic basis of life rather than only as a financial asset.

commonMisreadings: Agrarianism does not require rejecting all cities, machines, or scientific agriculture.
It is not identical to private-property absolutism; some agrarian traditions favor common land and cooperative cultivation.
criticisms: Critics argue that agrarian ideals can romanticize exhausting labor, ignore racial and gendered dispossession, and understate the productivity or cultural value of urban life.

lookalikes.note: Environmentalism is broader; agrarianism specifically links ecological care to cultivation, land tenure, and rural civic life.
Georgism focuses on land value and public revenue, while agrarianism is a wider social ideal about land-based life.

concepts.name: Agrippa's trilemma
concepts.summary: A skeptical trilemma claiming that a demand for reasons ends in dogma, circularity, or an infinite regress.
concepts.body:
Agrippa's trilemma targets the structure of justification. If a belief is supported by a reason, that reason may require another reason. Continuing produces an endless regress; returning to an earlier claim produces circularity; stopping without a further reason produces an arbitrary assumption or dogma. The argument does not itself say which response is correct.

Epistemologists answer in different ways: foundationalists allow basic justified beliefs, coherentists accept mutual support within a system, infinitists defend an open chain, and contextualists limit when further reasons are demanded. The trilemma is therefore a pressure test for theories of justification rather than a complete proof of skepticism.

examples.text: When a witness supports a claim with a memory, supports the memory with past reliability, and is asked for a reason for that reliability, each proposed stopping point invites another challenge.
examples.note: The example displays the three structural options without assuming that ordinary inquiry must literally continue forever.

commonMisreadings: The trilemma does not establish that no belief can be rational; it shows that a theory must explain where or how justification stops.
Circular support is not automatically vicious in every coherentist theory, which treats mutual support as a system property rather than a single proof.
criticisms: Foundationalists argue that the trilemma assumes every justified belief needs an inferential reason, while coherentists deny that linear grounding is the only model of justification.

lookalikes.note: The trilemma is a skeptical argument about justification, not a complete skeptical theory.

concepts.name: Ahimsa
concepts.summary: An ethical principle of non-harm or disciplined reduction of violence toward living beings.
concepts.body:
Ahimsa is a central ethical ideal in Jain, Buddhist, and Hindu traditions, though its meaning and practical demands differ among them. It can govern physical action, speech, intention, diet, occupation, and political conduct. In stringent Jain practice, careful movement and diet aim to minimize harm to even small living beings; in Gandhian politics, nonviolence becomes a method of resistance that exposes injustice without reproducing domination.

Ahimsa is not a simple rule that every harm is avoidable. Traditions debate intention, necessity, self-defense, livelihood, and responsibility for indirect effects. Its distinctive demand is to treat the reduction of harm as a discipline of character and social action rather than as mere passivity.

examples.text: A nonviolent campaign refuses attacks on persons while organizing boycotts, public fasts, and deliberate arrest to make an unjust law politically costly.
examples.note: The resistance is active, but its means aim to avoid injury and transform the opponent's relation to the conflict.

commonMisreadings: Ahimsa is not simple inaction; it can require courageous intervention and acceptance of personal risk.
It is not identical to pacifism in every tradition, because the scope of permissible defensive or indirect action is debated.
criticisms: Critics argue that strict nonviolence can leave victims exposed when coercive force is the only realistic way to stop immediate violence; defenders distinguish refusal to harm from refusal to resist.

lookalikes.note: Violence is the harm that ahimsa seeks to avoid or minimize; the concepts are opposed rather than synonymous.

concepts.name: Aidagara
concepts.summary: Watsuji Tetsurō's account of human existence as structured by the between-space of relational, historical, and ethical life.
concepts.body:
Watsuji uses aidagara, or betweenness, for an ontological and ethical account of the conditions of personhood. Human beings are embodied in climates, languages, customs, families, and institutions, yet they can also withdraw, criticize, and transform those relations. Individual and community are not two finished substances later connected; each is intelligible through the between-space that organizes obligations and possibilities.

The insight helps explain why responsibility is neither purely private nor reducible to social conformity. A promise, for example, depends on shared practices and a particular relationship, but the person who made it can still be judged for sustaining or breaking it. Critics worry that Watsuji's language of communal life can naturalize nation or tradition. The concept needs a place for dissent, unequal membership, and relationships that should be escaped rather than honored.

examples.text: A person's responsibility for a neighborhood flood response depends on shared infrastructure, local history, and roles that neither an isolated individual nor an abstract state fully describes.
examples.note: The example treats agency as situated in relationships without reducing the person to those relationships.

commonMisreadings: Aidagara is not relationalism about geometric space or a claim that people have no individuality.
It does not make every communal expectation ethically legitimate; relationships can sustain domination as well as care.
criticisms: Critics argue that Watsuji's emphasis on communal ethics can romanticize national or cultural unity and understate dissenting or marginalized standpoints.

concepts.name: Akan personhood
concepts.summary: A family of Akan views in which full personhood develops through moral and social participation rather than being exhausted by biological humanity.
concepts.body:
Akan accounts of personhood, especially as interpreted in the work of Kwasi Wiredu and Kwame Gyekye, distinguish being a human organism from becoming a person in the normative and social sense. Character, responsibility, membership, and the fulfillment of obligations can mark degrees of achieved personhood. The framework highlights that personhood is not only an inner possession but also a status recognized and formed in relations with others.

The distinction should not be detached from Akan institutions or converted into a universal license to deny infants or vulnerable people moral worth. Contemporary interpreters disagree about how sharply biological humanity, social recognition, and moral achievement should be separated, and about how the view bears on rights.

examples.text: An Akan elder who has acquired responsibilities, demonstrates judgment, and sustains communal obligations may be described as having achieved a fuller social status than a newborn.
examples.note: The contrast concerns developed moral and civic standing, not a claim that the newborn is outside human concern or protection.

commonMisreadings: Akan personhood is not a single doctrine shared identically by every Akan community or philosopher.
It should not be paraphrased as saying that infants lack human dignity, interests, or claims against mistreatment.
criticisms: Critics worry that making personhood depend on achievement can endanger people with severe cognitive disabilities; defenders distinguish social-moral status from basic human rights.

lookalikes.note: Both emphasize social formation, but Akan personhood has specific historical and philosophical contexts.

concepts.name: Akrasia
concepts.summary: Acting against one's own considered judgment or settled intention about what should be done.
concepts.body:
Akrasia occurs when an agent judges that one option is better or required yet voluntarily performs another because a competing desire, emotion, habit, or temptation prevails. The puzzle is not merely that the agent changes their mind: the agent acts while retaining the judgment that the alternative is better. Philosophers use the case to examine practical knowledge, weakness of will, desire, and responsibility.

Some accounts explain akrasia as a conflict between better judgment and short-term motivation; others deny that the agent fully believes the better option at the moment of action, or distinguish all-things-considered judgment from a local desire. The phenomenon therefore does not settle whether reason alone motivates action.

examples.text: A person decides that submitting a tax form tonight is necessary, opens a streaming service instead, and continues watching while judging that the form should be completed.
examples.note: The diversion is akratic because the agent's retained practical judgment conflicts with the chosen action.

commonMisreadings: Akrasia is not simply revising a plan after learning new facts.
It is not every failure caused by coercion or incapacity; the classic problem involves a degree of voluntary control.
criticisms: Socratic intellectualists argue that genuine knowledge of what is best would control action, so apparent akrasia reflects ignorance, misdescription, or divided judgment.

lookalikes.note: Akrasia is a conflict within intentional agency, not the capacity for agency itself.

concepts.name: Alienation
concepts.summary: Estrangement from one's activity, products, self, relationships, or social world.
concepts.body:
Alienation describes a relation in which something a person does or is connected to appears foreign, imposed, or controlled by an external power. In Marx's analysis of capitalist labor, workers can be separated from the product they make, the activity of production, their human powers of self-development, and their relations with other workers. Other traditions use the concept for existential estrangement, bureaucratic domination, or social exclusion.

Alienation is more than unpleasantness. A difficult job can still be one's own if it is intelligible and self-directed; alienation concerns the loss of authorship, recognition, or meaningful relation. Diagnosing it therefore requires attention to institutions, ownership, division of labor, and the agent's experience.

examples.text: A warehouse worker follows opaque algorithmic quotas, has no say over pacing, never sees the finished supply chain, and is penalized for slowing down to protect their body.
examples.note: The work is alienating because activity, product, and bodily capacity are governed as external powers rather than as a shared human project.

commonMisreadings: Alienation is not just loneliness, boredom, or temporary dislike of a task.
Marxian alienation is not solved merely by changing an individual's attitude if ownership and control remain external.
criticisms: Critics argue that the concept can be too subjective to measure or can idealize self-directed labor while overlooking unavoidable coordination and dependence in social production.

concepts.name: Altruism
concepts.summary: Concern for others expressed in action that may impose a cost on the agent.
concepts.body:
Altruism can refer to a motive, a behavior, or a normative ideal, and these should not be conflated. An action may benefit another at a cost without being motivated by concern, while a caring motive may fail to help. Ethical theories debate whether altruism requires self-sacrifice, whether concern for others can coexist with personal satisfaction, and whether impartial aid is preferable to special care.

Psychological egoists argue that every motivated action ultimately serves the agent's desire, but that thesis does not follow merely from the fact that helping can feel good. The philosophical question is whether another person's welfare can be an object of motivation rather than only an instrument for one's own state.

examples.text: A compatible donor gives a kidney anonymously to a stranger after understanding the medical risks and without seeking recognition or repayment.
examples.note: The case separates substantial concern for another's welfare from exchange, praise, or an expectation of direct return.

commonMisreadings: Altruism does not require the absence of all satisfaction; enjoying helping does not prove that the beneficiary was only a means.
It is not identical to effective charity, since a generous motive can still produce little benefit.
criticisms: Critics question whether altruism is psychologically distinct from enlightened self-interest and whether demanding impartial concern can overwhelm legitimate personal commitments.

lookalikes.note: Altruism can be impartial or relationship-based; agent-relative reasons classify the source of normative force.

concepts.name: Analogy
concepts.summary: A comparison that transfers insight from a familiar case to a less familiar case through relevant similarity.
concepts.body:
An analogy maps relations, roles, or structures between two domains and uses the mapping to suggest a conclusion about the less familiar one. Its strength depends on whether the shared features are relevant to the target conclusion, whether important disanalogies are absent, and whether the comparison generates testable expectations. Analogies can guide discovery and explanation without proving that the cases are identical.

A useful analogy preserves a pattern, not merely a surface resemblance. Comparing electrical current to water flow may illuminate pressure and resistance, but it can mislead if the analogy is extended to claims about discrete particles or conservation without qualification.

examples.text: A public-health team models the spread of misinformation using an epidemic model because transmission, exposure, and immunity have structurally similar relations.
examples.note: The analogy is useful only for the mapped dynamics; it does not imply that beliefs are pathogens in every respect.

commonMisreadings: An analogy supports a defeasible inference; it does not establish the conclusion simply because two things resemble each other.
A vivid comparison can be weak when the similarity is superficial or when a decisive disanalogy is ignored.
criticisms: Critics note that selecting which similarities count as relevant can presuppose the conclusion, making analogical arguments vulnerable to confirmation and rhetorical manipulation.

lookalikes.note: Metaphor can reshape understanding through figurative language, while analogy more explicitly maps relations to support inference.
Analogical reasoning is a form of defeasible induction, but it transfers relational structure rather than projecting a measured frequency.

concepts.name: Analytic philosophy
concepts.summary: A diverse philosophical tradition emphasizing precise argument, conceptual clarification, logic, and attention to language.
concepts.body:
Analytic philosophy is better understood as a family of methods and styles than as one doctrine. Its practitioners often make claims explicit, distinguish senses of a term, use formal or informal logic, test counterexamples, and examine how language relates to thought and world. The tradition includes naturalists, realists, pragmatists, ordinary-language philosophers, and metaphysicians who disagree sharply about method and substance.

Its strengths include argumentative transparency and sensitivity to hidden equivocation. Its critics argue that local analysis can lose historical, social, embodied, or political context, while many analytic philosophers now work directly on those subjects rather than treating them as outside the tradition.

examples.text: An analytic philosopher tests a definition of knowledge against cases involving justified true belief, luck, testimony, and memory rather than relying on an intuitive slogan alone.
examples.note: The method makes the proposed conditions precise and checks where they succeed or fail.

commonMisreadings: Analytic philosophy is not a single commitment to formal logic or a ban on history, literature, or political questions.
Clarity does not mean that every philosophical problem can be reduced to dictionary definitions.
criticisms: Continental and other critics argue that analytic problem-solving can fragment inquiry and conceal assumptions by treating context as an optional supplement rather than part of meaning.

lookalikes.note: The labels identify broad historical styles with substantial internal diversity, not mutually exclusive doctrines.
Conceptual analysis is one analytic method, not a complete definition of the whole tradition.

concepts.name: Analytic–synthetic distinction
concepts.summary: The distinction between truth grounded in meaning or logical form and truth depending on substantive facts.
concepts.body:
An analytic proposition is traditionally characterized as true in virtue of meanings or logical form, while a synthetic proposition is true, if at all, because of how the world is. “All bachelors are unmarried” is analytic under the standard definition because denying it conflicts with the meaning of bachelor; “some bachelors are happy” is synthetic because its truth requires information about actual people.

The distinction is not identical to a priori versus a posteriori. Analyticity is semantic or logical, whereas a priori status concerns the route of justification. Kant also defended synthetic a priori judgments, and Quine later challenged whether analyticity can be separated cleanly from the wider web of empirical belief.

examples.text: The sentence “a square has four sides” is analytic under the ordinary definition of square, while “the classroom contains a square table” is synthetic.
examples.note: The first follows from a concept; the second requires checking a contingent arrangement in the world.

commonMisreadings: Analytic does not mean trivial, uninformative, or psychologically innate.
A proposition learned from a teacher can still be analytic in content, while a synthetic proposition can sometimes be justified a priori on a philosophical theory.
criticisms: Quine argues that no sharp boundary separates truths by meaning from highly entrenched empirical claims because definitions and background theories are revisable together.

lookalikes.note: A priori concerns epistemic justification; analytic concerns semantic or logical grounds for truth.

concepts.name: Anarchism
concepts.summary: A family of political theories that rejects unjustified domination and seeks non-authoritarian forms of cooperation.
concepts.body:
Anarchism begins with criticism of coercive hierarchy, especially the state's claim to a standing monopoly of legitimate force, but its traditions disagree about property, markets, community, technology, and violence. Socialist anarchists emphasize mutual aid, common provision, and federated self-management; individualist versions stress autonomy and voluntary association. The positive aim is not the absence of rules but institutions whose rules are made and revisable by those subject to them.

Anarchist proposals must answer practical questions about defense, coordination, conflict, scale, and the risk that informal power recreates domination. The tradition's central test is whether an institution enables free cooperation or converts dependence into authority that escapes accountability.

examples.text: A federation of worker and neighborhood assemblies coordinates transport through recallable delegates whose mandates come from the assemblies rather than from a permanent ruling office.
examples.note: The example preserves large-scale coordination while trying to keep decision-makers subordinate to those affected.

commonMisreadings: Anarchism does not mean chaos, isolation, or the absence of all norms and institutions.
It is not one position on markets or violence; anarchist schools divide sharply on both.
criticisms: Critics argue that decentralized arrangements may struggle with large-scale coordination, defense, or accountability and may allow informal elites to replace formal rulers.

lookalikes.note: Libertarianism in politics often permits a minimal state, while anarchism rejects the state's standing authority more fundamentally.

concepts.name: Anarcho-capitalism
concepts.summary: A theory of stateless order based on private property, voluntary exchange, and competing private providers of protection.
concepts.body:
Anarcho-capitalism extends strong property rights and market exchange into functions usually performed by the state, including arbitration, security, roads, and money. Its defenders argue that voluntary contracts and competition can supply protection without taxation or a territorial monopoly of coercion. The theory therefore differs from minarchism, which retains a limited state, and from socialist anarchisms, which reject capitalist ownership and wage dependence.

Its key problem is institutional power. A market in protection may produce unequal agencies, conflicts among legal systems, exclusion from essential services, or a dominant provider that becomes state-like. The theory must explain how contracts remain voluntary when basic safety and property access are controlled by powerful private actors.

examples.text: A proposed community lets residents buy different arbitration and security plans, with contracts specifying jurisdiction and procedures for disputes between subscribers.
examples.note: The arrangement replaces public monopoly with competing contractual providers, creating the coordination problem the theory must solve.

commonMisreadings: Anarcho-capitalism is not simply ordinary libertarianism; it rejects even a minimal state.
Voluntary exchange does not by itself prove that initial property holdings or bargaining power are legitimate.
criticisms: Critics argue that private protection agencies could collude, exploit people who cannot pay, or consolidate into a coercive monopoly, reproducing the state under another name.

lookalikes.note: Anarchism includes socialist and anti-capitalist traditions that reject the property relations defended here.

concepts.name: Anarcho-collectivism
concepts.summary: A socialist anarchist doctrine favoring collective ownership of productive resources with distribution linked to labor contribution.
concepts.body:
Anarcho-collectivism, associated with Bakunin and parts of the First International, combines opposition to the state with opposition to capitalist ownership of land and productive capital. Workers' associations or federations would control production collectively, while individuals could receive certificates or shares corresponding to work performed. The proposal rejects private control of the means of production without immediately adopting distribution according to need.

This makes it distinct from anarcho-communism, which generally aims at common provision without labor-proportional exchange. Collectivist anarchism must address how labor is measured, how care and disability are valued, and how federations coordinate without creating a new centralized authority.

examples.text: A federation of metalworkers owns its foundry in common, elects rotating managers, and issues labor certificates while providing essential services through shared funds.
examples.note: Ownership is collective and management is accountable, but distribution still recognizes measured contribution rather than immediate need alone.

commonMisreadings: Anarcho-collectivism is not identical to state socialism; its defining institutional commitment is workers' control without a ruling state.
It is not anarcho-communism, because labor-linked compensation and conditional exchange remain central in many formulations.
criticisms: Critics question whether labor certificates reproduce status differences, how complex work can be compared fairly, and whether federations can prevent administrative power from hardening into hierarchy.

lookalikes.note: Anarcho-communism emphasizes distribution by need and common access, while collectivism retains a stronger labor-proportional element.

concepts.name: Anarcho-communism
concepts.summary: An anarchist communist proposal for abolishing the state and private ownership of productive resources through voluntary common provision.
concepts.body:
Anarcho-communism joins two claims: political authority should not command social life, and productive resources should not be owned as assets from which others must buy access. Its positive alternative is a federation of self-governing communes, workplaces, and mutual-aid associations that coordinate production and distribution without a central sovereign. Distribution according to need is meant to make survival a social guarantee rather than a reward for market power. The model therefore depends on practical institutions for conflict resolution, information sharing, and protection against informal domination.

It must answer an institutional question that slogans leave open: who decides when needs conflict, how are indispensable skills shared, and how can a federation prevent a local majority from becoming a new ruling class? Advocates appeal to recallable delegates, open accounts, federated planning, and norms of mutual aid rather than a permanent apparatus above society. The proposal is therefore not simply equal distribution; it is a theory of social ownership and accountable coordination.

Its strongest contrast with state socialism concerns the location of authority, while its contrast with anarcho-collectivism concerns the principle of distribution. A commune might still keep records, make difficult rationing decisions, and ask for specialized work, but those activities are supposed to remain contestable and oriented toward shared provision rather than accumulation by owners or officials.

examples.text: Several food-producing communes pool harvests and let residents request supplies while delegates coordinate transport between them.
examples.note: The example separates common ownership and need-based access from both wage exchange and centralized state rationing.

commonMisreadings: Anarcho-communism is not a proposal for a one-party communist state; abolishing state command is part of its definition.
Common ownership does not require identical consumption or the disappearance of every local decision.
criticisms: Critics question whether decentralized federations can allocate scarce or technically complex goods reliably without recreating coercive administration.

concepts.name: Anarcho-feminism
concepts.summary: An anarchist-feminist analysis of how patriarchy and other hierarchies operate in intimate life, work, and political organization.
concepts.body:
Anarcho-feminism treats domination as broader than laws issued by a state. Gendered expectations, economic dependence, sexual coercion, unpaid care, and movement leadership can reproduce authority even inside an anti-state organization. Its political practice therefore links liberation from government with changing the household, workplace, and habits of collective decision-making. Rotating roles, shared care, bodily autonomy, and resistance to compulsory gender roles are not merely private reforms; they are tests of whether a movement has removed hierarchy from everyday relations.

The analysis also changes what counts as political organization. A meeting can be formally horizontal while speakers, expertise, money, safety, or sexual access remain distributed unequally. Anarcho-feminists therefore examine who performs reproductive labor, who is believed when harm is reported, and whether a movement's procedures let dependent people refuse participation without losing necessities. Autonomy is material and relational, not only a legal right.
