Constitutionalism is the principle that governmental power must be legally limited and exercised under fundamental rules. It includes institutional checks, rights protections, and procedures for lawful government.

A constitutionalist system requires officials to follow law and permits institutions to review or challenge their decisions. Written limits matter only when courts, legislatures, and the public can make them effective in practice.

examples.text: Judicial review can enforce constitutionalism by invalidating actions that exceed legal authority.
examples.note: It fits because it concerns limits on rulers rather than merely the existence of a constitution.

commonMisreadings: A state can possess a written constitution without practicing constitutionalism.

concepts.name: Constructive dilemma
concepts.summary: A constructive dilemma is an argument form that derives a disjunction from two conditionals and a disjunction of their antecedents.
concepts.body:
A constructive dilemma is an argument form that derives a disjunction from two conditionals and a disjunction of their antecedents. Its pattern is If P then R, if Q then S, P or Q, therefore R or S.

From “if it rains, the match is canceled,” “if the field floods, the match is canceled,” and “it rains or the field floods,” one may infer that the match is canceled. The form is valid; whether its premises are true is a separate question.

examples.text: If rain causes flooding and snow causes closures, and rain or snow occurs, flooding or closures follows.
examples.note: It fits because the inference constructs an alternative conclusion from alternative sufficient conditions.

commonMisreadings: It is not a destructive dilemma, which uses negated consequents to infer negated antecedents.

concepts.name: Constructivism in philosophy
concepts.summary: Constructivism in philosophy holds that some truths, norms, or objects are constituted through procedures, practices, or conceptual activity.
concepts.body:
Constructivism in philosophy holds that some truths, norms, or objects are constituted through procedures, practices, or conceptual activity. Moral constructivism can ground principles in what agents would accept under suitable conditions.

A constructivist about justice may ground principles in a fair procedure of reasoning among persons rather than in a moral order discovered independently of any procedure. Constructivist views differ over what the procedure assumes and what kinds of truth it can establish.

examples.text: Kantian constructivism derives moral requirements from the structure of rational agency.
examples.note: It fits because the relevant standards are constructed through a specified standpoint or procedure.

commonMisreadings: It does not necessarily claim that physical reality is invented by human minds.

concepts.name: Content externalism
concepts.summary: Content externalism is the view that the content of some mental states depends partly on factors outside the thinker.
concepts.body:
Content externalism is the view that the content of some mental states depends partly on factors outside the thinker. A person can have the same internal physical state while a different environment changes what a word or thought refers to.

Two people with internally similar thoughts about water may mean different substances if one lives where the word refers to H2O and the other where it refers to a different liquid. Externalism says environment can partly determine content, while disputes remain about which external factors matter.

examples.text: Twin Earth arguments suggest that the content of water-thoughts depends on whether the surrounding liquid is H2O or XYZ.
examples.note: It fits because external environmental relations help determine mental content.

commonMisreadings: It differs from internalism, which makes content depend only on factors inside the subject.

concepts.name: Context-dependent memory
concepts.summary: Context-dependent memory is the tendency for recall to improve when the retrieval context resembles the context of learning.
concepts.body:
Context-dependent memory is the tendency for recall to improve when the retrieval context resembles the context of learning. The context can include a physical setting, internal state, or surrounding cues.

A diver may recall training details more readily underwater if the learning and retrieval settings match. Context is only one retrieval cue, and matching a setting does not guarantee recall or overcome weak encoding.

examples.text: A diver who learns words underwater may recall more of them underwater than on land.
examples.note: It fits because memory retrieval is helped by matching contextual cues.

commonMisreadings: It is not the claim that memories are stored only in the original context.

concepts.name: Contextualism in epistemology
concepts.summary: Contextualism in epistemology holds that the truth conditions of knowledge claims can vary with conversational or practical context.
concepts.body:
Contextualism in epistemology holds that the truth conditions of knowledge claims can vary with conversational or practical context. A person may correctly be said to know a fact in an ordinary context but not in a skeptical context with stricter standards.

In an ordinary conversation, someone may know they left keys on the table; after skeptical alternatives are raised, “know” may demand stronger evidence. Contextualists treat the standards in knowledge claims as shifting with conversational stakes, a thesis critics distinguish from changes in the person's evidence.

examples.text: Whether someone knows that a bank is open can depend on how much is at stake in the conversation.
examples.note: It fits because the standards for the verb know shift with context.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that truth itself changes whenever a speaker changes context.

concepts.name: Continental philosophy
concepts.summary: Continental philosophy is a broad tradition associated with European movements such as phenomenology, existentialism, hermeneutics, and critical theory.
concepts.body:
Continental philosophy is a broad tradition associated with European movements such as phenomenology, existentialism, hermeneutics, and critical theory. It often emphasizes history, interpretation, embodiment, society, and lived experience.

A phenomenologist studying lived experience and a critical theorist studying social power may both be placed in this broad tradition. The label gathers diverse movements and is often contrasted with analytic philosophy, but that division is porous and historically simplified.

examples.text: Heidegger's analysis of being-in-the-world is a work commonly placed in the continental tradition.
examples.note: It fits because the term names a historical and methodological family of philosophical approaches.

commonMisreadings: It is not a precise doctrine shared by every philosopher outside the analytic tradition.

concepts.name: Contingency
concepts.summary: Contingency is the condition of being possible but not necessary, so that something could have been otherwise.
concepts.body:
Contingency is the condition of being possible but not necessary, so that something could have been otherwise. A contingent fact is true in the actual world but false in at least one possible world.

A particular tree is contingent if it exists but could have failed to grow, unlike something that exists necessarily on the relevant theory. Modal claims depend on what possibilities are considered genuine and which features are held fixed.

examples.text: That a particular tree exists is contingent because the tree might never have grown.
examples.note: It fits because it marks dependence on circumstances rather than inevitability.

commonMisreadings: Contingency is not impossibility, which means that a thing cannot occur in any possible case.

concepts.name: Contingent being
concepts.summary: A contingent being is an entity that exists but could have failed to exist.
concepts.body:
A contingent being is an entity that exists but could have failed to exist. Contingent beings depend on conditions or causes outside themselves for their existence.

A house is contingent because it depends on materials, builders, and circumstances and might never have been built. The notion is used in arguments about explanation and existence, but showing that something is contingent does not alone establish a necessary cause.

examples.text: A human being is contingent because the individual would not exist without particular biological and historical conditions.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns non-necessary existence.

commonMisreadings: A contingent being is not the same as a dependent object in every philosophical theory, since dependence can be defined more narrowly.

concepts.name: Contractarianism
concepts.summary: Contractarianism is the view that moral or political principles are justified by agreement among rational agents.
concepts.body:
Contractarianism is the view that moral or political principles are justified by agreement among rational agents. The agreement may be hypothetical rather than an actual historical contract.

People may accept a rule against theft because everyone gains security by living under a mutually beneficial arrangement. Contractarian theories differ over who counts as a party and whether hypothetical agreement can justify duties to people unable to bargain.

examples.text: Hobbesian contractarianism explains political obligation through an agreement to escape insecurity.
examples.note: It fits because mutual agreement supplies the basis for norms or authority.

commonMisreadings: Contractarianism is distinct from contractualism, which typically derives morality from principles no one could reasonably reject.

concepts.name: Contractualism
concepts.summary: Contractualism is the moral theory that principles are justified when no one could reasonably reject them as a basis for shared conduct.
concepts.body:
Contractualism is the moral theory that principles are justified when no one could reasonably reject them as a basis for shared conduct. It evaluates principles from the standpoint of each affected person rather than simply aggregating welfare.

A policy is objectionable on contractualist grounds if someone affected could reasonably reject it as a rule for everyone, even when it increases total benefit. The theory focuses on justifiability to persons; what counts as a reasonable rejection remains contested.

examples.text: A contractualist may reject a policy if its burden on one person cannot be justified to that person.
examples.note: It fits because reasonable rejectability is its central test of moral principles.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily based on an actual signed contract or explicit bargain.

concepts.name: Contradiction
concepts.summary: A contradiction is a statement or pair of statements that cannot be true together in the same respect and at the same time.
concepts.body:
A contradiction is a statement or pair of statements that cannot be true together in the same respect and at the same time. In classical logic, a proposition and its negation form a contradiction.

“The light is on” and “the light is off” contradict one another when they concern the same light and moment. Contradictions are not mere disagreements: both sides might be false, and careful specification can reveal that apparently opposing claims concern different conditions.

examples.text: The claims The door is open and The door is not open contradict when they refer to the same door and time.
examples.note: It fits because incompatibility between truth claims is the defining relation.

commonMisreadings: A contradiction is not merely a disagreement between people, which may arise without logical incompatibility.

concepts.name: Contraposition
concepts.summary: Contraposition is the valid transformation of a conditional into one with the negated consequent as antecedent and negated antecedent as consequent.
concepts.body:
Contraposition is the valid transformation of a conditional into one with the negated consequent as antecedent and negated antecedent as consequent. The conditional If P then Q is logically equivalent to If not Q then not P.

From “if a number is divisible by four, it is even,” contraposition gives “if it is not even, it is not divisible by four.” This is logically equivalent in classical logic; reversing a conditional without negating both parts is generally invalid.

examples.text: If a shape is a square then it has four sides entails that if it lacks four sides then it is not a square.
examples.note: It fits because the inference preserves truth by reversing and negating the conditional.

commonMisreadings: Contraposition is not the same as affirming the consequent, which is invalid.

concepts.name: Conventionalism
concepts.summary: Conventionalism is the view that some truths, meanings, or standards depend on human conventions rather than on facts independent of convention.
concepts.body:
Conventionalism is the view that some truths, meanings, or standards depend on human conventions rather than on facts independent of convention. It can treat geometrical frameworks or linguistic meanings as selected systems of rules.

Driving on the right side is a convention that could have been coordinated differently, while its practical force depends on people following it. Conventionalists disagree about which truths depend on convention and how much reality or constraint remains independent of human agreement.

examples.text: The meaning of the word bicycle depends on linguistic conventions shared by speakers.
examples.note: It fits because convention is presented as constitutive of the relevant standard.

commonMisreadings: Conventionalism does not imply that every fact is arbitrary or socially chosen.

concepts.name: Cooperative principle
concepts.summary: The cooperative principle is Grice's idea that conversational participants generally contribute what is appropriate to the shared purpose of an exchange.
concepts.body:
The cooperative principle is Grice's idea that conversational participants generally contribute what is appropriate to the shared purpose of an exchange. It is expressed through maxims concerning quantity, quality, relation, and manner.

If asked for the time, a listener normally assumes a relevant and adequately informative answer rather than an unrelated fact. Grice's principle helps explain implicatures, but real conversation includes jokes, deception, and competing purposes that can suspend cooperation.

examples.text: Answering a question with relevant information normally follows the maxim of relation.
examples.note: It fits because it explains how shared conversational expectations support interpretation.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that speakers always cooperate sincerely or obey every maxim literally.

concepts.name: Corporatism
concepts.summary: Corporatism is a political system that organizes representation through occupational or social corporations rather than primarily through individual competition or class conflict.
concepts.body:
Corporatism is a political system that organizes representation through occupational or social corporations rather than primarily through individual competition or class conflict. Corporations in this sense can include employers, workers, professions, or other recognized groups.

A corporatist arrangement may give organized unions, employers, and professional bodies formal roles in negotiating national policy. Such representation can coordinate interests but may privilege officially recognized organizations and restrict independent political competition.

examples.text: A state may require labor and business associations to negotiate policy through officially recognized councils.
examples.note: It fits because organized social groups are given a formal role in governance.

commonMisreadings: Corporatism is not the same as rule by private corporations or ordinary corporate capitalism.

concepts.name: Correspondence theory of truth
concepts.summary: The correspondence theory of truth holds that a proposition is true when it corresponds to the relevant facts or reality.
concepts.body:
The correspondence theory of truth holds that a proposition is true when it corresponds to the relevant facts or reality. Its central idea connects truth with how the world is rather than only with coherence or usefulness.

“The kettle is boiling” is true, on a correspondence account, when the world contains the relevant state of affairs. The account captures an intuitive link to reality, but theories must explain what facts are and how propositions correspond to them.

examples.text: The proposition Snow is white is true when snow is in fact white under the intended conditions.
examples.note: It fits because truth is defined by agreement between statement and fact.

commonMisreadings: Correspondence does not mean that a true statement must resemble its fact pictorially.

concepts.name: Cosmopolitanism
concepts.summary: Cosmopolitanism is the view that all people belong to a shared moral or political community beyond particular nations.
concepts.body:
Cosmopolitanism is the view that all people belong to a shared moral or political community beyond particular nations. It gives universal duties or equal moral concern priority over exclusive national loyalty.

A cosmopolitan may argue that a distant person's basic interests deserve moral consideration regardless of nationality. Cosmopolitans differ over whether this entails global institutions, open borders, or simply duties that cross national boundaries.

examples.text: A cosmopolitan may support international institutions that protect human rights across borders.
examples.note: It fits because the concept treats global membership as morally significant.

commonMisreadings: Cosmopolitanism does not require eliminating all local cultures or political communities.

concepts.name: Cost–benefit analysis
concepts.summary: Cost–benefit analysis compares the expected costs and benefits of an option, often by expressing them in monetary or comparable terms.
concepts.body:
Cost–benefit analysis compares the expected costs and benefits of an option, often by expressing them in monetary or comparable terms. It can incorporate discounting, uncertainty, distributional effects, and opportunity costs.

A transport agency can compare a proposed rail line's construction and maintenance costs with travel-time savings and other benefits over time. Valuing lives, distributional effects, and uncertain future outcomes in common units involves ethical and methodological judgments, not just arithmetic.

examples.text: A transport agency may compare a bridge's construction cost with monetized travel-time savings and avoided accidents.
examples.note: It fits because systematic comparison guides the choice among policies or projects.

commonMisreadings: It is not a claim that every moral value is inherently reducible to money.

concepts.name: Council communism
concepts.summary: Council communism is a socialist current that advocates workers' councils as the basis of political and economic decision-making.
concepts.body:
Council communism is a socialist current that advocates workers' councils as the basis of political and economic decision-making. It rejects party-led state control in favor of direct worker self-management through councils.

In council communism, workers' councils would make decisions about production and governance through delegates accountable to assemblies. This current rejects party-state control as a substitute for workers' self-rule, though proposals differ on how councils coordinate at larger scales.

examples.text: A council communist model would have workplace councils coordinate production and delegate revocable representatives.
examples.note: It fits because workers' councils are the central institution of the proposed socialism.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to trade unionism, which can operate within capitalist ownership.

concepts.name: Counterexample
concepts.summary: A counterexample is a specific case that disproves a universal claim or invalidates an alleged general rule.
concepts.body:
A counterexample is a specific case that disproves a universal claim or invalidates an alleged general rule. One counterexample is sufficient to refute a statement of the form all objects have property P.

The claim “all birds fly” is refuted by a penguin, assuming penguins count as birds and the claim has no qualification. A counterexample defeats a universal claim but does not show how common the exception is or what narrower rule might survive.

examples.text: The number 9 is a counterexample to the claim that every odd number is prime.
examples.note: It fits because an individual case defeats a universal assertion.

commonMisreadings: A counterexample does not prove the opposite universal claim that no objects have the property.

concepts.name: Counterfactual
concepts.summary: A counterfactual is a conditional statement about what would or might have happened under a condition contrary to fact or not settled as actual.
concepts.body:
A counterfactual is a conditional statement about what would or might have happened under a condition contrary to fact or not settled as actual. Counterfactuals are often evaluated using relevant possible-world comparisons.

“If the driver had braked sooner, the collision would have been avoided” describes an alternative to what happened. Assessing it requires judgments about which background details stay fixed and how close the imagined scenario is to actuality.

examples.text: If the alarm had been set, the train would not have been missed is a counterfactual claim.
examples.note: It fits because it reasons about an alternative to the actual course of events.

commonMisreadings: A counterfactual is not simply a prediction about an event that has not happened yet.

concepts.name: Counterfactual thinking
concepts.summary: Counterfactual thinking is the mental process of imagining alternatives to events that actually occurred.
concepts.body:
Counterfactual thinking is the mental process of imagining alternatives to events that actually occurred. It can generate upward alternatives that improve on reality or downward alternatives that worsen it.

After missing a train, someone may imagine leaving home five minutes earlier and feel regret or relief. Such alternatives can guide learning and emotion, but they can also invite hindsight bias because the actual outcome makes one alternative seem obvious.

examples.text: After missing a flight, a traveler may imagine that leaving home ten minutes earlier would have prevented the loss.
examples.note: It fits because it constructs alternative causal paths from an actual outcome.

commonMisreadings: It is not the same as factual recall, which represents what actually happened.

concepts.name: Countermodel
concepts.summary: A countermodel is an interpretation or structure in which premises are true but a proposed conclusion is false.
concepts.body:
A countermodel is an interpretation or structure in which premises are true but a proposed conclusion is false. Finding a countermodel demonstrates that an argument form is invalid.

To show that “all birds fly” does not follow from a set of premises, an interpretation can make those premises true while assigning a nonflying bird to the domain. A countermodel establishes invalidity relative to the formal language and interpretation being used.

examples.text: An interpretation where P is true and Q is false countermodels the inference from P to Q.
examples.note: It fits because the model provides a formal case against logical consequence.

commonMisreadings: A countermodel is not merely an informal example unless it satisfies the formal interpretation requirements.

concepts.name: Counterpart theory
concepts.summary: Counterpart theory is David Lewis's account of modality in which an object has counterparts in other possible worlds rather than literally existing in them.
concepts.body:
Counterpart theory is David Lewis's account of modality in which an object has counterparts in other possible worlds rather than literally existing in them. Counterpart relations are similarity relations and need not be unique or exact identity relations.

On counterpart theory, a person in another possible world is a counterpart resembling the actual person in relevant ways, not literally that same person transported there. The account avoids one object existing in many worlds but makes judgments of possibility depend on similarity.

examples.text: A person in another possible world may be a counterpart of the actual person without being numerically identical to them.
examples.note: It fits because modal claims are analyzed through counterparts across worlds.

commonMisreadings: It differs from transworld identity, which says one object can literally exist in multiple worlds.

concepts.name: Courage
concepts.summary: Courage is the virtue of facing a significant danger or difficulty for a worthy end despite fear.
concepts.body:
Courage is the virtue of facing a significant danger or difficulty for a worthy end despite fear. Courage requires appropriate judgment because reckless exposure to danger is not necessarily virtuous.

A firefighter entering a burning building to rescue someone can act courageously despite reasonable fear. Courage is not recklessness: it requires judgment about the danger and worth of the end, and cultures may disagree about which risks merit praise.

examples.text: A firefighter enters a burning building to rescue a trapped person despite recognizing the risk.
examples.note: It fits because courageous action combines fear, risk, and a justified purpose.

commonMisreadings: Courage is not fearlessness, since a person can be courageous while feeling afraid.

concepts.name: Credence
concepts.summary: A credence is a degree of belief represented as a confidence level that a proposition is true.
concepts.body:
A credence is a degree of belief represented as a confidence level that a proposition is true. In Bayesian reasoning, credences are commonly represented by probabilities between zero and one.

A weather forecaster might assign a 70 percent credence to rain based on available evidence. A credence measures confidence rather than truth itself, and whether probabilities should follow particular mathematical rules is a further question.

examples.text: A researcher may assign a credence of 0.8 to the hypothesis that a treatment is effective.
examples.note: It fits because it measures graded belief rather than simple acceptance or rejection.

commonMisreadings: Credence is not evidence itself, but a rational response to evidence may change it.

concepts.name: Critical rationalism
concepts.summary: Critical rationalism is the philosophy that knowledge advances through bold conjectures and attempts at refutation rather than through final verification.
concepts.body:
Critical rationalism is the philosophy that knowledge advances through bold conjectures and attempts at refutation rather than through final verification. It treats criticism and falsifiability as central methods for correcting error.

A scientist proposes a theory that makes risky predictions and revises it when reliable tests conflict with them. Critical rationalism treats criticism as central but does not imply that one failed test mechanically settles a theory, since instruments and auxiliary assumptions can also be questioned.

examples.text: A scientific theory survives when repeated tests fail to refute its risky predictions, not because it is proven conclusively.
examples.note: It fits because rational inquiry is organized around criticism of proposed explanations.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim that every idea is equally rational merely because it can be criticized.

concepts.name: Critical theory
concepts.summary: Critical theory is an approach that examines and seeks to transform social structures that produce domination, inequality, or distorted understanding.
concepts.body:
Critical theory is an approach that examines and seeks to transform social structures that produce domination, inequality, or distorted understanding. It links social analysis with emancipatory aims rather than treating society as a neutral object of description.

A critical theorist might examine how workplace rules presented as neutral reproduce unequal control over workers. The approach combines explanation with evaluation and possible transformation, while critics challenge its standards of critique or its account of social change.

examples.text: A critical theorist may study how workplace rules reproduce class power while appearing impartial.
examples.note: It fits because critique is directed at hidden structures and possibilities for emancipation.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than simply criticizing a particular theory or argument.

concepts.name: Cross-race recognition effect
concepts.summary: The cross-race recognition effect is the tendency to recognize faces of one's own racial group more accurately than faces of unfamiliar racial groups.
concepts.body:
The cross-race recognition effect is the tendency to recognize faces of one's own racial group more accurately than faces of unfamiliar racial groups. The effect is influenced by experience, attention, and perceptual learning rather than proving an innate inability.

Someone may more accurately distinguish faces from a group they have had more experience seeing, partly because attention is tuned by experience. The effect is an average tendency in some settings, not a fixed limit on recognition, and social context and individual experience matter.

examples.text: A person who has mostly encountered one racial group may have greater difficulty distinguishing unfamiliar-group faces.
examples.note: It fits because it describes a measurable difference in face recognition across racial categories.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that people cannot recognize faces from other groups or that race alone determines accuracy.

concepts.name: Cue-dependent forgetting
concepts.summary: Cue-dependent forgetting is failure to retrieve stored information because the cues available at recall do not sufficiently match those present during encoding.
concepts.body:
Cue-dependent forgetting is failure to retrieve stored information because the cues available at recall do not sufficiently match those present during encoding. Providing an appropriate cue can recover information that was not erased from memory.

A student who cannot recall a name during an exam may remember it when given the first letter or when returning to the place where they studied. The information may be stored but temporarily inaccessible; forgetting can also reflect weak learning or interference.

examples.text: A forgotten name may return when a friend mentions the place where the meeting occurred.
examples.note: It fits because retrieval depends on access cues rather than storage failure alone.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to decay, which attributes forgetting to weakening over time.

concepts.name: Cultural appropriation
concepts.summary: Cultural appropriation is the adoption or use of elements of a culture by outsiders, especially when power inequalities, exploitation, or loss of context are involved.
concepts.body:
Cultural appropriation is the adoption or use of elements of a culture by outsiders, especially when power inequalities, exploitation, or loss of context are involved. Assessment depends on factors such as consent, representation, compensation, and whether sacred or marginalized practices are used commercially.

Using a sacred garment as a costume can strip it of meaning, especially when members of its source community face discrimination for wearing it. The term covers disputed cases, so analysis should identify power, consent, context, benefit, and the voices of people involved.

examples.text: Selling sacred Indigenous designs without permission or benefit to the community can constitute cultural appropriation.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns unequal cultural borrowing and its consequences.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply any cultural exchange between people from different backgrounds.

concepts.name: Cultural hegemony
concepts.summary: Cultural hegemony is the maintenance of social dominance by making a ruling group's values and assumptions appear natural or universally valid.
concepts.body:
Cultural hegemony is the maintenance of social dominance by making a ruling group's values and assumptions appear natural or universally valid. Antonio Gramsci linked hegemony to consent produced through institutions, education, and common sense.

If a society treats one group's economic priorities as simply common sense, its dominance may be sustained through education, media, and everyday norms as well as force. Hegemony is not total control: subordinate groups can reinterpret or resist prevailing ideas.

examples.text: A class may accept an economic hierarchy as meritocratic even when its institutions systematically favor that class.
examples.note: It fits because domination operates through accepted meanings as well as direct coercion.

commonMisreadings: Hegemony is not the same as propaganda, which is only one possible means of shaping belief.

concepts.name: Cultural relativism
concepts.summary: Cultural relativism is the methodological or moral view that beliefs and practices should be understood relative to their cultural context rather than judged automatically by another culture's standards.
concepts.body:
Cultural relativism is the methodological or moral view that beliefs and practices should be understood relative to their cultural context rather than judged automatically by another culture's standards. Methodological relativism suspends premature judgment, while moral relativism may deny universal moral standards.

A researcher studying a marriage practice may first understand its local history and meanings instead of applying an unfamiliar standard immediately. Contextual understanding does not settle whether criticism is warranted, and descriptive cultural relativism differs from the moral claim that no cross-cultural judgment is valid.

examples.text: An anthropologist interprets a marriage ritual through the community's own norms before evaluating it.
examples.note: It fits because cultural context is treated as essential to understanding or assessment.

commonMisreadings: Cultural relativism does not require accepting every practice as morally permissible.

concepts.name: Culture industry
concepts.summary: Adorno and Horkheimer's critique of mass cultural production as standardized commodities that organize pleasure, attention, and social conformity.
concepts.body:
Adorno and Horkheimer's claim is about a mode of production, not a verdict that every audience is passive or every popular work is worthless. Profit-oriented routines sort genres, stars, formats, and attention into repeatable packages. Standardization makes consumption predictable; pseudo-individualization supplies surface variation that lets consumers experience personal choice within a narrow range of options. Pleasure can therefore coexist with social conformity.

The thesis also explains why entertainment can absorb critique. A rebellious style may become a market segment, while exhaustion from work makes consumers seek relaxation that leaves the underlying organization untouched. Critics point to fan creativity, independent production, and works that genuinely disrupt expectations. These cases challenge any totalizing reading, but they do not by themselves refute the structural pressure toward commodified repetition.

examples.text: A streaming service offers hundreds of shows whose plots, pacing, and cliffhangers vary within a narrow formula optimized by audience data.
examples.note: The example shows pseudo-choice and standardization operating together.

commonMisreadings: The culture industry is not just a synonym for culture that many people enjoy.
Adorno and Horkheimer did not claim every popular work has identical effects or that audiences have no interpretive agency.
criticisms: Critics argue that the thesis underestimates audience creativity, subcultures, cultural difference, and the possibility that commercial media can support dissent.

concepts.name: Cynicism
concepts.summary: Cynicism is a skeptical attitude that distrusts the sincerity, motives, or goodness of people and institutions.
concepts.body:
Cynicism is a skeptical attitude that distrusts the sincerity, motives, or goodness of people and institutions. Modern cynicism often assumes that apparent altruism conceals self-interest.

A cynical voter may interpret every public promise as a bid for personal advantage. Such suspicion can notice real incentives but become self-sealing if no evidence is allowed to count as sincere action.

examples.text: A cynical observer interprets a charitable campaign mainly as a publicity strategy.
examples.note: It fits because suspicion of professed motives is its defining disposition.

commonMisreadings: Cynicism is not the ancient Cynic philosophy, which criticized convention through austere living.

concepts.name: Daoism
concepts.summary: Daoism is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in accordance with the Dao, the generative way or order of reality.
concepts.body:
Daoism is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in accordance with the Dao, the generative way or order of reality. Daoist texts often emphasize wuwei, meaning effective action that avoids forced or artificial striving.

A Daoist approach may favor responsive action that works with circumstances rather than forcing an abstract plan onto them. Daoist texts and religious practices are diverse, and the Dao is not simply a personal god or a synonym for passive inaction.

examples.text: A leader practicing wuwei may shape conditions so that a resolution emerges with minimal coercion.
examples.note: It fits because harmony with the Dao and non-forcing are central Daoist themes.

commonMisreadings: Daoism is not simply a synonym for passivity, since wuwei can involve skillful decisive action.

concepts.name: Decision theory
concepts.summary: Decision theory studies how agents should choose among actions under certainty, risk, or uncertainty.
concepts.body:
Decision theory studies how agents should choose among actions under certainty, risk, or uncertainty. It commonly represents preferences, probabilities, and utilities to evaluate options.

A traveler choosing a route can compare likely travel times and delays, assigning probabilities where outcomes are uncertain. Descriptive and normative decision theories answer different questions, and a mathematically coherent choice can still depend on questionable values or estimates.

examples.text: An investor may choose a portfolio by comparing the expected utilities of uncertain returns.
examples.note: It fits because the field analyzes rational choice under different information conditions.

commonMisreadings: Decision theory is not limited to financial decisions or to choices with known probabilities.

concepts.name: Decolonization
concepts.summary: Decolonization is the process of dismantling colonial rule and the political, economic, cultural, and epistemic structures that sustain it.
concepts.body:
Decolonization is the process of dismantling colonial rule and the political, economic, cultural, and epistemic structures that sustain it. It can include sovereignty, land restitution, institutional reform, and recovery of suppressed knowledge.

A newly independent country may change land ownership, education, and public language policies as well as replace colonial officials. Formal independence does not automatically end economic or cultural dependence, and decolonization can involve competing visions among formerly colonized people.

examples.text: A formerly colonized state may replace imposed land laws while restoring authority to Indigenous communities.
examples.note: It fits because it addresses both formal independence and continuing colonial relations.

commonMisreadings: Decolonization is not complete merely because a colony receives a new national flag.

concepts.name: Deconstruction
concepts.summary: Deconstruction is a method of reading that exposes tensions, exclusions, and unstable oppositions within texts or concepts.
concepts.body:
Deconstruction is a method of reading that exposes tensions, exclusions, and unstable oppositions within texts or concepts. It shows how a text can undermine the fixed meanings it appears to assert.

A deconstructive reading of a text may show that its opposition between reason and emotion relies on the very element it ranks as inferior. This is not simply destroying a text or claiming it means anything; the reading traces specific tensions and exclusions.

examples.text: A deconstructive reading may examine how a text's contrast between speech and writing depends on the supposedly inferior term.
examples.note: It fits because it analyzes internal instability rather than supplying a replacement doctrine.

commonMisreadings: Deconstruction is not the destruction of a text or a claim that texts have no meaning at all.

concepts.name: Deductive reasoning
concepts.summary: Deductive reasoning derives a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true and the inference is valid.
concepts.body:
Deductive reasoning derives a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true and the inference is valid. Validity concerns the structure of the inference, while soundness also requires true premises.

From “all sealed containers are closed” and “this jar is sealed,” it follows necessarily that this jar is closed, if the premises are true. Deduction preserves truth through valid form but cannot guarantee that the starting premises are true.

examples.text: From All mammals are warm-blooded and whales are mammals, deduction yields that whales are warm-blooded.
examples.note: It fits because necessity of the conclusion is the defining feature.

commonMisreadings: Deduction is not synonymous with certainty about the premises themselves.

concepts.name: Defeasible reasoning
concepts.summary: Defeasible reasoning draws a provisional conclusion that can be withdrawn when new information defeats it.
concepts.body:
Defeasible reasoning draws a provisional conclusion that can be withdrawn when new information defeats it. It is useful when generalizations have exceptions and complete information is unavailable.

A person may infer that a shop is open because its posted hours say so, then withdraw that conclusion on learning it is closed for a holiday. The first inference was reasonable but revisable; not every revision shows the original reasoning was irrational.

examples.text: A bird is normally assumed to fly until learning that the bird is a penguin.
examples.note: It fits because the inference remains open to revision by exceptions.

commonMisreadings: Defeasible reasoning is not deductively valid reasoning whose conclusion cannot be overturned by added facts.

concepts.name: Defeater
concepts.summary: A defeater is information that undermines the justification or evidential support for a belief without necessarily making the belief false.
concepts.body:
A defeater is information that undermines the justification or evidential support for a belief without necessarily making the belief false. A rebutting defeater supports the belief's negation, while an undercutting defeater attacks the connection between evidence and belief.

A witness's poor lighting conditions can defeat confidence in an identification without proving that the identification is false. Defeaters may undercut the evidence itself or provide evidence for the opposite conclusion, and a belief can remain true despite losing justification.

examples.text: Learning that a thermometer is broken defeats the reading's support for believing the room is cold.
examples.note: It fits because the new information removes or weakens epistemic justification.

commonMisreadings: A defeater is not automatically a refutation of the proposition believed.

concepts.name: Definite description
concepts.summary: A definite description is a phrase that purports to refer to a unique object by describing it, commonly using the.
concepts.body:
A definite description is a phrase that purports to refer to a unique object by describing it, commonly using the. Its standard logical analysis treats it as asserting existence, uniqueness, and possession of the described property.

In “the current chair of the committee,” the phrase typically presupposes or asserts that one person uniquely fits the description. Russell's analysis treats such phrases using quantifiers rather than assuming every grammatical description names an object.

examples.text: The tallest building in Perth refers only if exactly one building satisfies the description in the relevant context.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns uniquely identifying descriptions rather than ordinary names.

commonMisreadings: A definite description is not guaranteed to refer merely because its grammar is definite.

concepts.name: Definitional equivalence
concepts.summary: Definitional equivalence is a relation between formal theories that can define each other's primitive concepts without changing their deductive content.
concepts.body:
Definitional equivalence is a relation between formal theories that can define each other's primitive concepts without changing their deductive content. Equivalent theories may use different basic vocabularies while expressing the same structure.

Two formal theories may count as definitionally equivalent when each can explicitly define the other's basic terms and translate its claims without losing theorems. This is a strong technical relation, not mere similarity of subject matter or vocabulary.

examples.text: Two formulations of geometry can be definitionally equivalent if each system explicitly defines the other's primitive relations.
examples.note: It fits because mutual definability connects the theories at the level of formal language.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than merely having some logically equivalent theorems.

concepts.name: Deflationism about truth
concepts.summary: Deflationism about truth holds that the truth predicate does not name a substantial property beyond the logical or expressive role captured by instances such as saying that Snow is white is true.
concepts.body:
Deflationism about truth holds that the truth predicate does not name a substantial property beyond the logical or expressive role captured by instances such as saying that Snow is white is true. The equivalence schema This proposition is true if and only if the proposition is often does the explanatory work.

Saying “It is true that the train is late” can often be replaced by “The train is late” without adding a new claim about a special property. Deflationists differ on the truth predicate's useful roles, and critics argue that some explanatory questions need a richer theory.

examples.text: A deflationist can use true in The theorem is true to endorse the theorem without positing a deep truth substance.
examples.note: It fits because truth is treated as a minimal expressive device rather than a metaphysical relation.

commonMisreadings: Deflationism does not deny that people make true and false assertions.

concepts.name: Deism
concepts.summary: Deism is the theological view that a creator exists but does not ordinarily intervene through revealed miracles or ongoing providential acts.
concepts.body:
Deism is the theological view that a creator exists but does not ordinarily intervene through revealed miracles or ongoing providential acts. Deists typically rely on reason and nature rather than institutional revelation as the basis of religious belief.

A deist may believe that reason supports belief in a creator while rejecting ongoing miraculous intervention as necessary to explain the world. Deism has taken varied forms and should not be confused with atheism or with every belief in a distant deity.

examples.text: A deist may believe that God created the universe but reject the historical authority of miracle reports.
examples.note: It fits because a creator is affirmed while regular supernatural intervention is denied or minimized.

commonMisreadings: Deism is not atheism, since it retains belief in a creator.

concepts.name: Deliberative democracy
concepts.summary: Deliberative democracy is a model of democracy in which legitimate decisions result from public reasoning among free and equal participants.
concepts.body:
Deliberative democracy is a model of democracy in which legitimate decisions result from public reasoning among free and equal participants. Deliberation requires exchanging reasons, listening, and revising views rather than merely counting preferences.

Citizens in a deliberative process hear arguments and evidence about a proposed water policy before voting, with a chance to challenge assumptions. Good deliberation requires access and fair participation; it does not guarantee consensus or eliminate unequal influence.

examples.text: A citizens' assembly that studies evidence and publicly justifies its recommendations exemplifies deliberative democracy.
examples.note: It fits because reason-giving discussion is central to democratic legitimacy.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to direct democracy, which concerns who votes rather than how decisions are reasoned about.

concepts.name: Demarcation problem
concepts.summary: The demarcation problem asks how to distinguish science from non-science or pseudoscience.
concepts.body:
The demarcation problem asks how to distinguish science from non-science or pseudoscience. Proposed criteria include falsifiability, empirical testability, methodological norms, and research traditions, but no single criterion is universally accepted.

A claim that a treatment cures disease may imitate scientific language yet avoid tests that could reveal failure. Philosophers disagree about a single boundary between science and non-science; useful assessment often examines methods and evidence rather than relying on one label.

examples.text: Popper argued that a scientific theory should make predictions that could in principle be falsified.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns the boundary of scientific inquiry.

commonMisreadings: It is not the problem of distinguishing one scientific field from another.

concepts.name: Democracy
concepts.summary: Democracy is a form of political rule in which the people exercise ultimate authority, directly or through accountable representatives.
concepts.body:
Democracy is a form of political rule in which the people exercise ultimate authority, directly or through accountable representatives. Democratic systems require mechanisms for participation, contestation, and peaceful transfer or accountability of power.

In a representative democracy, voters choose officials who can be replaced through regular elections and remain subject to legal constraints. Elections alone do not ensure democratic rule if people cannot organize, access information, or contest decisions freely.

examples.text: A country with competitive elections, universal suffrage, and protected opposition parties has democratic institutions.
examples.note: It fits because popular political authority is the defining principle.

commonMisreadings: Democracy is not guaranteed by elections alone when elections are noncompetitive or unaccountable.

concepts.name: Democratic confederalism
concepts.summary: Democratic confederalism is a decentralized political model based on local assemblies, participatory democracy, gender equality, and ecological responsibility.
concepts.body:
Democratic confederalism is a decentralized political model based on local assemblies, participatory democracy, gender equality, and ecological responsibility. It favors a network of self-governing communities over a centralized nation-state.

A democratic confederalist model links local assemblies through delegates while seeking gender equality and ecological responsibility. It is a political proposal associated with particular movements; its ideals and practical institutions should be assessed separately.

examples.text: A federation of neighborhood councils that delegates limited, recallable responsibilities illustrates the model.
examples.note: It fits because confederal local autonomy and participatory governance are its organizing principles.

commonMisreadings: It is not conventional federalism, which can retain a powerful central government and representative institutions.

concepts.name: Democratic legitimacy
concepts.summary: Democratic legitimacy is the justified authority of a decision or institution because affected people can participate in, contest, or hold it accountable through democratic procedures.
concepts.body:
Democratic legitimacy is the justified authority of a decision or institution because affected people can participate in, contest, or hold it accountable through democratic procedures. Legitimacy can depend on inclusion, representation, transparency, and responsiveness as well as electoral results.

A city decision may gain legitimacy when affected residents can scrutinize evidence, participate, and challenge officials who implement it. Participation is not sufficient if it is only symbolic or if powerful groups control the process.

examples.text: A law gains democratic legitimacy when citizens can vote, organize opposition, and challenge its application through independent institutions.
examples.note: It fits because the concept explains why collective decisions deserve political compliance.

commonMisreadings: Democratic legitimacy is not the same as popularity at a single moment.

concepts.name: Democratic socialism
concepts.summary: Democratic socialism is a political tradition seeking social or collective ownership of major productive resources through democratic institutions and civil liberties.
concepts.body:
Democratic socialism is a political tradition seeking social or collective ownership of major productive resources through democratic institutions and civil liberties. It differs from authoritarian state socialism by treating political democracy and participation as essential.

A democratic socialist may support public or cooperative ownership of major industries while defending competitive elections and civil rights. The tradition includes reformist and more transformative programs, so the label does not specify one route or institutional design.

examples.text: A democratic socialist program may expand worker ownership while preserving multiparty elections and free association.
examples.note: It fits because socialism is pursued through democratic control rather than one-party rule.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply any welfare-state policy within a predominantly private economy.

concepts.name: Denotation
concepts.summary: Denotation is the literal or referential meaning of a word, distinct from its associated emotional or cultural meanings.
concepts.body:
Denotation is the literal or referential meaning of a word, distinct from its associated emotional or cultural meanings. A term's denotation can remain stable while its connotations differ among speakers.

“Rose” denotes a kind of flowering plant, while its associations may include romance or a particular cultural symbol. Denotation can depend on context and reference, so the contrast with connotation is useful without being a complete theory of meaning.

examples.text: The denotation of snake identifies a legless elongated reptile, while fear may be a connotation.
examples.note: It fits because it identifies what an expression directly refers to or means.

commonMisreadings: Denotation is not always identical to a single physical object, since abstract terms can denote properties or concepts.

concepts.name: Deontology
concepts.summary: Deontology is an ethical approach that evaluates actions by duties, rules, or constraints rather than solely by consequences.
concepts.body:
Deontology is an ethical approach that evaluates actions by duties, rules, or constraints rather than solely by consequences. Some deontological theories hold that certain actions are wrong even when they would produce better outcomes.

A deontologist may hold that lying is wrong even when a lie would produce a better immediate outcome, because a duty constrains action. Deontological theories vary in which duties are fundamental and how conflicts between duties should be resolved.

examples.text: A deontologist may reject lying to an innocent person even if the lie would increase overall happiness.
examples.note: It fits because obligation and prohibition are central to moral assessment.

commonMisreadings: Deontology is not the claim that consequences never matter in any moral theory.

concepts.name: Description theory of names
concepts.summary: The description theory of names holds that a proper name refers through an associated description or cluster of descriptions.
concepts.body:
The description theory of names holds that a proper name refers through an associated description or cluster of descriptions. It explains reference by treating names as shorthand for identifying information available to speakers.

A description theory might explain “Aristotle” as referring to whoever uniquely fits a description such as “the teacher of Alexander.” A name can still refer when speakers know little about its bearer, which motivates objections and alternative causal-historical accounts.

examples.text: On one version, Aristotle might refer through descriptions such as the ancient Greek philosopher who wrote the Metaphysics.
examples.note: It fits because descriptive content is used to explain how names refer.

commonMisreadings: It is challenged by causal theories that allow reference despite mistaken or incomplete descriptions.

concepts.name: Desert
concepts.summary: Desert is the idea that a person merits a benefit, burden, praise, or blame because of a relevant fact about them.
concepts.body:
Desert is the idea that a person merits a benefit, burden, praise, or blame because of a relevant fact about them. Desert differs from entitlement, which can arise from a rule, promise, or legal status without merit.

A worker may deserve credit for a difficult achievement because of effort and skill, while need-based allocation may point to a different distribution. Desert claims require a relevant basis and do not alone determine how competing claims should be weighed.

examples.text: A runner may deserve recognition for completing a difficult race through sustained effort.
examples.note: It fits because it concerns what someone merits rather than what they merely receive.

commonMisreadings: Desert is not identical to need, since a person can need help without having earned it.

concepts.name: Desire theory of well-being
concepts.summary: The desire theory of well-being holds that a person's life goes better when their desires or preferences are fulfilled.
concepts.body:
The desire theory of well-being holds that a person's life goes better when their desires or preferences are fulfilled. The theory can count fulfilled desires even when the person is not consciously aware of the fulfillment.

If a person wants to complete a long project and succeeds, desire theory may count that success as improving their life even if it brings little pleasure. The theory must address mistaken, harmful, or uninformed desires and whether fulfillment matters when a person never knows it occurred.

examples.text: A person's well-being may increase when a long-held goal is achieved, even if the person learns of it later.
examples.note: It fits because desire satisfaction supplies the account of welfare.

commonMisreadings: It is not the same as hedonism, which identifies well-being with pleasure and absence of pain.

concepts.name: Despotism
concepts.summary: Despotism is rule by an authority that exercises power with little effective legal, institutional, or popular constraint.
concepts.body:
Despotism is rule by an authority that exercises power with little effective legal, institutional, or popular constraint. Despotic rule can be arbitrary even when it maintains formal administrative institutions.

A despot may issue rules and punish opponents without independent courts or meaningful public checks. The term describes unconstrained rule, but actual systems vary in how power is organized and what informal limits remain.

examples.text: A ruler who can confiscate property or imprison opponents without independent review governs despotically.
examples.note: It fits because unchecked arbitrary power is the defining feature.

commonMisreadings: Despotism is not synonymous with monarchy, since a monarchy can be constitutionally limited.

concepts.name: Developmentalism
concepts.summary: Developmentalism is the view or policy approach that prioritizes economic development through active state coordination, industrialization, and structural transformation.
concepts.body:
Developmentalism is the view or policy approach that prioritizes economic development through active state coordination, industrialization, and structural transformation. Developmentalist states often use planning, infrastructure investment, trade policy, and targeted industrial support.

A developmentalist government might direct credit and investment toward domestic manufacturing to change the structure of its economy. State coordination can build capacity, but it can also misallocate resources or entrench favored industries; outcomes depend on institutions and context.

examples.text: South Korea's state-directed industrial policies during the late twentieth century are commonly studied as developmentalist.
examples.note: It fits because development is pursued through coordinated transformation rather than laissez-faire alone.

commonMisreadings: Developmentalism is not equivalent to any economic growth, since it names a particular strategy and governing orientation.

concepts.name: Dharma
concepts.summary: Dharma is a concept in Indian traditions referring, depending on context, to duty, moral order, right conduct, or the law that sustains reality.
concepts.body:
Dharma is a concept in Indian traditions referring, depending on context, to duty, moral order, right conduct, or the law that sustains reality. Its meaning differs across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and other traditions.

A text may use dharma to mean a person's duty, a teaching, or the order sustaining the world, depending on tradition and context. It has no single translation shared by Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and other uses, so interpretation requires care.

examples.text: In the Bhagavad Gita, fulfilling one's dharma is discussed in relation to role, duty, and disciplined action.
examples.note: It fits because it names a normative order connecting conduct and the structure of life.

commonMisreadings: Dharma is not reducible to a single English translation such as religion or duty.

concepts.name: Dialectic
concepts.summary: Dialectic is a method or process of inquiry in which opposing claims, forces, or positions interact to produce clarification or transformation.
concepts.body:
Dialectic is a method or process of inquiry in which opposing claims, forces, or positions interact to produce clarification or transformation. Socratic questioning uses dialogue to expose contradictions in a person's assumptions.

A debate can clarify a position by forcing it to answer a serious objection, and the exchange may change what either side initially thought. Dialectic has different meanings from Socratic questioning to theories of historical development; it is not always a simple thesis-antithesis-synthesis formula.

examples.text: A discussion may refine a definition by testing it against objections and revising it.
examples.note: It fits because development occurs through structured engagement with opposition.

commonMisreadings: Dialectic is not simply any argument or disagreement without a productive method.

concepts.name: Dialectical materialism
concepts.summary: Dialectical materialism is a Marxist framework that explains social and historical change through material conditions and conflicts developing within systems.
concepts.body:
Dialectical materialism is a Marxist framework that explains social and historical change through material conditions and conflicts developing within systems. It treats contradictions in economic and social relations as drivers of transformation.

A dialectical-materialist analysis might explain political conflict through changing production relations and tensions between social groups. Marxist thinkers disagree about the framework's laws and scope; it should not be treated as a mechanical prediction that history must follow one fixed sequence.

examples.text: Conflict between capital owners and wage workers is analyzed as a contradiction within capitalism.
examples.note: It fits because material organization and dialectical conflict jointly explain change.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely a synonym for economic determinism, since dialectical relations include active social struggle.

concepts.name: Dialetheism
concepts.summary: Dialetheism is the view that some contradictions are genuinely true.
concepts.body:
Dialetheism is the view that some contradictions are genuinely true. It rejects the classical principle that no proposition and its negation can both be true in every case.

A dialetheist may treat some paradoxical claims, such as certain self-referential sentences, as both true and false while using a logic that blocks arbitrary conclusions. This is a minority position; accepting a true contradiction does not mean accepting every contradiction.

examples.text: A dialetheist may treat certain semantic paradoxes as involving both a true statement and its negation.
examples.note: It fits because acceptance of true contradictions is its defining thesis.

commonMisreadings: Dialetheism does not say that every contradiction is true or that reasoning becomes useless.

concepts.name: Direct democracy
concepts.summary: Direct democracy is a system in which citizens decide policies or laws themselves rather than delegating all decisions to representatives.
concepts.body:
Direct democracy is a system in which citizens decide policies or laws themselves rather than delegating all decisions to representatives. Referendums, citizen initiatives, and assemblies are common direct-democratic mechanisms.

A referendum lets voters decide a proposed law directly rather than leaving the choice entirely to elected representatives. Direct participation can increase control but may favor simple questions, low-information campaigns, or groups with greater resources.

examples.text: Voters directly approve or reject a proposed constitutional amendment in a referendum.
examples.note: It fits because the electorate exercises decision-making authority on the measure itself.

commonMisreadings: It is not representative democracy, even though representative systems may include direct-democratic tools.

concepts.name: Direct realism
concepts.summary: Direct realism is the view that ordinary perception gives us direct awareness of mind-independent objects and their properties.
concepts.body:
Direct realism is the view that ordinary perception gives us direct awareness of mind-independent objects and their properties. It denies that perception always requires awareness of an internal intermediary representation.

When someone sees a tree, direct realism says their perception is of the tree itself, not only of an internal image from which a tree is inferred. The view must explain illusions and perceptual variation without turning ordinary perception into awareness of private intermediaries.

examples.text: When someone sees a tree, direct realism says the perceived tree itself is an object of perceptual awareness.
examples.note: It fits because external objects are treated as directly perceived.

commonMisreadings: Direct realism does not claim that perception is infallible or unaffected by conditions.

concepts.name: Disagreement
concepts.summary: Disagreement is a situation in which two or more parties hold incompatible answers, beliefs, judgments, or preferences about a matter.
concepts.body:
Disagreement is a situation in which two or more parties hold incompatible answers, beliefs, judgments, or preferences about a matter. Disagreement can concern facts, values, meanings, or practical choices.

Two doctors may agree on a patient's symptoms yet disagree about the diagnosis because they interpret evidence differently. Disagreement can concern facts, meanings, or values, and identifying which kind is involved helps determine what could resolve it.

examples.text: Two scientists disagree when one accepts a hypothesis and the other rejects it based on competing evidence.
examples.note: It fits because incompatible positions are the essential feature.

commonMisreadings: Disagreement is not necessarily irrational conflict, since reasonable people can disagree under uncertainty.

concepts.name: Disciplinary power
concepts.summary: Foucault's account of power that produces useful, observable, and self-regulating individual bodies through routines, surveillance, examination, and normalization.
concepts.body:
Discipline produces individual bodies as observable, comparable, and trainable units. It arranges space, schedules time, distributes tasks, records performance, and uses examinations to connect visibility with a norm. The person internalizes the possibility of being assessed and begins to regulate conduct even when no supervisor is visibly intervening. Power thus creates capacities and skills at the same time that it makes people useful and governable.

Its object differs from biopolitics. A timetable and grade rank a pupil; a demographic table manages a population's attendance, health, or fertility rates. The same institution can use both techniques, but their scales and operations are not identical. Critics note that Foucault can understate learning, consent, and resistance. The concept is strongest when it identifies the concrete routines through which support and control are combined.

examples.text: A school timetable, graded examination, seating plan, and attendance register make each pupil continuously comparable and correctable.
examples.note: The system produces individual visibility and normalized performance rather than relying only on a single sovereign command.

commonMisreadings: Disciplinary power is not just physical punishment and does not require a guard to be visibly present.
It is not the same as biopolitics: discipline individualizes bodies, while biopolitics regulates populations.
criticisms: Critics argue that Foucault's account can understate resistance, consent, and the ways institutions genuinely enable learning or care.

lookalikes.note: Discipline trains individual bodies; biopolitics manages the rates and risks of populations, with overlap but no identity.

concepts.name: Discounting
concepts.summary: Discounting is the practice of assigning lower present value to benefits or costs that occur later.
concepts.body:
Discounting is the practice of assigning lower present value to benefits or costs that occur later. A discount rate represents the relative weight given to future outcomes in an evaluation.

A project that costs money now but yields benefits decades later may compare those future benefits at a lower present value. Discounting can reflect opportunity cost or time preference, but the chosen rate strongly affects long-term projects and intergenerational judgments.

examples.text: A policy analyst may value a benefit received in twenty years less than the same benefit received today.
examples.note: It fits because temporal distance changes the value assigned to outcomes.

commonMisreadings: Discounting is not the same as ignoring future generations, although high rates can have that effect.

concepts.name: Discourse
concepts.summary: Discourse is an organized use of language or communication that shapes how a subject is understood and discussed.
concepts.body:
Discourse is an organized use of language or communication that shapes how a subject is understood and discussed. In social theory, discourse can include institutions, practices, categories, and accepted ways of speaking.

The way a society talks about illness can shape which experiences count as symptoms and who is treated as an authority. Discourse includes patterned language and practices, but it does not follow that material conditions are only words.

examples.text: Medical discourse can define which conditions count as illness and which treatments are considered legitimate.
examples.note: It fits because meaning is produced through structured patterns of communication.

commonMisreadings: Discourse is broader than a single conversation or speech.

concepts.name: Discourse ethics
concepts.summary: Discourse ethics is the theory that valid moral norms must be justifiable to all affected participants in free and noncoercive practical discourse.
concepts.body:
Discourse ethics is the theory that valid moral norms must be justifiable to all affected participants in free and noncoercive practical discourse. It emphasizes equal participation, reasons that others can accept, and the possibility of challenging claims.

A rule affecting workers would need justification in discussion where those affected could question it without coercion. The theory makes inclusion and reason-giving central, while critics ask whether ideal conditions can be achieved and how urgent decisions proceed.

examples.text: A law has discourse-ethical support when affected citizens can contest it under fair deliberative conditions.
examples.note: It fits because moral validity is tied to communicative justification.

commonMisreadings: It is not the rule that whatever people happen to agree on is automatically moral.

concepts.name: Discourse theory
concepts.summary: Discourse theory is a social and political approach that studies how language, communication, and shared meaning structure knowledge, identity, and power.
concepts.body:
Discourse theory is a social and political approach that studies how language, communication, and shared meaning structure knowledge, identity, and power. It examines how categories and institutions are produced and maintained through communicative practices.

A discourse-theoretical analysis might trace how official categories shape who can speak credibly about a policy. Different theories emphasize communication, institutions, or power, and their claims should not be conflated into the idea that language alone creates every social fact.

examples.text: A discourse theorist may analyze how the term security frames migration as a threat and enables exceptional policies.
examples.note: It fits because discursive practices are treated as constitutive of social understanding.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely the study of grammar or formal speech patterns.

concepts.name: Disjunction
concepts.summary: A disjunction is a compound proposition formed by joining alternatives with or.
concepts.body:
A disjunction is a compound proposition formed by joining alternatives with or. In inclusive logic, P or Q is true when at least one of P and Q is true.

“The key is in the drawer or in the bag” asserts at least one alternative in inclusive logic, though everyday “or” can suggest exclusivity. Formal reasoning must state which meaning is intended because the alternatives affect what follows.

examples.text: The statement The package is at home or at work is true if either location, or both, satisfies the alternatives.
examples.note: It fits because alternatives are combined into one logical proposition.

commonMisreadings: A disjunction need not be exclusive, since ordinary or can allow both alternatives.

concepts.name: Disjunctive syllogism
concepts.summary: Disjunctive syllogism is the inference form from P or Q and not P to Q.
concepts.body:
Disjunctive syllogism is the inference form from P or Q and not P to Q. Its validity depends on the disjunction and negation applying to the same alternatives.

From “the package is at the office or at home” and “it is not at the office,” one can infer that it is at home, assuming the alternatives are exhaustive. The inference form is valid, but a false or incomplete disjunction can mislead.

examples.text: From The key is in the drawer or the bag and not in the drawer, one may infer that it is in the bag.
examples.note: It fits because eliminating one disjunct leaves the other.

commonMisreadings: It is not valid when or is being used with an unrelated ambiguity or when both alternatives can be false.

concepts.name: Disposition
concepts.summary: A disposition is a stable tendency or capacity of an object or person to behave or react in a certain way under suitable conditions.
concepts.body:
A disposition is a stable tendency or capacity of an object or person to behave or react in a certain way under suitable conditions. Dispositions can exist even when they are not currently manifested.

Glass is fragile because it tends to break under certain impacts, even when it is currently intact. A disposition can exist without being manifested, and its triggering conditions may be more complex than a simple stimulus-response pair.

examples.text: A fragile glass has a disposition to shatter when struck with sufficient force.
examples.note: It fits because the concept describes conditional powers rather than only actual events.

commonMisreadings: A disposition is not identical to an occurrence, since the glass can remain unbroken while fragile.

concepts.name: Distinction making
concepts.summary: Distinction making separates senses or cases whose differences matter to an argument.
concepts.body:
Distinction making separates senses or cases whose differences matter to an argument. A useful distinction identifies a relevant difference and explains why it changes the conclusion. Merely assigning different labels does not show that two cases deserve different treatment.

Separating legal permission from moral justification can expose why “it is allowed” does not settle whether an action is right. A useful distinction tracks a real difference in the question; excessive distinctions can obscure rather than clarify.

examples.text: Separate explaining why a person acted from justifying the action as morally acceptable.
examples.note: Causal explanation and moral justification answer different questions.

commonMisreadings: Making a distinction does not by itself prove that the distinction matters.

concepts.name: Distributism
concepts.summary: Distributism is an economic view favoring widespread private ownership of productive property among families and small associations.
concepts.body:
Distributism is an economic view favoring widespread private ownership of productive property among families and small associations. It criticizes both concentrated capitalism and centralized state ownership.
