A distributist proposal would spread ownership of farms, workshops, or businesses across many households instead of concentrating it in a few corporations or the state. It favors broad property ownership, not equal wealth in every respect, and critics question its scalability in modern economies.

examples.text: A distributist policy might support small farms, worker cooperatives, and limits on monopolistic landholding.
examples.note: It fits because ownership distribution, rather than only income redistribution, is central.

commonMisreadings: Distributism is not socialism, since it generally preserves private property.

concepts.name: Distributive justice
concepts.summary: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of benefits, burdens, opportunities, and resources among members of a society.
concepts.body:
Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of benefits, burdens, opportunities, and resources among members of a society. Theories of distributive justice differ over whether allocation should track equality, need, desert, contribution, or priority to the worst off.

A fair allocation of medical care might prioritize urgency, equal access, or expected benefit, each producing different choices. Distributive justice asks which principles should govern and how they treat inequality, need, contribution, and historical disadvantage.

examples.text: A tax system can be evaluated for whether it distributes public burdens fairly across income groups.
examples.note: It fits because it addresses who should receive or bear what.

commonMisreadings: Distributive justice is not identical to corrective justice, which addresses repair after a wrong.

concepts.name: Divine command theory
concepts.summary: Divine command theory holds that moral obligations are grounded in the commands of God or a divine authority.
concepts.body:
Divine command theory holds that moral obligations are grounded in the commands of God or a divine authority. On many versions, an action is obligatory because God commands it and wrong because God forbids it.

If an act is obligatory because God commands it, divine-command theory grounds duty in divine authority. Critics ask whether commands make actions good arbitrarily or reflect an independent goodness; religious versions answer this dilemma in different ways.

examples.text: A believer who grounds a duty to give charity in a divine command uses this theory.
examples.note: It fits because divine authority supplies the source of moral requirement.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply the view that God knows moral truths, since knowledge does not itself ground obligation.

concepts.name: Divine foreknowledge
concepts.summary: Divine foreknowledge is the doctrine that God knows in advance all future events, including future human actions.
concepts.body:
Divine foreknowledge is the doctrine that God knows in advance all future events, including future human actions. It creates a philosophical problem about how exhaustive knowledge can coexist with human freedom and alternative possibilities.

If God infallibly knows tomorrow's choice, a question arises about whether the agent could choose otherwise. Theological accounts distinguish certainty from causal determination or use different views of time and knowledge; the tension has no universally accepted resolution.

examples.text: If God infallibly knows tomorrow's choice, philosophers ask whether the agent could choose differently.
examples.note: It fits because complete prior divine knowledge is the defining claim.

commonMisreadings: Foreknowledge is not the same as predestination, which concerns divine determination rather than knowledge alone.

concepts.name: Divine simplicity
concepts.summary: Divine simplicity is the theological doctrine that God has no distinct parts or separable properties and is not composed of act and potentiality.
concepts.body:
Divine simplicity is the theological doctrine that God has no distinct parts or separable properties and is not composed of act and potentiality. Classical versions identify God's attributes with one another and with God's being.

On divine simplicity, God's goodness is not one separable feature alongside existence and power; God is not composed of independent parts or properties. The doctrine aims to preserve divine unity, while critics question how it can make sense of distinct descriptions and relations.

examples.text: On a strong doctrine of simplicity, God's goodness is not an added feature but is identical with the divine essence.
examples.note: It fits because it denies metaphysical composition in God.

commonMisreadings: Simplicity does not mean that God is uncomplicated in the ordinary psychological sense.

concepts.name: Doctrine of double effect
concepts.summary: The doctrine of double effect holds that an action with both a foreseen good effect and a foreseen bad effect can be permissible under specified conditions.
concepts.body:
The doctrine of double effect holds that an action with both a foreseen good effect and a foreseen bad effect can be permissible under specified conditions. Typical conditions distinguish the intended effect from the merely foreseen harmful effect and require proportionality.

A surgeon may foresee a harmful side effect while intending a therapeutic benefit, and the doctrine asks whether the harm is intended as a means or merely foreseen. Permissibility also depends on proportionality and alternatives; application is disputed and sensitive to the case details.

examples.text: Administering high-dose pain relief that foreseeably shortens life may be defended when relieving severe pain is intended and proportionate.
examples.note: It fits because moral evaluation turns partly on intention and side effects.

commonMisreadings: It does not permit any harmful means merely because a good consequence is also expected.

concepts.name: Dogmatism
concepts.summary: Dogmatism is unjustified confidence in a belief or doctrine combined with resistance to relevant criticism or evidence.
concepts.body:
Dogmatism is unjustified confidence in a belief or doctrine combined with resistance to relevant criticism or evidence. Dogmatic commitment can occur in religious, political, scientific, or everyday contexts.

A person is dogmatic when they treat a belief as beyond challenge despite relevant counterevidence or criticism. Firm conviction alone is not dogmatism; the key issue is whether confidence is responsive to reasons and open to correction.

examples.text: A person who refuses to examine contrary evidence because a claim is declared unquestionable is dogmatic.
examples.note: It fits because uncritical certainty and closed inquiry define the attitude.

commonMisreadings: Dogmatism is not the same as holding a firm belief supported by strong evidence.

concepts.name: Doing and allowing
concepts.summary: The doing-and-allowing distinction separates actively causing a harm from permitting a harm to occur by failing to intervene.
concepts.body:
The doing-and-allowing distinction separates actively causing a harm from permitting a harm to occur by failing to intervene. Some moral theories judge doing harm more strictly than allowing comparable harm, while others reject that distinction.

Cutting a rope that supports someone differs intuitively from failing to throw a rope, even if the outcome is similar. Moral theories dispute when this distinction matters, and omission can itself be culpable when there is a duty to help.

examples.text: Pushing a person into danger is doing harm, whereas refusing to rescue may be allowing harm.
examples.note: It fits because the concept classifies moral cases by the agent's causal involvement.

commonMisreadings: Allowing is not always morally neutral, especially when the agent has a duty to rescue.

concepts.name: Domain of discourse
concepts.summary: The domain of discourse is the set of objects or values that a formal statement or discussion treats as its possible subjects.
concepts.body:
The domain of discourse is the set of objects or values that a formal statement or discussion treats as its possible subjects. Quantifiers range over the domain fixed by the interpretation or conversational context.

In a logic exercise about prime numbers below ten, the domain contains only the numbers 2, 3, 5, and 7. Quantified claims can change truth when the domain changes, so its boundaries must be made clear.

examples.text: In a discussion restricted to integers, the domain excludes noninteger real numbers.
examples.note: It fits because it specifies what the variables and claims are about.

commonMisreadings: The domain of discourse is not necessarily the whole universe of everything that exists.

concepts.name: Dominant strategy
concepts.summary: A dominant strategy is an action that gives a player at least as good an outcome as every alternative for every possible action by others, and a better outcome in some case.
concepts.body:
A dominant strategy is an action that gives a player at least as good an outcome as every alternative for every possible action by others, and a better outcome in some case. Choosing it does not require predicting what other players will do.

If a company earns more by lowering its price whether its rival keeps or cuts price, lowering is dominant for that company in the model. Real decisions rarely have fully known payoffs, and a dominant strategy need not produce the best joint outcome.

examples.text: In a prisoner's dilemma, confessing is dominant when it yields a better result regardless of the other prisoner's choice.
examples.note: It fits because the strategy is superior or equal across all responses by others.

commonMisreadings: A dominant strategy is not merely the strategy with the highest expected payoff under one probability estimate.

concepts.name: Domination
concepts.summary: Domination is a condition in which one person or group has the power to interfere arbitrarily with another's choices or standing.
concepts.body:
Domination is a condition in which one person or group has the power to interfere arbitrarily with another's choices or standing. Republican theories of freedom define domination by dependence on uncontrolled power, even when interference does not occur.

A landlord who can arbitrarily evict tenants may dominate them even if the power is rarely exercised, because their choices depend on unchecked discretion. Republican theories emphasize this standing power; not every influence or interference qualifies as domination.

examples.text: A worker dependent on an employer who can arbitrarily withhold essential housing is dominated by that power.
examples.note: It fits because vulnerability to arbitrary control, not only actual coercion, is central.

commonMisreadings: Domination is not identical to any unequal outcome, since inequality can exist without arbitrary power.

concepts.name: Double consciousness
concepts.summary: W. E. B. Du Bois's account of experiencing oneself through one's own identity and through the hostile or distorting gaze of a dominant society.
concepts.body:
Du Bois describes double consciousness as the experience of seeing oneself through one's own standpoint and through the eyes of a dominant society that marks Blackness as a problem. The resulting self-monitoring is not a split personality. It is a social contradiction: one must develop a self while negotiating an imposed image, measuring how one's actions will be interpreted and whether a stereotype will be projected onto the whole group.

The concept explains both injury and insight. The dominant gaze can produce exhaustion, shame, and constrained action, but navigating incompatible standards can also yield a critical view of the society that imposes them. It should not be universalized into one experience of all racialized people; gender, class, nation, colorism, and historical context alter the forms the contradiction takes.

examples.text: A Black student excels in a classroom while continually calculating whether a mistake will be read as evidence about the whole group.
examples.note: The example shows self-monitoring under a stereotype rather than ordinary awareness of an audience.

commonMisreadings: Double consciousness is not a claim that Black people lack an authentic self or possess a clinical disorder.
It is not simply code-switching, although language and presentation can be sites where the imposed double perspective appears.
criticisms: Critics note that the concept can be generalized too broadly and that gender, class, sexuality, and national location shape racialized self-perception differently.

lookalikes.note: Both describe divided experience, but double consciousness specifically concerns racialized selfhood under an external dominant gaze.

concepts.name: Double negation
concepts.summary: Double negation is the logical relation in which negating a negation returns a proposition in classical logic.
concepts.body:
Double negation is the logical relation in which negating a negation returns a proposition in classical logic. The classical equivalence is not not P if and only if P.

In classical logic, “it is not true that the alarm did not ring” is equivalent to “the alarm rang.” Some nonclassical logics handle negation differently, so the equivalence depends on the logical system.

examples.text: From It is not the case that the switch is not on, one may infer that the switch is on in classical logic.
examples.note: It fits because two negations cancel under the relevant logical rules.

commonMisreadings: Double negation elimination is not accepted in the same form by intuitionistic logic as a general inference.

concepts.name: Drowning child
concepts.summary: The drowning child is a thought experiment in which a person can save a drowning child at a small personal cost but chooses not to do so.
concepts.body:
The drowning child is a thought experiment in which a person can save a drowning child at a small personal cost but chooses not to do so. Peter Singer uses it to argue that people should prevent serious suffering when they can do so without sacrificing something of comparable moral importance.

The case asks whether one should ruin an expensive suit to save a child in a shallow pond, then compares that small cost with distant preventable deaths. It makes moral demands vivid, but analogies to aid and rescue differ in efficacy, obligation, and institutional context.

examples.text: Walking around a shallow pond to save a child while ruining inexpensive clothing illustrates the case.
examples.note: It fits because the example tests the moral significance of proximity and small personal sacrifice.

commonMisreadings: The thought experiment does not by itself settle every question about demandingness or institutional responsibility.

concepts.name: Dual-aspect theory
concepts.summary: Dual-aspect theory holds that mental and physical descriptions are two aspects of one underlying reality rather than two separate substances.
concepts.body:
Dual-aspect theory holds that mental and physical descriptions are two aspects of one underlying reality rather than two separate substances. It seeks to avoid both reduction of mind to matter and interaction between independent substances.

A dual-aspect theorist may describe one event as neural activity from a physical perspective and as experience from a mental perspective. The view avoids two separate substances but must explain what the underlying reality is and why its aspects correlate.

examples.text: A single event can be described neurally as brain activity and experientially as a pain.
examples.note: It fits because one reality is approached through distinct mental and physical aspects.

commonMisreadings: It is not property dualism if it treats the aspects as descriptions rather than separate fundamental properties.

concepts.name: Dual-process theory
concepts.summary: Dual-process theory proposes that cognition involves at least two interacting modes, one fast and automatic and another slower and more controlled.
concepts.body:
Dual-process theory proposes that cognition involves at least two interacting modes, one fast and automatic and another slower and more controlled. The fast mode uses learned associations, while the slower mode can monitor and revise intuitive responses.

A driver may react automatically to a sudden obstacle, then deliberately reason through a complex route choice. The two-mode framework is a useful broad model, not a claim that the brain contains exactly two systems or that fast thinking is always biased.

examples.text: Recognizing a familiar face is typically rapid, whereas checking a difficult calculation requires deliberate reasoning.
examples.note: It fits because distinct processing modes explain differences in speed and control.

commonMisreadings: It does not imply that all thinking cleanly belongs to exactly two isolated systems.

concepts.name: Dualism
concepts.summary: Dualism is the view that reality or a particular domain contains two fundamentally distinct kinds or principles.
concepts.body:
Dualism is the view that reality or a particular domain contains two fundamentally distinct kinds or principles. In philosophy of mind, substance dualism holds that mind and body are different substances.

Mind-body dualism distinguishes mental from physical reality, while other forms of dualism divide a domain along different basic principles. The term alone does not specify which two kinds are fundamental or how they interact.

examples.text: A Cartesian dualist treats thinking mind and extended matter as fundamentally different types of substance.
examples.note: It fits because irreducible twofold structure is the defining commitment.

commonMisreadings: Dualism is not always substance dualism, since it can concern properties, values, or cosmic principles.

concepts.name: Duck test
concepts.summary: The duck test identifies something by whether its observable behavior resembles the kind of thing it is claimed to be.
concepts.body:
The duck test identifies something by whether its observable behavior resembles the kind of thing it is claimed to be. It is an abductive heuristic, not deductive proof.

If a system repeatedly behaves like a database and supports database operations, the duck test suggests classifying it by those observable features. The test is a heuristic, not a proof: similar behavior can have different underlying mechanisms or important hidden differences.

examples.text: A bird that swims, walks, and quacks like a duck is treated as a duck.
examples.note: Several characteristic behaviors jointly support the classification.

commonMisreadings: Resemblance alone does not establish biological identity.

concepts.name: Duhem–Quine thesis
concepts.summary: The Duhem–Quine thesis says a scientific hypothesis is tested with auxiliary assumptions and background conditions.
concepts.body:
The Duhem–Quine thesis says a scientific hypothesis is tested with auxiliary assumptions and background conditions. A failed prediction does not uniquely identify which assumption is false.

A failed prediction may challenge a theory, but the test also relies on assumptions about instruments, initial conditions, and calculations. Scientists can revise any part of this network, so evidence rarely identifies a single falsified claim without further judgment.

examples.text: An unexpected orbit could reflect faulty gravity theory or instrument calibration.
examples.note: The observation tests a network rather than one isolated claim.

commonMisreadings: It does not make scientific rejection impossible.

concepts.name: Dukkha
concepts.summary: Dukkha is Buddhist suffering, unsatisfactoriness, and instability in conditioned experience.
concepts.body:
Dukkha is Buddhist suffering, unsatisfactoriness, and instability in conditioned experience. It includes pain and frustration caused by attachment to changing things.

A pleasant meal can still be dukkha in the broader Buddhist sense if it is impermanent and cannot provide lasting security. The term includes suffering and unsatisfactoriness, not only acute pain, and its interpretation varies across Buddhist traditions.

examples.text: A new phone’s pleasure becomes anxiety when its owner fears losing it.
examples.note: Impermanence makes satisfaction vulnerable to distress.

commonMisreadings: Dukkha does not mean every moment is equally miserable.

concepts.name: Dunning–Kruger effect
concepts.summary: The Dunning–Kruger effect is impaired self-assessment caused by limited competence in a domain.
concepts.body:
The Dunning–Kruger effect is impaired self-assessment caused by limited competence in a domain. It concerns metacognitive calibration rather than universal arrogance.

A novice may lack the skills needed to spot errors in their own work and therefore rate it too highly. Research on this effect is more nuanced than the popular claim that the least competent always feel most confident; measurement and domain matter.

examples.text: A novice programmer judges flawed code correct because they cannot detect its errors.
examples.note: The missing skill prevents accurate evaluation.

commonMisreadings: It does not affect every domain or every inexperienced person.

concepts.name: Duty
concepts.summary: A duty is an obligation giving an agent a reason to act or refrain from acting.
concepts.body:
A duty is an obligation giving an agent a reason to act or refrain from acting. Duties can arise from promises, roles, laws, relationships, or principles.

A promise can create a duty to arrive at an agreed time even when doing so becomes inconvenient. Duties may arise from roles, rules, relationships, or moral principles and can conflict, requiring an account of priority and exceptions.

examples.text: A lifeguard has a duty to respond to a drowning swimmer.
examples.note: The entrusted professional role creates the obligation.

commonMisreadings: A duty is not merely a preferred action.

concepts.name: Dvaita Vedanta
concepts.summary: Dvaita Vedanta, founded by Madhva, holds that God, souls, and matter are really distinct.
concepts.body:
Dvaita Vedanta, founded by Madhva, holds that God, souls, and matter are really distinct. It identifies Vishnu as supreme and liberation as dependence on divine grace without identity with God.

Dvaita Vedanta maintains an enduring distinction between God, individual souls, and matter, with souls dependent on God. It is one school within Vedanta and contrasts with nondual interpretations; its terms and arguments belong to a specific theological setting.

examples.text: A liberated soul worships Vishnu while remaining distinct from him.
examples.note: The worship relation depends on real difference.

commonMisreadings: Dvaita is not Advaita nondualism.

concepts.name: Eclecticism
concepts.summary: Eclecticism combines doctrines or methods from different traditions according to perceived merits.
concepts.body:
Eclecticism combines doctrines or methods from different traditions according to perceived merits. An eclectic position need not accept every borrowed element.

A thinker may combine one tradition's account of virtue with another's method for analyzing institutions because each addresses a different problem. Eclecticism can be selective and reasoned, but without an account of compatibility it risks assembling claims that conflict.

examples.text: A therapist combines cognitive-behavioral, mindfulness, and family-systems techniques.
examples.note: Different tools are selected for complementary purposes.

commonMisreadings: Eclecticism is not indiscriminate mixing.

concepts.name: Eco-anarchism
concepts.summary: Eco-anarchism links ecological protection with decentralized, non-hierarchical social organization.
concepts.body:
Eco-anarchism links ecological protection with decentralized, non-hierarchical social organization. It commonly criticizes state domination and resource systems that treat nature as unlimited.

An eco-anarchist community might manage forests through local cooperation and shared limits rather than centralized state command or private extraction. The approach links ecological care to opposition to hierarchy, while questions remain about large-scale coordination and accountability.

examples.text: Self-governing communities might manage a watershed through shared ecological rules.
examples.note: Local autonomy and ecological interdependence are combined.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply every environmental movement opposing government.

concepts.name: Eco-socialism
concepts.summary: Eco-socialism combines socialist criticism of capitalism with ecological criticism of profit-driven growth.
concepts.body:
Eco-socialism combines socialist criticism of capitalism with ecological criticism of profit-driven growth. It argues that democratic control of production can prevent systematic ecological destruction.

An eco-socialist may argue that firms' pressure to expand production for profit contributes to resource depletion and emissions. Proposed alternatives vary, and ecological limits alone do not determine how ownership or democratic decision-making should be organized.

examples.text: A publicly governed energy system could replace fossil-fuel profits with planned renewable transition.
examples.note: Ownership and production decisions are linked to environmental limits.

commonMisreadings: It differs from environmental reform preserving capitalist ownership.

concepts.name: Ecofeminism
concepts.summary: Ecofeminism examines connections between women’s oppression and domination of nature.
concepts.body:
Ecofeminism examines connections between women’s oppression and domination of nature. Theories explain those connections through culture, social structure, or political economy.

An ecofeminist analysis may connect the devaluation of care work with practices that treat land and animals as resources to control. Ecofeminist theories differ, and the connection should be explained through specific institutions rather than assumed as a universal link between women and nature.

examples.text: Plantation analysis may connect gendered labor exploitation with deforestation.
examples.note: One economic arrangement burdens people and ecosystems together.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim women are naturally closer to nature.

concepts.name: Ecological rationality
concepts.summary: Ecological rationality means a decision rule fits the structure of the environment where it operates.
concepts.body:
Ecological rationality means a decision rule fits the structure of the environment where it operates. Simple heuristics can outperform complex methods when they exploit reliable environmental regularities.

A simple rule such as “choose the familiar route” can work well in a stable neighborhood but fail in a city where roads change often. Ecological rationality evaluates a strategy against the environment's structure, not against an abstract ideal of unlimited calculation.

examples.text: Familiarity may help choose the larger of two unknown cities.
examples.note: The environmental cue correlates with city size in that setting.

commonMisreadings: It does not make every instinct rational.

concepts.name: Economic justice
concepts.summary: Economic justice concerns fair distribution and exercise of resources, opportunities, and economic burdens.
concepts.body:
Economic justice concerns fair distribution and exercise of resources, opportunities, and economic burdens. It can involve wages, property, taxation, necessities, and decision-making power.

A policy can raise average income yet leave some workers without safe conditions or a fair share of gains, raising questions of economic justice. The concept covers distribution, opportunity, power, and procedure, and theories disagree about which should take priority.

examples.text: A progressive tax funding universal healthcare is defended as economically just.
examples.note: It combines access to care with unequal capacity to pay.

commonMisreadings: It does not require identical incomes.

concepts.name: Effective altruism
concepts.summary: Effective altruism uses evidence and reason to choose actions producing the most good with available resources.
concepts.body:
Effective altruism uses evidence and reason to choose actions producing the most good with available resources. It often compares impact, neglectedness, and cost-effectiveness.

An effective altruist might compare charities by evidence about how much preventable illness each dollar reduces. The approach emphasizes impact and revisability, while critics question how to compare unlike goods, account for systemic change, and avoid neglecting duties or relationships.

examples.text: A donor funds malaria nets after evidence shows they prevent illness cheaply.
examples.note: Estimated outcomes guide the choice more than emotional vividness.

commonMisreadings: It does not require one fixed charity or total self-sacrifice.

concepts.name: Egalitarianism
concepts.summary: Egalitarianism holds that people should be equal in a morally significant respect.
concepts.body:
Egalitarianism holds that people should be equal in a morally significant respect. Versions differ over equality of welfare, resources, opportunity, status, or power.

An egalitarian may argue that everyone should have equal legal status while allowing differences in income based on choice or contribution. Egalitarian views specify the relevant equality; they do not all demand identical outcomes in every respect.

examples.text: Equal voting rights provide equal formal political influence.
examples.note: The specified political dimension is equalized.

commonMisreadings: It need not demand identical outcomes everywhere.

concepts.name: Ego depletion
concepts.summary: Ego-depletion theory proposed that prior self-control temporarily reduces later self-control capacity.
concepts.body:
Ego-depletion theory proposed that prior self-control temporarily reduces later self-control capacity. Its original resource model has faced major replication and measurement challenges.

The classic ego-depletion hypothesis predicted that resisting one temptation would leave less capacity for a later self-control task. Replication results and measurement choices have challenged the effect's robustness, so it should be described as a debated hypothesis rather than settled fact.

examples.text: Researchers test whether resisting food affects persistence on a tedious task.
examples.note: The tasks examine transfer of regulatory fatigue.

commonMisreadings: Ego depletion is not an established finite mental fuel.

concepts.name: Eleatic philosophy
concepts.summary: Eleatic philosophy, associated with Parmenides, emphasizes the unity and stability of being.
concepts.body:
Eleatic philosophy, associated with Parmenides, emphasizes the unity and stability of being. Its arguments challenge the coherence of change, plurality, and coming into existence.

Parmenides argued that genuine being cannot come from nonbeing, leading toward a stark challenge to ordinary talk of change. Later Eleatic thinkers developed arguments about motion and plurality; the school is historically varied and not simply the claim that nothing changes.

examples.text: Zeno’s motion paradoxes involve infinitely divisible distances.
examples.note: They challenge ordinary assumptions about motion.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely abstract reasoning.

concepts.name: Eliminative materialism
concepts.summary: Eliminative materialism says mature neuroscience may eliminate common-sense psychological categories.
concepts.body:
Eliminative materialism says mature neuroscience may eliminate common-sense psychological categories. Beliefs or desires could resemble obsolete scientific entities rather than reduce to neural facts.

An eliminativist expects neuroscience to replace some everyday categories, perhaps by showing that familiar beliefs about memory or desire divide mental processes poorly. The view targets theories, not the existence of experience, and critics ask whether ordinary psychological concepts can be discarded so radically.

examples.text: An eliminativist may expect neuroscience to replace belief with another neural taxonomy.
examples.note: The ordinary category need not map onto a real kind.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than physical reductionism.

concepts.name: Emancipation
concepts.summary: Emancipation is release from a legal, political, social, or economic condition of domination.
concepts.body:
Emancipation is release from a legal, political, social, or economic condition of domination. It can mean formal liberation and practical capacity to use freedom.

Ending a legal status that permits forced labor is one form of emancipation, while lasting freedom may also require access to land, education, and political power. The term can name a process or an achieved condition, and formal release may leave other structures intact.

examples.text: The Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in specified rebellious areas free.
examples.note: It legally attacked a status of coerced ownership.

commonMisreadings: It does not automatically remove later inequality.

concepts.name: Embodied cognition
concepts.summary: Embodied cognition holds that thought is shaped by bodily, sensory, motor, and environmental interaction.
concepts.body:
Embodied cognition holds that thought is shaped by bodily, sensory, motor, and environmental interaction. It rejects explaining cognition solely as detached brain computation.

A person solving a spatial problem may use gestures and move objects, with bodily action helping structure thought. Embodied cognition ranges from modest claims about bodily influence to stronger claims that cognition extends into environment; evidence for one version does not establish them all.

examples.text: Learning bicycle balance involves continuous corrective movements.
examples.note: The skill is enacted through bodily action and feedback.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny neural involvement.

concepts.name: Emergence
concepts.summary: Emergence is the appearance of system-level patterns arising from component interactions.
concepts.body:
Emergence is the appearance of system-level patterns arising from component interactions. An emergent property depends on parts without belonging to one part alone.

A flock's coordinated shape can arise from each bird following local rules without any bird planning the whole pattern. Emergent behavior depends on interactions and can be surprising, but “emergent” alone does not explain the mechanism or show that higher-level laws are irreducible.

examples.text: A fish school’s spiral arises from local spacing and alignment behaviors.
examples.note: No individual fish has the collective formation as its property.

commonMisreadings: Emergence need not be supernatural.

concepts.name: Emergentism
concepts.summary: Emergentism says organized physical systems can have novel properties requiring higher-level concepts.
concepts.body:
Emergentism says organized physical systems can have novel properties requiring higher-level concepts. Some emergentists assign higher-level properties new causal powers; others claim only explanatory novelty.

An emergentist may hold that consciousness depends on brain organization but has features that cannot be captured by describing neurons individually. The position preserves physical dependence while debating whether higher-level properties have distinct causal powers or explanatory status.

examples.text: Life processes may be emergent from biochemical organization.
examples.note: Organization creates a level not captured by listing molecules.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to mystery.

concepts.name: Emotivism
concepts.summary: Emotivism says moral judgments express attitudes or emotions rather than report objective moral facts.
concepts.body:
Emotivism says moral judgments express attitudes or emotions rather than report objective moral facts. “Stealing is wrong” functions like disapproval or a directive on a classic version.

On an emotivist account, saying “cruelty is wrong” expresses condemnation and may encourage others to share it rather than report a moral property. The view explains some practical force of moral language, but must also account for moral disagreement and reasoning.

examples.text: “Do not steal” expresses condemnation and seeks to influence conduct.
examples.note: The utterance performs a motivational function.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely the claim that emotion affects morality.

concepts.name: Empiricism
concepts.summary: Empiricism holds that experience, especially sensory experience, fundamentally contributes to knowledge or justification.
concepts.body:
Empiricism holds that experience, especially sensory experience, fundamentally contributes to knowledge or justification. Empiricists may use reasoning while rejecting substantial innate knowledge.

An empiricist points to observation and experiment as central sources of knowledge about whether a metal expands when heated. Empiricists disagree about the role of innate structures and reasoning, and experience alone may not settle abstract or necessary truths.

examples.text: A scientist accepts a reaction claim after controlled observations support it.
examples.note: Experience supplies evidence beyond deduction.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean trusting every personal impression.

concepts.name: Enactivism
concepts.summary: Enactivism says cognition arises through active organism-environment engagement, not passive internal representation alone.
concepts.body:
Enactivism says cognition arises through active organism-environment engagement, not passive internal representation alone. It emphasizes sensorimotor skill, autonomy, and mutual shaping.

A person learns to navigate by moving through a space and adjusting to what their actions make available, rather than building a complete inner map first. Enactivist theories vary, and they need not deny internal processes or representations in every form.

examples.text: Bicycle balance is learned through ongoing action and changing feedback.
examples.note: The skill exists in agent-environment coupling.

commonMisreadings: It does not exclude the brain.

concepts.name: End-of-history illusion
concepts.summary: The end-of-history illusion is underestimating future change in one’s preferences, values, or personality.
concepts.body:
The end-of-history illusion is underestimating future change in one’s preferences, values, or personality. People recognize past change while treating the present self as nearly complete.

A person may expect to change little after age thirty while recognizing that they changed greatly during the previous decade. The effect concerns judgments about future personal change, not a claim that people stop changing; forecasts may be affected by memory and uncertainty.

examples.text: A twenty-year-old predicts identical musical tastes at forty.
examples.note: The prediction ignores earlier transformations.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim people stop changing at a particular age.

concepts.name: Endurantism
concepts.summary: Endurantism says an object is wholly present at every time at which it exists.
concepts.body:
Endurantism says an object is wholly present at every time at which it exists. It contrasts with perdurantism, which treats objects as temporal parts.

An endurantist says the child and adult are the same person wholly present at different times, despite changes in height and beliefs. This account contrasts with views that objects have different temporal parts; puzzles about change and persistence motivate both sides.

examples.text: The same tree is wholly present as sapling and mature tree.
examples.note: Persistence consists in complete presence at each time.

commonMisreadings: It allows different properties at different times.

concepts.name: Engaged Buddhism
concepts.summary: Engaged Buddhism applies Buddhist compassion and contemplation to social, political, and environmental suffering.
concepts.body:
Engaged Buddhism applies Buddhist compassion and contemplation to social, political, and environmental suffering. It treats collective action as compatible with personal spiritual cultivation.

An engaged Buddhist group might respond to displacement or environmental harm through relief work and advocacy informed by compassion and non-harming. The tradition applies Buddhist practice to public problems, but participants disagree about strategy and how to balance action with contemplative practice.

examples.text: Buddhists organizing nonviolent refugee relief practice engaged Buddhism.
examples.note: The practice addresses suffering beyond private meditation.

commonMisreadings: It does not say meditation is unnecessary.

concepts.name: Entailment
concepts.summary: Entailment holds when truth of one proposition guarantees truth of another under relevant interpretation.
concepts.body:
Entailment holds when truth of one proposition guarantees truth of another under relevant interpretation. The first proposition cannot be true while the entailed proposition is false.

“The number is divisible by four” entails “the number is even” under the usual arithmetic interpretation. Entailment is stronger than evidence or implication in casual speech: it means no relevant interpretation makes the first true and the second false.

examples.text: “Every raven is a bird” entails “Every raven is an animal.”
examples.note: Raven membership guarantees animal membership.

commonMisreadings: Entailment is stronger than probability.

concepts.name: Environmental ethics
concepts.summary: Environmental ethics studies moral status and obligations concerning nature, organisms, ecosystems, and nonhuman entities.
concepts.body:
Environmental ethics studies moral status and obligations concerning nature, organisms, ecosystems, and nonhuman entities. It asks whether value extends beyond human welfare.

A proposal to protect a wetland may weigh human livelihoods alongside the standing of species and ecosystems themselves. Environmental ethics asks what has moral value and what duties follow; different theories assign weight to individuals, species, systems, or future generations.

examples.text: A forest may be protected because it has value beyond timber.
examples.note: The justification assigns moral significance to an ecosystem.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than pollution policy.

concepts.name: Environmentalism
concepts.summary: Environmentalism is a movement seeking ecological protection and reduced environmental harm.
concepts.body:
Environmentalism is a movement seeking ecological protection and reduced environmental harm. Its approaches include conservation, regulation, restoration, activism, and changed consumption.

An environmental campaign may seek cleaner air by limiting pollutants and expanding public transport. Environmentalism includes diverse priorities and methods, and a policy's ecological benefit must be assessed alongside its social effects and implementation.

examples.text: A campaign for lower industrial sulfur emissions is environmentalist.
examples.note: It aims to reduce pollutant damage.

commonMisreadings: It is not one single political theory.

concepts.name: Epicureanism
concepts.summary: Epicureanism teaches that prudent pleasure, friendship, and freedom from irrational fear produce tranquility.
concepts.body:
Epicureanism teaches that prudent pleasure, friendship, and freedom from irrational fear produce tranquility. It values simple stable pleasure and absence of disturbance.

An Epicurean may choose a modest meal and friendship over luxury because stable pleasure and freedom from needless fear matter more than excess. Epicureanism is not crude indulgence; its account of pleasure emphasizes tranquility and thoughtful limitation of desire.

examples.text: An Epicurean chooses a modest meal with friends over an anxious lavish feast.
examples.note: The choice favors durable tranquility.

commonMisreadings: It is not unrestricted luxury.

concepts.name: Epiphenomenalism
concepts.summary: Epiphenomenalism says mental events are caused by physical events but do not cause physical events.
concepts.body:
Epiphenomenalism says mental events are caused by physical events but do not cause physical events. Conscious experience accompanies neural processes without altering bodily behavior.

An epiphenomenalist holds that brain activity produces the experience of pain, while the experience itself does not cause withdrawal of the hand. This creates a challenge about how mental states seem to influence speech and action, and whether the view can explain that appearance.

examples.text: Neural circuitry causes withdrawal while pain is merely produced alongside it.
examples.note: The mental episode is an effect, not a physical cause.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny mental-physical correlation.

concepts.name: Epistemic closure
concepts.summary: Epistemic closure is the principle that knowledge of a proposition transfers to propositions known to follow from it.
concepts.body:
Epistemic closure is the principle that knowledge of a proposition transfers to propositions known to follow from it. A common form says knowing p and knowing p entails q yields knowledge of q.

If someone knows a book is on the desk and knows that implies it is in the room, closure suggests they know it is in the room. Skeptical arguments exploit this principle; philosophers debate its scope and whether knowing the implication requires additional conditions.

examples.text: Knowing keys are in a drawer and that this excludes the garden yields knowledge they are not there.
examples.note: A known entailment transmits knowledge.

commonMisreadings: It concerns knowledge, not physical containment.

concepts.name: Epistemic humility
concepts.summary: Epistemic humility is recognizing limits in one’s evidence, competence, and perspective.
concepts.body:
Epistemic humility is recognizing limits in one’s evidence, competence, and perspective. It allows confidence when evidence warrants it and openness to correction.

A careful analyst marks which conclusions are uncertain and seeks expertise outside their own field. Epistemic humility is calibrated recognition of limits, not automatic deference or refusal to reach conclusions when evidence is strong.

examples.text: A surgeon calls a scan inconclusive and requests another test.
examples.note: The confidence level matches the evidence.

commonMisreadings: It is not refusing every belief.

concepts.name: Epistemic injustice
concepts.summary: Epistemic injustice wrongs someone specifically as a knower or contributor to knowledge.
concepts.body:
Epistemic injustice wrongs someone specifically as a knower or contributor to knowledge. Testimonial injustice discounts credibility through prejudice; hermeneutical injustice involves interpretive gaps.

A patient's report may be discounted because a clinician stereotypes them as unreliable, harming their standing as a knower. Other forms arise when shared concepts fail to make an experience intelligible; remedies require attention to credibility and gaps in collective understanding.

examples.text: A patient’s pain report is dismissed because of a group stereotype.
examples.note: Prejudice creates an unfair credibility deficit.

commonMisreadings: It is not every factual mistake.

concepts.name: Epistemic luck
concepts.summary: Epistemic luck is luck affecting truth or justification in a way relevant to knowledge.
concepts.body:
Epistemic luck is luck affecting truth or justification in a way relevant to knowledge. Gettier cases show justified true belief can be true accidentally.

A person glances at a clock that stopped by chance and forms a true belief about the time at the exact moment it stopped. The belief's truth depends on luck in a way that threatens knowledge, though theories differ over which kinds of luck are disqualifying.

examples.text: A person sees the only real barn among many fake façades.
examples.note: The true perception depends on accidental circumstances.

commonMisreadings: It is not any fortunate life event.

concepts.name: Epistemic modality
concepts.summary: Epistemic modality concerns what is possible, necessary, or certain relative to information or knowledge.
concepts.body:
Epistemic modality concerns what is possible, necessary, or certain relative to information or knowledge. It differs from metaphysical modality, which concerns reality’s underlying possibilities.

Before checking the schedule, a traveler may say the train could have left already, meaning the available information does not rule that out. Epistemic possibility is relative to what someone knows and differs from what is metaphysically or physically possible.

examples.text: Current evidence leaves it epistemically possible that a suspect is elsewhere.
examples.note: The claim reports compatibility with evidence.

commonMisreadings: Epistemic possibility is not metaphysical possibility.

concepts.name: Epistemic peerhood
concepts.summary: Epistemic peerhood relates agents comparably competent, informed, and conscientious about a question.
concepts.body:
Epistemic peerhood relates agents comparably competent, informed, and conscientious about a question. Peer disagreement can give reason to reduce confidence.

Two researchers with similar training, access to the same data, and careful methods may count as peers on a particular question. Peerhood is domain-specific and defeasible; credentials alone do not guarantee equal evidence or conscientiousness.

examples.text: Two equally qualified climatologists disagree over a forecast using the same data.
examples.note: Neither has an obvious epistemic advantage.

commonMisreadings: A peer need not equal one in every ability.

concepts.name: Epistemic rationality
concepts.summary: Epistemic rationality forms beliefs in ways responsive to evidence and truth-directed reasons.
concepts.body:
Epistemic rationality forms beliefs in ways responsive to evidence and truth-directed reasons. It differs from instrumental rationality, which concerns achieving goals.

If reliable measurements strongly favor one forecast, an epistemically rational agent updates confidence accordingly rather than preserving a preferred answer unchanged. Rational belief need not guarantee truth, since evidence can be incomplete or misleading.

examples.text: Updating a probability after reliable contrary data is epistemically rational.
examples.note: Evidence rather than convenience drives revision.

commonMisreadings: It does not guarantee truth.

concepts.name: Epistemic relativism
concepts.summary: Epistemic relativism says standards of knowledge or justification vary relative to frameworks, cultures, or conceptual schemes.
concepts.body:
Epistemic relativism says standards of knowledge or justification vary relative to frameworks, cultures, or conceptual schemes. Some versions deny one universally binding epistemic standard.

An epistemic relativist may hold that what counts as justified belief depends on standards internal to a framework. The view faces questions about cross-framework criticism and whether different standards can be compared without assuming a neutral standard.

examples.text: A relativist may say laboratory and oral-tradition communities rank evidence differently.
examples.note: Evaluation depends partly on a social framework.

commonMisreadings: It need not say every belief is equally supported.

concepts.name: Epistemic vigilance
concepts.summary: Epistemic vigilance monitors communicated information for reliability, deception, and relevance.
concepts.body:
Epistemic vigilance monitors communicated information for reliability, deception, and relevance. It checks a speaker’s competence, intentions, and coherence.

A reader checks whether a viral health claim names credible evidence, fits what is known, and comes from a source with relevant expertise. Vigilance helps filter communication but can misfire through excessive distrust or misplaced confidence in familiar sources.

examples.text: A journalist verifies quoted statistics before publication.
examples.note: Verification guards against error and misinformation.

commonMisreadings: It is not automatic distrust.

concepts.name: Epistemology
concepts.summary: Epistemology studies knowledge, belief, justification, evidence, and related concepts.
concepts.body:
Epistemology studies knowledge, belief, justification, evidence, and related concepts. It asks what knowledge is and whether skepticism can be answered.

A person may have a true belief about tomorrow's weather by guessing, prompting the question of whether truth alone is enough for knowledge. Epistemology examines such cases alongside evidence, justification, skepticism, and how inquiry should proceed.

examples.text: Analyzing whether justified true belief suffices for knowledge is epistemological.
examples.note: The inquiry concerns conditions of knowing.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely laboratory method.

concepts.name: Equality
concepts.summary: Equality is sameness of status, treatment, share, or opportunity along a specified relevant dimension.
concepts.body:
Equality is sameness of status, treatment, share, or opportunity along a specified relevant dimension. A claim of equality requires identifying the dimension and comparison class.

Equal treatment may mean giving every applicant the same test, while equal opportunity may require accommodations for disability. A claim about equality should name the dimension and explain why it is relevant; identical treatment is not always fair treatment.

examples.text: Equal voting rights give each citizen the same formal vote.
examples.note: The political entitlement is equalized.

commonMisreadings: Equality does not mean sameness in every trait.

concepts.name: Equilibrium
concepts.summary: Equilibrium is a state where opposing influences balance and the relevant system has no net change.
concepts.body:
Equilibrium is a state where opposing influences balance and the relevant system has no net change. Dynamic equilibrium permits continuing microscopic change with stable aggregate conditions.

In a market model, prices may settle where planned supply and demand match, so there is no pressure for further change within the model. Equilibrium can be stable or fragile and is a modeling condition, not necessarily a fair or desirable outcome.

examples.text: A chemical reaction has equal forward and reverse rates at equilibrium.
examples.note: Concentrations remain stable while molecules react.

commonMisreadings: Equilibrium does not require total stillness.

concepts.name: Error theory in ethics
concepts.summary: Error theory says moral judgments purport to state objective facts but are all false because no such facts exist.
concepts.body:
Error theory says moral judgments purport to state objective facts but are all false because no such facts exist. It combines cognitivist moral language with anti-realist metaphysics.

An error theorist says “cruelty is objectively wrong” makes a factual claim, but no objective moral properties exist, so the claim is false. This differs from saying moral language only expresses attitudes; the theory must explain why moral practice persists and what replaces it.

examples.text: “Cruelty is wrong” asserts a property the error theorist says nothing instantiates.
examples.note: The judgment is false, not merely emotional.

commonMisreadings: It differs from emotivism.

concepts.name: Essence
concepts.summary: An essence is the set of properties making an entity the kind of thing it is.
concepts.body:
An essence is the set of properties making an entity the kind of thing it is. Essential properties contrast with accidental properties an entity can lose while remaining itself.

A theory might say being a chemical element depends essentially on having a particular number of protons, while color is accidental. Which properties are essential depends on the entity and theory; apparent definitions can be revised by scientific discovery.

examples.text: Having three sides is essential to a triangle.
examples.note: Removing it makes the object non-triangular.

commonMisreadings: Essence is not the most noticeable feature.

concepts.name: Essentialism
concepts.summary: Essentialism says entities or categories possess necessary underlying properties.
concepts.body:
Essentialism says entities or categories possess necessary underlying properties. In social theory it can mean treating groups as fixed and homogeneous.

An essentialist account of a biological kind holds that membership depends on necessary underlying features rather than superficial resemblance alone. Essentialism can clarify some classifications but risks treating socially constructed categories or diverse groups as fixed and uniform.

examples.text: Species essentialism treats every member as sharing one immutable defining nature.
examples.note: Variation is ignored beneath a presumed essence.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely recognizing genetic influence.

concepts.name: Eternalism
concepts.summary: Eternalism about time says past, present, and future events all exist in a tenseless spacetime.
concepts.body:
Eternalism about time says past, present, and future events all exist in a tenseless spacetime. It contrasts with presentism, where only the present exists.

Eternalism treats a past meeting and a future eclipse as equally part of spacetime, although they occupy different temporal locations. It contrasts with presentism, which says only the present exists; neither view alone says time feels the same from every perspective.

examples.text: A past eruption and future eclipse are both spacetime events for an eternalist.
examples.note: Temporal location is treated like spatial location.

commonMisreadings: It does not say all events are simultaneous.

concepts.name: Ethical egoism
concepts.summary: Ethical egoism says each person ought to act in their own self-interest.
concepts.body:
Ethical egoism says each person ought to act in their own self-interest. It is normative, unlike the psychological claim that people are actually self-interested.

An ethical egoist may say a person ought to save money for their own future rather than donate it, because self-interest is the governing moral standard. This is a normative theory, distinct from the psychological claim that people always act selfishly.

examples.text: It may judge accepting a profitable opportunity morally required despite no benefit to strangers.
examples.note: Self-interest supplies the fundamental standard.

commonMisreadings: It does not say every person always acts selfishly.

concepts.name: Ethical hedonism
concepts.summary: Ethical hedonism says pleasure is the only intrinsic good and pain the only intrinsic bad, or grounds right action in pleasure over pain.
concepts.body:
Ethical hedonism says pleasure is the only intrinsic good and pain the only intrinsic bad, or grounds right action in pleasure over pain. Pleasure need not mean intense physical sensation.

An ethical hedonist counts a painful illness as bad and a joyful friendship as good because pleasure and pain ground value. Versions differ on whether pleasure makes an action right or is the only intrinsic good, and critics point to meaningful goods beyond enjoyment.

examples.text: A hedonist may choose lasting friendship over a brief thrill.
examples.note: The choice maximizes durable pleasant experience.

commonMisreadings: It is not careless indulgence.

concepts.name: Ethical intuitionism
concepts.summary: Ethical intuitionism says some moral truths are directly knowable through rational intuition.
concepts.body:
Ethical intuitionism says some moral truths are directly knowable through rational intuition. It treats some moral properties or principles as irreducible and self-evident.

An intuitionist may judge that deliberately harming an innocent person for amusement is wrong without deriving that judgment from a further rule. Intuition is meant as rational moral insight, not a passing gut reaction, and philosophers dispute its reliability and scope.

examples.text: An intuitionist may see gratuitous cruelty as wrong without utility calculation.
examples.note: The judgment is basic rather than derived.

commonMisreadings: It does not equate every feeling with intuition.

concepts.name: Ethical naturalism
concepts.summary: Ethical naturalism says moral facts or properties are natural features of the world.
concepts.body:
Ethical naturalism says moral facts or properties are natural features of the world. It rejects a sharp metaphysical divide between moral and natural facts.

A naturalist might identify goodness with features such as flourishing or the satisfaction of needs, treating moral facts as part of the natural world. The theory must explain how moral concepts relate to empirical facts and respond to arguments that the concepts are not interchangeable.

examples.text: A theory may identify goodness with natural human flourishing.
examples.note: The moral property is analyzed through worldly conditions.

commonMisreadings: It does not say whatever is natural is good.

concepts.name: Ethical non-naturalism
concepts.summary: Ethical non-naturalism says moral properties are real but irreducible to natural or scientific properties.
concepts.body:
Ethical non-naturalism says moral properties are real but irreducible to natural or scientific properties. It is objective moral realism without natural reduction.

A non-naturalist may hold that goodness is real but cannot be reduced to pleasure, fitness, or another scientific property. The view aims to preserve moral truths while facing questions about how we know such facts and how they fit into a natural world.

examples.text: Justice’s goodness may not equal any measurable amount of pleasure.
examples.note: The moral property remains objective but non-natural.

commonMisreadings: It is not moral nihilism.

concepts.name: Ethics
concepts.summary: Ethics studies right action, character, value, obligation, and the good life.
concepts.body:
Ethics studies right action, character, value, obligation, and the good life. It includes normative ethics, applied ethics, and metaethics.

A decision about whether to disclose confidential information can involve duties, consequences, rights, and character. Ethics includes theories and practical reasoning about such cases; disagreement often reflects different principles or views of the facts.

examples.text: Allocating scarce organs by urgency is an applied ethical problem.
examples.note: The case requires reasoning about competing values.

commonMisreadings: Ethics is not etiquette alone.

concepts.name: Ethnic nationalism
concepts.summary: Ethnic nationalism defines a nation through shared ancestry, culture, language, or inherited identity.
concepts.body:
Ethnic nationalism defines a nation through shared ancestry, culture, language, or inherited identity. It makes political membership depend on an ethnic community rather than only citizenship.

An ethnic nationalist movement may define national membership through ancestry, language, or inherited cultural identity. These criteria can exclude citizens and minorities, and real movements vary in how much they combine ethnic claims with civic institutions.

examples.text: A movement seeks a state for people sharing a language and historical origin.
examples.note: Ethnic belonging grounds sovereignty.

commonMisreadings: It differs from civic nationalism.

concepts.name: Ethnonationalism
concepts.summary: Ethnonationalism seeks political authority or borders to correspond to an ethnically defined people.
concepts.body:
Ethnonationalism seeks political authority or borders to correspond to an ethnically defined people. It can support autonomy, separation, assimilation, or exclusion.

An ethnonationalist project seeks political borders or authority aligned with a people defined by ethnicity. Such claims can overlap with self-determination movements but may marginalize residents who do not share the favored identity.

examples.text: A party restricts citizenship to members of a favored ethnicity.
examples.note: Ethnic membership controls political belonging.

commonMisreadings: It is not ordinary cultural pride.

concepts.name: Ethnophilosophy
concepts.summary: An approach that presents a community's shared oral, religious, or cultural beliefs as a collective philosophy, and the debate over whether that presentation counts as philosophy.
concepts.body:
Ethnophilosophy refers to presentations of a people's proverbs, myths, religion, language, and customs as a collective philosophical worldview, especially in debates about African philosophy. It can preserve intellectual materials neglected by colonial scholarship, but it becomes problematic when an interpreter turns diverse voices into one timeless subject and treats description as proof of philosophy. The issue is authorship, argument, disagreement, and historical change.

Hountondji's criticism presses for philosophy as a critical practice in which identifiable thinkers make contestable claims; it does not entail that oral or communal traditions lack reflection. The opposing concern is that a strict academic model can exclude forms of thought whose authority is distributed through performance, memory, and practice. The debate is methodological: how should researchers represent collective intellectual life without either romanticizing it or denying its philosophical questions?

examples.text: A researcher compiles proverbs from one society and declares them a complete philosophy without naming speakers, disagreements, or historical changes.
examples.note: The example exposes the risk of turning cultural materials into a timeless collective subject.

commonMisreadings: Ethnophilosophy is not simply any study of African thought, and Hountondji's criticism should not be misreported as his endorsement.
A collective tradition can contain philosophical questions without proving that it is a single person's argument or a uniform worldview.
criticisms: Critics of Hountondji's strict author-centered model argue that oral, communal, and nonacademic practices can carry reflection even when authorship is distributed.

concepts.name: Eudaimonia
concepts.summary: Eudaimonia is the Greek ideal of flourishing through a complete and excellent human life.
concepts.body:
Eudaimonia is the Greek ideal of flourishing through a complete and excellent human life. Aristotle treats it as virtuous activity rather than a passing feeling.

For Aristotle, eudaimonia is a life going well through virtuous activity over a complete span, not a passing feeling of happiness. The concept is tied to ancient Greek accounts of human function, and modern interpretations differ on how to translate or apply it.

examples.text: A person cultivating courage, practical wisdom, friendship, and civic responsibility exemplifies it.
examples.note: The whole life is judged successful in human activity.

commonMisreadings: It is not momentary pleasure.

concepts.name: Eudaimonism
concepts.summary: Eudaimonism says human flourishing or well-being is the ultimate moral standard.
concepts.body:
Eudaimonism says human flourishing or well-being is the ultimate moral standard. Virtues may be valued as constituents or conditions of flourishing.

A eudaimonist theory may judge habits and actions by whether they contribute to a person's flourishing across a whole life. It treats flourishing as a central standard, though theories disagree about its contents and whether morality can demand sacrifice of one's own good.

examples.text: Honesty is praised because it supports trust and practical excellence.
examples.note: The virtue contributes to a good human life.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than psychological egoism.

concepts.name: Euroscepticism
concepts.summary: Euroscepticism is skepticism or opposition toward some or all European Union integration.
concepts.body:
Euroscepticism is skepticism or opposition toward some or all European Union integration. It ranges from policy criticism to support for withdrawal.

A Eurosceptic may oppose transferring more authority to European Union institutions while supporting membership or cooperation in other areas. The label spans degrees of criticism and withdrawal advocacy; its meaning depends on the policy and political context.

examples.text: A party supports the single market but opposes transferring more powers to EU institutions.
examples.note: The stance rejects deeper integration without rejecting every European link.

commonMisreadings: It is not hostility to all European countries.

concepts.name: Euthyphro dilemma
concepts.summary: The Euthyphro dilemma asks whether actions are good because a deity commands them or commanded because they are good.
concepts.body:
The Euthyphro dilemma asks whether actions are good because a deity commands them or commanded because they are good. It challenges simple divine-command foundations through arbitrariness or dependence concerns.

If actions are right only because God commands them, morality may seem arbitrary; if God commands them because they are right, goodness seems independent of command. The dilemma probes grounding, and theistic philosophers offer accounts involving divine nature, reason, or other relations.

examples.text: If command alone makes generosity good, command could seemingly make cruelty good.
examples.note: The example raises the arbitrariness problem.

commonMisreadings: It does not prove religious people lack moral reasons.

concepts.name: Event
concepts.summary: An event is a happening located in a temporal and sometimes spatial framework.
concepts.body: An event is something that happens, bounded by when it occurs and sometimes by where. This separates an occurrence from the objects, people, or conditions involved: the bridge is a structure, while its collapse is an event. Events may be brief or extended, planned or accidental. Historians can treat a revolution as one large event while also examining its many component events; which boundaries matter depends on the explanatory question.

examples.text: A bridge collapse at noon is an event.
examples.note: It occurs rather than persists as a thing.

commonMisreadings: An event need not be planned.

concepts.name: Evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence is information that supports, undermines, or bears on a claim’s truth or justification.
concepts.body: Evidence is information whose relevance bears on whether a claim should be accepted, rejected, or assigned more or less confidence. A fingerprint, a witness account, and a controlled measurement can each support a hypothesis, but their force depends on reliability, context, and alternatives. A DNA match may raise the probability that a suspect left biological material; it does not alone establish when or why it was left. Evidence therefore needs interpretation, not mere accumulation.

examples.text: A DNA match links a suspect to biological material.
examples.note: Reliable matching changes the probability of involvement.

commonMisreadings: Evidence is not always certainty.

concepts.name: Evidentialism
concepts.summary: Evidentialism says belief justification depends on evidence available to the believer.
concepts.body: Evidentialism makes the believer’s evidence the basis for whether a belief is epistemically justified. If two people have the same relevant evidence, their confidence should be proportionate to it rather than to preference or convenience. A researcher who encounters a carefully replicated contrary result should lower confidence in the original hypothesis. The view does not require certainty: evidence can be incomplete, and evidentialists disagree about what counts as evidence and how strongly it supports a conclusion.

examples.text: A researcher lowers confidence after a controlled contrary experiment.
examples.note: Evidence governs revision rather than attachment.

commonMisreadings: It need not require only verbal evidence.

concepts.name: Existence
concepts.summary: Existence is being real or instantiated, though theories disagree about abstract entities.
concepts.body: To ask whether something exists is to ask whether it is part of reality, though philosophers disagree about what kinds of things reality includes. A table occupies space and has causal effects; numbers do not behave that way, yet mathematical reasoning appears to quantify over them. Platonists treat numbers as abstract objects, while nominalists seek accounts that avoid such entities. The dispute matters because assumptions about existence determine what a theory must explain and what its commitments are.

examples.text: A Platonist treats numbers as abstract objects, unlike a nominalist.
examples.note: The dispute concerns which entities are real.

commonMisreadings: Existence is not limited to observability.

concepts.name: Existential import
concepts.summary: Existential import is an assumption that a categorical statement presupposes or entails subject-class members exist.
concepts.body: Existential import is the commitment that a statement about a class presupposes or entails that the class has members. In modern predicate logic, “All unicorns are white” can be true when there are no unicorns: there is no counterexample. A traditional reading may instead treat the sentence as implying that unicorns exist. This difference affects syllogisms and ordinary claims about empty categories; readers must distinguish what a sentence says about every member from whether any member is present.

examples.text: “All unicorns are white” is true in an empty-unicorn domain.
examples.note: Universal quantification does not require a witness.

commonMisreadings: It differs from existential quantification.

concepts.name: Existential quantification
concepts.summary: Existential quantification asserts that at least one object satisfies a predicate or formula.
concepts.body: Existential quantification says that at least one thing in the domain satisfies a condition. The symbol ∃x in “∃x(Penguin(x) and Swims(x))” requires a witness that is both a penguin and a swimmer. It does not identify which penguin or claim that all penguins swim. The quantifier is fundamental to formalizing claims such as “someone left,” and its truth depends on the chosen domain and on whether an object meets every predicate in the formula.

examples.text: ∃x(Penguin(x) and Swims(x)) says some penguin swims.
examples.note: A particular penguin can witness the formula.

commonMisreadings: It does not say every object swims.

concepts.name: Existentialism
concepts.summary: Existentialism emphasizes freedom, responsibility, situated choice, anxiety, and meaning.
concepts.body: Existentialism foregrounds a person’s situated freedom: people inherit circumstances they did not choose, yet their responses help shape who they become. Choice brings responsibility because a person cannot always appeal to a fixed role or universal rule to decide for them. Someone torn between caring for a parent and joining a resistance movement faces competing commitments rather than a formulaic answer. Existentialist writers differ, but commonly examine anxiety, self-deception, and the effort to create meaning under uncertainty.

examples.text: Sartre’s person choosing between caring for a parent and joining resistance faces conflicting responsibility.
examples.note: Concrete choice shapes identity under uncertainty.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply pessimism.

concepts.name: Expected utility
concepts.summary: Expected utility is the probability-weighted average of utilities across possible outcomes.
concepts.body: Expected utility evaluates a risky choice by multiplying each possible outcome’s value to the decision-maker by its probability, then adding the results. The value is utility, not necessarily money: an extra dollar matters less to a wealthy person than to someone facing eviction. A gamble with a 50 percent chance of $100 and a 50 percent chance of nothing has expected monetary value of $50, but its expected utility depends on how the person values each outcome. The rule helps compare risk, given probabilities and a utility scale.

examples.text: A fair $100-or-$0 gamble has expected monetary utility of $50 under linear utility.
examples.note: Each outcome is weighted before summing.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily the most probable outcome.

concepts.name: Expected value
concepts.summary: Expected value is the probability-weighted average numerical outcome of a random variable.
concepts.body: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of the numerical outcomes of a random process. For a fair six-sided die, each face has probability one-sixth, so the average is 3.5 even though no roll shows 3.5. This makes expected value useful for repeated decisions and long-run averages, but it does not predict an individual result. It can also conceal risk: two bets may share the same average while one has a much wider spread of possible outcomes.

examples.text: A fair die has expected value 3.5 although no roll does.
examples.note: The number describes the long-run average.

commonMisreadings: It is not a one-trial prediction.

concepts.name: Experience machine
concepts.summary: The experience machine is Nozick’s device producing any desired pleasurable experience.
concepts.body: Nozick’s experience machine asks whether a life would be good if a device could provide any desired experiences while the person remained unaware that they were simulated. Refusing to plug in suggests that pleasure is not the only thing people value: they may care about actually accomplishing something, being a certain kind of person, or relating to a real world. The thought experiment challenges simple hedonism, but a refusal does not prove that authenticity always outweighs happiness; people may also distrust the machine or value agency itself.

examples.text: Someone refusing permanent connection may value doing real things and being a certain person.
examples.note: The refusal assigns value to authenticity or reality.

commonMisreadings: It does not prove pleasure has no value.

concepts.name: Explanation
concepts.summary: An explanation accounts for why or how something occurs through causes, mechanisms, laws, reasons, or structures.
concepts.body: An explanation answers a why-or-how question by showing relevant causes, mechanisms, laws, reasons, or structural relations. A fever may be explained by an infection: pathogens trigger immune responses that alter body temperature. Merely repeating that the patient has a fever describes the fact without accounting for it. Different questions call for different explanations: a physician may need the biological mechanism, while a historian asks why an outbreak spread through a city. Explanations can be informative without being complete or certain.

examples.text: An infection and its physiological effects explain a fever.
examples.note: The account identifies a producing mechanism.

commonMisreadings: Restatement is not explanation.

concepts.name: Explanatory power
concepts.summary: Explanatory power is a theory’s capacity to account for evidence and diverse phenomena.
concepts.body: A theory has explanatory power when it accounts for evidence, connects otherwise separate observations, and supports understanding or prediction. Natural selection can explain adaptations, shared anatomical structures, and patterns in fossils through one mechanism of inherited variation and differential reproduction.
