A theory that fits only one example by adding a special exception has less reach. Explanatory breadth is not proof, however: a theory must also fit the evidence, avoid ad hoc patches, and outperform plausible rivals.

examples.text: Natural selection explains adaptation, homologous structures, and fossil succession.
examples.note: One mechanism connects several observations.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to simplicity.

concepts.name: Exploitation
concepts.summary: Exploitation is unfair use of another’s vulnerability, labor, or resources for disproportionate benefit.
concepts.body: Exploitation occurs when one party takes unfair advantage of another’s vulnerability, labor, or resources, typically securing a disproportionate benefit. An employer who pays migrant workers below legal wages while threatening retaliation gains from the workers’ constrained alternatives. The injustice is not simply that one party benefits; ordinary exchange can benefit both sides. Analysis asks how power, dependence, and the terms of exchange shape what each party can refuse, and theories disagree about whether unfairness lies chiefly in outcomes, process, or background inequality.

examples.text: An employer pays migrant workers illegally low wages while threatening retaliation.
examples.note: Constrained options make refusal costly while the employer gains.

commonMisreadings: It is not every unequal mutually beneficial exchange.

concepts.name: Explosion principle
concepts.summary: The explosion principle says a contradiction entails any proposition in classical logic.
concepts.body: In classical logic, the explosion principle says that a contradiction entails any proposition: from P and not-P, one can derive an unrelated Q. This follows from classical inference rules, not from a claim that contradictions are harmless in real reasoning. If a database contains inconsistent records and every conclusion becomes derivable, it is unusable. Paraconsistent logics reject unrestricted explosion so reasoning can continue despite contradiction. The principle matters when choosing a logic for inconsistent information, where preserving useful conclusions may be more important than classical completeness.

examples.text: From P and not-P, classical logic derives unrelated Q.
examples.note: An inconsistent premise set becomes deductively trivial.

commonMisreadings: Explosion is not a physical claim.

concepts.name: Expression theory of art
concepts.summary: Expression theory says an artwork’s artistic identity or value centrally involves expressing emotion or experience.
concepts.body: Expression theories connect art to the communication or embodiment of emotion and experience. A composer may shape dissonance, pacing, and silence so a piece conveys grief; on some accounts, the artist clarifies an initially inchoate feeling and gives it perceptible form. The view explains why expressive qualities can matter beyond technical skill, but faces cases such as abstract art, which may be valued without a clear emotion, and works whose makers’ feelings are unknown. Expression is one account of art, not a universal test for artistic status.

examples.text: A composer’s dissonant slow piece conveys mourning.
examples.note: Musical form communicates an emotional quality.

commonMisreadings: Art need not express autobiography.

concepts.name: Expressivism
concepts.summary: Expressivism says normative statements express attitudes, commitments, or plans rather than describe normative facts.
concepts.body: Expressivism interprets normative statements as expressing practical attitudes or commitments rather than reporting independent moral facts. Saying “Cruelty is wrong” may express disapproval and a commitment to oppose cruelty, rather than describe a property detectable like color. This explains why moral language can motivate action and guide disagreement. A challenge is to explain logical relations: someone who condemns cruelty but approves a cruel act seems inconsistent. Expressivists develop accounts of how attitudes combine and how moral arguments can be valid without treating norms as ordinary factual reports.

examples.text: “Cheating is wrong” expresses opposition and a practical commitment.
examples.note: The statement guides action without describing a moral object.

commonMisreadings: It does not make moral language meaningless.

concepts.name: Extended mind
concepts.summary: The extended-mind thesis says cognitive processes can include suitably integrated external resources.
concepts.body: The extended-mind thesis holds that a cognitive process can include an external resource when it is reliably integrated into thinking, rather than merely used occasionally as a tool. A person with severe memory impairment who constantly consults a trusted notebook may use it as part of the practical memory system, much as another person relies on biological recall. A book read once is not thereby part of the mind. The thesis shifts attention from where a resource sits to how it functions, while raising questions about access, reliability, and ownership.

examples.text: Otto’s constantly consulted notebook functions as external memory.
examples.note: It performs retrieval work that internal memory performs for another agent.

commonMisreadings: Not every tool automatically becomes part of mind.

concepts.name: Extension
concepts.summary: The extension of a term is the set of things to which it correctly applies.
concepts.body: The extension of a word or predicate is the set of things to which it correctly applies. The extension of “planet” includes Earth and Mars under the accepted astronomical classification; the extension of “red” includes objects that meet the relevant color standard. Extension contrasts with intension, the meaning or conditions that determine membership. Two expressions can refer to the same set while differing in meaning, and an extension may change when scientific classifications or the relevant context changes.

examples.text: The extension of “planet” includes bodies satisfying the chosen astronomical definition.
examples.note: Those bodies are the term’s members.

commonMisreadings: Extension is not word length.

concepts.name: Externalism in epistemology
concepts.summary: Epistemic externalism says factors outside conscious access can contribute to knowledge or justification.
concepts.body: Epistemic externalism allows factors beyond a person’s reflective access to help make a belief knowledge or justified. A person may know that a tree is in the garden by seeing it in good light, even if they cannot explain the reliability of their vision. Reliabilists, for example, emphasize whether the belief was produced by a dependable process. Externalist accounts can explain ordinary knowledge without requiring elaborate self-checking, but critics ask whether a believer must be able to recognize or defend the conditions that make the belief trustworthy.

examples.text: Normal perception can yield knowledge even when a person cannot prove perception reliable.
examples.note: The process’s truth connection is externally relevant.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny internal reasons.

concepts.name: Externality
concepts.summary: An externality is an unpriced cost or benefit of an activity imposed on third parties.
concepts.body: An externality is a cost or benefit of an activity that falls on people outside the transaction and is not reflected in its price. A factory may sell goods profitably while nearby residents bear pollution-related health costs. The market price then omits part of the social cost, which can lead to too much pollution. Taxes, regulation, or negotiated compensation may address the mismatch, but measuring the harm and assigning responsibility can be difficult. Not every effect on a third party is an externality in the technical economic sense; the unpriced impact is central.

examples.text: Factory smoke imposes respiratory costs on nearby residents.
examples.note: Outsiders bear harm absent from the product price.

commonMisreadings: It is not any unpaid producer cost.

concepts.name: Fabianism
concepts.summary: Fabianism is a socialist tradition favoring gradual democratic institutional reform over revolution.
concepts.body: Fabianism is a socialist tradition that seeks change through gradual reform, elections, public institutions, and evidence-based policy rather than an immediate revolutionary break. A Fabian strategy might expand public services and labor protections step by step, building durable support for social ownership or redistribution. The name comes from the Roman general Fabius, associated with delay and attrition. Gradualism can reduce upheaval and make reforms administratively workable, but critics argue that slow change may leave entrenched power intact or blunt more transformative aims.

examples.text: A Fabian strategy expands public ownership through parliamentary reforms.
examples.note: Socialist objectives are pursued incrementally.

commonMisreadings: It is not opposition to all state intervention.

concepts.name: Fairness
concepts.summary: Fairness treats people by impartial, relevant, and consistently applied standards.
concepts.body: Fairness requires treating people according to relevant, impartial standards and applying those standards consistently. A teacher grading identical work by the same rubric acts fairly in one sense; a rule that ignores a student’s disability may still produce an unjust result. Fairness therefore involves both consistency and judgment about which differences matter. It is central to decisions about opportunity, punishment, and sharing scarce goods, but different theories prioritize equal treatment, need, merit, rights, or repair of past disadvantage.

examples.text: Extra exam time for a student with a disability can be fair.
examples.note: The adjustment equalizes opportunity rather than treatment.

commonMisreadings: Fairness is not always identical treatment.

concepts.name: Fallibilism
concepts.summary: Fallibilism says justified beliefs remain open to error.
concepts.body: Fallibilism holds that a belief can be rationally justified or count as knowledge even though it might turn out to be wrong. A doctor may have strong evidence for a diagnosis and begin treatment while recognizing that later tests could reveal another cause. This rejects the demand for absolute certainty as a condition of knowledge. Fallibilism does not make all beliefs equally credible: confidence should track the strength of evidence, and openness to correction is compatible with firm conclusions when the evidence is strong.

examples.text: A geologist accepts a fault model while allowing future revision.
examples.note: The belief is responsible without being guaranteed true.

commonMisreadings: It is not total skepticism.

concepts.name: False fame effect
concepts.summary: The false fame effect is judging an unfamiliar previously seen name as famous because it feels familiar.
concepts.body: The false-fame effect is a memory error in which a previously encountered unfamiliar name later feels familiar and is mistaken for the name of a famous person. In an experiment, people who saw obscure names earlier may judge those names famous on a later list, even without recalling the first exposure. Familiarity supplies a misleading cue when its source is forgotten. The effect shows that judgments can rely on a feeling of recognition rather than explicit knowledge, though it does not mean that every fame judgment is based on familiarity alone.

examples.text: After seeing a fictional author’s name, participants may call it a celebrity name.
examples.note: Exposure creates familiarity without fame evidence.

commonMisreadings: It does not make the person famous.

concepts.name: Falsifiability
concepts.summary: Falsifiability is vulnerability of a claim to observations that could show it false.
concepts.body: A claim is falsifiable when some possible observation would count against it. “Every swan is white” is challenged by a verified black swan; a claim designed to explain every possible outcome has no such test. Falsifiability helps distinguish empirical hypotheses from claims insulated against evidence and encourages researchers to specify risky predictions. It is not a complete measure of scientific value: broad theories are tested alongside auxiliary assumptions, and a single anomaly may indicate a faulty instrument rather than a false central theory.

examples.text: “One measured metal contracts when heated” could challenge “all metals expand.”
examples.note: The universal claim permits a counterexample.

commonMisreadings: Falsifiable does not mean false.

concepts.name: Family resemblance
concepts.summary: Family resemblance is category membership through overlapping similarities without one feature common to all members.
concepts.body: Family resemblance describes categories whose members overlap in several ways without sharing one feature possessed by every member. Board games, for example, include activities with competition, chance, strategy, or shared goals in different combinations. Wittgenstein used this pattern to question whether every word has a single essence. The idea explains flexible everyday categories, but it should not become a license to classify anything: practical inquiry still needs to identify which similarities matter for the purpose at hand.

examples.text: Games include sports, board games, and solitary puzzles sharing different features.
examples.note: No one feature must define every game.

commonMisreadings: The category is not thereby arbitrary.

concepts.name: Fascism
concepts.summary: Fascism is authoritarian ultranationalism subordinating individuals to a mythic national community and often using leader rule and violence.
concepts.body: Fascism is an authoritarian ultranationalist politics that imagines the nation as a unified body in decline and promises renewal through hierarchy, leader rule, and mobilization against internal or external enemies. Fascist movements have historically attacked liberal pluralism, organized labor, and democratic opposition, often using paramilitary violence. The label should be applied with attention to defining political features, not as a synonym for any disliked policy. Historians debate boundaries and national variations, but the combination of national rebirth myth, authoritarianism, and suppression of pluralism is central.

examples.text: Mussolini’s regime combined one-party rule, censorship, paramilitaries, and nationalism.
examples.note: The institutions express authoritarian militant nationalism.

commonMisreadings: Fascism is not every dictatorship or patriotism.

concepts.name: Fatalism
concepts.summary: Fatalism says some outcomes occur regardless of what agents choose or do.
concepts.body: Fatalism says that some outcome will occur regardless of what an agent chooses or does. If a person believes a storm will destroy a house whatever repairs are attempted, they may see action as futile. This differs from determinism: a determined outcome can depend on choices that are themselves part of the causal chain, so acting still makes a difference. Fatalism matters to debates about responsibility and motivation, but it can also be a mistaken inference from certainty about an outcome to the claim that efforts cannot affect it.

examples.text: A fatalist refuses exam study because the result is fixed anyway.
examples.note: Deliberation is treated as causally irrelevant.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely difficulty changing an outcome.

concepts.name: Federalism
concepts.summary: Federalism divides constitutional authority between central and regional governments.
concepts.body: Federalism constitutionally divides governing authority between a central government and regional units, with each level holding powers it cannot simply take from the other. In a federation, states or provinces may control education while the national government handles defense and currency. This arrangement can bring decisions closer to local populations and accommodate regional differences, while making coordination and accountability harder when responsibilities overlap. Federalism is distinct from ordinary decentralization because the regional authority is constitutionally protected rather than delegated at the center’s discretion.

examples.text: The United States assigns national defense federally and many local matters to states.
examples.note: Both government levels possess legally assigned authority.

commonMisreadings: It differs from a unitary state.

concepts.name: Feedback loop
concepts.summary: A feedback loop returns a system’s output as input that alters later behavior.
concepts.body: A feedback loop occurs when a system’s output returns as an input and changes its later behavior. A thermostat measures room temperature and turns heating on or off; the resulting temperature then affects the next measurement. Negative feedback tends to stabilize a system, while positive feedback amplifies change, as when warming reduces reflective ice and increases further warming. The direction and delay of the feedback matter. Identifying a loop helps explain why interventions can have indirect or unexpected effects over time.

examples.text: A thermostat turns heating on when measured temperature falls below its set point.
examples.note: Measurement controls action that reduces deviation.

commonMisreadings: It is not every temporal sequence.

concepts.name: Feminism
concepts.summary: Feminism seeks to understand and end gender-based subordination and secure gender justice.
concepts.body: Feminism encompasses movements and theories that analyze and oppose gender-based subordination while pursuing equal dignity, agency, and social standing. A feminist account of workplace inequality might examine hiring rules, care responsibilities, harassment, and pay rather than treating each outcome as an isolated choice. Feminism is not a single doctrine: liberal, socialist, radical, intersectional, and other traditions disagree about causes and remedies. Its core concern is how gendered power operates and how institutions and relationships can be changed to make people less constrained by it.

examples.text: Equal-pay campaigns challenge gendered workplace disadvantage.
examples.note: They target institutional effects of gender roles.

commonMisreadings: Feminism does not seek women’s domination.

concepts.name: Feminist epistemology
concepts.summary: Feminist epistemology studies how gendered power shapes knowledge, credibility, inquiry, and justification.
concepts.body: Feminist epistemology studies how gender and power shape what is known, whose testimony is trusted, and which questions research treats as important. A patient whose pain is dismissed because of gendered assumptions illustrates how credibility can be distributed unfairly. The field also asks whether social position can reveal features of institutions invisible from dominant perspectives. It does not claim that identity automatically guarantees truth; it investigates how situated experience, methods, and power affect evidence and correction in inquiry.

examples.text: Studying women’s exclusion from drug trials reveals distorted medical knowledge.
examples.note: Research design affects what is known and for whom.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim only women know.

concepts.name: Feminist ethics
concepts.summary: Feminist ethics critiques moral theories neglecting dependency, unequal power, emotion, and care.
concepts.body: Feminist ethics challenges moral theories that treat people as isolated, equally powerful decision-makers and overlook dependency, care, emotion, and social inequality. In a hospital, a decision about treatment may involve a patient’s agency alongside the unpaid labor and obligations of family caregivers. The approach asks how relationships and unequal power shape what responsibility requires. It is not simply the claim that women are naturally more caring; feminist ethicists differ about the role of care and how to combine it with rights, justice, and autonomy.

examples.text: Discharge planning may consider an unpaid caregiver’s constrained labor.
examples.note: Relationships and structural burdens become morally relevant.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply kindness over rules.

concepts.name: Fermi paradox
concepts.summary: The Fermi paradox is the tension between probable extraterrestrial life and absence of clear advanced-civilization evidence.
concepts.body: The Fermi paradox names the tension between the vast number of potentially habitable worlds and the absence of confirmed evidence for technologically advanced extraterrestrial civilizations. If life and technological societies arise often, one might expect signs such as signals or probes; none has been verified. Possible resolutions include rare abiogenesis, short-lived civilizations, limits on interstellar travel, or our inadequate search. The paradox is a prompt for framing hypotheses, not evidence that aliens must exist or that the silence has one known explanation.

examples.text: The Drake equation may suggest many communicators while searches find no confirmed technosignatures.
examples.note: Expectation conflicts with observation.

commonMisreadings: It does not prove aliens do not exist.

concepts.name: Feudalism
concepts.summary: Feudalism is a label for landholding, military obligation, and hierarchical dependence especially associated with medieval Europe.
concepts.body: Feudalism is a broad label for social orders in which landholding, political authority, and military or service obligations were linked through hierarchical relationships, especially in medieval Europe. A lord might grant land rights to a vassal in return for service, while peasants owed labor or dues. The arrangement varied by region and period, and historians debate whether “feudalism” compresses too many distinct institutions into one model. Use of the term should specify which relationships are meant rather than imply a uniform system across medieval societies.

examples.text: A lord grants a fief to a vassal for military service.
examples.note: Land tenure is tied to personal political obligation.

commonMisreadings: It was not one identical universal system.

concepts.name: Fictional discourse
concepts.summary: Fictional discourse discusses entities and events represented in stories.
concepts.body: Fictional discourse is talk about characters, places, and events represented in stories. “Sherlock Holmes lives on Baker Street” can be understood as true within Conan Doyle’s fictional world, even though Holmes is not an actual person. Readers use narrative conventions to distinguish what a story establishes from what is merely imagined by a character. The topic matters to semantics and metaphysics because ordinary language appears to make claims about fictional entities; theories explain this without assuming that every named character exists in reality.

examples.text: Readers infer that Sherlock Holmes is a detective from the stories.
examples.note: The inference uses information authorized by the fiction.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily deceptive real-world speech.

concepts.name: Fictionalism
concepts.summary: Fictionalism uses a discourse as useful make-believe while denying literal existence of its entities.
concepts.body: Fictionalism treats a discourse as a useful make-believe practice while withholding literal commitment to the entities it appears to describe. A mathematical fictionalist might use talk of numbers to calculate and communicate while denying that numbers are abstract objects. The view aims to preserve a practice’s usefulness without accepting its apparent ontology. It must explain why the discourse remains reliable and what makes its claims correct within the practice; fictionalism is not simply pretending that every statement is false or useless.

examples.text: A mathematical fictionalist calculates with numbers while denying abstract numbers exist.
examples.note: Mathematical practice is retained without Platonist commitment.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny truth within fiction.

concepts.name: Fideism
concepts.summary: Fideism holds that faith is independent of or superior to reason for certain religious commitments.
concepts.body: Fideism gives religious faith a role independent of, or sometimes prior to, rational demonstration. A fideist may argue that trust in God is grounded in commitment or revelation and cannot be established by neutral proof. The label covers different positions, from skepticism about reason’s reach to stronger claims that faith should take precedence. It raises the question of how belief can be responsible when evidence is inconclusive, and critics worry that it can insulate beliefs from criticism. It need not mean that believers never reason.

examples.text: A fideist grounds belief in God in faith rather than cosmological demonstration.
examples.note: Trust, not inference, supplies the commitment.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely faith cooperating with reason.

concepts.name: Filial piety
concepts.summary: Filial piety is respect, care, and obligation toward parents and ancestors.
concepts.body: Filial piety is the ethical importance given to respect, care, and appropriate obligation toward parents and ancestors, especially in Confucian traditions. An adult child may feel duties to support an aging parent while also balancing work and other family responsibilities. The ideal can sustain gratitude and intergenerational care, but it does not settle every conflict: obedience may be limited when a parent acts unjustly or when obligations become coercive. Interpretations vary, so filial piety should not be reduced to unquestioning submission.

examples.text: An adult child caring for an ill parent while preserving dignity exemplifies it.
examples.note: The conduct expresses sustained family responsibility.

commonMisreadings: It does not require obeying every harmful demand.

concepts.name: Final cause
concepts.summary: A final cause is the end or purpose for which something occurs in Aristotelian teleology.
concepts.body: In Aristotle’s account of explanation, a final cause is the end or purpose for which a thing exists or an activity is performed. The final cause of a house is shelter; that purpose helps explain why builders arrange materials in a particular way. This differs from the efficient cause, such as the builders’ labor, and the material cause, such as wood and stone. Final-cause explanations are especially relevant to living functions and intentional action, but they should not be confused with claims that every natural event was consciously designed.

examples.text: The heart’s final cause is circulating blood, while contraction is an efficient process.
examples.note: Function explains what the organ is for.

commonMisreadings: A final cause need not be a conscious intention.

concepts.name: First-order logic
concepts.summary: First-order logic quantifies over individual objects but not over predicates or properties.
concepts.body: First-order logic quantifies over individual objects in a domain and uses predicates to state their properties or relations. “Every student submitted an assignment” can be represented by saying that for each object, if it is a student, then it submitted an assignment. Unlike higher-order logic, first-order logic does not directly quantify over predicates or properties themselves. Its balance of expressive power and formal tractability makes it central to mathematics and computer science; the choice of domain affects what the quantified claims say.

examples.text: “All mammals are animals” can be formalized as every object that is a mammal being an animal.
examples.note: The formula quantifies over objects and applies predicates to them, which is the defining scope of first-order logic.

commonMisreadings: It is not propositional logic, because it represents internal subject-predicate structure.

concepts.name: First-person perspective
concepts.summary: A first-person perspective presents experience or narration from the standpoint of an experiencing subject.
concepts.body: A first-person perspective presents an experience or account from the standpoint of a subject, often using “I” and reporting what that person can perceive or know. A diary entry about a storm conveys what the writer saw and feared, not necessarily the full event as an outside observer would reconstruct it. The perspective can give direct access to felt experience while remaining partial or mistaken about causes. In fiction, shifting first-person narrators changes which information readers receive and how trustworthy the account seems.

examples.text: A diary entry describing the writer’s fear during an earthquake uses a first-person perspective.
examples.note: The account reports the event through the writer’s own point of view rather than an external observer.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely a story containing a character, because the relevant perspective is the character’s own.

concepts.name: First-principles reasoning
concepts.summary: First-principles reasoning analyzes a problem by reducing it to basic facts and deriving conclusions from them.
concepts.body: First-principles reasoning breaks a problem into basic assumptions or facts and derives an answer from them instead of relying on convention or analogy alone. To estimate whether a delivery route is feasible, one might calculate distance, speed, and loading time rather than assume that a familiar schedule will work. The method can expose hidden assumptions and open alternatives, but identifying “basic” premises is difficult; reasoning from an incomplete or false starting point produces a confident error. It complements experience rather than making expertise unnecessary.

examples.text: A battery designer may derive a pack’s cost from cell price, materials, assembly, and losses instead of copying an existing pack price.
examples.note: The calculation rebuilds the answer from underlying components rather than accepting a conventional design as given.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply being skeptical, because it requires constructive derivation after questioning assumptions.

concepts.name: Flourishing
concepts.summary: Flourishing is a condition of living well in which a person develops capabilities and exercises them across a worthwhile life.
concepts.body: Flourishing is living well through the development and exercise of human capacities across a life, not merely feeling pleasure at a given moment. A person may flourish through meaningful relationships, learning, health, and worthwhile work, even while experiencing temporary frustration. The concept is prominent in virtue ethics, where a life is assessed as a whole and within social conditions. Disagreement concerns which capabilities are essential and who gets to define them; an account of flourishing can become paternalistic if it ignores people’s own aims and circumstances.

examples.text: A community nurse who cultivates skill, friendship, civic responsibility, and personal health illustrates flourishing.
examples.note: The example includes integrated activity and development, not just a temporary pleasant feeling.

commonMisreadings: Flourishing is broader than happiness understood as positive mood alone.

concepts.name: Folk psychology
concepts.summary: Folk psychology is the ordinary framework of beliefs, desires, intentions, and emotions used to explain and predict behavior.
concepts.body: Folk psychology is the everyday practice of explaining behavior through beliefs, desires, intentions, and emotions. We predict that someone will bring an umbrella because they believe it will rain and want to stay dry. These concepts let people interpret one another and coordinate without measuring brain states. The framework can be inaccurate or culturally shaped, and cognitive science may revise it, but it remains useful for describing reasons and responsibility. Treating a person’s action as intentional is different from identifying its neural mechanism.

examples.text: Saying that Maya took an umbrella because she believed it would rain is a folk-psychological explanation.
examples.note: The explanation uses an ordinary belief and desire vocabulary rather than a laboratory theory.

commonMisreadings: Folk psychology is not necessarily primitive science; it is the common interpretive framework people routinely use.

concepts.name: Forer effect
concepts.summary: The Forer effect is the tendency to accept vague, broadly applicable personality descriptions as uniquely accurate.
concepts.body: The Forer effect is the tendency to accept a vague, generally applicable personality description as uniquely accurate. A person told they are sometimes sociable but also need time alone may recognize ordinary experiences and conclude the profile is highly personal. Astrologic readings and some personality claims exploit this effect by combining broad statements with perceived authority. It warns against judging a test by how resonant its feedback feels; reliable assessment needs specific predictions and independent validation, not just subjective recognition.

examples.text: A person may rate “You sometimes doubt yourself but value independence” as an unusually precise assessment.
examples.note: The statement combines common traits and flexible wording, allowing the reader to fit it to personal experience.

commonMisreadings: It is not evidence that the assessment measured an individual trait with high specificity.

concepts.name: Forgiveness
concepts.summary: Forgiveness is the deliberate relinquishing of resentment or a demand for retaliation after a wrong.
concepts.body: Forgiveness is a deliberate change in how a person responds to a wrong, often by relinquishing resentment or the wish to retaliate. Someone harmed by a friend may forgive while still naming the injury, setting boundaries, or declining to restore trust. Forgiveness is therefore distinct from excusing the act, forgetting it, or reconciling with the offender. It can free a person from being governed by grievance, but moral and religious traditions disagree about its duties and timing; pressuring victims to forgive can compound the original harm.

examples.text: A victim may stop seeking revenge against an apologetic offender while still reporting the crime.
examples.note: The victim releases personal vengeance but does not deny harm or remove institutional consequences.

commonMisreadings: Forgiveness is distinct from reconciliation, which requires renewed relationship and usually mutual participation.

concepts.name: Formal language
concepts.summary: A formal language is a set of strings generated or recognized according to explicit symbolic rules.
concepts.body: A formal language is a precisely specified set of symbol strings, defined by rules for forming or recognizing valid expressions. In arithmetic, rules can determine that “2 + 3” is well formed while “+ 2 3” is not in ordinary infix notation. Formal languages let logicians and computer scientists reason about syntax without relying on ambiguous natural-language interpretation. A grammar defines which strings belong; it does not by itself establish what those strings mean or whether a program using them behaves correctly.

examples.text: The language of balanced parentheses contains strings such as “()()” and “(())” but excludes “)(”.
examples.note: Membership is determined by a formal rule for matching delimiters rather than by interpretation.

commonMisreadings: A formal language need not be a natural human language or have semantic content.

concepts.name: Formalism in aesthetics
concepts.summary: Formalism in aesthetics evaluates artworks primarily through perceptible relations such as form, composition, color, rhythm, or structure.
concepts.body: Aesthetic formalism gives primary importance to an artwork’s perceptible organization: composition, rhythm, color, line, or structural relations. A painting may be compelling because its balance and contrasts guide the eye, regardless of the artist’s biography or political message. Formal qualities can be described and compared, but focusing on them alone may miss context, subject matter, or the work’s social effects. Formalism is best understood as a critical emphasis, not the claim that meaning and history never matter to art.

examples.text: A formalist analysis of a painting may focus on geometric balance and contrast without discussing its political subject.
examples.note: The analysis explains the work’s aesthetic organization through features directly present in its arrangement.

commonMisreadings: Formalism does not mean that an artwork must lack meaning; it means meaning is not the primary evaluative basis.

concepts.name: Formalism in mathematics
concepts.summary: Formalism in mathematics treats mathematical practice as manipulation of symbols according to stipulated rules, with consistency as a central concern.
concepts.body: Mathematical formalism treats mathematics as the manipulation of symbols according to explicit rules, emphasizing consistency and proof within formal systems. On this view, a proof shows that a formula follows from axioms by permitted steps, as in deriving a theorem from the rules of arithmetic. The position helps clarify what mathematical rigor requires, but a purely symbolic picture faces questions about why mathematics applies so effectively to the physical world and what mathematical statements mean. Formalists differ over whether mathematics is merely a game or a useful structural practice.

examples.text: In a formal arithmetic system, a proof is a finite sequence of formulas each licensed by an axiom or inference rule.
examples.note: The proof’s validity depends on syntactic derivability rather than intuitive reference to numbers.

commonMisreadings: Formalism is not the claim that mathematicians never use intuition or interpretation in practice.

concepts.name: Foundationalism
concepts.summary: Foundationalism is the epistemological view that some beliefs are basic and support other justified beliefs without depending on them.
concepts.body: Foundationalism says that some beliefs are justified without being inferred from other beliefs, and that these basic beliefs help support the rest of what a person knows. A belief that one is in pain may be basic because it is directly felt; the belief that a distant storm is approaching may depend on instruments and testimony. The theory offers an answer to the regress of reasons, but must explain which beliefs can be basic and how their support extends to complex claims. Competing coherentist views treat justification as mutual support among beliefs.

examples.text: A foundationalist may hold that a present perceptual experience directly justifies belief that a red object is visible.
examples.note: That perceptual belief is treated as an immediate support from which further beliefs can be inferred.

commonMisreadings: Foundationalism differs from coherentism, which makes mutual fit within a belief system central.

concepts.name: Four noble truths
concepts.summary: The Four Noble Truths state that suffering or unsatisfactoriness exists, has craving as a cause, can cease, and has a path leading to cessation.
concepts.body: The Four Noble Truths organize the Buddha’s teaching around dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness), its arising through craving and ignorance, its cessation, and a path of practice leading to cessation. A person may notice that clinging to a desired outcome intensifies distress, and train in ethical conduct, meditation, and insight to loosen that pattern. The truths function as a diagnosis and prescription, not merely a pessimistic claim that life is bad. Buddhist schools interpret their scope and practice differently, and “suffering” can understate the wider sense of dukkha.

examples.text: The Noble Eightfold Path is presented as the practical path associated with ending suffering.
examples.note: It supplies the fourth truth’s prescribed route rather than merely describing Buddhist ethics in general.

commonMisreadings: The first truth does not assert that every experience is equally painful; it concerns pervasive unsatisfactoriness and vulnerability.

concepts.name: Four-dimensionalism
concepts.summary: Four-dimensionalism is the metaphysical view that objects extend through time as well as through the three spatial dimensions.
concepts.body: Four-dimensionalism treats an object as extended through time as well as space: a person is a whole made up of temporal parts, much as a road has spatial segments. The child and adult are stages of one life, analogous to different cross-sections of a spacetime object. This account can explain change without saying that one and the same part both has and lacks a property. It contrasts with three-dimensionalism, where objects persist wholly through time, and raises questions about identity, responsibility, and which temporal parts count as oneself.

examples.text: A four-dimensionalist can describe a tree as a spacetime worm containing distinct temporal parts across its life.
examples.note: The tree’s change is represented as differences among temporal parts rather than alteration of one wholly present object.

commonMisreadings: Four-dimensionalism is not the claim that physical space has four spatial dimensions.

concepts.name: Frankfurt cases
concepts.summary: Frankfurt cases are thought experiments in which an agent acts freely even though a counterfactual mechanism would have prevented alternative action if needed.
concepts.body: Frankfurt cases are thought experiments intended to show that moral responsibility may not require the ability to do otherwise. A controller stands ready to force a person’s choice if they begin to choose differently, but the person independently makes the desired choice, so the controller never intervenes. The agent seems responsible despite lacking a live alternative. Critics question whether the setup truly removes alternatives or whether responsibility depends on the actual sequence of causes. These cases sharpen the debate between alternative possibilities and responsibility for how an action was produced.

examples.text: A hidden controller would intervene only if Jones began choosing differently, but Jones chooses for his own reasons and the controller never acts.
examples.note: Because the intervention is inactive, the actual choice appears responsible despite the absence of a live alternative.

commonMisreadings: A Frankfurt case is not simply any deterministic scenario; its distinctive feature is the nonintervening backup mechanism.

concepts.name: Frankfurt School
concepts.summary: The Frankfurt School was a tradition of critical social theory associated with the Institute for Social Research and analyses of capitalism, culture, and domination.
concepts.body: The Frankfurt School refers to critical theorists linked to the Institute for Social Research, including Adorno, Horkheimer, and Marcuse. They studied how capitalism, mass culture, and administration can shape desires and reproduce domination even without direct force. A culture industry that packages entertainment as standardized choice, for example, may encourage passive consumption while appearing to offer freedom. The tradition draws on Marx, Freud, and other sources; it is not a single doctrine, and critics dispute its pessimism and its account of popular culture.

examples.text: Adorno and Horkheimer’s analysis of the culture industry examines how mass-produced entertainment can reproduce social conformity.
examples.note: The example connects cultural production with the maintenance of power, a characteristic Frankfurt School concern.

commonMisreadings: The name does not refer to a university department or a single uniform doctrine.

concepts.name: Free variable
concepts.summary: A free variable is a variable occurrence not bound by a quantifier or another binding operator within its scope.
concepts.body: A variable occurrence is free when no quantifier or binding operator governs it within the formula’s scope. In “P(x) and ∀y Q(y),” x is free, while y is bound by the universal quantifier. The distinction matters because a sentence with a free variable is more like a condition awaiting an assignment than a complete truth claim. Substituting values or adding a quantifier can change the formula’s meaning, so variable scope must be tracked carefully in proofs and programming languages.

examples.text: In “x is taller than y,” both x and y are free if no quantifier governs them.
examples.note: Their values must be supplied by an assignment before the formula receives a truth value.

commonMisreadings: A free variable is not the same as a variable that happens to be unquantified in an informal sentence.

concepts.name: Free will
concepts.summary: Free will is the capacity to exercise control over choices or actions in a way relevant to agency and responsibility.
concepts.body: Free will is the kind of control over action that could make a person responsible for choosing and acting. Theories disagree about what that control requires: compatibilists allow freedom within a causally determined world when action follows the agent’s reasons without coercion, while libertarians require genuine indeterminism. Someone signing a contract under a credible threat acts differently from someone choosing freely, even if both actions have causes. The concept matters to praise, blame, and law, but “free” can refer to distinct abilities such as alternative choice or self-governance.

examples.text: A person who considers reasons and voluntarily signs a contract is commonly described as exercising free will.
examples.note: The decision is attributed to the person’s deliberation rather than to coercion or reflex.

commonMisreadings: Free will is not identical to doing whatever one desires, since desires may be manipulated or compulsive.

concepts.name: Freedom
concepts.summary: Freedom is the condition of having meaningful scope to act, choose, or develop without unjustified constraint.
concepts.body: Freedom is meaningful scope to act, choose, and develop without unjustified constraint, and can also include participation in collective self-rule. A person may have formal permission to speak but lack practical freedom if employers can retaliate without recourse. Negative liberty emphasizes absence of interference; positive accounts ask whether people have the capacities and conditions needed to direct their lives. These dimensions can conflict: regulation may restrict one person’s choices while protecting another’s. Any claim about freedom should specify whose options, which constraints, and what standard of justification are at stake.

examples.text: A worker is freer when leaving a job is legally permitted and economically feasible than when exit is formally legal but impossible.
examples.note: The example shows that formal noninterference can differ from practical power to act.

commonMisreadings: Freedom is not equivalent to unlimited choice, because social rules can protect everyone’s agency.

concepts.name: Freedom of association
concepts.summary: Freedom of association is the liberty to form, join, maintain, or leave groups for lawful shared purposes.
concepts.body: Freedom of association protects people’s ability to form, join, maintain, or leave groups for shared purposes. Workers can organize a union, neighbors can create a community association, and a person can withdraw from either. The right supports political participation and personal relationships, but it can conflict with anti-discrimination rules or the rights of people excluded from powerful organizations. Its scope depends on the group’s function and the jurisdiction’s law; it is not an unlimited entitlement for every private group to exercise public authority without accountability.

examples.text: Employees forming a union exercise freedom of association by organizing around shared workplace interests.
examples.note: Their coordinated membership creates a group through which they pursue a common purpose.

commonMisreadings: It does not guarantee every group access to public resources or exemption from generally applicable law.

concepts.name: Freedom of expression
concepts.summary: Freedom of expression is the right to communicate ideas, information, opinions, and artistic or symbolic messages without unjustified state restriction.
concepts.body: Freedom of expression protects communication through speech, writing, art, and symbolic acts from unjustified restriction, especially by government. A protester burning a flag communicates a political message through conduct rather than words. The principle supports debate and criticism, but does not mean every expression is immune from regulation: threats, defamation, and incitement may be treated differently, with legal limits varying by country. The hard question is how to protect dissent while addressing concrete harms without giving authorities broad power to suppress unpopular views.

examples.text: Publishing criticism of a government policy in a newspaper is an exercise of freedom of expression.
examples.note: The communication conveys a political opinion, a core protected use of expressive liberty.

commonMisreadings: It is not a guarantee that private platforms must publish every message.

concepts.name: Freedom of religion
concepts.summary: Freedom of religion protects a person’s liberty to hold, change, practice, or decline religious beliefs.
concepts.body: Freedom of religion protects the liberty to adopt, change, practice, or reject religious beliefs. It can protect a person who wears religious clothing at work as well as someone who leaves a religious community. The right includes both belief and outward conduct, though conduct may be limited when it conflicts with others’ rights or neutral laws. It also protects nonbelief; state neutrality should not privilege religion over conscience. Different legal systems draw the line between accommodation, public order, and equal treatment in different ways.

examples.text: A state that permits a citizen to convert and attend worship without penalty protects religious freedom.
examples.note: The citizen’s belief and practice remain voluntary rather than imposed by government.

commonMisreadings: Religious freedom does not automatically exempt conduct from neutral laws that protect others.

concepts.name: Friendship
concepts.summary: Friendship is a voluntary relationship involving mutual goodwill, personal concern, and shared recognition between people.
concepts.body: Friendship is a voluntary relationship marked by mutual goodwill, personal concern, and recognition of one another as particular people. Friends may support each other during illness, share activities, and tell each other difficult truths because each matters to the other. The relationship differs from a purely transactional exchange, though reciprocity need not be equal at every moment. Friendship can create obligations without contract or law, and may conflict with impartial duties when loyalty is used to excuse favoritism or conceal wrongdoing.

examples.text: Two neighbors who reliably support one another and enjoy candid conversation exemplify friendship.
examples.note: Their relationship includes mutual concern and companionship rather than a merely transactional exchange.

commonMisreadings: Friendship is not identical to familiarity, popularity, or any relationship that happens to feel pleasant.

concepts.name: Functionalism in philosophy of mind
concepts.summary: Functionalism in philosophy of mind identifies mental states by the causal roles they play among inputs, internal states, and behavior.
concepts.body: Functionalism identifies a mental state by the role it plays among sensory inputs, other mental states, and behavior, rather than by the material it is made of. Pain, for example, is typically caused by injury, produces distress and a desire to avoid harm, and leads to protective behavior. A different physical system could realize the same role. This allows minds to be multiply realizable, but critics ask whether function captures the felt quality of pain or whether a system could perform the role without conscious experience.

examples.text: A functionalist can regard an appropriately organized silicon system as capable of pain if it occupies the relevant causal role.
examples.note: The theory defines pain by its response and interaction pattern rather than by biological tissue alone.

commonMisreadings: Functionalism is not behaviorism, because it includes internal causal states rather than only observable behavior.

concepts.name: Fundamentalism
concepts.summary: Fundamentalism is a movement that insists on authoritative foundational doctrines and often opposes perceived dilution by modern interpretation.
concepts.body: Fundamentalism is a movement that treats certain doctrines or authorities as foundational and resists interpretations seen as diluting them. Religious fundamentalists may insist that core scriptures or teachings govern modern life, often in response to social change. The term has historical roots in early twentieth-century Protestant movements but is now applied more broadly, sometimes imprecisely. It should describe a specific stance toward authority and interpretation, not serve as a synonym for devout belief or extremism; movements labeled fundamentalist differ significantly in doctrine and politics.

examples.text: Christian fundamentalism in the early twentieth century defended selected doctrines against liberal Protestant reinterpretation.
examples.note: The movement treated those doctrines as nonnegotiable foundations of religious authority.

commonMisreadings: Fundamentalism does not simply mean intense religious commitment or literal reading in every context.

concepts.name: Fuzzy logic
concepts.summary: Fuzzy logic represents degrees of membership or truth between the binary values of completely false and completely true.
concepts.body: Fuzzy logic represents degrees of truth or membership rather than forcing every claim into simply true or false. A temperature of 24 degrees might count as “warm” to degree 0.7 and “hot” to degree 0.3 under a chosen membership function. This is useful for control systems that handle gradual categories, such as adjusting air conditioning smoothly. The degrees are not automatically probabilities or uncertainty about a crisp fact; they model how strongly something belongs to a vague category. The choice of membership rules must fit the application.

examples.text: A thermostat can use the rule that if a room is somewhat cold, heating should increase moderately.
examples.note: The rule handles gradual temperature categories instead of forcing a sharp cold-versus-not-cold boundary.

commonMisreadings: Fuzzy truth is not the same as probability, which measures uncertainty about whether a proposition is true.

concepts.name: Game theory
concepts.summary: Game theory studies strategic situations in which each participant’s outcome depends partly on the choices of others.
concepts.body: Game theory models strategic situations where each participant’s outcome depends on their own choices and those of others. Two firms deciding whether to lower prices must anticipate how a rival will respond; the best move depends on those expectations. Models specify players, available actions, payoffs, and information, then analyze incentives and stable outcomes. They clarify conflict and cooperation but simplify motives and context. A mathematically stable strategy is not necessarily fair or realistic, and predictions depend on whether the model captures what participants actually know and value.

examples.text: In the prisoner’s dilemma, each prisoner’s best individual response can produce a worse joint outcome than cooperation.
examples.note: The payoff structure makes the conflict between individual incentives and collective benefit explicit.

commonMisreadings: Game theory is not limited to recreational games or necessarily to competitive situations.

concepts.name: Genealogical critique
concepts.summary: Genealogical critique investigates how a value, category, or practice emerged and acquired authority.
concepts.body: Genealogical critique traces how a concept, value, or institution emerged and gained authority, often to reveal interests and power concealed by claims that it is timeless or natural. A history of modern categories of normality might show how medical, legal, and administrative practices helped define them. The method can unsettle taken-for-granted standards without proving that every product of history is false or unjust. Its force depends on accurate historical evidence and an argument linking origins to present meaning or effects; origin alone does not refute a belief.

examples.text: Trace how a punishment practice became described as rehabilitation and ask which institutions benefited from the change.
examples.note: The inquiry examines how a justification became authoritative.

commonMisreadings: Inferring falsity solely from an origin would be a genetic fallacy.

concepts.name: General will
concepts.summary: Rousseau's idea of a people's common political will directed toward the shared conditions of freedom rather than the sum of private preferences.
concepts.body:
Rousseau's general will is the will directed toward the common good, not the sum of private preferences or the decision of whatever majority happens to prevail. Citizens participate as equals when they legislate for conditions they could accept as members of a shared political body. The idea tries to reconcile freedom with obligation: obeying a law one has jointly authorized can be a form of self-government rather than external submission.

The danger is interpretive authority. Leaders can claim to know the general will and silence dissenters as selfish or mistaken. Rousseau distinguishes the general will from all actual votes, but that distinction can either correct factional domination or authorize paternalism. The concept is most defensible when paired with equal membership, public justification, revisability, and safeguards against anyone monopolizing the definition of the common good.

examples.text: Citizens adopt a tax that applies by a public rule and funds services all can use, even though each household would prefer to pay less.
examples.note: The example contrasts a general law with a private bargain that privileges one group.

commonMisreadings: The general will is not identical to a simple majority vote or to the private will of a leader.
Rousseau's claim that citizens can be forced to be free is not a license for any government to label coercion freedom.
criticisms: Critics argue that the concept can erase plural interests and provide authoritarian governments with a vocabulary for claiming that dissenters misunderstand the common good.

lookalikes.note: The general will is part of Rousseau's account of legitimate collective authority, but it is a substantive standard for law rather than a mere agreement to obey.

concepts.name: Generation effect
concepts.summary: The generation effect is the memory advantage that occurs when people produce information themselves rather than merely read it.
concepts.body: The generation effect is the memory advantage for information a person actively produces over information merely read or heard. Trying to complete “hot and ___” may make “cold” easier to remember than seeing the pair printed. Generating an answer requires retrieval and elaboration, giving memory additional cues. The benefit varies with task and difficulty: a wrong answer can be remembered, and generation can take longer than passive review. The effect supports practice methods that require learners to recall or construct information rather than only reread notes.

examples.text: A student usually remembers a definition better after completing a missing word than after copying the completed sentence.
examples.note: The act of generating the word adds an active encoding operation that supports later recall.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean every generated answer is accurate or better than every form of study.

concepts.name: Georgism
concepts.summary: Georgism is the economic view that individuals should retain the value they create while socially generated land value should be captured for public benefit.
concepts.body: Georgism argues that people should keep the value they create through work and investment, while the value of land—which arises largely from location and social development—should be shared through public revenue. A parcel near a new railway becomes more valuable partly because the community built the transport network, not because its owner created the location. A land-value tax aims to recapture that socially generated value while discouraging idle landholding. Georgists differ on policy details, and measuring land value separately from buildings is a practical challenge.

examples.text: A city may fund services with a land-value tax that charges more for a centrally located vacant lot than for a remote lot of equal size.
examples.note: The tax targets location value created by community activity while avoiding a direct penalty on construction.

commonMisreadings: Georgism is not a general ban on private property in land.

concepts.name: German idealism
concepts.summary: German idealism is an early modern philosophical movement emphasizing the conditions under which reason, subjectivity, and freedom structure experience and reality.
concepts.body: German idealism is a movement, especially associated with Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel, that examines how reason and subjectivity shape the conditions of experience and knowledge. Kant argues that the mind contributes organizing forms through which objects can be experienced, rather than simply receiving a ready-made world. Later thinkers develop accounts of freedom, nature, and history. The movement is not the claim that individuals invent external reality at will; it concerns the relation between mind, concepts, and what can count as an object of knowledge.

examples.text: Hegel’s account of history as the development of freedom is a German idealist approach to social and metaphysical change.
examples.note: It treats rational self-development as central to understanding both thought and historical reality.

commonMisreadings: German idealism is not one claim that only private ideas exist; several of its thinkers defended objective structures.

concepts.name: Gettier cases
concepts.summary: Gettier cases are examples in which a person has justified true belief but seems not to know because the belief is true by luck.
concepts.body: Gettier cases present a person whose belief is justified and true but appears true by luck, challenging the idea that knowledge is simply justified true belief. Smith sees a job candidate with ten coins in a pocket get hired and infers that the person who gets the job has ten coins. By coincidence, Smith himself gets the job and has ten coins, making his conclusion true for the wrong reason. Such cases motivate adding a condition that rules out epistemic luck, though philosophers disagree about which condition succeeds.

examples.text: A person sees a stopped clock showing the correct time and believes it is noon, but the clock is correct only by coincidence.
examples.note: The belief is true and perceptually supported, yet its truth is disconnected from the evidence in the relevant way.

commonMisreadings: A Gettier case is not merely a false justified belief, because its defining conclusion is true.

concepts.name: Gettier problem
concepts.summary: The Gettier problem is the challenge to the claim that knowledge is simply justified true belief.
concepts.body: The Gettier problem is the challenge raised by cases where someone has a justified true belief that still seems not to be knowledge because the truth is accidental. A person may read a stopped clock that happens to show the correct time and form a justified belief, yet the belief’s accuracy is luck. This undermines the traditional analysis of knowledge as justified true belief and prompts theories to add reliability, causal connection, or safety conditions. The problem is not that justification is irrelevant, but that justification plus truth may leave a gap.

examples.text: The stopped-clock example motivates searching for a no-luck, causal, or safety condition on knowledge.
examples.note: The problem arises because truth, belief, and justification can all be present while knowledge still seems absent.

commonMisreadings: It does not show that justification is irrelevant to knowledge; it shows that the three-part analysis is insufficient.

concepts.name: Global justice
concepts.summary: Global justice concerns the fair distribution of rights, duties, resources, and political consideration across national borders.
concepts.body: Global justice asks what fairness and moral responsibility require across national borders, including the distribution of resources, rights, and political power. A supply chain may bring consumers low prices while workers abroad face unsafe conditions; the question is whether distant beneficiaries and governments owe remedies. Some theories ground duties in shared humanity, others in institutions or causal contribution. Global justice extends debates about equality and rights beyond a single state, while disputes remain over who has authority to enforce obligations and how duties should be shared.

examples.text: A global justice argument may require affluent states to reduce emissions because poorer populations bear disproportionate climate harms.
examples.note: The proposed duty crosses borders and responds to unequal effects on people worldwide.

commonMisreadings: Global justice is broader than international charity, because it also examines institutions and structural power.

concepts.name: Globalism
concepts.summary: Globalism is a perspective that emphasizes worldwide interdependence and cooperation across national boundaries.
concepts.body: Globalism is a perspective that emphasizes worldwide interdependence and cooperation among countries and peoples. Climate change, financial crises, and disease spread across borders, so a state’s actions can affect people far away. Globalist approaches favor institutions and agreements that coordinate responses to shared problems. The term can describe analysis or political advocacy and is not synonymous with globalization, the process of increasing cross-border flows. Supporters stress cooperation; critics warn that global institutions can lack democratic accountability or weaken local control.

examples.text: Support for an international climate agreement is a globalist policy orientation.
examples.note: The agreement addresses a shared planetary problem through coordinated action among states.

commonMisreadings: Globalism is not identical to globalization, which describes processes rather than a normative or political viewpoint.

concepts.name: Gnosticism
concepts.summary: Gnosticism refers to religious movements that make salvific knowledge of divine reality central and often portray the material world as deficient or alienating.
concepts.body: Gnosticism refers to diverse ancient religious movements in which salvific knowledge—gnosis—of divine reality is central, often alongside a view that ordinary material existence is flawed or alienating. Some texts portray a transcendent divine source and a lower creator associated with the world. These movements were not one unified church, and scholars debate which groups belong under the label. The concept helps describe a family of teachings about knowledge and liberation, but should not be used loosely for any secretive or anti-material belief.

examples.text: The Valentinian tradition presented spiritual knowledge as a route toward restoration to the divine realm.
examples.note: Its emphasis on revealed knowledge and a problematic material order fits recurring Gnostic themes.

commonMisreadings: Gnosticism is not simply any religion that values knowledge or private spiritual experience.

concepts.name: Goodhart's law
concepts.summary: Goodhart’s law states that when a measure becomes a target, it can cease to be a good measure.
concepts.body: Goodhart’s law warns that once a measure becomes a target, people may change behavior in ways that make it a poorer measure of the goal. If a school is judged only by test scores, it may teach narrowly to the test, raising scores without improving broad understanding. The mechanism is strategic adaptation: the incentive changes what is measured. The maxim is not a mathematical law that metrics always fail; it signals a risk to monitor and suggests using multiple measures, audits, and attention to unintended behavior.

examples.text: If a hospital rewards low average treatment time, staff may discharge patients prematurely to improve the metric.
examples.note: The metric becomes gameable and no longer reliably represents quality of care.

commonMisreadings: The law is not a mathematical theorem that every metric inevitably fails when used as a target.

concepts.name: Google effect
concepts.summary: The Google effect is the tendency to remember information less well when people expect to be able to retrieve it online.
concepts.body: The Google effect is the tendency to remember less of some information when people expect it to remain available online, while remembering where or how to retrieve it. A student may forget a trivia fact but recall which site contained it. Offloading memory can be efficient, freeing attention for other tasks, rather than simply damaging cognition. The effect depends on the material and expectation of future access; it does not show that internet users lose the ability to remember important information generally.

examples.text: After searching a fact repeatedly, a student may remember the website location but not the fact itself.
examples.note: External availability reduces the perceived need to encode the fact in durable memory.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to ordinary forgetting caused by time or lack of attention.

concepts.name: Governance
concepts.summary: Governance is the process by which collective affairs are directed, regulated, and held accountable through institutions and practices.
concepts.body: Governance is the way collective affairs are directed and coordinated through rules, institutions, decisions, and accountability. A city’s transport system is governed not only by elected officials but also by agencies, contracts, regulators, and public consultation. The term captures how authority operates, including outside a single government. Good governance often requires transparency, participation, and enforceable responsibility, but those standards can conflict or be unevenly realized. Identifying governance arrangements helps explain who makes decisions and who can challenge them.

examples.text: A city’s governance includes elected officials, agencies, public consultations, courts, and service contractors.
examples.note: These actors jointly shape decisions and accountability rather than government alone issuing every action.

commonMisreadings: Governance is broader than government, which usually denotes the formal public authority.

concepts.name: Green politics
concepts.summary: Green politics is a political tradition that prioritizes ecological sustainability, interdependence, social justice, and participatory democracy.
concepts.body: Green politics is a political tradition that places ecological limits and sustainability alongside social justice and democratic participation. A city plan might prioritize public transit, compact housing, and clean energy while considering who bears costs and who benefits. Green politics treats environmental degradation as connected to economic organization and unequal power, not only individual consumer choices. Movements differ on growth, technology, and state action; ecological concern by itself does not determine one policy program.

examples.text: A green platform may combine renewable energy investment, public transit, habitat protection, and community decision-making.
examples.note: The package links ecological limits with social and democratic reforms rather than treating pollution as an isolated technical issue.

commonMisreadings: Green politics is not reducible to conservation alone, because it includes institutional and distributive concerns.

concepts.name: Grounding
concepts.summary: Grounding is a metaphysical relation in which one fact or entity explains why another exists or obtains.
concepts.body: Grounding is a metaphysical relation in which one fact obtains in virtue of another, a relation often described as “because” rather than as efficient causation. A particular object’s being red may be grounded in its surface reflecting light in certain ways, on a physicalist account. Grounding is used to explain dependence between levels, such as social facts on facts about people and institutions. Philosophers disagree about whether it is a distinct relation or a useful explanatory pattern, and a grounding claim needs to specify what depends on what.

examples.text: The fact that a triangle has three sides is grounded in what it is to be a triangle.
examples.note: The definitional nature of triangularity explains the fact without one event causing another.

commonMisreadings: Grounding is not simply causal explanation, because causes operate through temporal or productive dependence.

concepts.name: Groupthink
concepts.summary: Groupthink is a pattern in which a cohesive group suppresses dissent and critical evaluation in pursuit of apparent agreement.
concepts.body: Groupthink is a group decision pattern in which pressure for unanimity suppresses dissent and careful evaluation. A team may approve a risky launch because members assume everyone else agrees and no one wants to appear disloyal. The result can be false confidence, ignored alternatives, and poor risk assessment. Cohesion alone does not cause groupthink; leadership style, isolation, and decision procedures matter. Inviting independent review and assigning someone to challenge assumptions can reduce the risk without treating all consensus as suspect.

examples.text: A committee may ignore warnings about a failed launch because members fear appearing disloyal.
examples.note: Pressure for unanimity prevents the group from examining serious contrary evidence.

commonMisreadings: Groupthink is not the same as ordinary consensus reached after open disagreement.

concepts.name: Guild socialism
concepts.summary: Guild socialism is a socialist theory proposing worker control of industry through self-governing occupational guilds coordinated within a democratic state.
concepts.body: Guild socialism proposes that workers govern industries through democratic, self-managing occupational guilds, coordinated with a democratic state. A transport guild might manage its industry while public bodies set broad social priorities and mediate competing claims. The model seeks to replace both private capitalist control and centralized state management with worker participation. It faces questions about consumers, non-workers, and coordination across sectors. Historical advocates differed on how guilds would relate to parliament and public ownership, so it is a family of proposals rather than a single blueprint.

examples.text: A transport guild could manage rail operations through elected workers while a public council coordinates regional needs.
examples.note: The arrangement gives producers institutional control while retaining broader democratic coordination.

commonMisreadings: Guild socialism is not simply trade-union bargaining within an otherwise unchanged capitalist system.

concepts.name: Haecceitism
concepts.summary: Haecceitism is the view that individual things possess primitive nonqualitative identities or thisnesses.
concepts.body: Haecceitism is the view that an individual has a primitive identity—its “thisness”—that is not reducible to its qualitative properties. Imagine two possible worlds containing qualitatively identical people who differ only in which individual occupies which place; a haecceitist may say the difference is real because the individuals’ identities differ. This matters to theories of possible worlds and identity. Critics argue that if no qualitative fact changes, the supposed distinction may be empty or unknowable.

examples.text: A haecceitist may say two intrinsically identical particles are nevertheless distinct because each has its own thisness.
examples.note: Their numerical difference is not reduced to a difference in observable qualities.

commonMisreadings: Haecceitism differs from the identity of indiscernibles, which denies such possibility under its strongest reading.

concepts.name: Haecceity
concepts.summary: Haecceity is the nonqualitative property or principle that makes an individual that particular individual.
concepts.body: Haecceity is the nonqualitative feature that makes an individual the particular individual it is, sometimes called its thisness. Two perfectly similar keys could share every observable quality while remaining numerically distinct; haecceity is proposed to account for that distinctness. The idea separates identity from descriptive features such as shape or material. It is controversial because a primitive thisness can seem mysterious and difficult to detect, and many philosophers hold that ordinary identity needs no additional property beyond the object itself.

examples.text: Socrates’s haecceity would be what makes him Socrates even if another person matched his qualitative description.
examples.note: It individuates the subject independently of general features such as height or occupation.

commonMisreadings: Haecceity is not simply a person’s distinctive collection of qualitative traits.

concepts.name: Harm principle
concepts.summary: The harm principle holds that coercive interference with a person’s liberty is justified primarily to prevent harm to others.
concepts.body: The harm principle, associated with John Stuart Mill, says coercion over a person is justified primarily to prevent harm to others, not simply for that person’s own good. A government may restrict reckless driving because it endangers others, while Mill would reject banning a harmless personal choice solely to protect the chooser. Applying the principle requires deciding what counts as harm, how direct it must be, and how to treat risks. It limits paternalism but does not automatically resolve disputes about offense, public goods, or vulnerable people.

examples.text: A law against reckless driving can be justified because the conduct creates an unjustifiable risk to other road users.
examples.note: The restriction targets danger imposed on others rather than mere moral disapproval of the driver’s choice.

commonMisreadings: The principle does not define every form of harm or settle all disputes about paternalism.

concepts.name: Hawthorne effect
concepts.summary: The Hawthorne effect is the change in behavior that occurs because people know they are being observed or studied.
concepts.body: The Hawthorne effect is the possibility that people alter their behavior because they know they are being observed or studied. Employees may work more carefully while a researcher is present, making a workplace intervention seem more effective than it is under ordinary conditions.
