concepts.name: Introspection
concepts.summary: Introspection is the directed examination of one's own conscious experiences or mental states.
concepts.body: Introspection is attending to one’s own conscious experiences or mental states. A person may notice that they feel anxious before a presentation or examine how a color appears to them. Introspection can provide first-person evidence, but it is not infallible: people may misidentify motives, overlook influences, or lack concepts for what they feel. Psychological experiments compare self-reports with behavior and other measures. The method is central to philosophy of mind, where the reliability and limits of access to one’s own experience remain disputed.

examples.text: Someone attends to the painful quality of a headache and reports its intensity.
examples.note: The person examines an occurring experience from the first-person perspective.

commonMisreadings: Introspection is not simply thinking about oneself in general because it specifically targets one's own mental states.

concepts.name: Intuitionism in mathematics
concepts.summary: Intuitionism in mathematics is the philosophy that mathematical objects and proofs depend on constructive mental or demonstrable activity.
concepts.body: Mathematical intuitionism holds that mathematical objects and truths are grounded in constructive mental activity, so existence claims require a method for constructing an example. A proof that a number exists should, on this view, provide a way to find or specify it rather than rely only on ruling out its nonexistence. This stance reshapes accepted proof methods and rejects some classical arguments that use unrestricted excluded middle. It is a philosophy of mathematics, not the claim that mathematics is mere subjective intuition; rigorous construction remains essential.

examples.text: An intuitionist accepts an existential theorem only when a construction can produce an example satisfying the stated condition.
examples.note: The proof supplies the object rather than merely ruling out its nonexistence.

commonMisreadings: Mathematical intuitionism is not the same as trusting informal hunches because it imposes formal constructive standards.

concepts.name: Intuitionistic logic
concepts.summary: Intuitionistic logic is a logic that treats a proposition as established only when a proof or construction is available.
concepts.body: Intuitionistic logic interprets a proof of a proposition as a construction establishing it, and therefore does not accept every classical inference. A proof of “A or B” must establish A or establish B, rather than merely show that denying both leads to contradiction. This changes the status of the law of excluded middle for unproven propositions. The logic is useful in constructive mathematics and computer science, where proofs can correspond to programs. Its meaning differs from classical logic; it is not simply a weaker system with careless reasoning.

examples.text: The formula P or not-P is not automatically accepted intuitionistically for an arbitrary unproved proposition P.
examples.note: Neither a proof of P nor a proof that P is impossible has been supplied in the arbitrary case.

commonMisreadings: Intuitionistic logic is not merely classical logic with uncertain truth values because its proof interpretation changes valid inferences.

concepts.name: Investigation of things
concepts.summary: A Confucian practice of extending knowledge by investigating things, affairs, and patterns through disciplined attention and ethical cultivation.
concepts.body:
In Zhu Xi's interpretation, investigation of things is a cumulative practice of learning patterns through attention to texts, affairs, relationships, and one's own conduct. Knowledge is not complete when a fact has been collected; it becomes adequate when understanding changes perception and action. Studying the duties of friendship, for example, involves examining cases, inherited explanations, and one's motives until the relevant order becomes practically intelligible.

The method is connected to li but not identical with it. Li is the pattern to be understood; investigation is a disciplined way of extending knowledge of such patterns. Wang Yangming objected that moral knowing is already active in conscience and that endless outward inquiry can become evasion. The disagreement concerns where learning begins and how knowledge, attention, and action should be integrated.

examples.text: A student studies how a family obligation works in concrete cases, compares classical discussions, and changes conduct when the relevant pattern becomes clear.
examples.note: The example joins inquiry to moral practice rather than treating knowledge of a thing as merely descriptive.

commonMisreadings: Investigation of things does not mean modern laboratory science alone and does not reduce Confucian learning to collecting facts.
Zhu Xi did not invent the phrase; he gave it a systematic interpretation within Neo-Confucianism.
criticisms: Wang Yangming and other critics argue that exhaustive external investigation can postpone moral action because principle is also accessible through reflective self-cultivation.

lookalikes.note: Investigation is a method of learning patterns; li is the ordering principle that the investigation seeks to understand.

concepts.name: Irreversibility
concepts.summary: Irreversibility is the feature of a process or change that cannot be completely undone under the relevant conditions.
concepts.body: A process is irreversible when it cannot be completely undone under the relevant conditions. Mixing ink into water cannot practically be reversed to recover the original drops, even though physical laws may permit an improbable rearrangement. In thermodynamics, irreversibility is tied to entropy increase; in policy, it may refer to changes such as species extinction that cannot be repaired. The qualifier matters: some processes are reversible in principle but not in practice. Identifying irreversibility helps assess costs, one-way decisions, and the limits of restoration.

examples.text: A glass shattered on a floor does not spontaneously return to its original form.
examples.note: The reverse arrangement is physically possible only through external intervention and is overwhelmingly unlikely microscopically.

commonMisreadings: Irreversibility is not the same as practical inconvenience because the relevant issue is whether the prior state can be restored in principle or under specified laws.

concepts.name: Islamic occasionalism
concepts.summary: Islamic occasionalism is the theological view that God directly creates each event and that created things have no independent causal efficacy.
concepts.body: Islamic occasionalism is a theological view, developed by thinkers such as al-Ghazali, that God directly creates events and that created things have no independent causal power. Fire touching cotton is the occasion on which God creates burning, rather than fire efficiently causing it by its own power. The view emphasizes divine sovereignty and challenges assumptions about necessary natural causation. It should not be reduced to the idea that events have no regular patterns; regularities can reflect customary divine action. Philosophers debate how this account explains human agency and scientific laws.

examples.text: When fire touches cotton, God creates the burning on the occasion of contact rather than fire autonomously causing it.
examples.note: The contact supplies an occasion for the divine act, not an efficient cause belonging to fire.

commonMisreadings: Occasionalism is not the denial that events follow regular patterns; it denies that created things produce them independently.

concepts.name: Islamism
concepts.summary: Islamism is a set of political ideologies that seek to organize government and public life according to an interpretation of Islam.
concepts.body: Islamism refers to political movements that seek to shape government and public life according to interpretations of Islam. Some movements pursue electoral participation and social services; others advocate revolutionary change or authoritarian rule. Because the category includes diverse organizations and ideologies, it should not be treated as synonymous with Islam, Muslim identity, or violence. Analysis should specify the group’s goals, methods, and context. The term is politically contested, and scholars differ over whether it best describes religiously inspired politics or a distinct modern ideology.

examples.text: The Muslim Brotherhood's political program is commonly studied as an Islamist movement.
examples.note: It treats Islamic principles as a basis for political organization rather than only private devotion.

commonMisreadings: Islamism is not synonymous with Islam or with ordinary Muslim religious practice.

concepts.name: Iterated game
concepts.summary: An iterated game is a strategic interaction in which the same or related game is played repeatedly by the same participants.
concepts.body: An iterated game repeats a strategic interaction among the same participants, allowing current choices to affect future responses. Two firms that compete repeatedly may avoid a price war today because each expects retaliation in later rounds. Repetition can support cooperation, reputation, or punishment, depending on information and the expected length of the relationship. Results from one-shot games may therefore change when participants meet again. The model assumes particular payoffs and knowledge; real relationships include uncertainty, communication, and power differences that can alter strategy.

examples.text: In an iterated prisoner's dilemma, a player may cooperate today because defection would provoke retaliation in later rounds.
examples.note: The future rounds make the opponent's response strategically relevant to the present choice.

commonMisreadings: An iterated game is not simply a longer one-shot game because the history of prior moves changes incentives.

concepts.name: Jacobinism
concepts.summary: Jacobinism is a revolutionary political tradition associated with the Jacobin Club and the French Revolution's emphasis on centralized republican authority.
concepts.body: Jacobinism is a revolutionary political tradition associated with the Jacobin Club and the French Revolution, often emphasizing popular sovereignty, centralized republican authority, and radical transformation. During the Revolution, Jacobin leaders defended a strong state as necessary to protect the republic from internal and external enemies. Later uses of the label vary, sometimes referring broadly to egalitarian republicanism and sometimes to authoritarian centralization. Historical context matters: calling a policy Jacobin does not by itself show that it reproduces revolutionary terror or the original movement’s aims.

examples.text: The Committee of Public Safety during the Reign of Terror is a historical example linked to Jacobin rule.
examples.note: The committee used centralized emergency power to protect and remake the revolutionary republic.

commonMisreadings: Jacobinism is not equivalent to all French republicanism because its distinctive features include revolutionary centralization and moralized political unity.

concepts.name: Jain anekantavada
concepts.summary: Jain anekantavada is the doctrine that reality is many-sided and that finite statements capture only particular aspects of it.
concepts.body: Anekantavada, a Jain doctrine, holds that reality has many aspects and that any finite statement captures only part of it. The parable of people describing an elephant by touching different parts illustrates how one observer’s account can be partial without being wholly false. Jain thinkers use qualified predication to express the conditions under which a claim holds. The doctrine encourages intellectual humility, but it is not the claim that all contradictory views are equally true; statements must be assessed relative to the aspect and standpoint they address.

examples.text: The claim that a clay pot exists can be true in relation to its substance and false in relation to a particular prior form.
examples.note: Different qualified descriptions track different real aspects or conditions of the same object.

commonMisreadings: Anekantavada is not simple skepticism because it permits context-qualified knowledge rather than denying truth.

concepts.name: Jainism
concepts.summary: Jainism is an Indian religious and philosophical tradition centered on liberation through nonviolence, disciplined conduct, and knowledge.
concepts.body: Jainism is an Indian religious and philosophical tradition that seeks liberation through nonviolence, disciplined conduct, and knowledge. Its central ethical commitment to ahimsa leads practitioners to reduce harm to living beings, while ascetic disciplines aim to free the soul from karmic bondage. Jain communities include monastic and lay paths with differing obligations. The tradition is not simply a form of Hinduism or Buddhism; it has its own scriptures, metaphysics, and history. Its practices vary, but care about the consequences of action is a defining thread.

examples.text: A Jain monk sweeps the path gently to reduce the chance of injuring small organisms.
examples.note: The practice expresses an unusually comprehensive commitment to avoiding harm.

commonMisreadings: Jainism is not a branch of Buddhism because it has distinct doctrines of soul, karma, liberation, and teacher lineage.

concepts.name: Jewish philosophy
concepts.summary: Jewish philosophy is philosophical reflection conducted within or in dialogue with Jewish texts, practices, theology, and historical experience.
concepts.body: Jewish philosophy is philosophical inquiry developed within or in dialogue with Jewish scripture, law, theology, and historical experience. Maimonides, for example, used Aristotelian philosophy to examine divine attributes and religious law, while modern Jewish thinkers respond to secularism and political upheaval. The field spans many periods and positions rather than a single worldview. Its questions often concern how reason, revelation, communal practice, and interpretation relate. A philosopher’s Jewish identity alone does not determine their position; the engagement with Jewish intellectual traditions is central.

examples.text: Maimonides's Guide for the Perplexed interprets Jewish theology through Aristotelian philosophical concepts.
examples.note: The work uses classical philosophy to clarify problems arising from Jewish religious commitments.

commonMisreadings: Jewish philosophy is not a single doctrine because medieval, modern, and contemporary thinkers disagree substantially.

concepts.name: Justice
concepts.summary: Justice is the normative ideal of giving people their due and arranging social relations fairly.
concepts.body: Justice is the ideal of giving people what they are due and structuring social relations fairly. A court aims at justice by applying law impartially, while a society may ask whether access to education and healthcare is distributed fairly. Justice can concern procedure, punishment, rights, recognition, and the allocation of benefits and burdens. These dimensions may conflict: equal treatment can preserve unequal starting conditions. The concept therefore names a standard for judgment, but theories disagree about whether fairness requires equality, desert, need, liberty, or repair.

examples.text: A court applies the same evidentiary rule to both a wealthy defendant and a poor defendant.
examples.note: Equal procedural treatment expresses one account of fairness in adjudication.

commonMisreadings: Justice is broader than kindness because a just arrangement can require impartial rules rather than personal benevolence.

concepts.name: Justice as fairness
concepts.summary: Justice as fairness is John Rawls's theory that principles of justice should be chosen for a society's basic structure from a fair hypothetical choice situation.
concepts.body: Rawls’s justice as fairness asks what principles people would choose for society’s basic institutions if they selected them behind a veil of ignorance, unaware of their own class, talents, or social position. The device is meant to prevent people from designing rules to favor themselves. Rawls argues that equal basic liberties and fair opportunity should be protected, with inequalities benefiting the least advantaged. The theory is a framework for political principles, not a prediction of actual bargaining. Critics dispute its assumptions, its treatment of culture, and the priority it assigns to different goods.

examples.text: Behind the veil, representatives may choose a principle protecting the least advantaged because they do not know their future social position.
examples.note: The information restriction makes the choice fair by preventing bargaining from inherited advantage.

commonMisreadings: Justice as fairness is not the claim that every outcome must be identical because Rawls permits inequalities that benefit the least advantaged under fair conditions.

concepts.name: Justification
concepts.summary: Justification is the support that makes a belief, action, or claim appropriate or warranted under a relevant standard.
concepts.body: Justification is the support that makes a belief, action, or claim warranted under a relevant standard. A witness’s consistent testimony and corroborating evidence may justify a court’s provisional conclusion, while a good reason for action might explain why it was permissible. Epistemic, moral, and legal justification use different standards, so the word’s meaning depends on the domain. Justification need not guarantee truth or success: a belief can be well-supported and false, and a justified action can have a bad outcome.

examples.text: A historian justifies dating a document by citing its ink composition, handwriting, and archival provenance.
examples.note: The evidence makes the dating claim warranted rather than a bare guess.

commonMisreadings: Justification does not guarantee truth because a well-supported belief can still be mistaken.

concepts.name: Justified true belief
concepts.summary: Justified true belief is the classical analysis of knowledge as a belief that is true and epistemically justified.
concepts.body: The justified-true-belief analysis says that a person knows a proposition when they believe it, it is true, and they are justified in believing it. Someone who sees a reliable weather report and believes it will rain has a true, supported belief if rain follows. Gettier cases challenge the analysis by showing that luck can make all three conditions hold without knowledge. The account remains historically important because it isolates three intuitive requirements, even though most philosophers accept that an additional condition or a different analysis is needed.

examples.text: A stopped clock gives a person a justified true belief that the time is eight when it happens to be eight.
examples.note: The belief is supported by an apparently reliable clock but is true only by coincidence.

commonMisreadings: Justified true belief is not generally accepted as sufficient for knowledge after Gettier's counterexamples.

concepts.name: Kalam
concepts.summary: Kalam is Islamic theological discourse that uses rational argument to clarify and defend religious doctrines.
concepts.body: Kalam is Islamic theological discourse that uses rational argument to clarify and defend doctrines. The cosmological argument associated with kalam, for example, reasons from the beginning of the universe to a cause beyond it. The discipline developed through debate about divine attributes, human action, and revelation, with schools such as Ash‘arism and Mu‘tazilism taking different positions. Kalam is not simply Islamic philosophy in general, nor does it refer only to one argument. Its methods and conclusions vary across historical contexts.

examples.text: An Ash'arite theologian argues that the universe is created and therefore depends on God.
examples.note: The argument employs philosophical reasoning in defense of a theological conclusion.

commonMisreadings: Kalam is not identical to all Islamic philosophy because it has its own theological methods and debates.

concepts.name: Kantian ethics
concepts.summary: Kantian ethics judges morality by rational principles of duty, especially principles that can be willed universally and respect persons as ends.
concepts.body: Kantian ethics grounds morality in rational duties and the requirement to treat persons as ends in themselves, never merely as tools. A person who lies to obtain a signature manipulates another’s capacity to choose and could not consistently will a rule permitting such deception for everyone. Kantian tests ask whether a maxim can be universalized and whether it respects rational agency. The view explains why some actions remain wrong despite beneficial consequences, but critics question how to resolve conflicts of duties or apply abstract principles to complex cases.

examples.text: A person refuses to make a lying promise because universalizing such promises would undermine the practice of promising.
examples.note: The proposed maxim defeats the institution it presupposes when made universal.

commonMisreadings: Kantian ethics is not simply obedience to any rule because only rationally universalizable and person-respecting principles have moral authority.

concepts.name: Kantianism
concepts.summary: Kantianism is the philosophical tradition developing Immanuel Kant's views about knowledge, metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics, and rational agency.
concepts.body: Kantianism is the broad philosophical tradition developing Immanuel Kant’s work on knowledge, metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics, and rational agency. A Kantian account of knowledge asks how the mind’s forms and concepts make experience intelligible; Kantian ethics emphasizes autonomy and duty. Later thinkers revise these ideas in different directions, so the label does not identify one complete doctrine. Kant’s influence lies partly in reframing philosophical questions around the conditions and limits of human reason, while debates continue over whether his solutions succeed.

examples.text: Kant's account of space and time as forms of sensibility is a central Kantian thesis.
examples.note: The thesis explains how experience has spatial and temporal structure without treating space and time as properties of things in themselves.

commonMisreadings: Kantianism is broader than Kantian ethics because it includes his theoretical philosophy and aesthetics.

concepts.name: Karma
concepts.summary: Karma is the principle that intentional actions have consequences that shape future experience, especially across rebirth in South Asian religious traditions.
concepts.body: Karma is the principle that intentional actions have consequences shaping future experience, especially across rebirth in South Asian traditions. In Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain accounts, the details differ: actions may condition future circumstances, reinforce patterns of desire, or bind a soul to rebirth. Karma is not a simple system in which every misfortune proves past wrongdoing; traditions vary in how they understand causation, intention, and social responsibility. The concept links ethical conduct with long-term consequences and is often paired with paths toward liberation from the cycle of rebirth.

examples.text: In Hindu thought, an act of generosity may produce favorable karmic results while attachment to its reward can affect liberation.
examples.note: The act and its intention enter a moral causal order rather than functioning as a simple social reward.

commonMisreadings: Karma is not merely fate because intentional action is itself part of the causal process.

concepts.name: Kindness
concepts.summary: Kindness is a disposition to recognize others' needs and respond with concern, helpfulness, or gentle treatment.
concepts.body: Kindness is a disposition to notice another person’s needs and respond with care, helpfulness, or considerate treatment. A colleague quietly covering a task for someone facing a family emergency acts kindly without needing recognition. Kindness can express respect and strengthen relationships, but it does not always mean agreeing or avoiding difficult truths; setting a boundary may be kinder than enabling harm. The concept names a quality of response rather than a fixed action, since what helps depends on the person’s circumstances and wishes.

examples.text: A stranger returns a lost wallet without demanding a reward.
examples.note: The action benefits another person through considerate and honest assistance.

commonMisreadings: Kindness is not the same as permissiveness because a kind response can include a firm boundary that prevents harm.

concepts.name: Kitsch
concepts.summary: Kitsch is art or design regarded as sentimental, formulaic, or cheaply appealing through familiar emotional effects.
concepts.body: Kitsch is art or design criticized as sentimental, formulaic, or cheaply appealing through familiar emotional effects. A mass-produced landscape print may use a predictable sunset and nostalgic cottage to invite an easy response. The label often reflects judgments about taste and class as much as properties of the object, and what one audience calls kitsch another may value sincerely. It is useful for discussing manufactured sentimentality, but should not be used as an objective synonym for bad art without explaining the standard of criticism.

examples.text: A mass-produced painting of a glowing sunset with a crying child may be called kitsch.
examples.note: Its predictable sentiment and inexpensive emotional symbolism exemplify the usual criticism.

commonMisreadings: Kitsch is not simply any popular or decorative work because the label depends on judgments about formula, sentimentality, and artistic value.

concepts.name: Knowledge
concepts.summary: Knowledge is a successful cognitive relation to facts, objects, skills, or propositions, though its precise analysis is disputed.
concepts.body: Knowledge is a successful cognitive relation to facts, objects, or skills, though its exact analysis is disputed. A person may know that water boils at a certain temperature, recognize a familiar face, or know how to ride a bicycle; these are not the same kind of knowing. Philosophers often focus on propositional knowledge and ask how truth, belief, and justification relate. Knowledge requires more than a lucky true guess, but no single account resolves every case. The domain and context determine what kind of knowledge is at issue.

examples.text: A botanist knows that water freezes near zero degrees Celsius under standard atmospheric pressure.
examples.note: The botanist possesses a fact-directed understanding of a proposition.

commonMisreadings: Knowledge is not identical to certainty because people can know many things without infallible assurance.

concepts.name: Knowledge argument
concepts.summary: The knowledge argument is Frank Jackson's thought experiment claiming that complete physical knowledge may not include knowledge of conscious experience.
concepts.body: The knowledge argument uses Frank Jackson’s case of Mary, a scientist who learns every physical fact about color vision while living in a black-and-white environment, then sees red for the first time. If she learns what red looks like, the argument concludes that physical knowledge left something out, challenging physicalism. Physicalists reply that Mary gains an ability or a new way to represent known facts, not a new nonphysical fact. The thought experiment distinguishes knowing all descriptions from undergoing an experience, but its force depends on what counts as new knowledge.

examples.text: Mary learns what seeing red is like after leaving the monochrome room.
examples.note: The new phenomenal knowledge is used to challenge the claim that physical facts exhaust all facts about mind.

commonMisreadings: The argument is not simply a claim that Mary lacks information because its target is the completeness of physicalism.

concepts.name: Knowledge-how
concepts.summary: Knowledge-how is practical or ability knowledge of how to perform an activity.
concepts.body: Knowledge-how is practical or ability knowledge: knowing how to perform an activity, such as tying a knot or riding a bicycle. A person may know many facts about swimming yet be unable to swim, showing that propositional knowledge does not automatically provide skill. Philosophers debate whether know-how is reducible to knowing propositions or involves embodied ability and practice. It matters in education and expertise because instruction must often build competent performance, not just transmit information.

examples.text: A pianist knows how to play a C-major scale smoothly.
examples.note: The pianist can execute the skill under suitable conditions rather than merely state instructions.

commonMisreadings: Knowledge-how is not automatically identical to explicit verbal knowledge of the steps.

concepts.name: Knowledge-that
concepts.summary: Knowledge-that is propositional knowledge of a fact or that a proposition is true.
concepts.body: Knowledge-that is propositional knowledge, the kind expressed by “knows that,” as in knowing that a bridge is closed. It typically involves a true proposition and a non-accidental basis for belief, though the precise conditions are disputed. This contrasts with knowledge-how, such as knowing how to cross a river safely. The distinction helps clarify what a person has learned: factual understanding may guide action but does not itself establish practical competence or reliable performance.

examples.text: A student knows that Canberra is the capital of Australia.
examples.note: The object of the student's knowledge is a proposition about a geographical fact.

commonMisreadings: Knowledge-that is not mere belief because knowledge normally requires truth and some further epistemic success condition.

concepts.name: Lag effect
concepts.summary: The lag effect is the finding that spaced repetitions are remembered better after a delay than repetitions presented close together.
concepts.body: The lag effect is the memory benefit of spacing repeated study sessions apart rather than clustering them together. Reviewing vocabulary today and again several days later often supports longer-term recall better than repeating it many times in one sitting. Spacing makes retrieval more effortful and allows some forgetting, which can strengthen later learning. The best interval depends on how long the information must be retained and how difficult it is. Spaced practice is not always superior for immediate performance or every task, but it is valuable for durable learning.

examples.text: A student remembers vocabulary better when reviewing it on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday than when repeating it three times in one sitting.
examples.note: The distributed schedule creates temporal spacing that strengthens later recall.

commonMisreadings: The lag effect is not simply the claim that more study always helps because the timing between repetitions is the distinctive variable.

concepts.name: Language game
concepts.summary: A language-game is a practice in which words acquire meaning through their use within a particular activity and rule-governed context.
concepts.body: A language-game is a rule-governed activity in which words get their meaning through how people use them. The word “check” means different things in chess, banking, and casual conversation because each practice supplies different criteria for correct use. Wittgenstein used language-games to resist the idea that every word has one hidden essence. Meaning is connected to forms of life and shared action, though this does not make usage arbitrary: participants learn and enforce practical rules within a community.

examples.text: The word “check” has different roles in chess, banking, and ordinary inspection.
examples.note: Each practice supplies different rules that determine how the word functions.

commonMisreadings: A language-game is not merely a private vocabulary because its use depends on shared practices.

concepts.name: Law of excluded middle
concepts.summary: The law of excluded middle states that for any proposition P, either P is true or not-P is true.
concepts.body: The law of excluded middle states that for any proposition P, either P or not-P is true. For example, either the train is delayed or it is not delayed, under classical logic’s two-valued interpretation. Intuitionistic logic rejects unrestricted use of the law when neither side has been constructively proved. The principle is distinct from the law of noncontradiction, which says P and not-P cannot both be true. Whether excluded middle is acceptable depends on the logical framework and on how truth and proof are understood.

examples.text: For the proposition that it is raining, the classical law asserts that it is raining or it is not raining.
examples.note: The disjunction exhausts the two classical truth possibilities.

commonMisreadings: Excluded middle differs from the law of noncontradiction because it asserts completeness of alternatives rather than incompatibility.

concepts.name: Law of identity
concepts.summary: The law of identity states that each thing is identical with itself, commonly symbolized as A is A.
concepts.body: The law of identity states that each thing is itself, often represented as A = A. It underlies substitution and ordinary reasoning: if this is the same key, it has the key’s properties. The principle seems simple, but philosophical disputes arise over identity across time, possible worlds, or changing objects. It should not be confused with the identity of indiscernibles, which claims that objects with all the same properties are identical. The law is a basic logical principle, not a substantive explanation of what makes an object persist.

examples.text: A particular tree is identical with that same tree at the time and reference under discussion.
examples.note: The statement preserves the referent's identity rather than comparing it with another object.

commonMisreadings: The law does not assert that an object never changes in its properties or history.

concepts.name: Law of noncontradiction
concepts.summary: The law of noncontradiction states that a proposition and its negation cannot both be true in the same respect at the same time.
concepts.body: The law of noncontradiction says that a proposition and its negation cannot both be true in the same respect at the same time. A door cannot be both fully open and not open at that moment in the same sense. The qualifications matter: a person can be both tall relative to children and not tall relative to professional basketball players without contradiction because the comparison changes. Some nonclassical logics question unrestricted versions of the law, especially for inconsistent information, but ordinary reasoning relies on keeping claims and contexts distinct.

examples.text: A door cannot be wholly open and wholly not open at the same time in the same sense.
examples.note: The qualification prevents an apparent contradiction caused by changing times or different meanings.

commonMisreadings: Noncontradiction differs from excluded middle because it rules out simultaneous opposites rather than requiring one of them to hold.

concepts.name: Law of unintended consequences
concepts.summary: The law of unintended consequences is the sociological observation that purposeful actions can produce outcomes not included in the actors' aims.
concepts.body: The law of unintended consequences is the observation that purposeful actions can produce effects their agents did not aim for. A rent cap intended to make housing affordable may reduce incentives to build new units, worsening scarcity in the long run. The phrase is not a strict law that every policy fails; it calls attention to complex systems, feedback, and limited foresight. Good analysis identifies likely side effects and asks who experiences them. Some unintended outcomes are beneficial, while others can be mitigated through monitoring and policy adjustment.

examples.text: A city lowers downtown parking fees to help shoppers, unintentionally increasing congestion and reducing available spaces.
examples.note: The policy's direct aim produces secondary effects through changed behavior.

commonMisreadings: The phrase is not a strict physical law guaranteeing that every action has an unexpected result.

concepts.name: Left communism
concepts.summary: Left communism is a communist tradition that rejects parliamentary participation, electoral compromises, and often centralized party tactics associated with Leninism.
concepts.body: Left communism is a communist tradition that rejects parliamentary participation and electoral compromises, often criticizing party strategies associated with Leninism. Left communists have argued that workers’ councils and direct collective action should lead revolutionary change rather than a centralized vanguard governing in workers’ name. The movement includes different strands and historical contexts. Its critique highlights the risk that revolutionary parties reproduce hierarchy, but critics question how decentralized organization can coordinate action and defend gains against counterrevolution.

examples.text: The German-Dutch council communist tradition criticized participation in bourgeois elections.
examples.note: It treated electoral activity as integrating workers into the existing order rather than building independent proletarian power.

commonMisreadings: Left communism is not synonymous with every left-wing communist movement because it specifically criticizes party and parliamentary strategies.

concepts.name: Left-libertarianism
concepts.summary: Left-libertarianism combines strong individual rights over oneself with an egalitarian claim about natural resources or social wealth.
concepts.body: Left-libertarianism combines strong rights over oneself with an egalitarian claim that natural resources or socially created wealth should be shared fairly. A person may own their labor while owing compensation for exclusive use of valuable land that no one created. This differs from right-libertarianism, which typically allows broader private appropriation of resources. Left-libertarians disagree about what equality requires and how compensation should work. The position aims to reconcile personal freedom with equal claims to the world’s unowned resources.

examples.text: A person may keep wages from their work while owing compensation for exclusive use of a previously unowned oil field.
examples.note: The proposal reconciles self-ownership with equal claims to natural opportunities.

commonMisreadings: Left-libertarianism differs from right-libertarianism by requiring an egalitarian resource principle rather than unrestricted appropriation.

concepts.name: Legal obligation
concepts.summary: A legal obligation is a requirement imposed by a valid legal rule that a person or institution is legally bound to fulfill.
concepts.body: A legal obligation is a duty imposed by a valid legal rule that a person or institution is bound to fulfill. A landlord may be legally required to repair a dangerous stairway, and failure can trigger penalties or liability. Legal duties differ from moral duties: an action can be morally required without being legally mandated, or legally required despite moral disagreement. The obligation’s content depends on jurisdiction, facts, and applicable law, so identifying it requires more than citing a general principle.

examples.text: A driver has a legal obligation to stop at a red traffic signal.
examples.note: The traffic code makes compliance enforceable by public institutions.

commonMisreadings: A legal obligation is not merely a strong social expectation because it is constituted and enforced through a legal system.

concepts.name: Legal positivism
concepts.summary: Legal positivism holds that the existence and content of law depend on social facts and institutional practices rather than on its moral merit.
concepts.body: Legal positivism holds that a rule’s status as law depends on social sources and institutional practices, not on whether the rule is morally good. A court may recognize a statute as legally valid because it was enacted through accepted procedures, even if the statute is unjust. Positivists do not necessarily deny that morality matters to lawmaking or interpretation; they distinguish legal validity from moral merit. The theory helps explain how legal systems identify rules, while critics argue that law’s moral principles may be built into its criteria of validity.

examples.text: A statute enacted through the constitutionally specified process is law even if its policy is morally objectionable.
examples.note: Its legal status rests on recognized social sources rather than its goodness.

commonMisreadings: Legal positivism does not claim that judges should ignore morality in every decision or that law is always just.

concepts.name: Legal realism
concepts.summary: Legal realism is the jurisprudential view that law in practice is shaped by judicial behavior, institutional context, facts, and social consequences, not only written rules.
concepts.body: Legal realism emphasizes how law works in practice, including judicial behavior, institutional constraints, facts, and social consequences, rather than treating written rules as complete predictors. A judge’s decision may depend on how evidence is evaluated and which remedies are feasible, not just the words of a statute. Realists draw attention to discretion and the gap between legal texts and outcomes. Their approach can become cynical if it reduces law to personal preference; rules and precedents still constrain judges, even when they do not mechanically dictate results.

examples.text: A judge's prediction of how an appellate court will treat evidence may matter more to a lawyer than an abstract rule's wording.
examples.note: The prediction focuses on law as administered by institutions and people.

commonMisreadings: Legal realism is not the claim that rules never matter because realists study how rules interact with actual decision-making.

concepts.name: Legitimacy
concepts.summary: Legitimacy is the quality that makes a rule, institution, or exercise of power accepted as rightful or justified by relevant people or standards.
concepts.body: Legitimacy is the quality that makes a rule or exercise of power count as rightful under relevant standards. A government may be legally constituted yet lack legitimacy among people excluded from political participation. Legitimacy can rest on consent, fair procedures, effective protection of rights, tradition, or other principles, depending on the theory. It helps explain why people accept authority beyond fear of punishment. Claims of legitimacy must identify whose judgment and which standard matter; public acceptance alone does not prove that power is justified.

examples.text: An elected government gains democratic legitimacy through a free and fair election.
examples.note: The procedure gives citizens a recognized basis for treating the government's authority as rightful.

commonMisreadings: Legitimacy is not identical to coercive effectiveness because a regime can control people without being regarded as rightful.

concepts.name: Leibniz's principle of plenitude
concepts.summary: Leibniz's principle of plenitude is the metaphysical idea that reality contains or expresses every genuine possibility in some form or across the full order of creation.
concepts.body: The principle of plenitude is the metaphysical idea that genuine possibilities are realized somewhere in the complete order of reality. In Leibniz’s version, God creates the best possible world, whose richness may include a full expression of what is compossible. The principle has older forms associated with the thought that nature leaves no genuine possibility empty. It matters to arguments about possible worlds and divine creation, but it is not the claim that every logically imaginable scenario exists together; incompatible possibilities cannot all be actual in one world.

examples.text: A Leibnizian may regard the diversity of species and worlds as evidence that divine creation realizes many possibilities.
examples.note: The example treats variety as part of a maximal order rather than as accidental scarcity.

commonMisreadings: The principle of plenitude is not the claim that every imagined description is possible or exists exactly as conceived.

concepts.name: Leninism
concepts.summary: Leninism is a revolutionary Marxist theory emphasizing a disciplined vanguard party, imperialism, and the seizure of state power by a proletarian revolution.
concepts.body: Leninism is a revolutionary Marxist theory emphasizing a disciplined vanguard party, imperialism, and the seizure of state power by a proletarian revolution. Lenin argued that a trained party could organize political struggle under conditions where workers’ spontaneous action might remain limited. After revolution, Leninist practice concentrated authority in the party-state, though interpretations vary about whether this was necessary or a betrayal of democratic aims. The doctrine has shaped communist movements worldwide, and its record raises questions about party leadership, pluralism, and the transition to socialism.

examples.text: The Bolshevik Party's organization and leadership during the 1917 Russian Revolution are associated with Leninist practice.
examples.note: The party sought centralized coordination for revolutionary transformation.

commonMisreadings: Leninism is not simply any belief in socialism because its distinctive strategy centers on the vanguard party and revolutionary state power.

concepts.name: Leveling and sharpening
concepts.summary: Leveling and sharpening are memory distortions in which recall omits details and emphasizes or exaggerates other details.
concepts.body: Leveling and sharpening describe distortions in memory: recall tends to omit some details while emphasizing or exaggerating others. Someone retelling a story may forget minor qualifications but make the central conflict seem sharper than it was. These processes can make a memory more coherent and memorable while less faithful to the original. They matter in eyewitness testimony and social transmission of stories. Memory is reconstructive rather than a literal recording, so checking original records can reveal how details changed over time.

examples.text: After retelling a story, a witness forgets minor background details but repeatedly emphasizes the suspect's red jacket.
examples.note: The account shows both loss of peripheral information and increased salience of one feature.

commonMisreadings: The terms do not mean improving or worsening a memory in an objective sense; they describe systematic changes in recall.

concepts.name: Levels-of-processing effect
concepts.summary: The levels-of-processing effect is the finding that information processed for meaning is generally remembered better than information processed only for superficial features.
concepts.body: The levels-of-processing effect is the finding that information processed for meaning is generally remembered better than information attended to only for surface features. A student asked to connect a new term to an example may retain it better than one who merely counts its letters. Semantic engagement creates richer retrieval cues. The effect is not a guarantee: deep analysis can be misdirected, and some tasks reward perceptual detail. Effective study uses meaningful elaboration and retrieval appropriate to what must later be remembered.

examples.text: A learner remembers the word “apple” better after deciding whether it names a fruit than after counting its letters.
examples.note: The semantic judgment creates deeper encoding than the orthographic task.

commonMisreadings: The effect does not mean that every semantic task guarantees memory or that depth is independent of task and context.

concepts.name: Li (principle)
concepts.summary: The Neo-Confucian concept of patterned order or principle that makes things and relationships intelligible, especially in Zhu Xi's systematic metaphysics.
concepts.body:
In Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian metaphysics, li is the intelligible pattern and normative order through which things and relationships are what they are. It is not a material ingredient or a second substance floating apart from the world. Every concrete situation has li, while qi supplies the dynamic, embodied conditions in which that pattern is realized with greater clarity or distortion. Moral cultivation seeks to understand and enact the pattern rather than invent values at will.

This li (理) must be distinguished from ritual propriety, also transliterated li (禮). Ritual li concerns forms of conduct, ceremony, and social distinction; principle li is the broader ordering intelligibility that Zhu Xi systematized using inherited vocabulary. Zhu Xi did not invent either term. Critics such as Wang Yangming worried that treating principle as an object to investigate could separate knowledge from immediate moral realization, while Zhu Xi emphasized disciplined learning and inquiry.

examples.text: A just family practice expresses a pattern of relationship, while the same principle can be obscured by selfish habit and social disorder.
examples.note: The example links metaphysical intelligibility to ethical cultivation without reducing li to a ritual rule.

commonMisreadings: Li as principle (理) differs from li as ritual propriety (禮), despite the shared transliteration.
Zhu Xi did not invent li or qi; he developed a distinctive systematic interpretation of inherited terms.
criticisms: Wang Yangming and other critics argue that treating principle as something to investigate externally can separate knowledge from immediate moral realization.

lookalikes.note: Confucian li concerns ritual propriety and patterned conduct; Neo-Confucian li is the broader ordering principle in Zhu Xi's metaphysics.
Li is patterned order; qi is the dynamic material force through which patterns become concrete, though the distinction is not a separation into two independent substances.

concepts.name: Liberal conservatism
concepts.summary: Liberal conservatism combines support for individual liberty and constitutional government with preference for gradual change, social continuity, and restrained state power.
concepts.body: Liberal conservatism combines constitutional liberties and individual rights with preference for gradual change, social continuity, and limits on state power. A liberal conservative may defend free speech and equal legal status while resisting rapid institutional redesign that could weaken stable norms. The tradition joins commitments that can pull in different directions, such as protecting individual choice while preserving inherited institutions. Its expression varies by country and era; it should not be confused with either laissez-faire liberalism or social conservatism alone.

examples.text: A liberal conservative may support free speech and market competition while opposing abrupt revolutionary restructuring.
examples.note: The position joins liberal rights with conservative caution about rapid institutional change.

commonMisreadings: Liberal conservatism is not identical to either unrestricted laissez-faire or traditionalist rejection of liberal rights.

concepts.name: Liberal democracy
concepts.summary: Liberal democracy is a political system combining popular elections with constitutional limits, individual rights, pluralism, and rule of law.
concepts.body: Liberal democracy combines competitive elections with constitutional constraints, individual rights, pluralism, and rule of law. A majority can choose a government, but courts and rights protections prevent that government from silencing opposition or stripping minorities of basic protections. Elections supply public authorization; liberal institutions limit arbitrary power. The system can still be unequal or imperfectly representative, and institutions may be captured. The concept distinguishes democratic rule from mere majority command and liberal rights from unelected rule.

examples.text: A parliament elected by universal suffrage remains subject to an independent court enforcing freedom of expression.
examples.note: Elections and rights-protecting institutions jointly define the system.

commonMisreadings: Liberal democracy is not mere majority voting because liberal constitutional constraints are essential.

concepts.name: Liberal feminism
concepts.summary: Liberal feminism seeks women's equality through individual rights, equal opportunity, legal reform, education, and access to institutions.
concepts.body: Liberal feminism seeks gender equality by extending individual rights, equal opportunity, education, and access to institutions. A campaign for equal pay or fair hiring challenges rules that exclude women from professions. The tradition emphasizes reform through law and policy and often treats autonomy and equal citizenship as central. Critics argue that formal equality may leave unpaid care burdens and class or racial inequalities untouched. Liberal feminists differ over how much state intervention is needed to make opportunities genuinely equal.

examples.text: A liberal feminist campaign supports equal pay laws and nondiscriminatory hiring procedures.
examples.note: The reforms aim to secure equal civic and economic opportunities under law.

commonMisreadings: Liberal feminism differs from radical feminism by not necessarily treating patriarchy as a total system requiring comprehensive social transformation.

concepts.name: Liberal nationalism
concepts.summary: Liberal nationalism holds that national belonging can support democratic self-government while remaining constrained by individual rights and civic equality.
concepts.body: Liberal nationalism holds that national community can support democratic self-government and solidarity while remaining limited by individual rights and civic equality. Shared institutions and language may enable citizens to deliberate and sustain public services, while minority rights constrain majoritarian nationalism. The view differs from ethnic nationalism that defines belonging by ancestry. It faces questions about who belongs, how borders are justified, and whether national solidarity can coexist with duties to outsiders. The position treats nationhood as potentially valuable, not automatically benign.

examples.text: A liberal nationalist supports a common language for public institutions while protecting minority citizenship and religious freedom.
examples.note: Shared civic practices coexist with equal rights for members of diverse backgrounds.

commonMisreadings: Liberal nationalism is not ethnic nationalism because national membership need not depend on ancestry.

concepts.name: Liberal socialism
concepts.summary: Liberal socialism combines liberal rights and democratic institutions with socialist aims such as social ownership, economic equality, or worker control.
concepts.body: Liberal socialism combines political liberties and democratic institutions with socialist aims such as social ownership, economic equality, or worker control. It might defend free elections and civil rights while placing key industries under public or cooperative ownership. The combination seeks to prevent both economic domination and authoritarian state power. Traditions differ on markets, planning, and property, and critics ask whether social ownership can preserve individual choice and innovation. Liberal socialism is a family of proposals, not a single settled institutional design.

examples.text: A liberal socialist may support constitutional free speech alongside worker cooperatives and universal public services.
examples.note: Political liberties and egalitarian economic institutions are treated as mutually supporting.

commonMisreadings: Liberal socialism is not social liberalism because it generally seeks more extensive changes in ownership or control of production.

concepts.name: Liberalism
concepts.summary: Liberalism is a political tradition centered on individual liberty, equal civic status, limited government, and institutions that protect rights.
concepts.body: Liberalism is a political tradition centered on individual liberty, equal civic standing, and institutions that limit power and protect rights. A liberal constitution may secure speech and religion even when majorities oppose them. Liberal thinkers disagree about property, welfare, and the role of government: some stress limited state action, while others argue public services are needed for real opportunity. The tradition’s core is not a single economic policy but a framework for protecting people from arbitrary authority and enabling plural ways of life.

examples.text: A constitutional liberal state protects speech and religious exercise while applying laws through independent courts.
examples.note: The institutions limit arbitrary power and recognize citizens as rights-bearing individuals.

commonMisreadings: Liberalism is not simply permissive individualism because many liberals support public institutions that make freedom effective.

concepts.name: Libertarian communism
concepts.summary: Libertarian communism advocates a classless, stateless society based on common ownership, voluntary association, and decentralized self-management.
concepts.body: Libertarian communism advocates a classless and stateless society based on common ownership, voluntary association, and decentralized self-management. A neighborhood might collectively manage essential services through assemblies and federations rather than private firms or a central state. The tradition argues that hierarchy and private control of production are sources of coercion. Practical questions concern coordination, conflict resolution, and distribution at scale. Historical anarchist movements have proposed different methods, so the concept describes a political aim rather than one detailed administrative blueprint.

examples.text: An anarcho-communist federation distributes goods through worker and neighborhood assemblies without a permanent state bureaucracy.
examples.note: Common resources and self-governing associations replace both capitalist ownership and hierarchical state command.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian communism is not state socialism because it rejects centralized state ownership as the route to liberation.

concepts.name: Libertarian free will
concepts.summary: Libertarian free will is the view that genuine free choice requires indeterminism and that agents can originate alternative actions.
concepts.body: Libertarian free will holds that agents have genuine alternatives not fixed by prior causes, and that this indeterminism is necessary for freedom. In a difficult decision, a person could truly choose either path, and the choice originates partly in the agent rather than being determined by the past. This aims to ground responsibility more robustly than compatibilist accounts. The challenge is explaining how an undetermined choice remains controlled rather than random. Libertarians offer agent-causal and event-causal theories, with no consensus on how either succeeds.

examples.text: A person deciding whether to donate may, with the same prior conditions, genuinely choose either donation or refusal.
examples.note: The agent's choice is treated as an undetermined source of action rather than a predetermined outcome.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian free will does not mean arbitrary behavior because reasons and character can still guide the choice.

concepts.name: Libertarian municipalism
concepts.summary: Libertarian municipalism is a political program of democratic local assemblies linked in confederations to replace hierarchical state administration.
concepts.body: Libertarian municipalism proposes that citizens govern through local face-to-face assemblies linked in confederations, gradually replacing hierarchical state administration. Residents might decide local budgets in assemblies, while delegates coordinate regional issues under clear mandates. The model, associated with Murray Bookchin, aims to combine direct democracy with coordination beyond a single town. It differs from simply granting municipalities more powers because it envisions a transformation of political authority. Critics ask how assemblies protect minorities, manage technical systems, and scale decisions to national or global problems.

examples.text: Residents of several towns deliberate in neighborhood assemblies and send recallable delegates to a regional confederation.
examples.note: Decision-making remains local while coordination occurs through accountable delegation.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian municipalism is not ordinary municipal administration because it aims to transform political authority and economic relations.

concepts.name: Libertarian socialism
concepts.summary: Libertarian socialism seeks social ownership and worker self-management without a coercive centralized state or capitalist class hierarchy.
concepts.body: Libertarian socialism seeks social ownership and worker self-management without capitalist class control or a coercive centralized state. A worker cooperative can let employees govern production while coordinating with other cooperatives through federations. The tradition includes anarchist, council communist, and other currents that disagree about organization and transition. Its central concern is that political and economic freedom require limiting hierarchy in both state and workplace. Critics question whether decentralized ownership can coordinate complex economies or defend collective choices without recreating centralized authority.

examples.text: Workers in a federation of cooperatives govern their workplaces and coordinate production through elected councils.
examples.note: The producers exercise control over economic decisions without private owners or state managers.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian socialism is not identical to laissez-faire libertarianism because it rejects capitalist ownership of productive assets.

concepts.name: Libertarianism in politics
concepts.summary: Libertarianism in politics gives primary importance to individual liberty, voluntary exchange, property rights, and limiting coercive government power.
concepts.body: Political libertarianism gives primary weight to individual liberty, voluntary exchange, property rights, and limits on coercive government. A libertarian may oppose licensing rules that restrict peaceful work or taxes used for expansive state programs. Versions differ: some treat self-ownership and property rights as near-absolute, while others allow limited public provision or regulation to protect liberty. The label does not settle questions about inherited property, public goods, or unequal bargaining power. Its central test is whether political coercion can be justified to the people subject to it.

examples.text: A minarchist supports courts, police, and national defense but opposes most other compulsory government programs.
examples.note: The state is limited to functions thought necessary for protecting rights and contracts.

commonMisreadings: Political libertarianism is not simply a preference for personal freedom because it includes institutional claims about coercion and authority.

concepts.name: Liberty
concepts.summary: Liberty is the condition of being free from undue coercion or able to direct one's conduct and participate in collective self-rule.
concepts.body: Liberty is freedom from undue coercion and, in some theories, the capacity to direct one’s conduct and participate in collective rule. A person legally free to choose a job may still lack meaningful options if discrimination blocks every route. Negative liberty focuses on noninterference; positive liberty asks about the power and resources needed for self-direction. These accounts can support different policies, so a dispute about liberty should specify whether it concerns absence of obstacles, protection from domination, or effective capacity to act.

examples.text: Freedom of speech protects a person's ability to criticize the government without legal punishment.
examples.note: The protection removes a form of state interference in expression.

commonMisreadings: Liberty is not identical to doing whatever one wants because rights and other people's liberty can limit action.

concepts.name: Lindy effect
concepts.summary: The Lindy effect is the heuristic that the expected remaining lifespan of a non-perishable thing increases with the length of time it has already survived.
concepts.body: The Lindy effect is a heuristic that estimates the remaining lifespan of a nonperishable thing from how long it has already survived: a book or practice with a long history may be more likely to persist. The idea is often applied to technologies, institutions, and knowledge, where continued use can signal resilience. It is not a law or guarantee; conditions can change abruptly, and survival may reflect power rather than quality. The effect is less applicable to things with predictable physical wear, such as a machine or a person.

examples.text: A programming language used successfully for fifty years may be expected to remain relevant longer than a newly released language.
examples.note: Past survival is treated as evidence of robustness or continued adoption.

commonMisreadings: The Lindy effect is a probabilistic heuristic, not a law that guarantees old things will outlast new ones.

concepts.name: Linguistic relativity
concepts.summary: Linguistic relativity is the view that the structures and categories of a language can influence how its speakers perceive, remember, or conceptualize experience.
concepts.body: Linguistic relativity is the view that a language’s structures and categories can influence how its speakers perceive, remember, or conceptualize experience. If a language routinely marks distinctions in direction or color, speakers may become more practiced at noticing them. The strongest claim—that language determines what can be thought—is not supported by the more modest evidence for influence. Language shapes attention and habits without necessarily imprisoning thought; bilingual speakers can learn new categories, and context and culture also affect cognition.

examples.text: Speakers of languages that grammatically mark evidential sources may attend more consistently to how they know a reported fact.
examples.note: The grammatical distinction can guide habitual attention to evidence.

commonMisreadings: Linguistic relativity is not linguistic determinism because influence does not entail that language fixes all thought.

concepts.name: List-length effect
concepts.summary: The list-length effect is the tendency for the proportion of correctly recalled items to decrease as the number of studied items increases.
concepts.body: The list-length effect is the tendency for the proportion of studied items recalled correctly to decrease as list size increases. A person may remember a larger share of a ten-word list than of a forty-word list, even if the absolute number recalled rises. Retrieval competition and memory limits can contribute. This matters when designing learning tasks and interpreting recall scores: performance depends on list size, not just ability. The effect can vary with encoding, retrieval cues, and whether recall is measured freely or with prompts.

examples.text: People usually recall a larger percentage of a ten-word list than of a forty-word list under the same testing conditions.
examples.note: The longer list creates greater competition and memory load.

commonMisreadings: The list-length effect concerns recall proportion or performance as list size changes, not merely the fact that a longer list contains more items.

concepts.name: Literal meaning
concepts.summary: Literal meaning is the conventional semantic content of an expression apart from figurative, pragmatic, or ironic implications.
concepts.body: Literal meaning is the conventional semantic content of an expression, considered apart from figurative, ironic, or context-driven implications. “It is raining cats and dogs” literally describes animals falling from the sky, but conventionally functions as an idiom meaning heavy rain. A listener often uses context to determine whether literal or figurative interpretation is intended. Literal meaning is not always the whole meaning of an utterance; sarcasm, metaphor, and implicature add content that cannot be recovered from word definitions alone.

examples.text: The literal meaning of “The cat is on the mat” states that a cat is located on a mat.
examples.note: The sentence directly describes a spatial relation rather than implying a metaphorical condition.

commonMisreadings: Literal meaning is not always the total communicated meaning because context can add implicatures.

concepts.name: Logical atomism
concepts.summary: Logical atomism is the philosophical view that reality consists of atomic facts and that meaningful propositions can be analyzed into logically independent elementary components.
concepts.body: Logical atomism holds that reality consists of atomic facts and that meaningful propositions can be analyzed into elementary components corresponding to those facts. In Russell’s version, a complex sentence is true or false depending on the arrangement of simple facts it represents. The view sought to connect logical analysis with the structure of the world, rather than treat language as an undifferentiated whole. It faces questions about whether facts are truly independent atoms and whether ordinary statements can be fully decomposed into this form.

examples.text: The statement “Socrates is mortal” may be treated as representing a simple fact involving an object and a property.
examples.note: The proposition is analyzed as a basic correspondence rather than as an unanalyzed whole.

commonMisreadings: Logical atomism is not the claim that physical matter consists of indivisible atoms because its atoms are logical or factual units.

concepts.name: Logical consequence
concepts.summary: Logical consequence is the relation in which a conclusion must be true whenever the premises are true under the relevant semantics.
concepts.body: A conclusion is a logical consequence of premises when it must be true whenever those premises are true under the relevant interpretation. From “All mammals are warm-blooded” and “Whales are mammals,” it follows that whales are warm-blooded. Validity concerns the structure of the inference, not whether the premises actually hold. Different logics specify different consequence relations, particularly for conditionals, contradictions, or modal claims. Checking consequence helps separate a sound argument, with true premises, from an invalid one that only seems persuasive.

examples.text: From “All mammals are animals” and “All dogs are mammals,” it follows logically that all dogs are animals.
examples.note: Every model satisfying the premises also satisfies the conclusion.

commonMisreadings: Logical consequence differs from causal consequence because validity concerns truth preservation rather than production of events.

concepts.name: Logical empiricism
concepts.summary: Logical empiricism is a twentieth-century movement combining formal logical analysis with the view that meaningful knowledge is grounded in experience and scientific method.
concepts.body: Logical empiricism was a twentieth-century movement that combined formal analysis of language with the view that factual knowledge must connect to experience and scientific method. Its members sought to clarify scientific claims and reject metaphysical statements they considered empirically empty. The movement included varied positions, not one simple verification rule; later thinkers revised its account of meaning and theory. It helped shape philosophy of science and analytic philosophy, while critics argued that strict verification criteria exclude meaningful claims or cannot themselves be verified.

examples.text: A logical empiricist analyzes a scientific claim's logical form and asks how observation could support it.
examples.note: Formal clarification and empirical testing operate together in evaluating the claim.

commonMisreadings: Logical empiricism is not a rejection of all theoretical entities because many members accepted theories that organize observable evidence.

concepts.name: Logical equivalence
concepts.summary: Logical equivalence is the relation between propositions that have the same truth value under every possible interpretation.
concepts.body: Two propositions are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value under every relevant interpretation. “It is not the case that both P and Q” is classically equivalent to “not P or not Q,” by De Morgan’s law. Equivalence lets logicians substitute one expression for another without changing logical behavior. The relation depends on the logic and semantics used; formulas equivalent in classical logic may differ in intuitionistic or modal systems. Equivalence is stronger than happening to be true together in one situation.

examples.text: P and not-not-P are classically logically equivalent.
examples.note: Both formulas are true in exactly the same classical valuations.

commonMisreadings: Logical equivalence is stronger than having the same truth value in one actual situation.

concepts.name: Logical form
concepts.summary: Logical form is the abstract structural pattern that determines how the parts of an expression combine for inferential or semantic purposes.
concepts.body: Logical form is the abstract structure of an expression that determines how its parts combine for inference or meaning. “Every student read a book” has a structure involving a universal quantifier, a condition for being a student, and an existential claim about a book. Two sentences with different words can share the same form and support the same inference. Formalizing structure can expose ambiguity hidden by grammar, though different analyses may be needed when scope or context changes the reading.

examples.text: “All birds are animals” and “All roses are plants” share a universal conditional structure.
examples.note: Their common form explains why the same deductive pattern applies to both.

commonMisreadings: Logical form is not identical to surface word order because grammatical appearance can conceal relevant structure.

concepts.name: Logical necessity
concepts.summary: Logical necessity is the status of a proposition that cannot be false under the relevant logical rules or interpretations.
concepts.body: A proposition is logically necessary when it cannot be false under the rules or interpretations of the relevant logic. “If P and Q, then P” is true under classical logic for every assignment of truth values. Logical necessity differs from physical necessity: a law of nature may hold in our universe while being logically consistent with alternatives. The relevant framework matters, since logics can disagree about which formulas are valid. Necessity marks a stronger status than truth by fact or regularity.

examples.text: The proposition “Either it is raining or it is not raining” is classically logically necessary.
examples.note: No classical truth assignment makes both disjunctive alternatives false.

commonMisreadings: Logical necessity differs from physical necessity because a physically impossible event can still be logically describable.

concepts.name: Logical positivism
concepts.summary: Logical positivism is the view that meaningful factual claims are tied to possible empirical verification or confirmation and that formal logic clarifies language.
concepts.body: Logical positivism is the view, associated with the Vienna Circle, that factual claims must be tied to possible empirical verification or confirmation and that formal logic clarifies language. The movement treated many traditional metaphysical statements as lacking factual meaning because no observation could bear on them. It aimed to make philosophy continuous with science, but its verification criterion faced problems: universal laws cannot be conclusively verified, and the criterion itself is not empirical. Later logical empiricists softened and revised the program.

examples.text: A logical positivist treats “Water boils at standard pressure near 100 degrees Celsius” as meaningful because observations can test it.
examples.note: The statement has an identifiable observational connection.

commonMisreadings: Logical positivism is not the claim that every meaningful sentence is itself an observation report because logical and mathematical statements are treated separately.

concepts.name: Logical possibility
concepts.summary: Logical possibility is the status of a proposition or scenario that contains no contradiction under a specified logical framework.
concepts.body: A scenario is logically possible if its description contains no contradiction under a specified logical framework. A world with different physical laws may be logically possible even if it cannot occur under the laws of our universe. Logical possibility is broader than physical possibility and narrower than mere imaginability: an unclear description may seem conceivable while containing hidden inconsistency. Modal reasoning uses this distinction to test claims about what must or could be true, though philosophers debate which logic and conception of worlds to use.

examples.text: A world in which gravity is weaker than on Earth is logically possible even if it is not physically accessible from Earth.
examples.note: The description is coherent without being compatible with actual physical laws or history.

commonMisreadings: Logical possibility is not the same as conceivability in every theory because some apparently conceivable descriptions may hide contradictions.

concepts.name: Logicism
concepts.summary: Logicism is the philosophical program that mathematics can be reduced to logic and definitions of mathematical objects.
concepts.body: Logicism is the philosophical program of reducing mathematics to logic and definitions, aiming to show that mathematical truths follow from logical principles. Frege attempted to derive arithmetic in this way, but his system encountered a contradiction known as Russell’s paradox. Later logicists developed more sophisticated foundations. The project matters because it asks whether mathematics has a distinctive subject matter or can be grounded in general reasoning. Its success depends on what counts as logic and whether the required axioms are genuinely logical rather than mathematical assumptions in disguise.

examples.text: Principia Mathematica attempts to derive arithmetic within a formal logical system.
examples.note: The derivation seeks to show that numerical truths follow from logical principles and definitions.

commonMisreadings: Logicism is not merely the use of logic in mathematics because it claims a foundational reduction of mathematics to logic.

concepts.name: Longtermism
concepts.summary: Longtermism is the ethical view that improving the long-run future of humanity has very great moral importance.
concepts.body: Longtermism is the ethical view that improving the long-run future has very great moral importance, partly because future generations could be numerous.
