Intelligence, for instance, cannot necessarily be reduced to one test score. Different operations may measure different aspects, so operational clarity must be balanced against the possibility that the concept exceeds any single procedure.

examples.text: A laboratory may define reaction time as the interval between a tone and a participant’s button press. This makes the measure precise without proving that reaction time captures every aspect of alertness.
examples.note: The operation gives the term experimental use.

commonMisreadings: It need not deny theoretical entities.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
concepts.summary: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up when a choice is made. It captures what a decision sacrifices, not just the money directly spent.
concepts.body: The forgone alternative may involve time, income, or another benefit, and only the most valuable rejected option counts as the opportunity cost in standard analysis. It can be difficult to estimate when options are uncertain or incomparable. Accounting for opportunity cost helps compare choices that appear free because they use existing resources.

examples.text: If a student spends Saturday volunteering instead of working a paid shift, the foregone wages are part of the opportunity cost, even if volunteering requires no fee.
examples.note: The rejected best alternative is the relevant cost.

commonMisreadings: It is not the value of every rejected option.

concepts.name: Ordinary language philosophy
concepts.summary: Ordinary-language philosophy examines how words are used in everyday contexts to clarify philosophical problems. It often argues that a puzzle arises from taking a word out of the circumstances that give it its ordinary function.
concepts.body: Rather than building a theory from abstract definitions alone, ordinary-language philosophers compare examples, distinctions, and conversational practices. Wittgenstein and J. L. Austin influenced the approach, though neither reduced philosophy to dictionary work. Critics argue that ordinary usage can be inconsistent or inadequate for technical questions.

examples.text: A question about whether someone “knows” a fact may be clarified by examining how people use “know” when evidence is incomplete. This may dissolve a verbal confusion without settling every epistemological theory.
examples.note: Usage distinctions replace an assumed hidden entity.

commonMisreadings: It can still employ rigorous argument.

concepts.name: Organicism
concepts.summary: Organicism explains living systems or societies as organized wholes whose parts depend on their relations to the whole. It emphasizes integration, function, and coordinated structure.
concepts.body: In biology, organismic approaches stress how processes and parts interact to sustain life; in political thought, organic metaphors can portray society as an interdependent community. The metaphor can illuminate dependence but also conceal conflict or suggest that individuals should submit to a supposed social whole. Biological and political uses require separate evaluation.

examples.text: A heart’s role depends on its place within the circulatory system, illustrating how a part’s function can be understood through its organization with other parts.
examples.note: Its function depends on the whole.

commonMisreadings: It does not say every system is literally biological.

concepts.name: Original position
concepts.summary: The original position is John Rawls’s hypothetical choice situation for deciding principles of justice. People choose rules for society without knowing their own class, abilities, race, or conception of the good.
concepts.body: The veil of ignorance blocks information that could let choosers tailor rules to their personal advantage. Rawls argues that this makes the choice fair and leads to principles protecting equal liberties and benefiting the least advantaged. The device is a model of impartial reasoning, not a historical contract or an empirical claim about how people would actually vote.

examples.text: A chooser who does not know whether they will be wealthy or poor has reason to reject rules that leave the poor without basic protections. This illustrates the veil’s role in limiting self-serving choices.
examples.note: Ignorance blocks bargaining for actual advantage.

commonMisreadings: It is not a historical founding meeting.

concepts.name: Pacifism
concepts.summary: Pacifism rejects war and, in stronger forms, rejects intentional violence more broadly. Pacifists may base the view on moral principles, religious commitments, political consequences, or a combination of these.
concepts.body: Some pacifists oppose all violence; others oppose war while allowing defensive force or nonviolent resistance. Pacifist arguments emphasize the harms of killing and the tendency of violence to reproduce conflict. Critics ask whether refusing force can permit aggression or leave vulnerable people unprotected. The scope of the position must be specified.

examples.text: A conscientious objector may refuse military service while supporting nonviolent relief for people threatened by war. That stance differs from indifference to the victims of conflict.
examples.note: Political resistance occurs without violence.

commonMisreadings: It is not passivity.

concepts.name: Paleoconservatism
concepts.summary: Paleoconservatism is a strand of conservatism that emphasizes inherited traditions, national sovereignty, local community, and skepticism toward expansive federal power and interventionist foreign policy. The term is especially associated with American politics.
concepts.body: Its proponents often criticize globalism, large-scale immigration, and nation-building abroad, while favoring social conservatism and decentralization. The movement is internally varied and has contested boundaries with other right-wing currents. Historical and national context matter when applying the label.

examples.text: A paleoconservative politician may oppose a prolonged overseas nation-building mission and argue that national resources should remain focused at home.
examples.note: Traditionalism and foreign-policy restraint combine here.

commonMisreadings: It is not all conservatism.

concepts.name: Pan-Africanism
concepts.summary: Pan-Africanism promotes solidarity and cooperation among African peoples and people of African descent worldwide. It has included political, cultural, and intellectual movements opposing colonial rule and racial oppression.
concepts.body: Pan-African thinkers have argued for unity, self-determination, cultural recovery, and shared political action, while disagreeing about whether these goals require continental federation, independent states, or transnational networks. The movement’s history spans Africa and the diaspora and cannot be reduced to one organization or ideology.

examples.text: A diaspora organization supporting African independence movements and cultural exchange expresses Pan-African solidarity across national borders.
examples.note: Independent states coordinated around shared African interests.

commonMisreadings: It is transnational rather than ethnic to one group.

concepts.name: Pan-Arabism
concepts.summary: Pan-Arabism holds that Arabic-speaking peoples share a collective cultural and political identity that can support solidarity or political unity. It became a major current in twentieth-century Middle Eastern politics.
concepts.body: Pan-Arabist movements have differed over whether unity should take the form of a federation, a single state, or coordinated regional action, and over the role of socialism, religion, and authoritarian rule. Their ambitions have often encountered competing national interests and diverse local identities.

examples.text: A proposal for Arab states to coordinate foreign policy and economic planning in the name of shared identity reflects Pan-Arabist aims, even if it stops short of a unified state.
examples.note: Egypt and Syria joined under shared Arab identity.

commonMisreadings: It is not Islamism.

concepts.name: Pan-Slavism
concepts.summary: Pan-Slavism promotes cultural, political, or national unity among Slavic peoples. It emerged in the nineteenth century amid debates about language, identity, empire, and national self-determination.
concepts.body: The movement includes distinct forms, from cultural cooperation to projects led by particular states seeking regional influence. Shared Slavic identity has not erased religious, linguistic, or political differences. Pan-Slavism has sometimes supported liberation from empire and sometimes served expansionist state interests.

examples.text: A cultural congress encouraging literary exchange among Slavic-language communities illustrates Pan-Slavic cooperation without requiring political unification.
examples.note: Common language and ancestry linked communities.

commonMisreadings: It was never one agreed political program.

concepts.name: Panentheism
concepts.summary: Panentheism holds that the world exists in God while God also exceeds the world. It differs from pantheism, which identifies God with the universe or totality of reality.
concepts.body: Panentheistic traditions describe divine immanence and transcendence in different ways: the world may depend on God, participate in God, or exist within divine life without exhausting it. The view is used in several religious philosophies and is not one settled theology. Critics ask how a transcendent God relates to a world that is part of divine reality.

examples.text: A panentheist may say every creature exists within God’s sustaining presence while God is more than the sum of creatures. This preserves both intimacy and transcendence.
examples.note: The claim includes nature without exhausting divinity.

commonMisreadings: It differs from pantheism.

concepts.name: Panexperientialism
concepts.summary: Panexperientialism is the view that experience, or a primitive form of experiential capacity, is present throughout nature. It holds that experience is not restricted to complex brains.
concepts.body: Panexperientialist theories often distinguish simple proto-experience from the rich consciousness of animals and humans. They aim to explain how experience could be fundamental rather than emerging from wholly non-experiential matter. A central challenge is the combination problem: how simpler experiential elements could form unified subjects.

examples.text: A panexperientialist might attribute rudimentary experiential aspects to basic physical entities while denying that an electron has thoughts or human-like awareness.
examples.note: The experience is rudimentary, not reflective.

commonMisreadings: It does not give every object a human mind.

concepts.name: Panpsychism
concepts.summary: Panpsychism holds that mentality or consciousness is a fundamental and widespread feature of reality, rather than something that appears only in complex organisms. Versions differ over what kinds of entities have mental properties.
concepts.body: Some panpsychists attribute basic experiential properties to fundamental particles; others argue that mentality is ubiquitous at the level of nature as a whole. The view aims to avoid explaining consciousness as arising from entirely non-conscious matter, but faces the problem of how many simple experiences combine into one unified mind. It does not claim that stones think like people.

examples.text: A panpsychist may hold that fundamental constituents have extremely simple experiential aspects, while a human mind depends on their complex organization. The combination problem asks how that organization yields one subject.
examples.note: Physical particles receive a mental aspect.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily animism.

concepts.name: Pantheism
concepts.summary: Pantheism identifies God with the universe or the totality of reality, rather than treating God as a being separate from the world. It appears in several philosophical and religious traditions.
concepts.body: Pantheists differ over whether the universe is divine in a literal, spiritual, or more abstract sense. The view contrasts with panentheism, where God includes but exceeds the world, and with classical theism, where God is distinct from creation. Pantheism does not necessarily involve worship of every individual object.

examples.text: A pantheist may describe the natural world as divine reality itself, not as a creation made by a separate deity.
examples.note: The universe and divine reality are equated.

commonMisreadings: It differs from panentheism because it denies a divine excess.

concepts.name: Paraconsistent logic
concepts.summary: Paraconsistent logic is a logic in which a contradiction does not entail every proposition. It allows reasoning with inconsistent information without collapsing into triviality.
concepts.body: In classical logic, from P and not-P one can infer any Q; this is the principle of explosion. Paraconsistent systems reject that inference while still permitting other valid reasoning. They are useful for inconsistent databases, legal records, or theories under revision, but they do not declare contradictions true or harmless in every context.

examples.text: A database may contain both “the shipment arrived” and “the shipment did not arrive.” A paraconsistent system can preserve that conflict without concluding that every unrelated claim is true.
examples.note: Contradiction does not cause explosion.

commonMisreadings: It does not make every contradiction harmless or true.

concepts.name: Paradigm
concepts.summary: A paradigm is a shared framework of concepts, methods, standards, and exemplary problems that guides inquiry in a field. In Thomas Kuhn’s account, a scientific paradigm shapes what researchers treat as legitimate questions and solutions.
concepts.body: A paradigm is more than a single theory: it includes training practices, instruments, and accepted examples of successful work. Scientists working within it engage in normal research, while persistent anomalies can contribute to crisis and change. The term is also used more loosely for any model, so its specific Kuhnian meaning should be distinguished from casual usage.

examples.text: Newtonian mechanics served as a paradigm for solving many problems in classical physics, providing equations, methods, and examples of acceptable solutions.
examples.note: It structured questions and acceptable solutions.

commonMisreadings: It is more than one isolated theory.

concepts.name: Paradigm shift
concepts.summary: A paradigm shift is a major change in the framework that organizes research in a field. In Kuhn’s account, such a change alters accepted problems, methods, standards, and explanations.
concepts.body: A shift may occur when anomalies undermine confidence in the existing framework and a competing one gains support. Evidence matters, but frameworks can differ in what they treat as a problem or a good explanation, making change more complex than simply adding facts. The phrase is often used loosely for any significant change and should not imply that all scientific standards disappear.

examples.text: The move from a geocentric to a heliocentric model changed astronomy’s account of planetary motion and the organization of its explanations. It was a gradual historical process, not a single overnight switch.
examples.note: The new framework reorganized basic categories.

commonMisreadings: It is not a minor improvement.

concepts.name: Pareto efficiency
concepts.summary: A situation is Pareto-efficient if no feasible change can make at least one person better off without making someone else worse off. It is a criterion for comparing allocations and outcomes.
concepts.body: Pareto efficiency does not imply fairness, equality, or maximum total welfare. An extremely unequal distribution can be efficient if improving the least advantaged would reduce someone else’s holdings. The criterion identifies opportunities for mutual improvement but does not choose among efficient outcomes or settle which trade-offs are just.

examples.text: If all available changes that would help one household also reduce another household’s resources, the current allocation may be Pareto-efficient even if one household has far more.
examples.note: No improvement is possible without a loss under the options.

commonMisreadings: Efficiency does not imply fairness.

concepts.name: Parfit's repugnant conclusion
concepts.summary: Parfit’s repugnant conclusion is the result that some plausible principles of population ethics rank a very large population whose members have lives only slightly worth living above a smaller population with very high well-being. Derek Parfit used it to expose difficult trade-offs in evaluating possible populations.
concepts.body: The conclusion is called repugnant because many judge the enormous population to be worse despite its greater total value under some aggregative theories. Avoiding it can require revising assumptions about total welfare, average welfare, or how populations are compared. The puzzle is not a policy recommendation to create such a population.

examples.text: Compare a small society where everyone flourishes with a vastly larger society where each life is barely positive. A total-sum theory may favor the second, which many find troubling.
examples.note: Adding positive lives drives the comparison.

commonMisreadings: Parfit presented it as troubling, not endorsed.

concepts.name: Part-list cueing effect
concepts.summary: The part-list cueing effect is the finding that being shown some items from a studied list can reduce later recall of the remaining items compared with receiving no cues. The cues may interfere with retrieval of uncued material.
concepts.body: The effect has been studied in memory research and can depend on how retrieval is organized. Seeing a subset may strengthen those items while making competitors harder to access, rather than helping recall of the whole list. It is distinct from ordinary forgetting caused simply by not being tested.

examples.text: After studying a list of bird names, a participant shown several of them as hints may recall fewer of the unshown names than a participant asked to recall the whole list unaided.
examples.note: The presented subset disrupts access to the remainder.

commonMisreadings: It is not ordinary forgetting alone.

concepts.name: Partiality
concepts.summary: Partiality gives special concern or priority to particular people, groups, or relationships, such as family, friends, or one’s community. It contrasts with impartial theories that require treating everyone’s interests equally.
concepts.body: Many ethical views allow some partiality because relationships create special responsibilities and personal attachments have value. The challenge is determining when special concern is justified and when it becomes favoritism or unfair discrimination. Partiality is not automatically selfish: caring for a dependent child can be a genuine duty.

examples.text: A parent spends time and resources caring for their own child rather than dividing them equally among all children. This is partiality grounded in a special relationship.
examples.note: The special relationship grounds priority.

commonMisreadings: Partiality need not be unjustified bias.

concepts.name: Participatory democracy
concepts.summary: Participatory democracy gives citizens meaningful opportunities to take part directly in political decisions, rather than limiting their role to choosing representatives. It aims to deepen democratic agency and public involvement.
concepts.body: Participation can include town assemblies, participatory budgeting, citizen juries, and workplace or community decision-making. Advocates argue that participation builds civic skills and makes policy more responsive; critics point to unequal time, information, and access, as well as the difficulty of scaling direct involvement. It can supplement representative institutions rather than replace them entirely.

examples.text: Residents who decide how part of a city budget is allocated through public meetings exercise participatory democracy. The process still requires safeguards so less powerful residents can participate.
examples.note: Citizens decide policy rather than only electing officials.

commonMisreadings: It can coexist with representative democracy.

concepts.name: Particular
concepts.summary: A particular is a specific, individual entity, contrasted with a universal or repeatable property that can be instantiated by many entities. The term appears in metaphysics, logic, and debates about properties.
concepts.body: This distinction helps frame questions such as how two red objects share a feature: they may instantiate one universal redness, resemble one another, or fall under a common predicate. Particulars can be concrete, such as a particular tree, or abstract on some theories. The category’s boundaries depend on the metaphysical account being used.

examples.text: This apple and that apple are two particulars, even if both are red. A realist may explain their shared color by saying each instantiates the same universal.
examples.note: It has a unique history despite shared color.

commonMisreadings: A particular need not be physical in every theory.

concepts.name: Pascal's wager
concepts.summary: A decision argument that religious commitment may be rationally favored when the possible gains and losses of belief are treated as vastly unequal.
concepts.body:
Pascal's wager is practical reasoning about religious commitment under uncertainty, rather than a proof that God exists. In its familiar form, a person considers a nonzero probability of God existing, an infinite benefit associated with the appropriate religious life, and finite costs of religious practice. Those assumptions appear to make commitment favorable even when the evidence does not settle the religious question.

The result depends on how the decision is modeled. Competing religions may associate incompatible choices with infinite rewards. Several options can then receive the same unbounded expected payoff, while combinations of infinite gain and loss can leave comparisons undefined. The problem is not simply that a probability is multiplied by infinity; it is whether the available alternatives can actually be ranked by the proposed calculation.

A further issue concerns belief itself. Choosing to attend worship or investigate a tradition does not guarantee sincere conviction, and a deity might reject belief motivated by advantage. Pascal's discussion therefore connects the wager to practices through which belief might develop. Even if that practical strategy persuaded someone, it would not establish the truth of the beliefs or resolve the many-religions objection.

examples.text: A person with no decisive evidence compares the finite costs of attending to a Christian life with the claimed infinite stakes of salvation.
examples.note: The case illustrates practical decision reasoning, not an inference that the Christian proposition is thereby true.

commonMisreadings: The wager is not a proof of God's existence and does not make faith sincere merely by choosing its benefits.
It does not automatically answer the many-gods objection, since different religions can attach different stakes to the same choice.
criticisms: Critics challenge infinite utility calculations, arbitrary credence assignments, the possibility of many rival deities, and the morality of believing for advantage.

lookalikes.note: The wager uses decision-theoretic comparison of outcomes, but its religious stakes and belief-voluntariness problems make it a distinctive application.

concepts.name: Paternalism
concepts.summary: Paternalism is interference with a person’s choices or freedom justified by concern for that person’s own welfare. It can be exercised by governments, professionals, institutions, or individuals.
concepts.body: A paternalistic measure may be soft when it ensures a choice is informed or voluntary, and hard when it overrides a competent person’s informed decision. Defenders appeal to preventing harm, correcting impaired judgment, or protecting future options; critics emphasize autonomy and the danger of imposing another person’s values. The justification depends on capacity, risk, and proportionality.

examples.text: A law requiring seat belts limits choice to reduce serious injury risk. Whether that paternalism is justified depends partly on how much the law burdens autonomy and prevents harm.
examples.note: The restriction protects the chooser rather than others.

commonMisreadings: Not every safety law is paternalistic.

concepts.name: Path dependence
concepts.summary: Path dependence means that present outcomes are shaped by the sequence of earlier events, so a different history could have produced a different current arrangement. It is used in economics, politics, technology, and institutional analysis.
concepts.body: Early choices can create switching costs, habits, infrastructure, or vested interests that make alternatives difficult even when they might now be better. Path dependence does not mean history determines every outcome or that change is impossible. Analysts distinguish self-reinforcing mechanisms from mere chronological influence.

examples.text: A keyboard layout may persist because users, schools, and manufacturers are already organized around it, even if another layout could be more efficient.
examples.note: Early adoption made later change costly.

commonMisreadings: It is more than mere historical influence.

concepts.name: Patient-centered ethics
concepts.summary: Patient-centered ethics gives priority to a patient’s values, preferences, interests, and informed participation in healthcare decisions. It treats the patient as an agent, not merely as the object of clinical judgment.
concepts.body: The approach requires understandable communication, respect for consent, and attention to a patient’s goals and circumstances. It does not mean clinicians must provide any requested treatment: professional duties, evidence, justice, and safety also matter. Patient-centered care balances expert knowledge with the person’s authority over their own life and body.

examples.text: A clinician discusses treatment options with a patient who values staying alert more than extending life at any cost, then considers that priority when recommending care.
examples.note: The patient's conception of a good outcome guides care.

commonMisreadings: It remains constrained by safety and professional duties.

concepts.name: Patriotism
concepts.summary: Patriotism is attachment to and concern for one’s country, often expressed through civic participation, service, or commitment to its people and institutions. It can be critical as well as celebratory.
concepts.body: Patriotism differs from nationalism in emphasis, although the terms overlap: patriotism often concerns loyalty and care for a country, while nationalism more explicitly links national identity to political sovereignty. Patriotism can motivate solidarity and reform, but uncritical loyalty can excuse injustice or hostility to outsiders.

examples.text: A citizen who protests discriminatory laws because they want their country to uphold its stated principles expresses critical patriotism.
examples.note: Opposition is motivated by concern for the country's character.

commonMisreadings: It need not be nationalism or superiority.

concepts.name: Peer disagreement
concepts.summary: Peer disagreement occurs when people with similar relevant expertise, evidence, and reasoning abilities reach conflicting conclusions. It raises the question of how much disagreement should reduce one’s confidence.
concepts.body: Conciliationists say a person should often move toward the peer’s view; steadfast views hold that one may retain confidence when one has reason to trust one’s own assessment. Whether someone is a true peer can itself be disputed, and disagreement may reveal overlooked evidence or differences in background assumptions.

examples.text: Two equally experienced clinicians independently reviewing the same test results reach opposite diagnoses. Each may have reason to reconsider confidence, even if they do not simply split the difference.
examples.note: Comparable expertise makes revision relevant.

commonMisreadings: Any disagreement is not automatically peer disagreement.

concepts.name: Perception
concepts.summary: Perception is the process through which sensory systems organize information about the environment into awareness of objects, events, and features. It includes more than passive reception: attention, expectation, and bodily capacities shape what is noticed.
concepts.body: Philosophers ask whether perception gives direct access to external objects, represents them through internal states, or is partly constructed by the perceiver. Psychology studies how perception supports action and how illusions arise. A perceptual experience can be informative without being infallible.

examples.text: A person perceives a distant road as wet because heat creates a mirage. The experience is perceptual, but the apparent water is not present.
examples.note: Sensory input is organized into world-directed experience.

commonMisreadings: Perception is not raw sensation alone.

concepts.name: Perdurantism
concepts.summary: Perdurantism is the view that an object persists through time by having different temporal parts at different times. A person or tree is, on this account, extended through time much as it is extended through space.
concepts.body: The view contrasts with endurantism, which says the whole object is wholly present at each time. Temporal parts allow perdurantists to explain change without saying that one thing has incompatible properties simultaneously: an earlier temporal part can be bent while a later one is straight. Critics question whether this account preserves ordinary identity.

examples.text: A tree’s short, leafless winter stage and its leafy summer stage are temporal parts of one persisting tree in a perdurantist account.
examples.note: Stages compose one four-dimensional object.

commonMisreadings: It differs from endurantism, where the whole is present at each time.

concepts.name: Perennialism
concepts.summary: Perennialism is the view that enduring spiritual or philosophical truths appear across different religious traditions, often beneath their distinct doctrines and practices. It is associated with the idea of a shared perennial philosophy.
concepts.body: Perennialists interpret similarities among traditions as evidence of a common metaphysical insight or experience. Critics argue that this can flatten real differences and impose a universal framework on traditions that understand themselves differently. The term is also used in education for a separate theory emphasizing enduring texts and ideas, so context matters.

examples.text: A perennialist may interpret contemplative accounts from different religions as expressions of a shared insight into ultimate reality. Critics ask whether the traditions’ own concepts support that reading.
examples.note: The comparison emphasizes shared essence.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than ordinary religious pluralism.

concepts.name: Perfect duty
concepts.summary: A perfect duty is a strict moral requirement that leaves little or no discretion about whether to perform it or how it applies. In Kantian ethics, perfect duties are often contrasted with imperfect duties that allow latitude in their fulfillment.
concepts.body: A duty not to make false promises is a common example: one must refrain from the prohibited act rather than choose when to comply. By contrast, helping others may be required while leaving discretion about whom and when to help. The exact classification depends on the ethical theory and how duties are formulated.

examples.text: A Kantian may treat a duty not to lie as perfect, while treating beneficence as an imperfect duty that allows a person to choose particular opportunities to help.
examples.note: The duty excludes choosing whether to honor it.

commonMisreadings: It concerns strictness, not guaranteed outcomes.

concepts.name: Performative utterance
concepts.summary: A performative utterance performs an action in being spoken under suitable circumstances, rather than merely describing a fact. Examples include promising, naming, apologizing, and declaring a meeting open.
concepts.body: For a performative to succeed, the speaker must have appropriate authority or standing, and the relevant procedure and context must be in place. “I pronounce you married” has no effect when said by someone without the required role or at the wrong occasion. J. L. Austin’s analysis of speech acts broadened the study of how language does things.

examples.text: A chair opens a meeting by saying “I call this meeting to order,” thereby performing the opening in the proper context.
examples.note: The speech act changes a social situation rather than reporting one.

commonMisreadings: It can fail when context is inappropriate.

concepts.name: Persistence
concepts.summary: Persistence is the continued existence of an entity through change or across different times. The problem is to explain when an object at one time is identical with an object at another.
concepts.body: Theories of persistence differ over whether an object is wholly present at each time or has temporal parts, and over which changes preserve identity. Ordinary criteria vary by kind: a river, a person, and a repaired ship persist in different ways. Persistence is related to identity but focuses on its application across time.

examples.text: A ship remains in service after routine repairs, but replacing every plank over time raises the question of whether it is still the same ship.
examples.note: Organizational continuity supports identity.

commonMisreadings: Persistence is not mere resemblance.

concepts.name: Personal identity
concepts.summary: Personal identity concerns what makes a person at one time the same person at another time. It matters to responsibility, survival, memory, and practical concern about the future.
concepts.body: Theories emphasize bodily continuity, psychological continuity such as memory and character, or more complex relations among them. Thought experiments involving brain transfer or memory loss test these accounts, but everyday cases may not uniquely determine one answer. Personal identity is distinct from similarity: two people can be alike without being numerically the same person.

examples.text: If someone’s memories and personality change gradually after an injury, we ask whether they remain the same person, and what continuity is relevant to responsibility.
examples.note: Mental relations connect the later person to the earlier one.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to unchanged personality.

concepts.name: Personalism
concepts.summary: Personalism is a family of philosophical and theological views that treats persons as fundamental and places special emphasis on their dignity, agency, and relationships. It often uses personhood to frame ethics and social life.
concepts.body: Personalists differ on whether persons are metaphysically basic, how personhood relates to the body, and which rights follow from personal dignity. The approach has influenced religious thought, political philosophy, and bioethics. It does not refer to one uniform theory or simply to being personable.

examples.text: A personalist account of healthcare may insist that a patient be treated as a participant with goals and relationships, rather than only as a set of symptoms.
examples.note: The patient remains an end with intrinsic dignity.

commonMisreadings: It differs from individualism because persons can be relational.

concepts.name: Personhood
concepts.summary: Personhood is the status or set of characteristics associated with being a person. It is used in debates about rights, moral responsibility, legal recognition, and the treatment of humans and other entities.
concepts.body: Proposed criteria include consciousness, rationality, self-awareness, agency, relationships, and biological membership, but no single criterion is universally accepted. Some theories distinguish being a human organism from being a person; others reject that separation. Personhood can be a moral or legal category, and the criteria may differ by context.

examples.text: A debate over whether an advanced artificial system qualifies as a person may examine its consciousness and agency as well as the social and legal consequences of recognition.
examples.note: The corporation receives legal standing without being human.

commonMisreadings: Personhood and humanity are not identical in every context.

concepts.name: Perspectivism
concepts.summary: Perspectivism holds that knowledge and interpretation are always situated from particular standpoints. What can be seen or understood depends partly on the knower’s position, interests, and conceptual resources.
concepts.body: Perspectivism need not imply that every view is equally true or that objective knowledge is impossible. Multiple perspectives may reveal different aspects of a subject, and some can be better informed or more comprehensive. The term is associated especially with Nietzsche but is used in diverse epistemological and cultural theories.

examples.text: A historian and a nurse may describe the same hospital policy from different standpoints, revealing administrative aims and patient effects that neither account captures alone.
examples.note: Each account reflects position and available information.

commonMisreadings: It is not automatically relativism.

concepts.name: Phenomenal consciousness
concepts.summary: Phenomenal consciousness is the felt, subjective character of experience: what it is like to see blue, feel pain, or hear a melody. It distinguishes conscious experience from information processing that may occur without awareness.
concepts.body: The concept motivates the “hard problem” of explaining how physical processes give rise to subjective feeling. Philosophers disagree about whether phenomenal properties are physical, functional, or irreducible. Reports of experience provide evidence about consciousness but do not by themselves settle its metaphysical explanation.

examples.text: The sting of a pin has a felt quality beyond the fact that the body detects damage and withdraws. That felt quality is an example of phenomenal consciousness.
examples.note: The focus is subjective experience, not withdrawal behavior.

commonMisreadings: It differs from access consciousness.

concepts.name: Phenomenalism
concepts.summary: Phenomenalism analyzes claims about physical objects in terms of actual or possible sensory experiences. On some versions, saying that an object exists means that certain experiences would occur under suitable conditions.
concepts.body: The view aims to explain material-object talk without positing objects beyond experience. It must account for unobserved objects, the stability of the world, and how different people’s experiences fit together. Phenomenalism is not the claim that physical things are imaginary; it offers a particular analysis of what claims about them mean.

examples.text: To say that a tree exists unseen may be analyzed as saying that people would have tree-like visual and tactile experiences if they approached it in suitable conditions.
examples.note: Counterfactual experience supplies object stability.

commonMisreadings: It does not require objects to vanish when unobserved.

concepts.name: Phenomenological description
concepts.summary: Phenomenological description carefully describes how something is experienced from the first-person perspective before explaining its causes or reducing it to a theory. It attends to the structure, qualities, and meaning of appearance.
concepts.body: The method asks what is present in experience and how attention, embodiment, time, or expectation shape it. It does not claim that appearances are always accurate or that causal science is irrelevant. Rather, it isolates lived experience as a phenomenon worth describing in its own terms.

examples.text: A phenomenological description of waiting may attend to how time feels prolonged and attention shifts toward small sounds, before explaining the experience through clocks or brain activity.
examples.note: The description distinguishes what is directly presented from what is anticipated.

commonMisreadings: Description of experience alone does not establish the external causes of experience.

concepts.name: Phenomenology
concepts.summary: Phenomenology is the philosophical study of structures and meanings of lived experience. It examines how objects, time, other people, and the self appear to consciousness.
concepts.body: Husserl developed phenomenology as a disciplined investigation of experience, while later thinkers such as Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, and Sartre transformed its aims. Some approaches emphasize intentionality, the directedness of experience toward things; others stress embodiment, practical involvement, or social existence. It is a family of methods and theories, not simply introspection.

examples.text: A phenomenologist studying a tool may examine how it is experienced as ready for use within an activity, rather than first treating it as a neutral object with measurable properties.
examples.note: The temporal structure of experience is described.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely introspective psychology.

concepts.name: Philosophical behaviorism
concepts.summary: Philosophical behaviorism analyzes mental states in terms of behavior and dispositions to behave, rather than as hidden inner entities. To be in pain, on one account, is to show or be disposed to show characteristic behavior under suitable conditions.
concepts.body: The view aims to connect mental concepts to publicly observable criteria and avoid a private mental theater. Critics argue that people can feel pain without displaying it, hide their states, or behave differently for reasons unrelated to them. Philosophical behaviorism differs from methodological behaviorism, which restricts psychological science to observable behavior.

examples.text: A person may be in pain while staying still to avoid detection, which challenges a simple behavioral definition. A behaviorist may respond by including counterfactual dispositions and context.
examples.note: Behavioral criteria replace an occult inner object.

commonMisreadings: It does not eliminate mental vocabulary.

concepts.name: Philosophical pessimism
concepts.summary: Philosophical pessimism is the view that suffering, frustration, or unfulfilled desire is a deep and pervasive feature of life, often outweighing its positive value. It is a broad orientation rather than a single doctrine.
concepts.body: Pessimists such as Schopenhauer emphasize desire as a source of recurring dissatisfaction, while later thinkers develop different arguments about suffering and existence. Philosophical pessimism is not simply a gloomy mood or clinical depression. Critics argue that it undervalues joy, achievement, and the possibility of improving conditions.

examples.text: A pessimist may argue that satisfying one desire commonly gives way to another, so pleasure does not permanently resolve dissatisfaction. That claim requires philosophical argument, not merely a personal feeling.
examples.note: The judgment concerns existence's structure, not one setback.

commonMisreadings: It is not clinical depression.

concepts.name: Philosophical quietism
concepts.summary: Philosophical quietism is the approach of dissolving or clarifying philosophical problems instead of solving them with a new explanatory theory. It often treats apparent puzzles as arising from misuse of language or confused assumptions.
concepts.body: Quietists may show how ordinary concepts work and why a demand for an underlying metaphysical explanation is misplaced. The approach can end a debate without answering it on its original terms. Critics argue that clarification can become evasive when genuine explanatory questions remain. Quietism names a method or stance, not necessarily silence about every philosophical issue.

examples.text: A quietist response to “where is the mind located?” may question whether the question treats mental activity as a spatial object in the first place.
examples.note: Linguistic clarification removes the apparent problem.

commonMisreadings: It is not intellectual inactivity.

concepts.name: Philosophical zombie
concepts.summary: A philosophical zombie is a hypothetical being physically and behaviorally identical to a conscious human but with no subjective experience. The thought experiment tests whether physical facts fully determine phenomenal consciousness.
concepts.body: If such a zombie is genuinely conceivable, some argue that consciousness is not reducible to physical facts. Physicalists reply that conceivability does not establish metaphysical possibility, or that a complete physical duplicate would necessarily be conscious. The zombie is a philosophical device, not an empirical claim that such beings exist.

examples.text: Imagine a person who says “that hurts,” withdraws from a hot surface, and has the same brain activity as a human, yet feels nothing. The scenario asks whether behavior and physical structure exhaust experience.
examples.note: Physical duplication is stipulated without subjective experience.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely an unusual person.

concepts.name: Philosophy of liberation
concepts.summary: Philosophy of liberation is a tradition that analyzes oppression and knowledge from the standpoint of people and communities subject to domination, with the aim of supporting emancipatory change. It emerged prominently in Latin American philosophy.
concepts.body: Thinkers such as Enrique Dussel criticize Eurocentric histories and ask how philosophical concepts serve colonial and economic power. The tradition includes ethical, political, and historical work and is connected to broader liberation movements. It is not only abstract reflection: it evaluates theory by its relation to lived injustice and transformation.

examples.text: A liberation philosopher may examine whose voices are excluded when a political theory defines justice, then develop concepts that address colonial histories and present inequalities.
examples.note: Oppressed experience guides diagnosis and theory.

commonMisreadings: It is philosophy as well as activism.

concepts.name: Philosophy of literature
concepts.summary: Philosophy of literature examines what literature is, how literary works mean, how they should be interpreted, and what value or knowledge they can provide. It connects aesthetics with language, ethics, and imagination.
concepts.body: Questions include whether authors’ intentions determine meaning, how fiction can teach about real life, and whether moral features affect literary value. Different genres and traditions complicate any single definition of literature. The field studies philosophical problems raised by literary works as well as the nature of literary art itself.

examples.text: A reader may ask how a novel can provide insight into grief without reporting a true event. The question concerns the relation between fictional representation and knowledge.
examples.note: The question concerns literature's philosophical contribution.

commonMisreadings: It is not every form of literary criticism.

concepts.name: Philosophy of religion
concepts.summary: Philosophy of religion critically examines religious concepts, arguments, practices, and claims. It studies topics such as God, faith, evil, religious experience, miracles, and religious diversity.
concepts.body: The field includes arguments both for and against religious claims and analyses concepts without requiring the philosopher to adopt a religious commitment. It differs from theology, which often reasons from within a tradition, though the two overlap. Philosophical methods clarify premises and assess whether conclusions follow.

examples.text: A philosopher of religion may assess whether suffering is logically compatible with an all-good and all-powerful God. That analysis is distinct from describing how a community responds pastorally to suffering.
examples.note: It tests compatibility between divine goodness and suffering.

commonMisreadings: It differs from theology's usual internal commitment.

concepts.name: Philosophy of science
concepts.summary: Philosophy of science studies the concepts, methods, assumptions, and aims of scientific inquiry. It asks what makes explanations good, how evidence supports theories, and how scientific knowledge changes.
concepts.body: Topics include causation, models, laws, measurement, confirmation, realism, and the role of values in research. Philosophers of science draw on actual scientific practice while analyzing its logic and limits. The field does not replace science; it examines questions about how scientific claims are justified and interpreted.

examples.text: A philosopher of science may ask whether a climate model explains temperature patterns or merely predicts them accurately, and what evidence distinguishes those roles.
examples.note: The issue concerns what scientific success warrants.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely scientific history.

concepts.name: Physicalism
concepts.summary: Physicalism is the view that everything is physical or depends wholly on the physical. It is a general metaphysical position, often used to explain the mind in relation to the body and brain.
concepts.body: Physicalists disagree about what counts as physical and whether mental properties can be reduced to physical properties or only depend on them. The view must account for consciousness, meaning, and abstract entities. Physicalism does not mean that only objects visible to the naked eye exist; it includes entities and processes described by mature physical science.

examples.text: A physicalist may argue that pain depends entirely on brain and bodily processes, even if the concept of pain is not interchangeable with a neural description.
examples.note: Mind is included in a physically complete ontology.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to behaviorism.

concepts.name: Picture-superiority effect
concepts.summary: The picture-superiority effect is the tendency for pictures to be remembered better than corresponding words under some learning conditions. It is a finding about memory performance, not a universal rule for all material or tasks.
concepts.body: Pictures can provide distinctive visual information and connect to verbal labels, creating multiple retrieval routes. The advantage varies with imageability, familiarity, attention, and how memory is tested. It does not show that pictures always teach concepts more effectively than words or that text is unnecessary.

examples.text: After studying a list containing a line drawing of a key and the word “key,” a person may later recognize the drawing more reliably than the word.
examples.note: The image supplies visual features as well as meaning.

commonMisreadings: It is a tendency, not an exceptionless law.

concepts.name: Placebo effect
concepts.summary: The placebo effect is a change in symptoms or outcomes associated with the treatment context, expectation, learning, or care, rather than with an active ingredient specific to the condition. Placebos can produce real changes in experience and some bodily responses.
concepts.body: The term should not be used to imply that symptoms are imaginary or that an inactive treatment can cure any disease. Clinical trials distinguish placebo responses from natural symptom change, reporting effects, and treatment-specific efficacy. Expectation and conditioning can influence pain and other symptoms, but the size and mechanism vary.

examples.text: A patient’s pain may lessen after receiving a treatment they believe is effective, even when the pill contains no active analgesic. That response does not show that the pill treats the underlying cause.
examples.note: Expectation and context influence pain experience.

commonMisreadings: It does not show illness is imaginary.

concepts.name: Platonism
concepts.summary: Platonism holds that abstract entities such as numbers, propositions, or universals exist independently of human minds and language. It is named for Plato but also describes later realist positions about abstract objects.
concepts.body: Platonists argue that mathematics and logic concern truths that are discovered rather than invented. They must explain how humans can know abstract entities that have no causal contact with us. The term also refers to Plato’s broader philosophy, so the relevant sense depends on context.

examples.text: A mathematical Platonist may hold that prime numbers existed before humans developed a notation for them. The claim is about abstract existence, not physical objects hidden somewhere.
examples.note: The number is mind-independent and abstract.

commonMisreadings: Modern Platonism need not reproduce all of Plato's philosophy.

concepts.name: Pluralism in metaphysics
concepts.summary: Metaphysical pluralism holds that reality contains multiple irreducible fundamental kinds, principles, or modes of being. It rejects the claim that everything ultimately reduces to one basic kind.
concepts.body: Pluralist theories vary in what they treat as fundamental: mind and matter, several basic substances, or distinct categories that resist reduction. The view must explain how fundamental kinds relate and whether there is a unified account of reality at all. It is broader than political pluralism or cultural diversity.

examples.text: A metaphysical pluralist may argue that mental properties and physical properties are both fundamental, rather than reducing one to the other.
examples.note: Several basic ontological categories remain.

commonMisreadings: It concerns reality, not political pluralism.

concepts.name: Political obligation
concepts.summary: Political obligation is the alleged moral duty citizens have to obey laws or support the political institutions that govern them. Philosophers ask what could make such a duty binding.
concepts.body: Possible grounds include consent, fairness, membership, gratitude, or the need to sustain just institutions. Each faces challenges: many citizens never explicitly consent, and unjust laws may not deserve obedience. Political obligation is distinct from legal liability, since a law can impose penalties even when its moral authority is disputed.

examples.text: A citizen may obey a fair tax law because they benefit from and help sustain a cooperative system. The argument does not establish that every law creates a moral duty.
examples.note: Membership and cooperation explain the requirement.

commonMisreadings: Legal obligation and moral obligation can diverge.

concepts.name: Political representation
concepts.summary: Political representation is the practice of acting, speaking, or making decisions on behalf of a constituency. It connects citizens to institutions that govern at a scale where direct participation is difficult.
concepts.body: Representatives may be expected to follow constituents’ instructions, exercise independent judgment, resemble the people they represent, or advocate their interests. These models can conflict, especially when constituents disagree or representatives face urgent decisions. Representation requires accountability and inclusion, not just formal election.

examples.text: An elected member who weighs constituent views before voting on a national budget represents those constituents, but must also answer for the judgment they exercise.
examples.note: The official decides under an authorized relationship.

commonMisreadings: Representation does not require personal resemblance.

concepts.name: Political sovereignty
concepts.summary: Political sovereignty is the highest authority to make and enforce decisions within a political community or territory. It concerns who has final say over laws and governance.
concepts.body: Sovereignty may be located in a monarch, parliament, people, or constitutional order, and it can be divided or constrained by treaties and federal arrangements. The concept is contested when external powers, Indigenous nations, or supranational institutions claim authority. Legal sovereignty and effective control may also diverge.

examples.text: A constitution may declare that sovereignty rests with the people while assigning lawmaking to an elected parliament. The formal source of authority differs from who exercises each power.
examples.note: Citizens are the ultimate source of binding authority.

commonMisreadings: Sovereignty need not mean unlimited practical power.

concepts.name: Polytheism
concepts.summary: Polytheism is the religious belief in or worship of multiple gods. Polytheistic traditions differ in how they understand the gods’ powers, relationships, and connection to the world.
concepts.body: Some traditions treat gods as distinct beings with specialized roles; others place them within a larger cosmic order or recognize one deity as supreme without denying others. Polytheism is not necessarily opposed to every form of unity or hierarchy. It differs from monotheism, which reserves ultimate divinity for one God.

examples.text: A worshipper who offers prayers to several deities associated with healing, harvest, and protection follows a polytheistic practice.
examples.note: Several divine agents occupy one religious system.

commonMisreadings: It is more specific than belief in many supernatural beings.

concepts.name: Populism
concepts.summary: Populism frames politics as a conflict between an allegedly virtuous people and a corrupt elite, and claims that political authority should express the people’s will. It can attach to left-wing or right-wing programs.
concepts.body: Populist movements differ in whom they define as “the people” and which elites they oppose. The framing can challenge entrenched power, but it can also portray opponents and minorities as illegitimate and weaken pluralist institutions. Populism is often treated as a political style or logic rather than a complete ideology.

examples.text: A campaign that claims only its leader represents the “real people” and labels courts or journalists enemies of that people uses populist framing.
examples.note: People-versus-elite rhetoric supplies the core frame.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to democracy.

concepts.name: Positive liberty
concepts.summary: Positive liberty is the effective capacity to direct one’s life and pursue chosen purposes. It concerns whether a person can actually act, not only whether others refrain from interference.
concepts.body: Education, health, resources, and freedom from internal compulsion can affect positive liberty. Policies that expand capability may also involve state action, raising questions about who defines a person’s real interests and whether assistance becomes coercive. The concept is often contrasted with negative liberty, but both can matter to the same choice.

examples.text: A person is formally free to attend university but lacks the preparation or funds to do so. Expanding access can increase positive liberty by making the option usable.
examples.note: Resources expand what people can actually do.

commonMisreadings: It need not dictate a person's ends.

concepts.name: Positivism
concepts.summary: Positivism is a family of views that grounds reliable knowledge in observation, scientific method, or formal analysis and is skeptical of claims that cannot be tested or clarified. The term has different meanings in philosophy and social science.
concepts.body: Logical positivists sought to connect meaningful factual claims with possible verification and treated many metaphysical statements as lacking cognitive content. Comtean positivism emphasized scientific knowledge and social laws. Later critics challenged strict verification and the idea that science rests on neutral observation. The historical varieties should be distinguished.

examples.text: A positivist approach to a social question may require measurable evidence and testable hypotheses before accepting a causal claim.
examples.note: Empirical or logical testability sets the standard.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than merely respecting science.

concepts.name: Positivity offset
concepts.summary: The positivity offset is the tendency for people in neutral or mildly stimulating conditions to experience slightly more positive than negative affect. It describes a baseline pattern in emotional response.
concepts.body: Researchers distinguish the positivity offset from the negativity bias, which concerns stronger responses to negative events. Both can occur: ordinary neutral situations may elicit mild positive affect, while salient threats receive disproportionate attention. The effect varies by context, measurement, and individual differences.

examples.text: A person waiting in a quiet room may feel mild interest or contentment rather than distress, even though nothing especially rewarding is happening.
examples.note: Positive affect occurs without a special happy event.

commonMisreadings: It differs from optimism about the future.

concepts.name: Possible world
concepts.summary: A possible world is a complete way reality could have been. Philosophers use possible worlds to analyze possibility, necessity, counterfactuals, and the truth conditions of modal statements.
concepts.body: Some theories treat worlds as concrete realities; others regard them as abstract representations or useful models. A possible world need not be a distant planet or an actual universe accessible to observation. The framework helps compare alternatives, but debates remain about what worlds are and which descriptions count as genuinely possible.

examples.text: The claim “the glass could have remained unbroken” can be analyzed by considering a possible world in which the same relevant circumstances differ and the glass does not break.
examples.note: The structured scenario represents an alternative condition.

commonMisreadings: It need not be a parallel physical universe.

concepts.name: Post-anarchism
concepts.summary: Post-anarchism is a contemporary approach that rethinks anarchist opposition to domination using poststructuralist accounts of power, identity, and discourse. It challenges the idea that liberation can rely on a fixed, unified human subject.
concepts.body: Post-anarchist writers often analyze how authority is reproduced through everyday norms and identities, not only through the state. They retain opposition to domination while questioning classical anarchism’s assumptions about nature, reason, or inevitable emancipation. The term covers a varied theoretical current rather than a single organization or program.

examples.text: A post-anarchist analysis may examine how workplace rules shape identity and self-discipline even where no manager gives direct orders.
examples.note: Anti-authoritarian politics combines with nonessentialist theory.

commonMisreadings: It extends rather than simply abandons anarchism.

concepts.name: Post-Marxism
concepts.summary: Post-Marxism refers to approaches that revise Marxist theory in response to changes in capitalism, culture, class politics, and political movements. It often rejects the idea that class alone determines social conflict.
concepts.body: Some post-Marxists analyze how political identities are constructed through discourse and alliances, while retaining attention to power and economic relations. The term encompasses different projects and can mark both continuity with and departure from Marxism. It is not simply Marxism that came after a certain date.

examples.text: A post-Marxist account may explain a political coalition through the linking of labor, environmental, and minority movements rather than assuming a single class identity unifies them.
examples.note: Conflict remains without one economic foundation.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply anti-Marxism.

concepts.name: Post-positivism
concepts.summary: Post-positivism accepts that evidence and testing are central to inquiry while rejecting strong positivist claims that observation is wholly neutral or that certainty is easily achieved. It is influential in social research methodology.
concepts.body: Post-positivists treat theories as fallible and observations as shaped partly by prior concepts, while still holding that claims can be compared against evidence and improved. The label covers varied positions and should not be confused with rejecting science or treating all interpretations as equal.

examples.text: A post-positivist researcher may use surveys and statistical tests while acknowledging that question wording and sampling choices shape the data collected.
examples.note: Empirical method is combined with fallibilism.

commonMisreadings: It is not relativism.

concepts.name: Postcolonialism
concepts.summary: Postcolonialism studies the continuing effects of colonial rule on politics, culture, economies, knowledge, and identity. It examines both historical empire and its enduring forms after formal independence.
concepts.body: Postcolonial thinkers analyze how colonial power classified peoples, extracted resources, shaped institutions, and represented colonized societies. The field also studies resistance and the recovery of suppressed perspectives. “Postcolonial” does not mean colonial effects have ended; it marks the historical and analytic relation to colonialism.

examples.text: A postcolonial reading of a museum collection may ask how objects were acquired and how colonial categories continue to shape their display.
examples.note: Colonial power persists through knowledge and representation.

commonMisreadings: It includes colonial histories, not only post-independence events.

concepts.name: Posthumanism
concepts.summary: Posthumanism questions the idea that humans are uniquely central or sharply separate from animals, machines, and environments. It examines how human identity and agency depend on relations with other forms of life and technology.
concepts.body: Different posthumanist approaches challenge human exceptionalism, anthropocentrism, or the image of an autonomous individual. Some focus on technological transformation; others emphasize ecological interdependence and nonhuman agency. Posthumanism is not simply a prediction that machines will replace people.

examples.text: A posthumanist analysis of a city may treat its residents, transport systems, animals, and digital networks as interdependent participants in urban life.
examples.note: Moral and political analysis extends beyond isolated humans.

commonMisreadings: It need not be anti-human.

concepts.name: Postmodernism
concepts.summary: Postmodernism is a broad intellectual and cultural movement skeptical of universal foundations, grand explanations of history, and the idea that meaning is always stable and transparent. It appears in philosophy, architecture, literature, and criticism.
concepts.body: Postmodern thinkers examine how knowledge and identity are shaped by language, institutions, and power, while often resisting claims to a single neutral standpoint. The movement is diverse and difficult to define; critics argue that its skepticism can undermine shared standards of truth or political criticism. It should not be reduced to the claim that nothing is true.

examples.text: A postmodern novel may combine incompatible voices and genres to challenge the idea that one narrator can deliver a complete, authoritative account.
examples.note: Plurality and irony shape its design.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply anything contemporary.

concepts.name: Poststructuralism
concepts.summary: Poststructuralism is a set of approaches that questions the stability of structures, meanings, and identities. It builds on structuralist analysis while emphasizing that systems of signs and social relations remain open to change and conflict.
concepts.body: Poststructuralist thinkers analyze how meanings depend on differences among signs and how institutions shape what can be said or known. They do not claim that language has no structure; rather, structures do not fix meaning once and for all. The field includes distinct projects associated with Derrida, Foucault, and others.

examples.text: A poststructuralist reading may show how a legal text relies on distinctions such as normal/abnormal that shift across contexts and shape institutional treatment.
examples.note: A supposed essence is treated as historically constructed.

commonMisreadings: It studies structures rather than denying all structure.

concepts.name: Potentiality and actuality
concepts.summary: Potentiality and actuality distinguish what something can become or do from what it currently is or does. The distinction is central to Aristotle’s metaphysics and later accounts of change.
concepts.body: A seed is potentially a mature plant, while growth actualizes capacities under suitable conditions. Potentiality is not mere logical possibility: it depends on the nature and powers of the thing. Philosophers use the distinction to explain change without treating every new state as arising from nothing.

examples.text: A student who can learn to play piano has that potentiality, while performing a piece is one actualization of it. Practice and opportunity affect whether the capacity is realized.
examples.note: Capacity and realized form illustrate the distinction.

commonMisreadings: Potentiality is more than bare logical possibility.

concepts.name: Power
concepts.summary: Power is the capacity to influence actions, outcomes, resources, or the behavior of others. The term applies to individuals, institutions, states, and social structures.
concepts.body: Power can operate through direct commands, control of resources, agenda-setting, or shaping what people regard as possible and normal. It need not be exercised openly to affect outcomes. Political theorists disagree about whether power is mainly coercive, relational, productive, or dispersed through social practices.

examples.text: An employer can influence workers through the authority to set schedules, while a platform can shape public attention by ranking which posts users see.
examples.note: Authority and enforcement alter conduct.

commonMisreadings: Power is broader than physical force.

concepts.name: Practical reason
concepts.summary: Practical reason is the capacity to deliberate about what to do, which ends to pursue, and how to act. It contrasts with theoretical reasoning, which aims primarily at understanding what is true.
concepts.body: Theories disagree about whether practical reasoning starts from desires, moral principles, or rational requirements independent of desire. It can also evaluate ends, not just calculate efficient means. Practical reason underlies debates about autonomy, motivation, and the authority of moral demands.

examples.text: A person deciding whether to take a job weighs salary, family commitments, and long-term goals. This is practical reasoning about both means and ends.
examples.note: Means are evaluated relative to an intended end.

commonMisreadings: It can assess ends as well as calculate means.

concepts.name: Pragmatic encroachment
concepts.summary: Pragmatic encroachment is the view that practical stakes can affect whether a person knows or is justified in believing a proposition. On this view, the same evidence may suffice in a low-stakes setting but fall short when a costly decision depends on it.
concepts.body: The theory challenges accounts on which knowledge depends only on evidence and truth-related factors. Critics argue that stakes change what a person should do, not what they know. The debate turns on cases where ordinary confidence seems adequate for casual action but irresponsible when much is at risk.

examples.text: A traveler may know a train leaves at 9:00 for casual planning, yet need to check the schedule again before boarding an expensive international connection.
examples.note: The costly decision raises the practical standard relevant to the knowledge judgment.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that truth itself changes with a person's interests.

concepts.name: Pragmaticism
concepts.summary: Pragmaticism is Charles Sanders Peirce’s name for his version of pragmatism, which connects the meaning of a concept to the conceivable practical effects of its object. Peirce adopted the unusual spelling to distinguish his precise view from looser uses of “pragmatism.”
concepts.body: The method asks what habits of expectation or action would differ if a concept were true. It is not the claim that a belief is true whenever it is personally useful; Peirce tied inquiry to public, self-correcting investigation. Pragmaticism is one strand of a broader pragmatist tradition.

examples.text: To clarify the concept of “hardness,” one might ask what practical differences hardness makes in how an object resists scratching or deformation.
examples.note: Those possible experimental consequences express the concept's practical meaning.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply the advice to choose whatever works in an immediate situation.

concepts.name: Pragmatics
concepts.summary: Pragmatics studies how context affects what speakers mean and how listeners interpret utterances. It examines meaning in use, including implication, reference, presupposition, and speech acts.
concepts.body: A sentence’s literal content may differ from what it communicates in a situation. “It’s cold in here” can be a report or an indirect request to close a window. Pragmatics considers shared knowledge, speaker intention, and conversational norms; it complements semantics, which focuses on conventional meaning.

examples.text: If someone asks “Can you pass the salt?” at dinner, the expected response is to pass it, not merely answer whether one is physically able.
examples.note: The conversational setting supplies the intended force beyond the literal wording.

commonMisreadings: Pragmatics differs from semantics, which studies meaning encoded by linguistic expressions.

concepts.name: Pragmatism
concepts.summary: Pragmatism is a philosophical tradition that connects meaning and belief to inquiry, practice, and the consequences of acting on ideas. It treats concepts as tools for understanding and addressing problems.
concepts.body: Classical pragmatists such as Peirce, James, and Dewey differ in emphasis, but generally resist treating knowledge as detached from human practices. “Works in practice” does not mean that any convenient belief is true; consequences matter as part of testing ideas through sustained inquiry.

examples.text: A community tests a flood-control plan by examining whether it reduces damage across seasons and revising it when evidence changes.
examples.note: Its practical success is evidence within inquiry, not a license to call every useful belief true.

commonMisreadings: Pragmatism is not identical to short-term usefulness or opportunism.

concepts.name: Precautionary principle
concepts.summary: The precautionary principle says that uncertainty should not automatically delay protective action when there is a plausible risk of serious or irreversible harm. It is used in environmental, public-health, and technology policy.
concepts.body: Versions differ in how strong a risk is required, who bears the burden of proof, and how precaution should be balanced against the costs of intervention. The principle does not mean banning every activity with uncertain effects. It supports proportionate safeguards when waiting for complete evidence could make prevention impossible.

examples.text: A regulator may restrict a chemical with credible evidence of persistent ecological damage while requiring further study, even before every long-term effect is known.
examples.note: The restriction responds to potentially irreversible damage under uncertainty.

commonMisreadings: The principle does not require banning every activity that has any conceivable risk.

concepts.name: Predicate
concepts.summary: A predicate is an expression that attributes a property to an argument or relates multiple arguments. Completing it with the appropriate terms yields a sentence or proposition.
concepts.body: In “Socrates is wise,” “is wise” is a one-place predicate applied to Socrates; in “Socrates teaches Plato,” “teaches” relates two arguments. Predicates are central to logic and language analysis, though natural-language grammar and formal predicates do not always align neatly.

examples.text: “___ is taller than ___” is a two-place predicate; filling the blanks with “Ava” and “Noah” produces a claim that can be evaluated as true or false.
examples.note: The verb requires two arguments to express the stated relation.

commonMisreadings: A predicate is not the same thing as a complete proposition.

concepts.name: Predictive processing
concepts.summary: Predictive processing is a framework in cognitive science that models the brain as generating predictions about sensory input and updating them when incoming signals differ from expectations. It aims to explain perception, action, and learning through prediction and error correction.
concepts.body: The framework often treats the brain as minimizing prediction error, while allowing expectations to influence how sensory signals are interpreted. Researchers disagree about how broadly this model applies and how it can be tested against alternatives. It is not established that the brain literally contains a complete internal model of the world.

examples.text: In dim light, a person expecting to see a familiar face may initially interpret an ambiguous shape as that person, then revise the perception when closer inspection reveals a coat on a chair.
examples.note: Contextual expectations help explain the perceptual interpretation of ambiguous input.

commonMisreadings: The framework does not claim that perception is conscious guesswork in the ordinary sense.

concepts.name: Preference utilitarianism
concepts.summary: Preference utilitarianism evaluates actions or policies by how well they satisfy the preferences of everyone affected. It extends moral concern to what individuals want, rather than measuring value only by pleasure or happiness.
concepts.body: The theory must address uninformed, harmful, or adaptive preferences and compare preferences that conflict. It also asks how preferences should be aggregated and whether some deserve more weight. A preference-satisfaction measure can respect individual aims, but it does not automatically make every preference morally acceptable.

examples.text: A policy that improves access to clean water may be supported because it satisfies people’s strong preference for health and security, even if it does not maximize immediate pleasure.
examples.note: The outcome satisfies an autonomous preference rather than maximizing felt enjoyment.

commonMisreadings: A preference must still be relevant and informed enough to carry moral weight in the theory.

concepts.name: Premise
concepts.summary: A premise is a statement offered as support for a conclusion in an argument. Premises provide the reasons from which the argument asks a reader to accept its conclusion.
