concepts.body: An argument may have one or many premises, and they can be explicit or assumed. A valid inference does not guarantee a sound argument: the premises must also be true or well supported. Identifying hidden premises often reveals where disagreement actually lies.

examples.text: “All mammals breathe air; whales are mammals; therefore whales breathe air” has two premises and a conclusion. Someone challenging it may dispute a premise or the inference.
examples.note: Each premise contributes inferential support for the conclusion.

commonMisreadings: A premise need not be true merely because it appears in an argument.

concepts.name: Presentism in metaphysics
concepts.summary: Presentism is the metaphysical view that only present objects and events exist. Past things no longer exist and future things do not yet exist, although statements about them may still be meaningful.
concepts.body: Presentists must explain how past-tense truths are grounded if past events no longer exist and how future claims can be true. Eternalists hold that past, present, and future events all exist, while growing-block theories include the past and present. Presentism is a claim about what exists, not the everyday preference to focus on the present.

examples.text: A presentist says the Roman Empire does not exist now, though it did exist and left evidence. An eternalist instead treats it as located at an earlier time.
examples.note: The past is treated as no longer part of reality itself.

commonMisreadings: Presentism differs from eternalism, which regards past, present, and future entities as equally real.

concepts.name: Presupposition
concepts.summary: A presupposition is information a speaker treats as already accepted or available when making an utterance. It often remains in place when the sentence is negated or turned into a question.
concepts.body: “Mira stopped smoking” presupposes that Mira used to smoke; “Mira did not stop smoking” typically carries the same background assumption. Presuppositions can be challenged, accommodated, or cancelled in context. They shape communication without being asserted as the main point.

examples.text: “When did you return the book?” presupposes that the book was returned. A listener can reject the presupposition by replying that it has not been returned.
examples.note: The background assumption remains in both the affirmative and negative forms.

commonMisreadings: A presupposition is distinct from an entailment that disappears under ordinary negation.

concepts.name: Primacy effect
concepts.summary: The primacy effect is the tendency for items encountered early in a sequence to be remembered or to influence judgment more than later items. It is studied in memory, social judgment, and impression formation.
concepts.body: In list learning, early items may receive more rehearsal and transfer into long-term memory. In forming impressions, initial information can frame how later details are interpreted. The effect depends on task, attention, and delay, and should be distinguished from recency effects that favor the last items.

examples.text: A person may remember the first few names in a long introduction list because they had more time to rehearse them.
examples.note: Early items benefited from additional encoding opportunities.

commonMisreadings: It is not the same as the recency effect, which favors the last items.

concepts.name: Priming
concepts.summary: Priming is a change in how quickly or accurately a person processes a stimulus because of prior exposure to a related stimulus or context. It can occur without deliberate awareness of the influence.
concepts.body: Priming effects vary across perceptual, semantic, and behavioral tasks. A related word can speed recognition, while social or behavioral priming claims require careful replication and interpretation. Priming is not mind control: effects are usually limited and depend on context, measurement, and the strength of the association.

examples.text: After seeing the word “doctor,” a participant may recognize “nurse” more quickly because the concepts are related.
examples.note: The first word activates related representations before the second judgment.

commonMisreadings: Priming need not involve deliberate memory or conscious recollection.

concepts.name: Principal–agent problem
concepts.summary: The principal–agent problem arises when one person or organization (the principal) delegates a task to an agent whose interests or information differ from their own. The principal may not be able to observe the agent’s effort or decisions fully.
concepts.body: The problem can produce moral hazard, hidden action, or adverse selection. Contracts, monitoring, incentives, and professional norms can help align interests, but each has costs and may encourage gaming. The concept applies to shareholders and managers, voters and representatives, and clients and professionals.

examples.text: A company’s owners may not know how much effort its managers put into long-term projects. Performance measures can help monitor managers but may encourage them to focus on short-term targets.
examples.note: The executive controls daily decisions while the shareholder bears much of the resulting risk.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely any disagreement between two people.

concepts.name: Principle of charity
concepts.summary: The principle of charity advises interpreting another person’s argument or statement in its strongest reasonable form before criticizing it. It aims to make disagreement more accurate and productive.
concepts.body: Charity does not mean agreeing, inventing a position the speaker did not hold, or ignoring harmful implications. An interpreter should preserve the speaker’s commitments while resolving ambiguity in a plausible way. The principle is especially important when reconstructing arguments from brief or informal statements.

examples.text: If someone says “the policy is unfair because it burdens poorer families,” a charitable interpretation identifies the concern about unequal impact rather than treating the speaker as opposing every tax.
examples.note: The charitable restriction produces a more plausible claim for evaluation.

commonMisreadings: Charity does not permit changing a claim so much that the speaker's position disappears.

concepts.name: Principle of sufficient reason
concepts.summary: The principle of sufficient reason says that every fact, event, or truth has an adequate explanation or ground. It is associated especially with Leibniz and rationalist metaphysics.
concepts.body: Different versions require reasons for contingent things, for truths, or for why anything exists at all. The principle motivates cosmological arguments and demands explanation beyond brute facts. Critics question whether every fact must have a further reason and whether explanation can terminate without circularity or infinite regress.

examples.text: A person asking why a particular planet exists seeks an explanation in its formation history. The principle’s stronger form asks whether the existence of the universe as a whole also requires a sufficient reason.
examples.note: Those conditions provide an account of why the event occurred rather than another event.

commonMisreadings: The principle is stronger than the modest claim that many events have discoverable causes.

concepts.name: Prioritarianism
concepts.summary: Prioritarianism is a consequentialist view that gives extra moral weight to benefits received by people who are worse off. It values improving well-being while assigning greater priority to gains for those in greater need.
concepts.body: Unlike strict egalitarianism, prioritarianism does not require equal outcomes; unlike utilitarianism, it does not count equal-sized benefits identically regardless of who receives them. The theory must specify how disadvantage is measured and how much extra weight it receives.

examples.text: A prioritarian may prefer a modest health improvement for a severely ill person over the same improvement for someone already healthy, all else equal.
examples.note: The benefit to the worse-off patient has greater moral value under the weighting rule.

commonMisreadings: Prioritarianism differs from egalitarianism because it need not value equality as such.

concepts.name: Prisoner's dilemma
concepts.summary: The prisoner’s dilemma is a game in which each of two players has an incentive to defect regardless of the other’s choice, yet both would be better off if they cooperated. It illustrates tension between individual incentives and collective outcomes.
concepts.body: In the standard one-shot version, defection is each player’s dominant strategy, producing an equilibrium worse for both than mutual cooperation. Repeated interaction, trust, communication, and institutions can change incentives and make cooperation more stable. The dilemma is a model, not a claim that cooperation is impossible.

examples.text: Two firms can either keep prices stable or undercut each other. Each may gain by undercutting while the other holds steady, yet both earn less if they repeatedly drive prices down.
examples.note: Each confession is safer for the individual given the other's choice, but mutual confession is jointly worse.

commonMisreadings: The dilemma is not simply any conflict between individual and collective interests.

concepts.name: Private language argument
concepts.summary: The private-language argument is Wittgenstein’s case that a language whose signs refer only to experiences accessible to one person cannot have meaning fixed by purely private reference. It challenges the idea that words get meaning from pointing to wholly private inner objects.
concepts.body: Wittgenstein argues that correct use requires criteria for distinguishing right from seeming right, and purely private impressions cannot provide such standards. The argument does not deny that people have private experiences or use first-person language. It concerns whether private experience alone can establish a rule-governed language.

examples.text: A person invents a symbol for a private sensation and writes it down whenever it occurs. If there is no independent criterion for whether the symbol is used correctly, the practice cannot distinguish remembering the rule from merely seeming to remember it.
examples.note: Without criteria beyond seeming right, correctness collapses into mere inclination.

commonMisreadings: The argument does not deny that people have private experiences.

concepts.name: Private property
concepts.summary: Private property is a system of socially recognized rights that gives individuals or organizations control over resources, including rights to use, exclude others, receive income, and transfer ownership. The bundle of rights varies by legal system.
concepts.body: Private property can support personal autonomy and investment, but its distribution and limits are politically contested. Rights may be constrained by taxation, zoning, environmental rules, or public needs. The concept is not identical to personal possessions: theories distinguish personal-use goods from productive property in different ways.

examples.text: Owning a house may give a person rights to live in it and exclude others, while zoning law limits how the land can be used.
examples.note: The legal system assigns control and transfer powers to the owner.

commonMisreadings: Private property does not imply that every resource must be privately owned.

concepts.name: Problem of evil
concepts.summary: The problem of evil asks how suffering and wrongdoing can exist if God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good. It is one of the central challenges in philosophy of religion.
concepts.body: The logical problem argues that these divine attributes appear inconsistent with evil; the evidential problem argues that the amount or kinds of suffering count against God’s existence. Theodicies propose reasons God might permit evil, while critics question whether those reasons justify actual suffering. Natural disasters and human wrongdoing raise related but distinct issues.

examples.text: A child’s severe illness raises an evidential question about why a good and powerful God would permit apparently pointless suffering. A theodicy may offer a response, but its adequacy remains contested.
examples.note: The suffering appears difficult to explain as necessary for a greater good.

commonMisreadings: The problem concerns both natural evil and moral evil, not only human wrongdoing.

concepts.name: Problem of other minds
concepts.summary: The problem of other minds asks how we can know that other people or animals have conscious experiences rather than merely behaving as if they do. It concerns the evidence for minds beyond one’s own.
concepts.body: We infer other minds from behavior, shared biology, and analogy with our own case, but these do not provide direct first-person access. Skeptical scenarios challenge whether such evidence is conclusive. The problem does not mean that ordinary confidence in other people’s feelings is irrational; it examines what supports that confidence.

examples.text: A person cannot feel another’s toothache directly, but their words, behavior, and shared physiology provide strong grounds to believe they are in pain.
examples.note: The inference moves from publicly observed signs to privately experienced states.

commonMisreadings: The problem does not imply that belief in other minds is irrational or avoidable.

concepts.name: Problem of religious diversity
concepts.summary: The problem of religious diversity asks how widespread and persistent disagreement among religions affects the justification of claims that one tradition alone is true. It is an epistemological challenge to religious exclusivism.
concepts.body: The diversity may prompt reconsideration of one’s confidence, but disagreement can also be interpreted through claims about revelation, culture, or partial insight. Philosophers distinguish pluralist responses, which treat multiple traditions as valid paths, from exclusivist and inclusivist views. The existence of disagreement does not by itself settle which view is correct.

examples.text: A believer learning that sincere, informed people in other traditions report compelling religious experiences may ask whether those experiences should reduce confidence in their own interpretation.
examples.note: The variation makes cultural location and epistemic access relevant to religious justification.

commonMisreadings: The problem is about disagreement and justification, not merely the existence of many rituals.

concepts.name: Problem of the criterion
concepts.summary: The problem of the criterion is a circularity in theories of knowledge: to identify reliable methods, we seem to need examples of what we know; to identify what we know, we seem to need reliable methods. It asks where epistemological inquiry can begin.
concepts.body: One response starts with particular beliefs and builds a method from them; another starts with a method and uses it to assess beliefs. A third may accept mutual support between methods and cases. The problem shows that theories of knowledge face a choice about justification, not that knowledge is impossible.

examples.text: To decide whether memory is reliable, one might check memories against records; but trusting the records already depends on some reliable method of knowing.
examples.note: The attempted validation uses the very capacity whose reliability is under examination.

commonMisreadings: It is not just a complaint that some standards are difficult to agree on.

concepts.name: Procedural justice
concepts.summary: Procedural justice concerns whether the processes used to make decisions are fair and legitimate. It focuses on how decisions are reached, not only on the distribution of outcomes.
concepts.body: Common standards include consistency, impartiality, accurate information, opportunity to be heard, and respectful treatment. Fair procedures can increase trust even when a person dislikes the outcome, but good procedure does not guarantee a substantively just result. The concept is used in courts, workplaces, public administration, and social psychology.

examples.text: A disciplinary hearing is procedurally fairer when the accused can see the evidence, respond, and receive a decision from an impartial reviewer.
examples.note: The opportunity for a fair hearing supports the legitimacy of the decision process.

commonMisreadings: Procedural justice differs from distributive justice, which evaluates the allocation of outcomes.

concepts.name: Process philosophy
concepts.summary: Process philosophy treats becoming, change, events, and relations as fundamental features of reality rather than viewing stable substances as primary. It understands things through the processes that produce and sustain them.
concepts.body: Process thinkers such as Whitehead emphasize that entities are constituted by relations and temporal activity. The approach offers a different picture of persistence and causation from substance-based metaphysics. It has influenced theology, ecology, and philosophy of science, though critics question whether processes can be described without presupposing enduring entities.

examples.text: A river is understood as a continuing flow of water and interactions with its banks, not as a fixed object whose material stays the same.
examples.note: The organism's identity is explained through continuity of process and relation.

commonMisreadings: Process philosophy does not mean that every change is random or unstructured.

concepts.name: Process theology
concepts.summary: Process theology applies process philosophy to religious thought, portraying God and the world as dynamically related. God is not an entirely immutable controller who unilaterally determines every event.
concepts.body: In many versions, God influences the world through persuasive possibilities rather than coercive control and is affected by what occurs. This account aims to address change, freedom, and evil, but revises traditional ideas of divine omnipotence and immutability. Process theologians differ about how to describe God’s power and relation to creation.

examples.text: A process theologian may say God offers possibilities for healing after a disaster but does not override the causal processes that produced it.
examples.note: Divine action is conceived as persuasive rather than coercive control.

commonMisreadings: Process theology differs from classical theism on divine power and immutability.

concepts.name: Processing fluency
concepts.summary: Processing fluency is the subjective ease with which information is perceived, understood, or retrieved. People often use this feeling of ease as a cue when judging familiarity, truth, or preference.
concepts.body: Fluency can be increased by clear formatting, repetition, or simple phrasing, but ease is not reliable evidence that a claim is true. It can influence judgments without deliberate awareness, and context affects whether people interpret fluency as familiarity, confidence, or aesthetic appeal.

examples.text: A slogan repeated many times may feel more familiar and therefore more believable, even when repetition adds no evidence for its accuracy.
examples.note: The easier presentation creates a positive fluency signal that can bias judgment.

commonMisreadings: Fluency is not evidence that the statement is actually true.

concepts.name: Progressivism
concepts.summary: Progressivism is a political orientation that favors social reform and public action to address inequality, exclusion, or problems produced by economic and political institutions. Its meaning changes across eras and countries.
concepts.body: Historical progressivism often supported regulation of industry, expanded political participation, and social welfare. Contemporary progressives may emphasize civil rights, climate policy, and economic redistribution. The label does not specify one program, and critics dispute whether reforms improve justice or expand state power too far.

examples.text: A progressive campaign may support stronger workplace protections and public healthcare to reduce insecurity and unequal access.
examples.note: Both measures use public policy to improve workers' social and economic conditions.

commonMisreadings: Progressivism is a broad political tradition rather than one fixed platform.

concepts.name: Proof
concepts.summary: A proof is a sequence of justified steps showing that a conclusion follows from premises, definitions, axioms, or accepted rules. Proofs establish results in mathematics and formal logic.
concepts.body: A proof must make each inference valid and state the assumptions on which it depends. In informal settings, a proof can be persuasive without being fully formal; in mathematics, details may be compressed but must be recoverable. A convincing example or numerical check is not, by itself, a proof of a general claim.

examples.text: To prove every even integer is divisible by two, define an even integer as 2k for an integer k; the claim then follows directly from the definition.
examples.note: The definition supplies the exact form required for the conclusion.

commonMisreadings: A persuasive example or empirical measurement is not automatically a proof.

concepts.name: Proof by cases
concepts.summary: Proof by cases establishes a conclusion by dividing the possibilities into a set of exhaustive cases and proving the conclusion in every case. It is valid because one of the covered cases must apply.
concepts.body: The cases must be exhaustive; otherwise the proof leaves an unexamined possibility. Cases may overlap, though disjoint cases can make the argument clearer. The method is useful when a statement’s truth depends on a feature such as parity, sign, or which condition holds.

examples.text: To show that an integer n² is nonnegative, consider the cases n ≥ 0 and n < 0; in either case, squaring yields a nonnegative result.
examples.note: Every integer falls into one of the two cases, and each yields the target conclusion.

commonMisreadings: The method fails if an unconsidered case remains.

concepts.name: Proof by contradiction
concepts.summary: Proof by contradiction assumes the negation of a claim and derives an impossibility, thereby showing that the original claim must hold under the accepted logic and premises.
concepts.body: The contradiction may be a statement and its negation, or a result incompatible with a definition or established theorem. In classical logic, contradiction licenses the conclusion; some nonclassical systems treat contradictions differently. The method is especially useful when a direct construction is difficult.

examples.text: To show there is no largest integer, assume a largest integer n exists; then n + 1 is a larger integer, contradicting the assumption.
examples.note: The constructed divisor contradicts the claim that the list was complete.

commonMisreadings: A contradiction proof is not the same as showing that the conclusion is merely unlikely.

concepts.name: Proof theory
concepts.summary: Proof theory studies formal proofs as mathematical objects: their structure, rules, transformations, and relation to consistency and computation. It focuses on the syntactic side of logic.
concepts.body: Proof theorists compare systems by examining what can be derived and how proofs can be normalized or transformed. Results such as consistency proofs show what a formal system can establish about itself or related systems. Proof theory complements model theory, which studies truth in structures.

examples.text: A proof theorist may analyze whether every derivation using a certain rule can be transformed into a simpler form without that rule.
examples.note: The proof itself becomes the object whose structure and permitted transformations are examined.

commonMisreadings: Proof theory differs from model theory, which studies interpretations and structures satisfying sentences.

concepts.name: Proper name
concepts.summary: A proper name is an expression conventionally used to refer to a particular individual, place, institution, or other entity. Names such as “Ada Lovelace” or “Nairobi” typically function this way.
concepts.body: Philosophers debate whether a name refers through associated descriptions, a causal-historical chain of use, or some combination. Names can continue to refer even when a speaker knows little about the bearer, and the same name can refer to different entities in different contexts. Proper names contrast with general terms that apply to many things.

examples.text: A speaker can refer to Ada Lovelace by using her name without knowing the details of her life. The name’s reference depends on shared linguistic practices.
examples.note: The expression has a conventional reference to that geographic individual.

commonMisreadings: A proper name is not automatically synonymous with a definite description.

concepts.name: Property
concepts.summary: A property is a feature or attribute that can be predicated of an object or shared by multiple objects. Philosophers ask what properties are and how objects possess them.
concepts.body: Some theories treat properties as universals that can be instantiated many times; others treat them as particularized features or as useful ways of classifying objects. Properties can be intrinsic, such as mass, or relational, such as being taller than another person. The concept is central to metaphysics, logic, and scientific explanation.

examples.text: Two apples may both have the property of being red, while only one has the relational property of being larger than the other.
examples.note: Different objects share the same general attribute.

commonMisreadings: A property differs from a relation, which connects two or more entities.

concepts.name: Property dualism
concepts.summary: Property dualism holds that mental properties and physical properties are distinct kinds, even if there is only one underlying substance such as the body. It contrasts with substance dualism, which posits separate mental and physical substances.
concepts.body: Property dualists often argue that physical descriptions do not capture the felt quality of experience, even if experience depends on the brain. They must explain how mental properties relate causally to physical events and whether they can be reduced to physical properties. The view has several forms, including epiphenomenalism and nonreductive accounts.

examples.text: A property dualist may say that a brain state and the painful feeling associated with it are distinct properties of one embodied person.
examples.note: The two property types are attributed to the same physical system but are not identified.

commonMisreadings: Property dualism differs from substance dualism, which posits distinct kinds of substances.

concepts.name: Property rights
concepts.summary: Property rights are legally or socially enforceable claims governing how a resource may be used, controlled, excluded from, or transferred. They define relations among people as well as relations between people and things.
concepts.body: A property regime may divide rights among owners, tenants, communities, and the state. Rights can be limited by contract, regulation, or public-use rules, and their distribution shapes economic power. Property rights are not necessarily absolute ownership of every possible use.

examples.text: A tenant may have the right to occupy an apartment while the landlord retains ownership and the right to sell it, subject to the lease.
examples.note: Different parties hold different incidents of the overall property arrangement.

commonMisreadings: Property rights are not limited to absolute ownership of a physical object.

concepts.name: Proportionality
concepts.summary: Proportionality is the principle that a response, restriction, or penalty should be appropriately related to the aim pursued or the harm addressed. It is used in ethics, law, and public policy.
concepts.body: A proportionality analysis may ask whether a measure serves a legitimate aim, whether it is necessary, and whether its burdens are excessive compared with its benefits. Standards differ across legal systems and contexts. Proportionality does not mean numerical equality; it requires a reasoned fit between means and ends.

examples.text: A city may impose a modest fine for a minor parking violation but reserve license suspension for repeated or dangerous conduct.
examples.note: The unequal seriousness of the conduct calls for an unequal sanction.

commonMisreadings: Proportionality does not mean that the response must be numerically identical to the harm.

concepts.name: Proposition
concepts.summary: A proposition is an abstract content expressed by a declarative sentence and capable of being true or false. Different sentences can express the same proposition, and one sentence can express different propositions in different contexts.
concepts.body: Philosophers debate whether propositions are structured entities, meanings, or truth-bearers. The notion helps distinguish a statement’s content from its wording or from the act of asserting it. Questions about propositions matter in logic, language, belief, and disagreement.

examples.text: “Snow is white” and its translation into another language can express the same proposition, even though the sentences use different words.
examples.note: The wording differs while the asserted content remains equivalent.

commonMisreadings: A proposition is not the physical sentence token used to express it.

concepts.name: Propositional logic
concepts.summary: Propositional logic is a formal system that treats whole propositions as units and combines them using connectives such as not, and, or, and if–then. It studies valid inferences based on those structures.
concepts.body: The system abstracts from the internal content of simple propositions, representing them with letters such as P and Q. Truth tables determine how compound statements depend on their parts. Predicate logic extends the analysis by representing objects, properties, and quantifiers.

examples.text: From P and P → Q, propositional logic derives Q by modus ponens, regardless of what P and Q specifically describe.
examples.note: Its truth value depends on the values assigned to P and Q.

commonMisreadings: Propositional logic does not analyze the internal subjects and predicates of atomic propositions.

concepts.name: Prospect theory
concepts.summary: Prospect theory describes how people make choices under risk, emphasizing that outcomes are evaluated relative to a reference point and that losses often weigh more heavily than equal gains. It was developed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky.
concepts.body: The theory models nonlinear sensitivity to gains and losses and nonlinear weighting of probabilities, helping explain patterns that expected-utility theory does not predict. It is a descriptive account of observed choices, not a claim that those choices are always rational or a recommendation for how to decide.

examples.text: A person may reject a fair coin toss to win or lose the same amount because the possible loss feels more significant than the equal gain.
examples.note: The two choices reflect different distortions around losses and unlikely outcomes.

commonMisreadings: Prospect theory is descriptive of observed judgments rather than a rule for ideal rational choice.

concepts.name: Protectionism
concepts.summary: Protectionism is the use of tariffs, quotas, subsidies, or regulations to shield domestic producers from foreign competition. Governments may justify it by protecting jobs, strategic industries, or national security.
concepts.body: Protectionist measures can support some domestic firms but raise costs for consumers and provoke retaliation from trading partners. Their effects vary by industry and time horizon. The term describes policy instruments; evaluating them requires identifying who benefits, who pays, and whether the stated goals are achieved.

examples.text: A tariff on imported steel may help domestic steel producers compete while raising costs for construction companies that use steel.
examples.note: The tariff makes foreign steel more expensive relative to local production.

commonMisreadings: Protectionism is not the same as any policy that regulates international trade.

concepts.name: Pseudoscience
concepts.summary: Pseudoscience is a practice or body of claims presented as scientific while failing to meet reliable standards of evidence, testing, and correction. The label concerns methods and evidential behavior, not merely whether a claim is unusual.
concepts.body: Common warning signs include avoiding falsifiable predictions, ignoring contrary evidence, relying on anecdotes, and protecting claims from revision. Classification can be contested, and a mistaken scientific hypothesis is not automatically pseudoscience if it is tested and revised through sound methods. The distinction depends on how a field handles evidence over time.

examples.text: A treatment claimed to cure every illness may be pseudoscientific if its supporters dismiss controlled studies and never specify what result would count against it.
examples.note: The practice retains its claims despite weak and nonreproducible evidence.

commonMisreadings: Pseudoscience is distinguished from a genuine scientific hypothesis that remains uncertain but testable.

concepts.name: Psychological egoism
concepts.summary: Psychological egoism is the descriptive theory that every human action is ultimately motivated by self-interest. It claims to explain what people in fact want, not what they morally ought to want.
concepts.body: Supporters may reinterpret apparently altruistic acts as seeking satisfaction, avoiding guilt, or gaining approval. Critics argue that this makes the theory unfalsifiable and confuses acting from a desire with acting selfishly: a person can want another’s welfare for its own sake. Psychological egoism is distinct from ethical egoism, a normative theory.

examples.text: Someone donates anonymously to help a stranger despite receiving no recognition. An egoist may posit hidden self-satisfaction, but critics ask what evidence could distinguish that motive from genuine concern.
examples.note: The theory treats the donor's personal motive as self-interested even though the beneficiary gains.

commonMisreadings: Psychological egoism describes motivation and does not by itself say that selfishness is morally right.

concepts.name: Public goods
concepts.summary: Public goods are goods that are non-excludable and non-rivalrous: people are difficult to exclude from their benefits, and one person’s use does not substantially reduce what is available to others.
concepts.body: These features can create a free-rider problem, since people may benefit without paying. Governments or collective institutions often fund public goods, though actual goods can be only partly public and provision may be local or mixed. The economic definition differs from the everyday sense of something owned by the public.

examples.text: Street lighting is a public good in a neighborhood: passersby benefit without using up the light or being easily excluded.
examples.note: The same protection can be enjoyed by many people at once without ordinary exclusion.

commonMisreadings: A publicly provided good is not necessarily a public good if users can be excluded or consumption competes.

concepts.name: Public reason
concepts.summary: Public reason is the idea that coercive political rules should be justified with reasons that citizens can reasonably share despite deep religious or moral disagreement. It concerns the legitimacy of laws imposed on a diverse population.
concepts.body: Rawls’s account asks officials and citizens to justify fundamental political decisions through public political values, while other theories define admissible reasons differently. Public reason does not require people to abandon private beliefs; it asks what can justify coercion to fellow citizens. Critics dispute whether shared reasons exist and whether the standard excludes important religious or marginalized perspectives.

examples.text: A law restricting speech might be defended by reference to equal civic freedom and public safety rather than a doctrine accepted only by one religious group.
examples.note: The stated reason can be assessed by citizens with different comprehensive doctrines.

commonMisreadings: Public reason does not require citizens to abandon private religious motivations.

concepts.name: Pygmalion effect
concepts.summary: The Pygmalion effect is the tendency for higher expectations from a teacher or other authority figure to improve a person’s performance, partly through changes in treatment and opportunity. It is related to self-fulfilling expectations.
concepts.body: Expectations can influence attention, feedback, encouragement, and the difficulty of tasks offered. The effect is not automatic or equally strong in every setting, and early studies have been debated over methods and interpretation. Positive expectations cannot substitute for resources, skill, or appropriate support.

examples.text: A teacher who expects a student to improve may provide more challenging work and specific encouragement, helping the student develop. The change depends on the actual support, not expectation alone.
examples.note: The teacher's changed treatment can help produce the expected improvement.

commonMisreadings: The effect is not proof that expectations alone determine achievement in every case.

concepts.name: Pyrrhonism
concepts.summary: Pyrrhonism is an ancient form of skepticism that recommends suspending judgment when opposing arguments seem equally persuasive.
concepts.body:
A Pyrrhonist compares how a claim appears from different perspectives and weighs the arguments for and against it.

When neither side seems stronger, the appropriate response is epoché, or suspension of judgment. The aim is ataraxia, a less disturbed state that may follow when one stops insisting on certainty.

examples.text: A traveler may suspend judgment about which account of a disputed custom is objectively correct after hearing equally plausible explanations from each community.
examples.note: Suspension follows the apparent equality of support for the competing claims.

commonMisreadings: Suspension follows a balance in the evidence; it is not a settled claim that truth is unknowable.

concepts.name: Pythagoreanism
concepts.summary: Pythagoreanism is an ancient Greek philosophical and religious tradition linking mathematical order, the cosmos, and disciplined ways of life.
concepts.body:
Pythagorean thinkers treated number and proportion as clues to the structure of reality.

Musical intervals offered a vivid example: an octave corresponds to a 2:1 string-length ratio. The tradition also included communal rules, religious commitments, and ideas about the soul, though ancient reports are difficult to separate between Pythagoras and later followers.

examples.text: A musician notices that halving a vibrating string’s length produces an octave, and takes the simple ratio as evidence that mathematical structure helps explain harmony.
examples.note: The audible consonance corresponds to a simple numerical proportion.

commonMisreadings: Pythagoreanism is not just the theorem about right triangles; it was a broad school with mathematical, ethical, and religious dimensions.

concepts.name: Qi
concepts.summary: A Chinese philosophical term for dynamic material force or vital process, interpreted differently across cosmological, medical, and Neo-Confucian traditions.
concepts.body:
Qi has a long and varied history in Chinese thought, where it can name breath, vapour, material stuff, vitality, disposition, or dynamic process. Its meaning depends on the tradition and question; it should not be translated automatically as a measurable physical energy. In Zhu Xi's system, qi is the moving, embodied medium through which li is expressed, and differences in its clarity or turbidity help explain why a common moral pattern appears unevenly in particular beings.

The li-qi distinction is not a dualism of two independent substances. A thing is concrete through qi and intelligible through li, with the two inseparable in actual existence. Zhu Xi inherited both terms and gave them a systematic Neo-Confucian relation; he did not coin them. The model is criticized when qi becomes an elastic explanation for every variation, but its explanatory role is clearer when a tradition specifies the processes, qualities, and ethical consequences it attributes to qi.

examples.text: A person's temperament is described as clearer or more turbid qi, affecting how a shared moral pattern is expressed in conduct.
examples.note: The example uses qi to explain embodied variation without treating it as a measurable physical energy in the modern scientific sense.

commonMisreadings: Qi is not simply electricity, a supernatural fluid, or one concept with the same meaning in every Chinese tradition.
Zhu Xi did not coin qi or li; he arranged inherited terms into a distinctive metaphysical account.
criticisms: Critics argue that qi can become too elastic to explain anything unless a tradition specifies its processes and standards of evidence.

lookalikes.note: Qi is dynamic material force or process; li is patterned order. Zhu Xi treats them as inseparable aspects, not identical terms.

concepts.name: Qualia
concepts.summary: Qualia are the felt, first-person qualities of experience, such as the appearance of red or the sting of pain.
concepts.body:
The term highlights what an experience is like for the person having it.

Philosophers use it to ask whether a complete account of brain activity and behavior captures the character of experience, or leaves something out. They disagree about whether qualia are private, ineffable, or even a distinct feature beyond representational and functional facts.

examples.text: Two people might discriminate the same red light and use the same color word, while a thought experiment asks whether its appearance could feel different to each.
examples.note: It identifies the first-person character of that tasting episode.

commonMisreadings: Qualia are not the external object or its physical properties; the question concerns the character of experiencing it.

concepts.name: Quantifier
concepts.summary: A quantifier is a logical expression that says how many members of a domain satisfy a condition.
concepts.body:
The existential quantifier (∃) says that at least one object has a property; the universal quantifier (∀) says that every object in the chosen domain does.

The domain matters: “everyone is seated” can mean everyone in a room, not every person anywhere. Quantifiers also interact with one another, so their order can change a sentence’s meaning.

examples.text: “Every student read a book” can mean each student read some book, possibly different ones; “There is a book every student read” claims one shared book.
examples.note: It requires the predicate “mortal” to hold for each object in the quantified class.

commonMisreadings: A quantifier’s scope and domain affect what it asserts; “some” does not mean exactly one.

concepts.name: Radical democracy
concepts.summary: Radical democracy seeks to deepen popular self-government and widen participation in decisions that shape people’s lives.
concepts.body:
It treats democracy as an ongoing practice, not only periodic elections.

Radical democratic approaches examine how economic power, social hierarchy, and exclusion limit whose voices count, and favor institutions that let affected people contest decisions. They differ on how direct participation should be and how it can coexist with rights, expertise, and representative government.

examples.text: A city creates resident assemblies with real authority over part of its budget, while making participation accessible to groups usually left out of hearings.
examples.note: The people subject to the policy gain an active role in determining it.

commonMisreadings: “Radical” does not by itself mean violent revolution; it refers to extending democracy toward the roots of social power.

concepts.name: Radical empiricism
concepts.summary: Radical empiricism is William James’s view that experience includes relations between things as well as the things themselves.
concepts.body:
James argued that relations such as “next to,” “before,” and “because” are encountered in experience, rather than being added only by later thought.

This challenges accounts that treat experience as a heap of disconnected sensations. The view is meant to preserve both immediate experience and the connections through which it forms a continuous world.

examples.text: Seeing a cup on a table includes not only the cup and table but their experienced relation of being-on.
examples.note: The relation of succession is experienced along with the individual notes.

commonMisreadings: Radical empiricism is not the claim that all knowledge comes from isolated sensory data; relations are part of what is experienced.

concepts.name: Radical feminism
concepts.summary: Radical feminism explains women’s oppression through deep social structures of male power, often called patriarchy.
concepts.body:
Its analyses examine how institutions and practices organize sexuality, reproduction, violence, family life, and labor.

“Radical” means seeking causes at the roots of social arrangements, rather than limiting reform to formal legal equality. Radical feminists disagree substantially about gender, sexuality, race, class, and which strategies best transform these structures.

examples.text: An analysis of workplace inequality might trace it beyond hiring rules to unpaid care expectations and the unequal risks of sexual harassment.
examples.note: The practices are treated as structural mechanisms rather than isolated personal incidents.

commonMisreadings: Radical feminism is not a single doctrine or a synonym for hostility toward men; its schools disagree on both analysis and political priorities.

concepts.name: Rational choice theory
concepts.summary: Rational choice theory models choices as attempts to select the option that best fits an agent’s preferences and constraints.
concepts.body:
A model specifies the available options, the agent’s ranking or utility for them, and sometimes beliefs about uncertain outcomes.

It can clarify how incentives affect behavior without claiming that people consciously calculate every choice. Its conclusions depend on the assumptions: preferences may be incomplete, socially shaped, unstable, or difficult to observe.

examples.text: A commuter chooses a slower route when its reliability matters more to them than the quickest average travel time.
examples.note: The choice follows an assumed ranking of outcomes and an assessment of probabilities.

commonMisreadings: “Rational” here usually means consistent with a formal model of preferences, not morally good, perfectly informed, or emotionally detached.

concepts.name: Rational egoism
concepts.summary: Rational egoism is the normative view that a person ought to act in ways that advance their own long-term good.
concepts.body:
Unlike psychological egoism, which claims people always act from self-interest, rational egoism says what they should do.

The theory must explain what counts as one’s good and how present interests relate to future welfare. It also faces cases where helping another person seems required even when it brings the agent no compensating benefit.

examples.text: An egoist may recommend saving for future security over an immediately pleasurable purchase, because the former better serves the agent’s lasting interests.
examples.note: The action is judged by the agent's durable interests rather than immediate gain.

commonMisreadings: Rational egoism is not the claim that every selfish impulse is rational; long-term self-interest can require restraint or cooperation.

concepts.name: Rationalism
concepts.summary: Rationalism is the view that reason can provide substantial knowledge independently of particular sensory observations.
concepts.body:
Rationalists often point to mathematics, logic, or principles they regard as knowable a priori.

They need not deny that experience is important: experience can supply concepts, prompt inquiry, or reveal facts, while reasoning establishes some conclusions. Rationalist theories differ over which truths are independent of experience and how humans can know them.

examples.text: A person can infer that no square has five sides from the meanings and rules involved, without measuring any physical object.
examples.note: The claim holds for the concept of a triangle before any particular observation.

commonMisreadings: Rationalism does not mean trusting any argument that sounds logical or rejecting all empirical evidence.

concepts.name: Rationality
concepts.summary: Rationality is the standard of forming beliefs and choosing actions in a way that fits relevant reasons, evidence, or aims.
concepts.body:
The word covers different standards.

Epistemic rationality concerns whether beliefs fit the evidence; practical rationality concerns whether actions serve an agent’s goals or meet requirements of choice. A person can reason consistently from false assumptions, so rationality alone does not guarantee truth or good outcomes.

examples.text: It is epistemically rational to lower confidence in a forecast when repeated observations contradict it, even if one still hopes it will be right.
examples.note: The belief changes in response to relevant evidence.

commonMisreadings: Rationality does not always demand calculation or emotionlessness; emotions can convey information and values can shape reasonable aims.

concepts.name: Reactionary politics
concepts.summary: Reactionary politics seeks to restore a social or political order regarded as better than the changes that displaced it.
concepts.body:
Reactionaries frame current reforms or revolutions as losses and appeal to inherited authority, religion, hierarchy, or national tradition.

Their preferred past may be selective or idealized, and the political program can range from restoring specific institutions to reversing broad social change. The label describes a direction of political change, not one fixed platform.

examples.text: A movement may seek to reinstate a former constitutional arrangement after a revolution, arguing that it provided stability and legitimate authority.
examples.note: Its goal is reversal toward a prior hierarchy rather than incremental improvement of the current system.

commonMisreadings: Reactionary politics is not simply conservatism: it characteristically seeks reversal toward an earlier order rather than preserving the present.

concepts.name: Reactivity
concepts.summary: Reactivity is a change in behavior or results caused by being observed, measured, tested, or otherwise studied.
concepts.body:
In research, participants may alter their conduct because they know they are being watched; measurement tools can also disturb the systems they record.

Researchers try to reduce or estimate these effects through unobtrusive measures, comparison groups, repeated observations, or explicit modeling. Reactivity is context-dependent and does not make every observation useless.

examples.text: Employees may follow a safety procedure more carefully while an evaluator is visibly auditing the workplace than during ordinary shifts.
examples.note: The observation procedure itself changes the behavior being measured.

commonMisreadings: Reactivity is a possible measurement influence, not proof that an observed result is entirely artificial.

concepts.name: Realism
concepts.summary: Realism is the broad view that at least some things or facts exist independently of what people believe or say about them.
concepts.body:
Realists disagree about what is independent and how it is known.

There are realist positions about the external world, moral facts, mathematical objects, and the entities described by science. Realism contrasts with views that treat the relevant facts as constructed, mind-dependent, or only useful features of a representation.

examples.text: A scientific realist may hold that a virus existed before it was observed and that instruments provide evidence about it.
examples.note: The claim makes electron existence independent of human recognition.

commonMisreadings: “Realism” names different debates in different fields; commitment to an independent world does not settle what that world contains.

concepts.name: Recency effect
concepts.summary: The recency effect is the tendency to recall the last items in a sequence especially well.
concepts.body:
In immediate recall, recent items may remain active in short-term memory, making them easier to report.

The effect is strongest under some conditions and can weaken when a delay or distracting task intervenes. It is one part of the serial-position pattern, alongside the primacy advantage often seen for early items.

examples.text: After hearing a short list and being asked to repeat it at once, a person may remember the final few words better than words from the middle.
examples.note: The final items have had the shortest interval to decay or be displaced.

commonMisreadings: The recency effect concerns a statistical tendency in particular memory tasks, not a guarantee that the newest information is always remembered best.

concepts.name: Reciprocity
concepts.summary: Reciprocity is the practice or expectation of responding to another person’s benefit or harm with a related response.
concepts.body:
Reciprocity can sustain cooperation: people often return help, share obligations, or avoid exploiting those who have treated them fairly.

It may be direct between two people or generalized across a group. The norm can also create pressure, debt, or retaliation, and what counts as a fair return varies across relationships and cultures.

examples.text: A neighbor who receives help carrying furniture may later offer to help that person with a repair.
examples.note: The returned favor reflects an expectation of mutual exchange.

commonMisreadings: Reciprocity is not always an equal exchange, and mutual return can be a social norm without an explicit contract.

concepts.name: Reconstructionism
concepts.summary: Reconstructionism is the effort to rebuild a damaged institution or tradition by reinterpreting and reorganizing its inherited elements.
concepts.body:
The term is used in different settings, including religious movements, education, and post-conflict politics.

Reconstructionists do not simply reproduce the past: they decide which practices remain meaningful, which need revision, and how a community can function under changed conditions. The chosen reconstruction can itself be contested.

examples.text: After a school system is disrupted, educators may retain its language and community ties while redesigning its curriculum and governance.
examples.note: The institution is rebuilt to address changed conditions rather than simply restored unchanged.

commonMisreadings: Reconstructionism does not name one universal program; its meaning depends on the tradition or institution being rebuilt.

concepts.name: Recursive definition
concepts.summary: A recursive definition gives base cases and rules for building further cases from ones already defined.
concepts.body:
The base cases anchor the definition; the recursive clauses explain how to form new members.

A well-specified recursion must make clear which cases are generated and, for computations, how the process terminates. Recursive definitions are common in mathematics, logic, and computer science because complex structures can be described from simpler ones.

examples.text: Natural numbers can be defined by including 0 and saying that if n is a natural number, its successor n+1 is one too.
examples.note: Each later factorial is determined from a previously defined smaller one.

commonMisreadings: A recursive rule without a base case or stopping condition may fail to define anything useful or may produce a process that never ends.

concepts.name: Red-team reasoning
concepts.summary: Red-team reasoning deliberately tests a proposal by looking for weaknesses, hidden assumptions, and ways it could fail.
concepts.body:
A red team takes an adversarial perspective while serving the larger goal of improving a decision.

It can challenge evidence, simulate an opponent, or trace failure scenarios. Its usefulness depends on access to relevant information and a willingness by decision-makers to act on findings; criticism without a clear question can become performative.

examples.text: Before launching a service, a separate team tries to expose how a malicious user could bypass its safeguards.
examples.note: The adversarial test targets vulnerabilities that ordinary implementation review might overlook.

commonMisreadings: Red-team work is structured stress-testing, not a demand to oppose every idea or to treat speculative risks as established facts.

concepts.name: Reductio ad impossibile
concepts.summary: Reductio ad impossibile argues by assuming a claim and deriving a contradiction or other impossibility from it.
concepts.body:
The impossible result gives a reason to reject the initial assumption, provided the inference is valid and the contradiction is genuine.

In classical logic, a reductio can establish the negation of an assumption; some nonclassical systems treat contradictions differently. The method is often called proof by contradiction, though terminology varies.

examples.text: Assume there is a largest integer. Adding one produces a larger integer, contradicting the assumption that the original was largest.
examples.note: The derived object contradicts the assumed minimality.

commonMisreadings: A reductio depends on the steps from assumption to contradiction; merely calling a consequence absurd does not complete the proof.

concepts.name: Reductionism
concepts.summary: Reductionism explains a complex phenomenon by analyzing it in terms of simpler parts, processes, or levels.
concepts.body:
A reduction can be explanatory, methodological, or metaphysical: it may show how a higher-level pattern arises from lower-level mechanisms, recommend studying components first, or claim that only the lower-level entities are fundamental.

Success in one sense does not establish the others. Some patterns depend on organization and interactions that a parts list alone cannot explain.

examples.text: A biologist may explain a cell process by tracing the chemical reactions and molecular interactions that produce it.
examples.note: The higher-level process is analyzed by its constituent mechanisms.

commonMisreadings: Reductionism need not deny that higher-level descriptions are useful or that systems exhibit patterns requiring explanation.

concepts.name: Reductionist physicalism
concepts.summary: Reductionist physicalism holds that mental phenomena are physical and can in principle be fully identified with or explained by physical processes.
concepts.body:
The view combines physicalism about what minds are with a reductionist account of how mental facts relate to physical facts.

Proposals include identifying particular mental states with brain states or deriving psychological explanations from physical science. Critics question whether first-person experience, mental meaning, or higher-level regularities can be captured in that way.

examples.text: A reductionist might identify pain with a neural process and seek to explain its felt and behavioral features through that process.
examples.note: The mental property is treated as nothing over and above an appropriate physical basis.

commonMisreadings: Physicalism alone need not be reductionist; some physicalists treat mental properties as real higher-level features.

concepts.name: Reference
concepts.summary: Reference is the relation by which a word, name, or symbol stands for something.
concepts.body:
A name may refer to an individual, a predicate to a property or class, and a pronoun to an entity supplied by context.

Philosophers and linguists ask what fixes reference: a speaker’s intention, a description, social conventions, causal history, or features of the world. Reference is distinct from an expression’s meaning or the way it presents its object.

examples.text: In “Mina left her bag,” the name “Mina” refers to a particular person in the conversation.
examples.note: The expression systematically picks out that city in relevant contexts.

commonMisreadings: Expressions can have meaning without an actual referent, as with an empty name, and different expressions can refer to the same thing.

concepts.name: Reflective equilibrium
concepts.summary: Reflective equilibrium justifies principles by adjusting them alongside considered judgments and background theories until they fit coherently.
concepts.body:
The method is iterative rather than a one-way deduction from self-evident rules.

A conflict may lead someone to revise a general principle, reconsider a particular judgment, or alter assumptions about relevant facts. Wide reflective equilibrium also tests the resulting set against competing theories and broader evidence. Coherence is a method of support, not a guarantee that the conclusion is true.

examples.text: A person comparing fairness principles with judgments about a difficult distribution case may revise either the case judgment or the principle and check the fit again.
examples.note: The judgment and principle are adjusted until the resulting set is more coherent.

commonMisreadings: Reflective equilibrium does not mean choosing whichever belief feels comfortable; revisions should answer reasons and withstand scrutiny.

concepts.name: Reformism
concepts.summary: Reformism pursues significant political or social change through gradual changes to laws and institutions.
concepts.body:
Reformists work through methods such as legislation, elections, collective bargaining, and administrative change, often arguing that durable gains can be built without overthrowing the system.

Critics may see reform as too slow or as stabilizing unjust institutions; reformists may see rupture as risky or destructive. The term covers different goals and strategies.

examples.text: A labor movement may campaign for enforceable workplace protections through legislation and union negotiations.
examples.note: Its incremental means are directed toward a larger structural improvement.

commonMisreadings: Reformism describes a strategy for change; it does not imply that the changes sought are minor.

concepts.name: Regress testing
concepts.summary: Regress-testing asks whether repeated demands for a further explanation or justification prevent an inquiry from reaching a usable answer.
concepts.body:
A regress begins when each answer is challenged by asking for another answer of the same kind.

The test helps identify whether a chain needs a stopping point, a different kind of support, or a circular structure. The term can be used broadly, but it should not be confused with software regression testing, which checks whether code changes break existing behavior.

examples.text: If every proof requires a proof of its proof, and so on without end, one can ask what grounds the original conclusion.
examples.note: The issue is the transmission of justification, not simply the number of steps.

commonMisreadings: An infinite regress is not automatically vicious; the question is whether the chain undermines the task it is meant to perform.

concepts.name: Relation
concepts.summary: A relation is a way in which two or more things are connected or ordered.
concepts.body:
Examples include being taller than, owning, between, and being a parent of.

Relations can have different numbers of places and may be symmetric, asymmetric, or transitive. In metaphysics, a key question is whether a relation is an independent feature of reality or reducible to the properties of its relata.

examples.text: “Leah is older than Omar” expresses a two-place relation whose order matters: reversing the names changes the claim.
examples.note: The relation cannot be fully specified by describing either person alone.

commonMisreadings: A relation is not simply a property of one object; its structure depends on the number and roles of the things it connects.

concepts.name: Relationalism about space
concepts.summary: Relationalism about space says spatial facts consist in relations among objects or events, rather than in space as an independent container.
concepts.body:
On this view, facts such as distance and position depend on how material things are arranged.

The opposing substantivalist view treats space as something that exists in its own right, including possibly empty regions. Debates concern whether the theories explain motion and physical laws equally well, and whether an empty space could exist without objects.

examples.text: If every object disappeared, a relationalist would deny that there remained spatial distances among absent objects; a substantivalist may allow empty space to remain.
examples.note: The spatial fact is explained through the objects' relation rather than an empty absolute space.

commonMisreadings: Relationalism does not deny that spatial measurements are objective; it offers an account of what makes spatial facts obtain.

concepts.name: Relevance logic
concepts.summary: Relevance logic is a family of logics that requires a meaningful connection between premises and conclusions.
concepts.body:
Classical logic allows a conclusion to follow from an inconsistent set of premises, and permits some inferences where a premise is irrelevant to the conclusion.

Relevance logics revise these rules to block such inferences while preserving formal rigor. Different systems specify relevance differently, so the label covers multiple technical approaches.

examples.text: From “It is raining” and “It is not raining,” classical logic permits any conclusion; a relevance logician questions whether those premises bear on that conclusion.
examples.note: The inference is blocked because the arbitrary conclusion lacks the required relevance to the premises.

commonMisreadings: Relevance logic is not merely a preference for topical arguments; it gives formal rules governing which inferences count.

concepts.name: Reliabilism
concepts.summary: Reliabilism explains justification or knowledge partly by whether a belief comes from a process that tends to produce true beliefs.
concepts.body:
Perception, memory, and careful measurement can be reliable processes in suitable conditions.

A reliabilist may say a person knows something even if they cannot explain why their method is reliable, provided the process actually is truth-conducive. Challenges include specifying the relevant process and context, and explaining what to say when a generally reliable method misfires.

examples.text: A normally functioning thermometer provides a well-calibrated reading, so a person’s belief about the room temperature is formed by a reliable process.
examples.note: The perceptual process usually produces true beliefs in that environment.

commonMisreadings: Reliabilism concerns the reliability of belief formation, not whether a belief happens to be true by luck.

concepts.name: Religious nationalism
concepts.summary: Religious nationalism ties national identity and political authority to a particular religious tradition.
concepts.body:
It may treat a religion as central to the nation’s history, define citizenship through religious belonging, or seek laws shaped by religious norms.

The forms vary: some movements emphasize cultural heritage while others demand religious rule or unequal status for minorities. Its effects depend on how the state defines belonging and protects dissent.

examples.text: A party may campaign for a constitution that names one faith as the nation’s defining religion and gives its institutions a formal political role.
examples.note: Religious identity is made part of the political definition of the nation.

commonMisreadings: Religious nationalism is not identical to personal religious devotion; it makes a claim about the nation and political order.

concepts.name: Religious pluralism
concepts.summary: Religious pluralism holds that more than one religious tradition can have genuine religious value or access to truth.
concepts.body:
The term can describe a social ideal of peaceful coexistence, or a theological claim about how different religions relate to ultimate reality and salvation.

These claims are distinct: a person can support equal civic rights without believing all religions are equally true. Pluralists differ on whether traditions offer partial truths, distinct paths, or culturally shaped responses to the transcendent.

examples.text: A pluralist theologian may see two traditions’ different practices as meaningful ways of responding to a reality neither describes completely.
examples.note: The traditions are not reduced to mere error simply because they disagree.

commonMisreadings: Religious pluralism does not mean that all religions teach the same thing or that their disagreements are unimportant.

concepts.name: Reminiscence bump
concepts.summary: The reminiscence bump is the concentration of autobiographical memories from adolescence and early adulthood in older adults’ life stories.
concepts.body:
When asked to recall significant events across a lifetime, people often report more memories from this period than from nearby adult years.

Novel transitions, identity formation, and culturally shared milestones may contribute, though no single explanation accounts for every pattern. The effect concerns the distribution of remembered events, not necessarily superior memory for every event from that age.

examples.text: A person in their sixties may readily recount school transitions, first work, and early relationships when asked for important life memories.
examples.note: The earlier period contains memorable transitions that remain highly accessible.

commonMisreadings: The bump is a recall pattern across the lifespan; it does not mean childhood memories are absent or all early-adult memories are unusually vivid.

concepts.name: Reparative justice
concepts.summary: Reparative justice seeks to address harm caused by past wrongdoing through repair for those harmed.
concepts.body:
Repair can include compensation, restoration of land or rights, public acknowledgment, institutional change, or guarantees against recurrence.

The appropriate response depends on the wrong, who suffered it, and what can now be repaired; money alone may not restore lost status or opportunity. Reparative justice also raises questions about responsibility across generations and the design of remedies.

examples.text: A government may return land and fund community-led restoration after an official inquiry establishes that it was taken unlawfully.
examples.note: The measures respond to a concrete historical injury and its ongoing effects.

commonMisreadings: Reparation is not merely a symbolic apology, and a remedy cannot always undo the original harm.

concepts.name: Replication
concepts.summary: Replication repeats a study or analysis to see whether its findings recur.
concepts.body:
A close replication follows the original procedures as faithfully as practical; a conceptual replication tests the same hypothesis with different methods.

Results can differ because of sampling variation, context, measurement, or flaws in either study. Replication helps estimate how dependable a finding is, but a single failure does not by itself show the original result was false.

examples.text: A second laboratory uses the same task and measures with a new participant group to check whether the reported effect appears again.
examples.note: The new test examines the original claim beyond the first research team.

commonMisreadings: Replication is not simple copying: researchers must distinguish faithful repetition from a new test of the same underlying claim.

concepts.name: Representationalism
concepts.summary: Representationalism holds that mental states or perceptions represent objects, properties, or states of affairs.
concepts.body:
A perception of a red apple, for example, presents the world as containing an apple with a certain color.

The theory can explain how mental states have content and can be accurate or mistaken. Philosophers disagree about whether representation fully explains conscious experience, and about what makes an internal state represent one thing rather than another.

examples.text: A map represents a city layout and can guide a traveler while still containing an error about a street.
examples.note: The internal state carries information about the apple without being the apple itself.

commonMisreadings: Representationalism is not the claim that people consciously inspect internal pictures; representation can be a functional or informational relation.

concepts.name: Republican liberty
concepts.summary: Republican liberty is freedom from domination by another’s uncontrolled or arbitrary power.
concepts.body:
A person can be dominated even when a powerful party does not currently interfere, if that party can intervene at will and the person has no effective way to challenge it.

Republican theory therefore emphasizes safeguards, accountability, and citizens’ ability to contest public decisions. It differs from defining freedom only as the absence of actual interference.

examples.text: A tenant whose landlord can evict them without cause may lack republican freedom even if the landlord has never threatened eviction.
examples.note: The standing dependence itself constitutes domination even without constant interference.

commonMisreadings: Non-domination does not mean freedom from every rule; laws can protect freedom when they are public, accountable, and contestable.

concepts.name: Republicanism
concepts.summary: Republicanism is a political tradition centered on self-government and freedom from domination.
concepts.body:
Republicans have emphasized civic participation, public institutions, and a common political life in which no ruler can exercise unchecked power.

The tradition includes different accounts of civic virtue, representative government, and citizens’ rights. Modern republicanism often treats contestability and the control of arbitrary power as key tests for institutions.

examples.text: A constitution that lets citizens challenge an official’s decision and requires public reasons can express republican commitments.
examples.note: Accountability limits rulers' ability to exercise uncontrolled authority.

commonMisreadings: Republicanism is not the same as support for a republic as a constitutional form; it is a wider theory of political freedom and citizenship.

concepts.name: Resistance
concepts.summary: Resistance is action that opposes, disrupts, or refuses a force, authority, or condition.
concepts.body:
Resistance can be individual or collective, public or quiet, and may use legal protest, noncooperation, strikes, concealment, or armed force.

Its moral and political status depends on what is resisted, the methods used, the available alternatives, and likely consequences. The concept itself does not imply that the cause is just.

examples.text: Workers may collectively refuse unsafe duties until an employer corrects a documented hazard.
examples.note: Their coordinated refusal aims to change the imposed conditions.

commonMisreadings: Resistance is not automatically justified or successful; evaluating it requires examining its target and methods.

concepts.name: Respect
concepts.summary: Respect is recognition of another person’s standing, dignity, rights, or legitimate claims.
concepts.body:
Respect can mean treating someone as an equal moral agent, attending seriously to their views, or observing a role-specific form of regard.

These senses can come apart: one can respect a person’s rights while criticizing their choices, or show deference without believing they deserve moral admiration. Ethical theories disagree about what grounds respect and what it requires in practice.

examples.text: A doctor can disagree with a patient’s decision while explaining the options honestly and honoring the patient’s authority to choose.
examples.note: The patient is treated as an agent entitled to decide about their body.

commonMisreadings: Respect does not require agreement, admiration, or compliance with every request.

concepts.name: Restorative justice
concepts.summary: Restorative justice responds to wrongdoing by centering the harm and the people affected, alongside accountability by the person responsible.
concepts.body:
Processes may bring victims, offenders, and community members together to describe what happened and agree on steps to repair damage.

Participation should be informed and voluntary, with safeguards for safety and unequal power. Restorative processes can complement formal justice, but they are not suitable for every case and do not guarantee reconciliation.

examples.text: After a school incident, a facilitated conference may let the harmed student explain the impact and require the responsible student to make a concrete repair.
examples.note: The process addresses the victim's injury and the offender's responsibility directly.

commonMisreadings: Restorative justice is not simply leniency or forced forgiveness; accountability and protection remain central.

concepts.name: Retributive justice
concepts.summary: Retributive justice holds that culpable wrongdoing can deserve a proportionate punishment.
concepts.body:
It focuses on what the offender has done rather than treating punishment only as a tool to deter future crime or rehabilitate.

A defensible retributive account must connect culpability, seriousness, and severity, while respecting limits on punishment. The view does not imply that every wrong should be punished or that harsh penalties are automatically deserved.

examples.text: A court may distinguish a deliberate assault from an accidental injury when deciding whether a penalty is deserved and how severe it should be.
examples.note: The punishment is justified by the offender's culpable violation and its seriousness.

commonMisreadings: Retribution is not revenge: it appeals to public standards of culpability and proportionality.

concepts.name: Retrieval-induced forgetting
concepts.summary: Retrieval-induced forgetting is reduced later recall of related information that was not retrieved during practice.
concepts.body:
When someone repeatedly practices some items from a category, competing related items may become harder to recall later.

One explanation is that retrieval strengthens target memories while suppressing competitors. The effect is not universal across tasks, and forgetting here means impaired access on a test, not necessarily permanent erasure.

examples.text: Practicing several bird names from a category can make an unpracticed related bird name harder to produce immediately afterward.
examples.note: Retrieval strengthens the practiced items while reducing access to competitors.

commonMisreadings: The effect differs from ordinary decay: practicing one item can itself change access to other related memories.

concepts.name: Revolutionary socialism
concepts.summary: Revolutionary socialism holds that ending capitalism requires a fundamental break with its property and political structures.
concepts.body:
