examples.text: A person who loses a job can distinguish the event itself from the judgments and actions still available to them.
examples.note: Character is evaluated rather than an uncontrollable result.

commonMisreadings: Stoicism is not emotional numbness; it aims to transform harmful judgments and respond well to feelings.

concepts.name: Strong artificial intelligence
concepts.summary: Strong artificial intelligence is the idea that an artificial system could genuinely have a mind or understanding, not merely imitate intelligent behavior.
concepts.body:
The phrase is associated with debates about whether computation can produce consciousness, intentionality, or human-level cognition.

It contrasts with “weak AI,” where machines may be useful tools without literally understanding. The boundary is disputed because behavior alone may not settle what kind of mental state a system has.

examples.text: A machine that converses fluently raises the question whether it understands meaning or only generates appropriate responses.
examples.note: Understanding is treated as real rather than imitation.

commonMisreadings: Strong AI is a philosophical thesis, not simply a label for a capable or convincing software system.

concepts.name: Stroop effect
concepts.summary: The Stroop effect is slower or less accurate naming of a color when the printed word names a different color.
concepts.body:
Reading words is often automatic, so an incongruent word interferes with the task of naming its ink color.

The classic effect demonstrates competition between processes that are difficult to control voluntarily. Performance varies with practice, language, and task design.

examples.text: The word BLUE printed in red ink typically takes longer to name by ink color than a neutral string printed in red.
examples.note: Automatic reading competes with color naming.

commonMisreadings: The effect is not a general inability to ignore words; it is a measurable interference under particular conditions.

concepts.name: Structural injustice
concepts.summary: Structural injustice is harm or disadvantage produced by ordinary systems and social processes, even without one person intending the whole outcome.
concepts.body:
Housing, labor, education, and transport policies can interact over time to constrain some groups’ opportunities.

Responsibility may therefore be shared among institutions and people who sustain or can change the processes, rather than assigned only to a single wrongdoer. The concept directs attention to patterns, rules, and remedies.

examples.text: A hiring system may reproduce unequal access when schools, unpaid internships, and referral networks systematically favor already advantaged applicants.
examples.note: No single decision need intend exclusion for the pattern to restrict opportunity.

commonMisreadings: Structural injustice does not mean nobody is responsible; it asks how responsibility is distributed across a system.

concepts.name: Structural linguistics
concepts.summary: Structural linguistics studies language as a system in which signs gain value through their relations and contrasts with other signs.
concepts.body:
Rather than treating words as labels attached independently to things, structuralists examine how differences organize a language.

A word’s role depends partly on the alternatives and combinations available in that system. This approach influenced later work in anthropology, literary theory, and semiotics.

examples.text: The meaning of “sheep” differs from “goat” partly because speakers use the terms to mark a contrast within a shared vocabulary.
examples.note: The contrast gives each sound linguistic value.

commonMisreadings: Structural linguistics does not deny that words refer to the world; it emphasizes that linguistic value also depends on relations within the system.

concepts.name: Structural realism
concepts.summary: Structural realism holds that science may reveal real relations and structures even when theories change their accounts of the entities involved.
concepts.body:
The view responds to scientific change by emphasizing continuity in mathematical structure across successful theories.

Epistemic structural realists limit claims about what entities are intrinsically like; ontic structural realists give structure a more fundamental status. The positions differ, and the label does not settle which scientific structures are real.

examples.text: A physicist may argue that a theory preserves relations among measurable quantities even as its picture of underlying particles changes.
examples.note: Relations survive revision of object descriptions.

commonMisreadings: Structural realism is a realist position about structure, not a claim that science knows nothing about entities.

concepts.name: Structuralism
concepts.summary: Structuralism explains meaning or social patterns through underlying systems of relations rather than isolated elements.
concepts.body:
Across linguistics, anthropology, and literary theory, structuralists look for rules and contrasts that organize signs, myths, kinship, or texts.

A feature’s role depends on the system in which it appears. Structuralist approaches vary, and critics argue that they can understate history, individual agency, and change.

examples.text: An anthropologist may compare myths by examining recurring oppositions such as nature and culture rather than treating each story as unrelated.
examples.note: Each element gets significance from its relational position.

commonMisreadings: Structuralism is not one universal method; it names related approaches that differ by discipline.

concepts.name: Subjective well-being
concepts.summary: Subjective well-being is how people evaluate and experience their own lives.
concepts.body:
Researchers often distinguish life satisfaction judgments from positive and negative feelings.

Self-reports provide access to a person’s perspective but can be affected by memory, current mood, wording, and cultural expectations. Subjective well-being is one account of welfare, alongside objective goods and capabilities.

examples.text: A survey may ask someone to rate overall life satisfaction and separately report how often they felt joy, stress, or sadness recently.
examples.note: The measures target experienced and evaluated quality of life.

commonMisreadings: Subjective well-being is not a complete measure of justice or welfare; a person’s reported satisfaction may coexist with serious deprivation.

concepts.name: Sublime
concepts.summary: The sublime is an aesthetic experience of overwhelming scale, power, or difficulty that exceeds ordinary understanding.
concepts.body:
In eighteenth-century aesthetics and later Romanticism, the sublime was distinguished from beauty: it can involve awe, fear, or astonishment before something vast or forceful.

The experience is not simply the object itself; it also concerns how a perceiver confronts limits of imagination and control. Different theorists explain that response differently.

examples.text: A person viewing a vast storm from a safe distance may feel both threatened and awed by its scale.
examples.note: The scene exceeds comfortable sensory grasp while stimulating thought.

commonMisreadings: The sublime is not just “very beautiful”; it often involves tension, excess, or a sense that representation falls short.

concepts.name: Subsidiarity
concepts.summary: Subsidiarity holds that decisions should be made by the lowest level of authority capable of handling them well.
concepts.body:
Higher institutions should support smaller communities or individuals when needed, rather than take over tasks they can perform.

The principle appears in Catholic social thought and political arrangements such as federalism. It requires judgments about competence, resources, and spillover effects; local control is not always adequate.

examples.text: A municipality may manage local roads while a national government coordinates a highway crossing several regions.
examples.note: Higher authority supplies capacity without taking over competent local tasks.

commonMisreadings: Subsidiarity is not a blanket rule that the smallest unit should always decide; it also assigns support to higher levels when necessary.

concepts.name: Substance
concepts.summary: A substance is an entity understood to exist in its own right rather than as a feature of something else.
concepts.body:
In Aristotelian metaphysics, individual things such as a horse are primary substances, while qualities such as color belong to them.

Other philosophers use substance for an underlying bearer that persists through change. The term’s meaning varies across systems, and whether substances are needed is disputed.

examples.text: A tree may be treated as a substance that remains the same individual while changing its leaves and height.
examples.note: The horse bears properties that depend on it.

commonMisreadings: Substance does not simply mean a material chemical; it is a metaphysical category about what exists independently.

concepts.name: Substance dualism
concepts.summary: Substance dualism holds that mind and body are fundamentally distinct kinds of substance.
concepts.body:
The view treats mental subjects as nonphysical thinkers and bodies as physical things.

Descartes is its best-known modern defender. It faces the interaction problem: if mind and body are fundamentally different, how do mental decisions cause bodily movements and physical events shape experience?

examples.text: A substance dualist may say that an intention is a mental event that causes a person’s arm to rise.
examples.note: The distinction is taken to indicate distinct substances.

commonMisreadings: Substance dualism differs from property dualism, which allows one physical substance to have distinct mental properties.

concepts.name: Substance self
concepts.summary: Substance-self theory explains personal identity through a persisting underlying self or soul.
concepts.body:
On this account, the same self can remain numerically identical despite changes in body, memory, and character.

It is often contrasted with theories that make identity depend on psychological continuity or bodily persistence. Critics ask how the underlying self can be identified and whether positing it explains the connections that matter in survival.

examples.text: A person who forgets much of their past may still be the same self on a substance account if the soul persists.
examples.note: The soul remains through physical and psychological change.

commonMisreadings: A persisting substance is one proposed basis of identity, not an agreed explanation of what makes a person the same over time.

concepts.name: Substratum theory
concepts.summary: Substratum theory says that properties depend on an underlying bearer that is not itself identical to any of those properties.
concepts.body:
The theory addresses how one thing can have many changing features while remaining a single subject.

The substratum is often described as “bare particularity,” but critics question whether an unknowable bearer adds explanatory value beyond the properties and relations themselves. Different metaphysical accounts treat the bearer in different ways.

examples.text: A red apple can become green as it ripens; a substratum theorist says one underlying object bears both colors at different times.
examples.note: The bearer unifies the properties in one object.

commonMisreadings: A substratum is not an extra visible feature; it is a proposed underlying subject of properties.

concepts.name: Sufficient condition
concepts.summary: A sufficient condition guarantees that another condition is met whenever it is met.
concepts.body:
If A is sufficient for B, then A’s truth ensures B’s truth, though B may also be true for other reasons.

Sufficient conditions can be stated in logic, law, science, and everyday explanations. They differ from necessary conditions, which must be present for the target condition to occur.

examples.text: Being a square is sufficient for being a rectangle, though some rectangles are not squares.
examples.note: Every square is a rectangle, though not every rectangle is a square.

commonMisreadings: A sufficient condition need not be the only way to produce the result.

concepts.name: Sufficientarianism
concepts.summary: Sufficientarianism holds that justice gives special priority to ensuring everyone has enough of a good.
concepts.body:
The relevant threshold might concern income, health, education, capability, or another good.

Sufficientarians disagree about how “enough” should be defined and whether inequalities above the threshold matter. The view contrasts with theories that focus primarily on equality or improving the position of the worst-off regardless of a threshold.

examples.text: A sufficientarian policy may prioritize bringing everyone above a basic standard of health care before reducing smaller differences among those already served.
examples.note: The threshold sets initial distributional priority.

commonMisreadings: Sufficientarianism does not imply that inequality ceases to matter once everyone crosses a line; versions differ on what follows.

concepts.name: Suffix effect
concepts.summary: The suffix effect is poorer immediate recall of a list when an irrelevant sound follows it.
concepts.body:
In a classic task, participants hear a sequence of items and then a spoken suffix such as “go.” The extra sound interferes with recall of the final items, especially when they are presented auditorily.

The effect helps researchers study how attention and auditory memory preserve sequence information.

examples.text: After hearing a list of digits followed by an unnecessary spoken word, a person may recall the last digits less accurately.
examples.note: The suffix interferes with auditory short-term memory.

commonMisreadings: The suffix effect is a specific memory finding, not a general effect of any word appearing after written information.

concepts.name: Sufism
concepts.summary: Sufism is a diverse Islamic tradition emphasizing spiritual discipline, remembrance of God, and transformation of the self.
concepts.body:
Sufi paths may include prayer, recitation, ethical training, guidance from a teacher, and communal practices such as dhikr.

Sufism has taken many forms across Muslim societies and is rooted in Islamic sources, though its practices and institutions have also been debated. It cannot be reduced to mysticism detached from Islam.

examples.text: A Sufi gathering may recite divine names as a disciplined practice of attention and devotion.
examples.note: Repetition functions as spiritual transformation.

commonMisreadings: Sufism is not one uniform order or a separate religion; its schools and practices vary widely.

concepts.name: Supererogation
concepts.summary: A supererogatory act is morally good but goes beyond what duty requires.
concepts.body:
The concept explains how a person can do something admirable without being blameworthy for not doing it.

Giving time or resources at significant personal cost is a common example, though whether an act is required depends on the moral theory and circumstances. The category is important for distinguishing obligation from exceptional generosity.

examples.text: A passerby who risks significant inconvenience to help a stranger may perform an admirable act beyond ordinary duty.
examples.note: The rescue is admirable even if omission is not culpable.

commonMisreadings: Supererogatory means praiseworthy but optional; it does not mean morally irrelevant.

concepts.name: Supervenience
concepts.summary: One set of properties supervenes on another when no difference in the first can occur without some difference in the second.
concepts.body:
Supervenience expresses dependence or covariation without specifying the mechanism that explains it.

If mental properties supervene on physical properties, physically identical situations cannot differ mentally. That claim alone does not settle whether mental properties are reducible to physical ones or how the dependence works.

examples.text: If two worlds match in every physical detail, a physicalist may require them to match in every mental detail as well.
examples.note: A higher-level difference requires a base-level difference.

commonMisreadings: Supervenience is a relation of dependence, not by itself an explanation or identity claim.

concepts.name: Sustainability
concepts.summary: Sustainability is maintaining human well-being while preserving the ecological and social conditions needed over time.
concepts.body:
The concept links present decisions to future generations and asks whether resource use, institutions, and economic activity can continue without exhausting essential systems.

Environmental sustainability is prominent, but social and economic dimensions also matter. Different policies balance these aims differently, and the term needs a specified context to be precise.

examples.text: A fishery is more sustainable when harvest levels allow the population and ecosystem to replenish over time.
examples.note: The policy preserves the ecological basis for future harvests.

commonMisreadings: Sustainability is not simply keeping current practices unchanged; it may require substantial changes to remain viable.

concepts.name: Swampman
concepts.summary: Swampman is a thought experiment about whether an exact physical duplicate is the same person or has the same meanings as the original.
concepts.body:
Donald Davidson imagines a person destroyed by lightning and an identical being spontaneously formed from a nearby swamp.

The duplicate has matching memories and behavior but no causal history connecting it to the original world. The case tests whether meaning and mental content depend only on present internal states or also on history and environment.

examples.text: Swampman says “tree” just as the original did, prompting the question whether the word has the same reference without a history of learning it.
examples.note: The duplicate has the original's apparent memories and character but lacks the ordinary history that produced them.

commonMisreadings: The scenario is a philosophical test case, not a plausible account of how living beings originate.

concepts.name: Syllogism
concepts.summary: A syllogism is a deductive argument in which a conclusion follows from stated premises by a structured form.
concepts.body:
Traditional categorical syllogisms connect classes using claims such as “all,” “some,” and “no.” The validity depends on logical form, not on whether the premises happen to be true.

Modern logic generalizes beyond the traditional syllogistic patterns.

examples.text: All mammals are animals; all whales are mammals; therefore all whales are animals.
examples.note: The middle term links the premises while disappearing from the conclusion, preserving the inferential structure.

commonMisreadings: A syllogism is not automatically valid; its structure must preserve truth from premises to conclusion.

concepts.name: Syndicalism
concepts.summary: Syndicalism is a labor movement that treats trade unions as the main means of worker power and social transformation.
concepts.body:
Syndicalists seek to organize workers directly through unions, strikes, and workplace action, sometimes aiming for worker control of production.

They vary in their attitude toward political parties and the state. Historical syndicalist movements developed in different national contexts and should not be treated as one uniform strategy.

examples.text: Workers may use a general strike to pressure employers and government while building union structures that could manage production.
examples.note: Its organizing model seeks to unite workers as a class capable of taking over production.

commonMisreadings: Syndicalism is not simply support for unions; it gives organized labor a central political and economic role.

concepts.name: Syntax
concepts.summary: Syntax is the set of rules that governs how words or symbols combine into well-formed expressions.
concepts.body:
In natural language, syntax concerns patterns such as word order and agreement; in formal languages, it specifies exactly which strings count as formulas or programs.

Syntax concerns structure rather than meaning, although structural differences often change meaning. A sentence can be syntactically well formed yet false or nonsensical.

examples.text: “The dog chased the ball” follows a common English subject-verb-object pattern; “Dog the ball chased the” does not.
examples.note: Changing constituent order changes grammatical roles and therefore the proposition conveyed.

commonMisreadings: Syntax does not determine truth by itself; a well-formed sentence can still make a false claim.

concepts.name: Systems thinking
concepts.summary: Systems thinking studies how connected parts and feedback produce patterns in a whole system.
concepts.body:
Instead of treating each event as isolated, it traces interactions, delays, loops, and unintended consequences over time.

This approach is useful when a change in one part affects others, as in ecosystems, organizations, or public policy. A system map can clarify relationships but is only as good as its evidence and boundaries.

examples.text: A hospital reducing discharge delays may need to examine bed availability, staffing, and community care rather than focusing on one department alone.
examples.note: The model treats an outbreak as a dynamic network rather than as an isolated sequence of individual decisions.

commonMisreadings: Systems thinking does not mean every outcome is too complex to explain; it identifies relationships that single-cause accounts miss.

concepts.name: Taste
concepts.summary: Taste is the sensory capacity to detect qualities such as sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami through receptors in the mouth.
concepts.body:
Taste perception arises from chemical stimulation and is integrated with smell, texture, temperature, and other signals to produce flavor.

The everyday word “taste” often refers to this broader flavor experience. Sensitivity and preference vary among people and can change with context or learning.

examples.text: A blocked nose can make food seem less flavorful even though the tongue still detects basic tastes.
examples.note: Glutamate is a tastant whose characteristic savory quality is detected by gustatory receptors.

commonMisreadings: Taste and flavor are related but not identical; smell contributes greatly to what people call flavor.

concepts.name: Tautology
concepts.summary: A tautology is a formula that is true under every assignment of its variables.
concepts.body:
In classical propositional logic, “P or not P” is true whether P is true or false.

Tautologies are useful for checking arguments and simplifying logical expressions. The term can also mean a needless repetition in ordinary language, but that rhetorical sense is distinct from the formal one.

examples.text: The truth table for P→P contains true in every row, so P→P is a tautology.
examples.note: The disjunction covers both truth possibilities for the same proposition.

commonMisreadings: A tautology is necessarily true by its logical form, not merely a statement that happens to be true.

concepts.name: Technocracy
concepts.summary: Technocracy is a political model that gives technical experts a central role in making public decisions.
concepts.body:
Its advocates argue that complex problems require specialized knowledge and evidence-based administration.

Critics worry that expertise can conceal value choices, weaken democratic accountability, or privilege narrow measures of success. In practice, technical analysis and public judgment often need to work together because evidence does not decide every political tradeoff.

examples.text: A government may appoint engineers and economists to design infrastructure policy while elected officials remain responsible for the goals and tradeoffs.
examples.note: The policy authority is assigned according to technical expertise rather than electoral popularity alone.

commonMisreadings: Technocracy is not simply using expert advice; it gives experts unusually strong governing authority.

concepts.name: Teleology
concepts.summary: Teleology explains something by reference to an end, purpose, or goal.
concepts.body:
An account may say an action is done for a purpose, or that an organism’s structure is directed toward a function.

Aristotle used final causes as one kind of explanation; modern biology often explains function through evolutionary history without claiming nature consciously aims. Teleological language can be useful but needs care where no agent or goal exists.

examples.text: A thermostat switches on heating in order to maintain a set temperature, because it was designed to serve that function.
examples.note: The explanation identifies an outcome or function toward which the process is directed.

commonMisreadings: Teleology does not always imply conscious intention; purpose can be attributed by design or by a theoretical account of function.

concepts.name: Teletransportation paradox
concepts.summary: The teletransportation paradox asks whether a person survives when a machine destroys an original and reconstructs an exact copy elsewhere.
concepts.body:
The device records the person’s structure, destroys the body, and builds a duplicate with the same memories and character.

If psychological continuity matters, the duplicate seems to be the same person; if bodily or biological continuity matters, the original may have died. The case tests which features of persistence matter for identity and survival.

examples.text: A traveler who steps into a teleporter and wakes with all memories intact asks whether they arrived or were replaced by a copy.
examples.note: The recreated person has Alice's memories and personality, making psychological survival plausible while leaving identity disputed.

commonMisreadings: The paradox is not resolved by saying the copy is qualitatively identical; it asks whether qualitative similarity is enough for numerical identity.

concepts.name: Temperance
concepts.summary: Temperance is the virtue of regulating desires and pleasures in a proportionate way.
concepts.body:
In classical ethics, a temperate person does not merely suppress appetite but learns to desire appropriate things in fitting amounts and circumstances.

The virtue can concern food, drink, sex, anger, or other strong impulses. It differs from abstinence because it aims at good judgment and balance rather than rejecting pleasure altogether.

examples.text: A temperate person enjoys a meal while stopping when satisfied rather than being ruled by appetite.
examples.note: The choice permits pleasure while preventing appetite from dictating action.

commonMisreadings: Temperance is not self-denial for its own sake; it is the skill of keeping desire in proper measure.

concepts.name: Temporal parts
concepts.summary: Temporal parts are the time-limited stages of an object in a four-dimensional account of persistence.
concepts.body:
On this view, an enduring person or object is extended through time as well as space, with different temporal parts existing at different periods.

This can explain change without requiring one wholly unchanging object to have incompatible properties at once. Endurantists instead say objects are wholly present at each time.

examples.text: A person’s childhood stage and adult stage can be treated as distinct temporal parts of the same extended person.
examples.note: Each stage has its own location and age while belonging to the same temporally extended entity.

commonMisreadings: Temporal-parts theory is one account of persistence, not a claim that people are literally divided into physical pieces.

concepts.name: Term
concepts.summary: A term is a word or expression that functions as a name, subject, or predicate in a language or argument.
concepts.body:
In logic, terms may refer to individuals or help form predicates; in ordinary language, “term” can also mean a technical word or a time period.

A concept is a mental or abstract representation, so the two should not be treated as identical: a term is linguistic, while a concept is what it may express.

examples.text: In “Socrates is mortal,” “Socrates” is a singular term and “mortal” is a predicate term.
examples.note: Each expression contributes an element to the proposition but does not independently make a complete assertion there.

commonMisreadings: A term is not necessarily a single word; expressions such as “the first person on the Moon” can function as terms.

concepts.name: Testimonial injustice
concepts.summary: Testimonial injustice occurs when prejudice causes a hearer to give a speaker less credibility than they deserve.
concepts.body:
Miranda Fricker’s account treats this as a distinctive epistemic wrong: identity-based stereotypes distort the exchange of knowledge and can silence the speaker.

The harm may be compounded when a person lacks shared concepts for explaining their experience. Credibility judgments can be challenged by examining evidence and the social assumptions behind them.

examples.text: A patient’s report of pain may be discounted because a clinician relies on a stereotype about the patient’s group.
examples.note: The stereotype lowers the witness's credibility independently of the evidence supplied.

commonMisreadings: Testimonial injustice is not every disagreement or error about credibility; prejudice must play a role in the credibility deficit.

concepts.name: Testimony
concepts.summary: Testimony is information conveyed through another person’s report or assertion.
concepts.body:
Much ordinary knowledge depends on testimony, from news and history to what a trusted expert says.

Whether testimony justifies belief by itself or requires independent checking is debated. Reliability, competence, honesty, context, and access to corroboration all affect how much weight a report deserves.

examples.text: A person learns the train schedule from a station employee rather than checking the operating system themselves.
examples.note: The traveler obtains the information through the curator's communicated assertion rather than direct observation.

commonMisreadings: Testimony is a source of evidence, not a guarantee of truth; speakers can be mistaken or deceptive.

concepts.name: Testing effect
concepts.summary: The testing effect is improved later memory after actively retrieving material, compared with only restudying it.
concepts.body:
Trying to recall an answer strengthens access to it and reveals what has not been learned.

The benefit can persist even when retrieval practice feels harder than rereading. Feedback and appropriately spaced practice improve results, while a test that is too difficult may provide little benefit.

examples.text: A student who closes their notes and explains a concept from memory may retain it longer than one who rereads the same page repeatedly.
examples.note: The practice test requires retrieval, which exercises the memory route used in later recall.

commonMisreadings: The effect concerns retrieval practice, not the claim that formal exams are always beneficial or that feedback is unnecessary.

concepts.name: Theism
concepts.summary: Theism is belief in at least one god or divine reality, often understood as personal and active in the world.
concepts.body:
Theists differ about whether God created the universe, intervenes in events, or has attributes such as omniscience and perfect goodness.

Classical monotheism is one form, but theism can also include multiple gods. The term states a broad commitment and does not specify a complete theology.

examples.text: A theist may believe that a creator sustains the universe while also holding that natural processes operate consistently.
examples.note: The claim includes a divine reality with agency rather than an impersonal first principle alone.

commonMisreadings: Theism does not name one religion or imply agreement about God’s nature.

concepts.name: Theocracy
concepts.summary: A theocracy is a political system whose authority is grounded in divine rule, religious law, or religious leadership.
concepts.body:
Religious institutions or officials may directly govern, or state laws may be interpreted as deriving from a religious authority.

Historical systems vary in how power is shared and how minorities are treated. The label concerns the source and structure of political authority, not the personal faith of citizens.

examples.text: A state may reserve senior political decisions for clerics who claim authority to interpret religious law.
examples.note: Political decisions are institutionally subordinated to a religious authority or norm.

commonMisreadings: A religious population does not by itself make a state a theocracy; the question is how government authority is organized.

concepts.name: Theodicy
concepts.summary: A theodicy attempts to explain how a perfectly good and powerful God can permit evil and suffering.
concepts.body:
The problem arises because apparently preventable suffering seems difficult to reconcile with divine goodness, knowledge, and power.

Theodicies offer proposed reasons, such as free will or the possibility of moral growth, while critics ask whether those reasons justify the actual scale and distribution of suffering. A defense may show a view is logically possible without claiming to explain every case.

examples.text: A free-will theodicy argues that meaningful moral choice requires the possibility of harmful action, though it must address suffering not caused by human choices.
examples.note: The proposed justification connects the existence of evil with a greater good or necessary condition.

commonMisreadings: A theodicy is an attempted reconciliation, not a demonstrated explanation accepted by all theists.

concepts.name: Theory of mind
concepts.summary: Theory of mind is the ability to attribute beliefs, desires, intentions, and other mental states to oneself and others.
concepts.body:
It helps explain and predict behavior by recognizing that another person can know or believe something different from what one knows.

Developmental psychology studies how this capacity emerges; philosophy asks how we know other minds. The term can refer either to the capacity or to an explicit explanatory framework about mental states.

examples.text: A child understands that a character will search where they last saw a toy, even though the child knows it was moved.
examples.note: The child tracks Sally's belief rather than substituting the child's own knowledge.

commonMisreadings: Theory of mind does not mean reading minds directly; attributions can be mistaken and depend on context.

concepts.name: Theory underdetermination
concepts.summary: A theory is underdetermined when the available evidence fits more than one explanatory account.
concepts.body:
The problem can arise because different theories make the same predictions, or because auxiliary assumptions allow rival views to accommodate the same data.

More evidence may distinguish them, but sometimes choices also depend on simplicity, scope, or explanatory virtues. Underdetermination challenges claims that evidence uniquely dictates one theory.

examples.text: Two models may explain the same observed planetary motion but make different predictions about an unmeasured case.
examples.note: The evidence fails to select one theory uniquely because both accommodate the data.

commonMisreadings: Underdetermination does not mean all theories are equally good; evidence and other standards can still favor one.

concepts.name: Theory-ladenness
concepts.summary: Theory-ladenness is the influence of prior concepts and expectations on observation and its interpretation.
concepts.body:
Scientists do not encounter data as wholly uninterpreted facts: instruments are designed using theories, and observers classify what they see through learned concepts.

This influence can help make observations meaningful, but it also creates risks of bias. Shared methods, calibration, and independent checks can constrain interpretation.

examples.text: A researcher identifies a faint mark as a planet because a telescope’s readings and a predictive model make that interpretation plausible.
examples.note: Background concepts affect classification and attention without making the physical stimulus arbitrary.

commonMisreadings: Theory-ladenness does not make objective observation impossible; it shows why methods and checks matter.

concepts.name: Theravada Buddhism
concepts.summary: Theravada Buddhism is a major Buddhist tradition emphasizing the Pali Canon, monastic discipline, meditation, and liberation.
concepts.body:
Theravada communities are prominent in Sri Lanka and parts of Southeast Asia.

Its teachings include the Four Noble Truths, the path to end suffering, and the ideal of the arahant who attains liberation. Lay and monastic practice are linked, though their roles differ; the living tradition is diverse and historically changing.

examples.text: A lay practitioner may support a monastery and practice generosity, while monks undertake intensive meditation and discipline.
examples.note: The practices and textual tradition express its emphasis on disciplined cultivation and insight.

commonMisreadings: Theravada is not simply “the original Buddhism”; it has its own long history and should not be reduced to a single practice.

concepts.name: Thisness
concepts.summary: Thisness is the feature or principle that makes an individual the particular individual it is.
concepts.body:
The medieval term haecceity is associated with Duns Scotus and addresses individuation: what distinguishes two things that share all general properties.

The idea can be treated as a primitive identity-making feature or analyzed in other ways. It helps frame debates about whether individuals differ only by qualitative properties.

examples.text: Two identical-looking leaves may still be two distinct leaves; thisness names what makes each this particular leaf.
examples.note: The distinction depends on numerical identity rather than on a differing observable quality.

commonMisreadings: Thisness is not an ordinary observable quality such as color; it is a proposed account of individual identity.

concepts.name: Thomism
concepts.summary: Thomism is the philosophical and theological tradition based on Thomas Aquinas’s work.
concepts.body:
Thomists develop Aquinas’s accounts of being, causation, natural law, virtue, and the relation between faith and reason.

The tradition includes later interpretations and disagreements, rather than one unchanged doctrine. It has influenced Catholic thought as well as broader debates in metaphysics and ethics.

examples.text: A Thomist account of natural law may argue that practical reason identifies goods rooted in human nature.
examples.note: The analysis uses Aquinas's Aristotelian framework to address theological questions.

commonMisreadings: Thomism is not simply Catholic theology as a whole; it is a particular intellectual tradition.

concepts.name: Thought-experiment method
concepts.summary: A thought experiment uses an imagined case to test concepts, principles, or theories.
concepts.body:
By changing one feature of a scenario while holding others fixed, philosophers can reveal which judgments a theory implies.

Thought experiments can clarify possibilities and expose tensions, but their force depends on whether intuitions about the imagined case are reliable and relevant. They complement argument and evidence rather than replacing them.

examples.text: Imagine a person whose memories and personality are copied into a new body to ask whether psychological continuity is enough for survival.
examples.note: The variation tests whether intention and means change the moral assessment.

commonMisreadings: An invented scenario does not prove a conclusion by itself; the reasoning from the case must be made explicit.

concepts.name: Time
concepts.summary: Time is the ordering or dimension in which events are related as earlier, simultaneous, or later.
concepts.body:
Philosophers ask whether time flows, whether past and future events exist, and how temporal passage relates to physical theories.

Some accounts treat all times as equally real; others give the present special status. The everyday experience of duration and change does not by itself settle these metaphysical questions.

examples.text: A meeting scheduled after lunch is ordered later than lunch, though different theories explain what this temporal relation amounts to.
examples.note: The events stand in an ordered relation even though the eruption and observation are not simultaneous.

commonMisreadings: Time has physical, psychological, and metaphysical aspects; a clock’s measurement does not settle every question about its nature.

concepts.name: Tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon
concepts.summary: The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon is the temporary inability to recall a known word despite feeling that it is close.
concepts.body:
A person may retrieve partial information such as the word’s first sound, syllable count, or meaning without reaching the full form.

The episode suggests that access to a word’s meaning and its sound can come apart. Stress, age, and frequency of use can affect how often such retrieval failures occur.

examples.text: Someone knows an actor’s name and can describe the person but cannot produce the name until several minutes later.
examples.note: Partial access shows that semantic or phonological information can be available without complete word production.

commonMisreadings: A tip-of-the-tongue state is a temporary retrieval failure, not proof that the information has been permanently forgotten.

concepts.name: Titoism
concepts.summary: Titoism refers to the communist political system associated with Josip Broz Tito’s Yugoslavia and its independence from Soviet control.
concepts.body:
After the split with Stalin in 1948, Yugoslavia pursued a distinct path that included worker self-management and a federal structure among its republics.

The system remained one-party communist and had limits on political pluralism. The term can describe both its international independence and its specific domestic institutions.

examples.text: Yugoslav enterprises used worker councils to make some management decisions, within a state-led socialist economy.
examples.note: The arrangement gave workers an institutional role in management while retaining socialist political authority.

commonMisreadings: Titoism was not liberal multiparty democracy; independence from Moscow coexisted with communist party rule.

concepts.name: Tolerance
concepts.summary: Tolerance is allowing a belief or practice one disapproves of to continue within limits.
concepts.body:
Toleration involves a reason to object, a reason to refrain from interference, and some balance between them.

Its limits become important when conduct harms others or undermines the conditions of tolerance itself. Toleration can be a civic principle without requiring approval or indifference.

examples.text: A university protects a controversial speaker’s lawful expression while permitting listeners to criticize the views.
examples.note: The institution allows expression without endorsing the association's views.

commonMisreadings: Tolerance is not endorsement; it is a decision about how to respond to disagreement.

concepts.name: Totalitarianism
concepts.summary: Totalitarianism is a form of rule that seeks comprehensive control of society through ideology, coercion, and political organization.
concepts.body:
The concept is used for regimes that aim to mobilize the population and penetrate institutions, media, and private life, often through a dominant party and security apparatus.

Scholars debate how to distinguish totalitarian systems from other dictatorships and how much control is ever complete. The term should be applied with attention to historical evidence.

examples.text: A regime may use a ruling party, propaganda, surveillance, and repression to organize public life around an official ideology.
examples.note: The state pursued ideological conformity through coordinated institutions and coercive surveillance.

commonMisreadings: Totalitarianism describes an aspiration and system of control; it does not mean authorities literally control every private thought.

concepts.name: Traditionalism
concepts.summary: Traditionalism gives weight to inherited practices, beliefs, and institutions because of their continuity or accumulated wisdom.
concepts.body:
Traditionalists may argue that social practices embody knowledge no single generation can fully articulate.

The position does not require preserving every custom unchanged; traditions can be interpreted and adapted. Critics ask whether appeals to heritage protect unjust power or block needed reform.

examples.text: A community may retain a customary council because it provides trusted local dispute resolution while revising rules that exclude women.
examples.note: The ceremony is preserved because its lineage and meaning are treated as reasons for continuation.

commonMisreadings: Traditionalism is not simply resistance to all change; it concerns the authority and value assigned to inheritance.

concepts.name: Tragedy
concepts.summary: Tragedy is a dramatic form in which serious conflict leads to suffering, loss, or catastrophe.
concepts.body:
In classical tragedy, protagonists face difficult choices shaped by character, circumstance, and forces beyond their control.

The genre can expose limits in knowledge and agency without reducing events to simple moral lessons. Modern tragedy varies widely, but often examines the costs of conflict and failed judgment.

examples.text: A ruler’s attempt to prevent a prophecy may help bring about the disastrous outcome it predicts.
examples.note: The pursuit of knowledge is both admirable and bound to a devastating recognition.

commonMisreadings: Tragedy is not just any sad story; it involves consequential conflict and a distinctive examination of human limits.

concepts.name: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.summary: The tragedy of the commons occurs when individual incentives lead people to overuse a shared resource.
concepts.body:
Each user receives much of the gain from taking more while spreading the cost of depletion across everyone.

The result can be collective damage even when no one intends it. Shared resources can be protected through community rules, monitoring, rights, or other institutions; privatization is not the only solution.

examples.text: Fishers each catch extra fish for immediate income, eventually reducing the stock that all depend on.
examples.note: Each fleet has an incentive to increase its catch even though aggregate overfishing collapses the resource.

commonMisreadings: The tragedy is not inevitable for every commons; cooperation and effective governance can prevent overuse.

concepts.name: Transcendence
concepts.summary: Transcendence is going beyond an ordinary limit, domain, or condition.
concepts.body:
In religion, it often describes a divine reality beyond the created world; in philosophy it can mean exceeding the limits of a conceptual system or ordinary experience.

The contrasting term immanence emphasizes presence within the world. The intended sense depends on the discipline and argument.

examples.text: A theologian may describe God as transcendent because divine existence is not confined to the physical universe.
examples.note: The claim places the divine outside the ordinary order of finite entities.

commonMisreadings: Transcendence does not always mean supernatural existence; the word has broader philosophical uses.

concepts.name: Transcendental idealism
concepts.summary: Transcendental idealism is Kant’s view that experience is structured by features of human sensibility and understanding.
concepts.body:
Space and time are forms through which humans experience objects, while categories such as causality organize judgment.

We can know objects as they appear under these conditions, but not things as they are independently of them. Kant’s view combines this limit with realism about the empirical world we experience.

examples.text: We experience events as ordered in time and connected causally, but cannot simply infer that these are properties of things as they are apart from all human experience.
examples.note: These structures belong to the conditions of possible experience rather than being inferred from experience as raw properties.

commonMisreadings: Kant does not say the experienced world is imaginary; he distinguishes appearances from unknowable things in themselves.

concepts.name: Transcendentalism
concepts.summary: Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century American movement emphasizing intuition, individual conscience, nature, and spiritual insight.
concepts.body:
Writers such as Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau resisted conformity and argued that people could encounter moral or spiritual truth beyond established institutions.

The movement drew on Romanticism and several religious and philosophical sources. Its members differed in politics and in how they understood nature and society.

examples.text: Thoreau’s experiment at Walden Pond expressed a search for deliberate living outside some pressures of commercial society.
examples.note: Nature functions as a medium through which the individual can encounter meaning and insight.

commonMisreadings: American Transcendentalism is a specific historical movement, not simply the general idea of transcending limits.

concepts.name: Transhumanism
concepts.summary: Transhumanism supports using science and technology to expand human capacities and reduce limitations such as disease and aging.
concepts.body:
Advocates debate technologies including genetic intervention, prosthetics, cognitive enhancement, and life extension.

They also ask who will have access, how risks should be governed, and whether enhancement could change human identity or equality. Transhumanism includes both optimistic and cautious positions.

examples.text: A transhumanist may support safe gene therapies that prevent inherited disease while debating whether enhancement should be publicly available.
examples.note: The technology first repairs a disability and then extends a human capacity beyond the typical biological range.

commonMisreadings: Transhumanism is not the claim that every technology is beneficial or that people must abandon human values.

concepts.name: Trolley problem
concepts.summary: The trolley problem is a family of moral cases about whether to redirect a threat so fewer people are harmed.
concepts.body:
In a common version, a runaway trolley will kill five people unless a bystander diverts it onto a track where one person will die.

Variations change whether harm is direct, intended, or merely foreseen, testing how people weigh consequences against constraints on action. Real decisions are more complex than the stylized cases.

examples.text: A switch operator can divert a trolley from five people onto a track with one person, raising whether doing so is permissible.
examples.note: The decision compares saving more lives with directly causing one person's death through redirection.

commonMisreadings: The trolley problem is not one question with a universally agreed answer; its variations isolate different moral considerations.

concepts.name: Trope theory
concepts.summary: Trope theory holds that properties are particular instances rather than repeatable universals shared by many things.
concepts.body:
Instead of one universal redness present in every red object, trope theorists posit distinct red tropes belonging to each object.

Similar tropes resemble one another, and their resemblance may explain why objects count as having the same property. The view must explain how tropes are grouped without relying on the universals it rejects.

examples.text: The redness of one apple and the redness of another are two particular property instances that closely resemble each other.
examples.note: Its particular location and bearer distinguish it from the redness trope of another apple.

commonMisreadings: Trope theory does not deny that objects share descriptions; it offers a different account of what property sharing involves.

concepts.name: Trotskyism
concepts.summary: Trotskyism is a Marxist tradition associated with Leon Trotsky, emphasizing international revolution and opposition to Stalinist bureaucracy.
concepts.body:
Trotsky argued that socialism could not be secure in one country and defended “permanent revolution,” in which democratic and socialist struggles continue across stages.

Trotskyist movements have divided over strategy and interpretation. The label identifies a political lineage, not one unified organization.

examples.text: A Trotskyist may argue that workers’ movements in different countries must support one another rather than build isolated national socialism.
examples.note: The position connects the success of socialism to international extension and political control by workers.

commonMisreadings: Trotskyism is not interchangeable with every anti-Stalinist left movement; it has specific theoretical commitments.

concepts.name: Truth
concepts.summary: Truth is the status of a claim when it meets the relevant standard of correctness or accurately represents reality.
concepts.body:
Theories explain this in different ways.

Correspondence theories connect truth to how things are; coherence theories emphasize fit within a system of beliefs; pragmatic accounts link truth to inquiry and successful practice. These theories address what truth consists in, while ordinary judgments often use truth without settling the metaphysical debate.

examples.text: “The kettle is boiling” is true if the kettle is in fact boiling under the intended conditions.
examples.note: The fact described by the statement matches the statement's asserted condition.

commonMisreadings: Truth is not the same as confidence or consensus; people can be certain or widely agreed and still be wrong.

concepts.name: Truth conditions
concepts.summary: Truth conditions are the circumstances in which a sentence or proposition would be true.
concepts.body:
Specifying truth conditions makes content precise by stating what must be the case.

For a simple sentence, these may be straightforward; for complex statements, they depend on how parts combine and on context. Truth-conditional semantics uses this idea to explain meaning without requiring a sentence to be true in the actual world.

examples.text: “The door is open” is true under conditions where the relevant door is open at the time and place in context.
examples.note: The sentence is true exactly when the stated condition obtains, under the relevant interpretation.

commonMisreadings: Truth conditions state what would make a claim true; they do not assert that those conditions actually obtain.

concepts.name: Truth table
concepts.summary: A truth table lists the truth value of a logical formula for every possible assignment to its component propositions.
concepts.body:
Tables make it possible to test whether a formula is always true, always false, or true only in some cases.

They also check whether an argument is valid by looking for an assignment where all premises are true and the conclusion false. The method is systematic for propositional logic but grows quickly with more variables.

examples.text: For P→Q, the table shows the conditional is false only when P is true and Q is false.
examples.note: The rows exhaust the possible classical truth assignments and the conjunction column records the resulting value.

commonMisreadings: A truth table concerns formal truth values, not the factual truth of the propositions represented by its letters.

concepts.name: Truth value
concepts.summary: A truth value is the value assigned to a proposition, commonly true or false.
concepts.body:
Classical logic uses two truth values, while other systems allow additional values such as indeterminate or inconsistent.

A sentence’s truth value may depend on its interpretation and context. The concept lets logicians analyze how compound statements behave without interpreting every proposition in detail.

examples.text: If P is true and Q is false, then the conjunction P and Q is false in classical logic.
examples.note: Its truth status follows from the arithmetic relation asserted by the proposition.

commonMisreadings: True and false are standard values, but not every logical system assumes only two.

concepts.name: Truth-conditional semantics
concepts.summary: Truth-conditional semantics explains meaning by specifying the conditions under which a sentence is true.
concepts.body:
The approach treats understanding a sentence as knowing what the world would have to be like for it to be true or false.

Formal semanticists explain how meanings of words and grammatical structure combine to yield those conditions. Context still matters, especially for pronouns, tense, and expressions such as “here” or “I.”

examples.text: The meaning of “Every cat slept” can be represented by conditions requiring each relevant cat to have slept.
examples.note: The sentence's interpretation is characterized by the state of affairs required for its truth.

commonMisreadings: Truth-conditional semantics is an account of linguistic meaning, not the claim that all meaning is only truth or falsity.

concepts.name: Truthmaker
concepts.summary: A truthmaker is what in reality makes a proposition true.
concepts.body:
Truthmaker theories ask whether truths depend on corresponding facts, objects, or states of affairs.

For example, the existence and location of a particular tree may make “There is a tree in the garden” true. Theories differ over negative, universal, and necessary truths, where an obvious truthmaker may be hard to identify.

examples.text: A specific broken window can make “The window is broken” true.
examples.note: The actual snowy state explains why the proposition is true rather than false.

commonMisreadings: A truthmaker is not merely evidence that a statement is true; it is proposed as the reality on which its truth depends.

concepts.name: Twin Earth
concepts.summary: Twin Earth is Hilary Putnam’s thought experiment about whether a word’s meaning depends on the speaker’s environment.
concepts.body:
Imagine a planet matching Earth except that its clear drinkable liquid is XYZ rather than H₂O.

A speaker there and an Earth speaker may have identical internal experiences and use “water” alike, yet refer to different substances. Putnam uses the case to argue that reference can depend on external facts and a linguistic community.

examples.text: An Earth visitor on Twin Earth learns that the liquid that looks and tastes like water has a different chemical composition.
examples.note: The different substances fix different external references despite identical apparent experiences and linguistic behavior.

commonMisreadings: Twin Earth is a thought experiment about meaning and reference, not a prediction that such a planet exists.

concepts.name: Tyranny
concepts.summary: Tyranny is oppressive rule that uses power arbitrarily and disregards law, rights, or the common good.
concepts.body:
The term has been used for rule by one person, but also more broadly for institutions that dominate without effective accountability.

Classical political theory contrasts a ruler’s pursuit of private interest with governance for the public good. Whether a government is tyrannical depends on its practices, not merely its formal title.

examples.text: A leader who imprisons critics without legal process and rules by personal decree may be described as tyrannical.
examples.note: The ruler uses public authority as an instrument of arbitrary personal control.

commonMisreadings: Tyranny is more than unpopular government; it involves oppressive or unchecked power.

concepts.name: Ubuntu
concepts.summary: Ubuntu is an African ethical idea that human life and personhood are formed through relationships with others.
concepts.body:
Often expressed as “a person is a person through other persons,” ubuntu emphasizes mutual care, dignity, and shared responsibility.

Its interpretations vary across languages, communities, and thinkers; it should not be treated as a single pan-African doctrine. The concept has influenced discussions of reconciliation and public ethics.

examples.text: A community may use ubuntu to guide a restorative process that recognizes both the harmed person’s dignity and the offender’s responsibilities.
examples.note: The process treats social repair and shared human dignity as central to justice.

commonMisreadings: Ubuntu does not erase individual identity; it stresses that people develop and flourish through social relations.

concepts.name: Ultranationalism
concepts.summary: Ultranationalism treats the nation as supreme and demands intense loyalty, often at the expense of outsiders or internal minorities.
concepts.body:
It can combine mythic national identity, hostility to pluralism, militarism, and claims that the nation must dominate or purify itself.

The label is commonly applied to movements that go beyond ordinary national attachment toward exclusionary or authoritarian politics. Specific cases need historical context.

examples.text: A movement may portray minorities as threats to national purity and demand their removal to restore national greatness.
examples.note: National belonging is made absolute and used to justify coercion against groups defined as outside it.

commonMisreadings: Ultranationalism is not simply patriotism; it elevates the nation in ways that can legitimize exclusion and coercion.

concepts.name: Uncertainty
concepts.summary: Uncertainty is a lack of information that prevents a single definite belief, prediction, or outcome from being established.
concepts.body:
It may be represented by known probabilities, as in risk, or be deeper when probabilities and relevant possibilities are unknown.

Decision-makers can reduce some uncertainty by gathering information, but further evidence can also reveal new unknowns. The appropriate response depends on stakes and how much uncertainty matters to the choice.

examples.text: A doctor may know several diagnoses are possible and request a test that helps distinguish among them.
examples.note: The probability expresses incomplete determination of the event from current information.

commonMisreadings: Uncertainty is not the same as ignorance about everything; partial knowledge can narrow the possibilities without settling them.

concepts.name: Unconscious
concepts.summary: The unconscious refers to mental processes that influence a person without being present in conscious awareness.
concepts.body:
The term has different meanings in psychoanalysis and cognitive science.

Freud emphasized wishes and conflicts outside awareness; contemporary research also studies automatic perception, memory, and habits. Evidence for one kind of unconscious process does not establish every theory about hidden motives.

examples.text: A person may recognize a familiar face before consciously recalling where they met, showing processing outside awareness.
examples.note: The processing influences behavior while remaining unavailable to introspective awareness.

commonMisreadings: The unconscious is not one single hidden agent, and ordinary automatic processing is not proof of Freudian repression.

concepts.name: Underdetermination
concepts.summary: Underdetermination occurs when given evidence or premises do not uniquely settle which conclusion is correct.
concepts.body:
Multiple explanations may fit the observations, or a premise set may leave several models possible.

Additional evidence, methodological standards, or practical aims can help choose among them. In philosophy of science, the problem raises questions about whether evidence alone determines theory choice.

examples.text: The same temperature readings might fit two competing climate models until more observations distinguish their predictions.
examples.note: The data alone do not select one causal story because different models predict the observation.

commonMisreadings: Underdetermination does not mean no conclusion is better supported; it means the stated evidence alone leaves alternatives open.

concepts.name: Universal
concepts.summary: A universal is a repeatable property, relation, or kind that can be shared by multiple particular things.
concepts.body:
Realists about universals treat properties such as redness as entities that different objects instantiate.

Nominalists deny such entities and explain resemblance or classification in other ways. The debate concerns what makes many things count as alike, not whether people can use shared words.

examples.text: Two apples can both be red because each instantiates the universal redness, on a realist account.
examples.note: Different triangles can possess one repeatable geometric property despite being separate objects.

commonMisreadings: A universal is not a universal statement such as “all”; it is a metaphysical account of repeatable features.

concepts.name: Universal quantification
concepts.summary: Universal quantification asserts that a predicate applies to every object in a specified domain.
concepts.body:
In formal logic, ∀x P(x) says that every x in the domain satisfies P.

Its force depends on the domain and on how the variable is bound. A universal claim can be refuted by one counterexample, provided that case belongs to the intended domain.

examples.text: “Every registered voter is eligible” can be represented by quantifying over the domain of registered voters.
examples.note: The conditional restricts the claim to objects that satisfy the predicate Human.

commonMisreadings: Universal quantification ranges over a defined domain; it does not automatically refer to everything that exists.

concepts.name: Universals problem
concepts.summary: The problem of universals asks what explains properties or relations that many particular things appear to share.
concepts.body:
Realists posit repeatable entities such as redness; nominalists explain shared classification without universals; conceptualists locate generality in thought.

Each view must explain resemblance, predication, and how general knowledge is possible. The debate reaches from ancient metaphysics to contemporary philosophy.

examples.text: Two red objects seem alike in color, raising whether they share one real property or merely resemble each other.
examples.note: The case requires an account of common predication across distinct particulars.

commonMisreadings: The problem concerns the status of shared properties, not simply whether general words are useful.

concepts.name: Upaya
concepts.summary: Upaya, or skillful means, is the Buddhist idea that teachings and practices can be adapted to help people toward liberation.
concepts.body:
A teacher may use different explanations for people with different capacities or circumstances, while treating them as means rather than final truths.

The idea is especially developed in Mahayana texts. It raises questions about who can judge that a teaching is skillful and how adaptation avoids becoming an excuse for manipulation.

examples.text: A teacher may offer a simple practice to a beginner before introducing a more demanding account of emptiness.
examples.note: The different teachings serve the learners' conditions while aiming at transformative insight.

commonMisreadings: Skillful means does not mean that any convenient teaching is acceptable; its purpose and effects must be judged in relation to liberation.

concepts.name: Utilitarianism
concepts.summary: Utilitarianism says that actions, rules, or institutions should be assessed by their effects on overall well-being.
concepts.body:
Classical utilitarians emphasize maximizing aggregate happiness or pleasure; later versions use preference satisfaction, welfare, or other measures.

The approach offers a common way to compare outcomes but faces questions about measuring welfare, distributing benefits, and protecting rights. Act and rule versions apply the standard differently.

examples.text: A utilitarian policy-maker may compare two health programs by estimating which produces greater overall benefit across the affected population.
examples.note: The policy compares outcomes across all patients rather than privileging one patient's claim by status.

commonMisreadings: Utilitarianism is not simply “the ends justify the means”; it requires a theory of whose welfare counts and how consequences are assessed.

concepts.name: Utility
concepts.summary: Utility is the value an agent or theory assigns to an option, outcome, or state of affairs.
concepts.body:
In decision theory, utility can represent preference rankings or expected benefit without measuring pleasure directly.

In ethics, utilitarian theories often use utility to represent well-being that should be promoted. The meaning depends on the model, and numerical utility does not always mean a measurable amount of happiness.

examples.text: A commuter may assign higher utility to a reliable route than to a faster but unpredictable one.
examples.note: The ranking represents the commuter's relative preference among available options.

commonMisreadings: Utility is a technical measure of value in a framework, not always the same as usefulness or pleasure.

concepts.name: Utopian socialism
concepts.summary: Utopian socialism is an early socialist tradition that proposed ideal cooperative communities as alternatives to capitalist society.
concepts.body:
Thinkers such as Robert Owen, Charles Fourier, and Henri de Saint-Simon sought to demonstrate more equal arrangements through planned communities and social reform.

Later Marxists criticized these projects for lacking a theory of class conflict and political transformation. The label can be descriptive or dismissive, and the figures differed greatly.

examples.text: Owen established cooperative experiments intended to show that humane working and living conditions were possible.
examples.note: The settlement sought to demonstrate a different social order through organized communal practice.

commonMisreadings: “Utopian” does not mean the proposals were only fantasies; some involved concrete experiments and institutional plans.

concepts.name: Vagueness
concepts.summary: An expression is vague when it lacks a sharp boundary between cases where it clearly applies and cases where it clearly does not.
concepts.body:
Words such as “tall” have clear central cases and borderline cases.

Sorites reasoning exploits this: if one grain is not a heap and adding one grain never seems decisive, when does a heap begin? Theories handle vagueness through degrees, contextual boundaries, or other formal approaches.

examples.text: A person of average height is clearly not tall and a very tall person clearly is, while some cases resist a definite classification.
examples.note: Hair loss changes gradually while ordinary language does not fix an exact cutoff for baldness.

commonMisreadings: Vagueness is not the same as ambiguity; a vague word has imprecise boundaries, while an ambiguous word has distinct meanings.

concepts.name: Vaisheshika
concepts.summary: Vaisheshika is an ancient Indian philosophical school that analyzes reality through basic categories.
concepts.body:
Its categories include substance, quality, motion, universality, particularity, and inherence; later accounts added absence.

The school developed atomist explanations of physical objects and debated how categories relate to knowledge and causation. It later became closely associated with Nyaya, while retaining its own history.

examples.text: A Vaisheshika analysis of a clay pot distinguishes the substance, its qualities, and the motion involved in its making.
examples.note: The object is understood by classifying its constituents and the relations connecting them.

commonMisreadings: Vaisheshika is not merely an ancient physics; it is a metaphysical and epistemological system.

concepts.name: Validity
concepts.summary: An argument is valid when its conclusion must be true if its premises are true.
concepts.body:
Validity depends on the form of inference, not on whether the premises are actually true.

A valid argument can have false premises and a false conclusion; soundness requires validity plus true premises. In formal logic, validity is tested across all permitted interpretations.

examples.text: If all mammals are animals and all whales are mammals, then all whales are animals follows validly.
examples.note: If the premises were true, the conclusion could not be false given the argument's structure.

commonMisreadings: A valid argument need not persuade or have true premises; it must preserve truth from premises to conclusion.

concepts.name: Value
concepts.summary: Value is the worth, importance, or desirability assigned to an object, action, outcome, or state.
concepts.body:
Value can be instrumental, because something helps achieve another end, or intrinsic, because it matters for its own sake.

Ethical and political theories disagree about what has value and how competing values should be compared. Value can also refer to economic worth or the numerical output of a function.

examples.text: Education may be valued both intrinsically, as learning, and instrumentally, because it opens employment opportunities.
examples.note: The friendship is treated as worth having in itself and the ticket as useful for a further end.

commonMisreadings: Value is not always monetary and need not be reducible to a single scale.

concepts.name: Value of information
concepts.summary: The value of information is the expected benefit of obtaining information before making a decision.
concepts.body:
Information is valuable when it could change a choice or improve its result enough to justify its cost and delay.

Decision theory compares expected outcomes with and without the information. Perfect information is an ideal benchmark; real data may be incomplete, costly, or misleading.

examples.text: Before choosing a treatment, a test is worth taking if its result could guide a more effective option and the delay is safe.
examples.note: The forecast has value because it can prevent a costly mistake and alter the farming decision.

commonMisreadings: More information is not always better; its value depends on whether it can improve the decision relative to its cost.

concepts.name: Value pluralism
concepts.summary: Value pluralism holds that there are multiple fundamental values that cannot all be reduced to one common measure.
concepts.body:
Liberty, equality, loyalty, and compassion may each matter for their own reasons and can conflict in real choices.

Pluralists argue that some tradeoffs have no uniquely correct numerical conversion, though judgment and compromise remain possible. The view differs from relativism: values can be real even when they are plural and sometimes incommensurable.

examples.text: A policy may protect freedom of speech while limiting the harm of targeted harassment, requiring a judgment across values that cannot be fully collapsed into one score.
examples.note: The conflict is treated as a genuine normative trade-off rather than a failure to calculate one master value.

commonMisreadings: Pluralism does not mean every preference is equally valid or that difficult choices are impossible.

concepts.name: Variable
concepts.summary: A variable is a symbol whose value can vary over a specified range or domain.
concepts.body:
In algebra, a variable may stand for an unknown number; in logic, it ranges over objects; in programming, it can refer to stored data that changes during execution.

The role depends on the formal system. A variable is distinct from a constant, whose value is fixed within the relevant context.

examples.text: In x + 3 = 8, x is a variable whose value is determined to be 5.
examples.note: The symbol stands for a value that is constrained by the equation rather than fixed by its spelling.

commonMisreadings: A variable does not always represent an unknown; it can range over many possible values.

concepts.name: Vedanta
concepts.summary: Vedanta is a family of Indian philosophical traditions grounded in the Upanishads and related foundational texts.
concepts.body:
Major schools interpret the relation between Brahman, the ultimate reality, and atman, the self, differently.

Advaita teaches non-duality; Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita defend distinct forms of qualified or complete difference. These are living traditions with diverse teachers and practices, not one doctrine.

examples.text: An Advaita Vedantin interprets liberation as realizing the deepest identity of atman and Brahman.
examples.note: The doctrine explains liberation as knowledge overcoming the appearance of fundamental separateness.

commonMisreadings: Vedanta is not synonymous with Advaita; it includes schools with sharply different metaphysical commitments.

concepts.name: Veil of ignorance
concepts.summary: The veil of ignorance is John Rawls’s device for choosing principles of justice without knowing one’s place in society.
concepts.body:
People behind the veil know general facts about society but not their own class, abilities, religion, or conception of the good.

Because no one can tailor rules to personal advantage, the device tests whether principles are fair to people in different positions. It is a hypothetical model of impartial choice, not a claim about actual political history.

examples.text: A chooser unaware whether they will be rich or poor may favor basic liberties and protections against severe deprivation.
examples.note: The uncertainty makes the chooser assess institutions from every possible social position.

commonMisreadings: The veil removes knowledge of personal position, not all knowledge; parties still understand general social facts.

concepts.name: Verification theory of meaning
concepts.summary: The verification theory of meaning connects a statement’s meaning to the conditions or methods that would verify it.
concepts.body:
Logical positivists used versions of the principle to distinguish empirically testable claims from claims they regarded as cognitively meaningless.

Difficulties arose for universal laws, historical claims, and the verification principle itself. Later versions weakened the requirement to allow degrees or indirect forms of confirmation.

examples.text: The claim “This metal conducts electricity” has empirical meaning partly through tests that could support or challenge it.
examples.note: The testing procedure supplies an empirical route for determining the statement's truth.

commonMisreadings: Verification theory does not say a meaningful claim must already have been verified; it concerns possible tests or evidence.

concepts.name: Verificationism
concepts.summary: Verificationism holds that a claim is cognitively meaningful only if it can be empirically tested or is true by definition.
concepts.body:
The doctrine was associated with logical positivism and sought to distinguish factual claims from metaphysical assertions.

Strict versions struggled with scientific laws and with verifying the principle itself, leading to weaker accounts based on confirmation or testability in principle. It remains influential in debates about meaning and evidence.
